About · the purpose A publication about AI agents, security and the next generation of publishing, written in the open by Dinis Cruz with a desk of agents. This page says what it is for, what it is not, and what I would like from you.
agenda

Three things, stated plainly. Share what I know, as I learn it, with the evidence attached. Solve real problems in the open, so the method can be checked and copied. Build sgit.ai and RiskMandate. Most of these articles use them as evidence, and I have a stake in both.
open

Nothing here is behind a licence you have to ask about. Content is CC BY 4.0: copy it, translate it, quote it, build on it, and say where it came from. Code is Apache 2.0. Every idea here is free to take, adapt and build on.
written

The words start as my voice notes. A desk of named agents turns the notes into articles, under rules that are published. Every version is kept, so you can see what changed and when. The method is published so anyone can run a newsroom like it. It lives in the workshop, not on the front page.

model-coauthorship

This site argues that authorship and agenda should be disclosed structurally, not left for a reader to infer. It can point to its own track record on exactly that point. Across the ten-article library this site cites: most core articles credit "Dinis Cruz" and "ChatGPT Deep Research" jointly, several add Claude 3.5 or Claude 3.7, and the practice of naming an AI co-author in structured front matter runs back to the first article in February 2025 — eighteen months before this site existed. Preserving that credit verbatim on every republished or synthesised page here is not a courtesy; dropping a co-author on republication would be exactly the attribution failure this site exists to argue against. A site arguing for provenance and disclosed agenda, which has a two-year dated record of disclosing its own model co-authorship, is putting that record on this page rather than treating it as an awkwardness to manage.

licence

These are different grants over closely related material. CC0 is the more permissive of the two, so republishing CC0 material under this site's CC BY 4.0 is legally sound — but this site's pages cannot make the original more restrictive than it already is, which is why every provenance block states the source licence explicitly rather than defaulting silently to CC BY 4.0. The cleanest resolution, and the one this site argues for: align docs.diniscruz.ai to CC BY 4.0 going forward, leaving already-published articles as CC0. A site about attribution that dedicates its own foundational work to the public domain with no attribution requirement is making an argument about itself it may not intend to make.

T1 — Expand /rights/, /newsroom/ and /thesis/ from single comprehensive hub pages into the full multi-page trees specified in briefs/05, once N1 is resolved and the fuller scope is confirmed. T2 — Advanced, not closed. The reciprocal Risk Mandate statement named in the network page's inversion section now exists as a commissioning brief — the risk & governance newsroom, which is that machinery pointed at corporate risk, written as a news operation whose first customer is a risk product. What the network page actually promises is a page at /network/riskmandate/, and that is still unwritten. tasks

T5 — Build /provenance/the-citation-chain/, specified in briefs/05 and not yet written: the PKI-signed claim chain from researcher to journalist to outlet to social, and the worked HIGH vs LOW evidence-weight scoring. It is the page that connects this site's provenance argument to pki.sgit.ai, and its absence is why that boundary is currently stated but not demonstrated. T6 — Build /infographics/, step 10 of the brief's own build order and the only step not started. It inherits the evidence-backed infographic pipeline in which every claim traces to a source URL — which makes it a demonstration of the thesis rather than decoration, and is the reason it is tracked rather than dropped. Its source document is now summarised at /mvps/#report-tool, which makes T6 the most concretely specified of the open tasks. T4 — Decide site rendering (server-rendered vs. client-assembled) before this site moves off static HTML, given the crawler-invisibility risk stated on the network page.
tasks

T7 — Confirm the current state of the three open decisions and six open questions republished on /mvps/ and /mvps/portugal.html. They are reproduced from a register dated May 2026 and this site has no evidence any was closed since. Question 5 — who is the editor of record, and who carries legal responsibility for published content — is a precondition for any of these instances launching, not a detail to settle afterwards, and it should not stay open silently.
tasks

T10 — Build the ingestion path for /governance/: fetch, freeze, hash, anchor. It is the single thing standing between that section being a demonstration of a graph and being the verification layer it exists to provide. Until it lands, every fact there is secondary, nothing is anchored, the staleness detector cannot run, and the Researcher role's centre of gravity — no claim without a source somebody fetched — is aspirational. Official publications and news issued by regulatory bodies are the first source class to take.
tasks

T11 — Get a route to the primary sources our egress blocks. The Researcher's run of 28 August 2026 tried two Council of the EU press releases carrying the primary record of the AI Act deferral dates and both returned 403 to us. They are excluded from the register and recorded as unreachable from here — a fact about our network, not about those pages, and gate check 11 now enforces that distinction rather than trusting anyone to remember it. The cost is concrete: the strongest story on the beat cannot be published, because the half that matters would have to be labelled secondary. A publication whose reach is decided by whoever happens to block its user agent is not a publication of record, and this is the second capability — after T10 — without which the verification layer is a design.
tasks

T9 — Answer who is legally answerable for what a publication on this stack asserts. The commissioning brief answers the editorial half — the editor of record is whoever's signature is on the current interval — and is explicit that a signature is evidence of who asserted something, not a legal person and not a defence. This is the same gap as Portugal's open question 5, now carried by a second instance. It is a precondition for launching any publication described on this site, not a detail to settle afterwards. T8 — Resolve, at source, the contradiction between the two 12 May briefs on whether the first publication launches bilingual or in one language. Both readings are currently published, unresolved, because picking a side on this site would be editing the sources rather than reporting them.

node admin/build/validate.js. Structure, links, version agreement, canonical/CNAME agreement, the agent surface, block balance, the agent-block rule, the provenance contract, and the redaction watch-list. # Check Why it is here, specifically for this site 1–7 Version agreement, links, canonical, agent surface, key-leak, block balance, agent block The shared core, inherited from every sibling site 8 The provenance contract — every block marked class="provenance" must state a first-published date and link to the original This site's central argument is that most articles do not provide evidence and the link is never followed. A page here that failed its own contract would have refuted the site on page one 9 The redaction watch-list — a fixed list of Tier 3 strings (a named VC, an infra account number, live product pricing) may never appear anywhere in the published tree The source material contains real commercial and safety-sensitive detail. Send to my vault from any browser: an inbox on the reader vault, a link three ways, and the drain. Issue 049, in the release. The inbox (049), the feature request in Sixteen notes I did not want to lose. In the vault pane’s Vault tab, Make a link for another browser makes a key pair in the browser (RSA-OAEP 3072), configures an append lane on the reader vault and records both in the master. The link is shown as a URL, as text and as a QR code, and carries the lane, its write-only token and the public key, nothing else. A browser with no passkey opens it on vault/send.html: it keeps the link and takes it out of the address, says what it holds that the vault does not, and on Send to my vault seals its own records, as one device file in the format the vault already uses, with sgit’s hybrid envelope, and appends them. It can write and never read. Once it holds a link, the strip above the pane offers the same button on any page. The next time the vault is opened with the passkey, the Vault tab lists what is waiting: from which browser, when, and what it carries; it refuses a message sealed to another key, one changed on the way and one that is not an inbox message, each with the reason; and Bring them in writes each browser’s file into the reader vault and runs the merge every device already uses, so the records keep that browser as their author. Make a new link keeps the key, changes the token, and the old link can no longer write. The design is in the note. Not built: expiry, which the append routes have no way to enforce; signatures; purge; the reply lane (015). Checked. test_inbox.mjs, the thirteenth file in CI: the link, the envelope, the refusals and the combining of two files of one browser in Node; in Chromium against the mock of the vault API, now with the append routes, a browser with a virtual passkey makes the account and the link (its QR code decoded back with jsQR), a browser with no passkey at all reads, keeps notes and sends twice, three bad messages are appended beside them, and the first browser refuses the three, brings the two in, discards the rest and makes a new link that the old one cannot write past. What reached the lane is ciphertext; neither browser keeps the private key or the enum key.

The note gains the second provider’s result and the field notes. A second passkey, stored in iCloud Keychain, gave the same PRF bytes on a Mac, a current iPad and a current iPhone, in Safari and in Chrome, which is the common case the design is for; an older iPad that could not use the passkey locally offered only the QR path, which the first test showed to be its own path. The note now records both providers side by side, concludes that the article’s claim needs the qualifier “through the same kind of path” rather than a retraction, and adds the field notes from the two days: Chrome’s transient “can’t reach Google Password Manager”, the capability that reads neither true nor false, the two dialogs that name the site differently, the flags that do not reveal the path, the identical credential id and user handle on every path, the fingerprint that was a prefix of the secret, the key derivation times, and the browser store with no PRF. The lab’s note item says the same in one sentence. Nothing else changed.

One door per passkey path: a finding from the lab, the bug behind it, and the design change it forces. The finding. One Google Password Manager passkey, used through the provider on a Mac and then on an iPhone, gave one set of PRF bytes. The same passkey, answering a QR code from an iPad and then from the same Mac, gave a different set, and gave it consistently: same credential id, same user handle, same input, different bytes. The design in The passkey opens the vault rested on the same passkey giving the same bytes everywhere; it holds along one path and not across paths. Apple’s developer forums carry the same symptom for iCloud Keychain passkeys since late 2024, with an engineer calling it a bug, a fix announced for iOS 18.4, and a later tester reporting it persisting. The note records the four runs, what the extension is supposed to do, why two paths can disagree, and what the length of time this has sat unfixed says about how few people derive keys this way across the QR path. The design change. The unit is the path, not the passkey: every distinct set of bytes is its own door to the same master, and each door records where it came from. The middle layer the design kept, one small vault between the passkey and the master, is the reason a second path costs one small vault rather than a second identity. A door is added while unlocked, on a device where both paths run (a Mac with Chrome runs both in one session), by asking for the bytes again by the other path and writing the master’s key under the new door; no key is typed, pasted or shown, and the provider sees a PRF request and nothing else. Where no device has both paths, the recovery code opens the recovery door once and the new path’s door is written from there. Providers without PRF cannot be doors and can hold the recovery code, which is a weaker thing and is described as such. The master’s list of doors, with each door’s own key, is what lets a lost device’s door be retired from any other. All of it is designed, not built, and what runs lists it so. The lab. Card 2 now shows the path that answered, platform or cross-platform, so the two cases are told apart on the page; its text and the comparison box say that a different path can give different bytes; and its fingerprint is the first eight characters of the SHA-256 of the bytes, where before it was the first four bytes of the secret itself, a careless thing to put on a screen. The test checks the path row and the hashed fingerprint. The hub pages and llms.txt narrow the claim to “through the same kind of path”. The CI step that runs the browser tests now names all five.

The Industry Wire: a section of industry news read live from an encrypted vault that agents keep. What it is. The Industry Wire is a new section, apart from the newsroom’s own articles: a daily wire across five beats (building with AI, the AI business, open source, cybersecurity, risk and governance), every story with its primary source, who else covered it, one exact quote and why it matters. None of it is on this site. The data lives in an sgit vault (u9i9jp0l on the SG/Send server) whose read key is published on purpose, in admin/build/wire-vault.json, in llms.txt and on every wire page, the same arrangement sgit.ai uses for its own documents: the page fetches ciphertext, decrypts it in the browser with that key, and draws it. A write key is a different key and is not here. The vault is kept by a research agent, which can run on its own schedule and commit a new edition; the site notices a new head within two minutes and shows it, with no release of this site. The sources lists the 55 publications the agent reads, by tier and licence, and how the wire works renders the vault’s own design and runbook documents, read from the vault as markdown and rendered here, never its pre-rendered HTML. A lens per persona (the newsroom’s own six) shows what reached that reader, through which concern, and what was withheld with the reason, as the vault’s own join recorded it. The pages reach this site and the vault server, nothing else. Read before it was published. The vault was cloned and read in full first: no key, token or credential in it, no private address, nothing that is not public news and the agent’s own working notes. Two things are flagged rather than fixed, since they are the vault’s to decide: the vault carries a persona and a personal note aimed at one reader, which is that reader’s interest profile and is now public; and its runbook plans to keep frozen copies of paywalled sources and reader feedback “privately”, which a vault with a published read key cannot do, so those need a vault of their own. That contract is written on the how page. Publishing a read key cannot be undone for anyone who has already fetched the objects. What it is not. Reviewed. Every story is marked ai-generated, unreviewed and stays so until the vault says otherwise; in this first edition, 22 of the 40 stories have a primary source the research agent did not fetch, and those stories say so with a dashed border. The daily run is not scheduled by this site. snapshot.json holds the headlines and primary links as of this release, for agents and as the fallback the page shows when the vault cannot be reached. Checked. admin/build/test_wire.mjs opens the three pages in Chromium against the real vault, which is the brief’s rule for anything that needs a vault: the edition, the commit, 40 stories across five beats and a lead, every link http(s), nothing from the vault becoming a script, frame, image or handler, the lens with its reached and withheld counts and the reason on each withheld story, 55 sources, the documents rendered and switched, requests to this site and the vault server only, no sideways scroll at phone width. 23 checks, now the fifth test file CI runs. wire/vault-reader.js is sgit.ai’s own reader, vendored and reduced to what the wire needs. Also in this release: the passkey lab says so when a browser reports neither true nor false for PRF support.

The passkey lab: the pieces of a reader account with no server, as things you can press. What it is. The passkey opens the vault designs an account with no server, no sign-in and no email: a passkey’s PRF bytes derive a small door vault, the door holds the master vault’s key, the master holds the rest. Before any of it reaches the reading account, the passkey lab lets a person try each piece in their own browser. Card 0 reads what the browser can do. Card 1 makes a passkey for this host with the PRF extension and shows whether PRF is on and whether the passkey is synced (the browser’s backup flags); when PRF is off it shows the article’s ladder. Card 2 gets the 32 PRF bytes with the fixed input and shows a fingerprint to compare with another device, where the same passkey gives the same bytes. Card 3 derives the door from them, the article’s steps made exact (HKDF to a seed, a 64-character passphrase and an 8-character vault id with rejection sampling), then sgit’s own derivation of the read and write keys, PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 at 600,000 iterations each, timed. Card 4 makes a 26-character recovery code and shows it is a second door. Card 5 runs the same derivation from a fixed fake PRF output and compares every value with what sgit’s own Python produced (vectors.json, from admin/build/passkey_vectors.py, which uses sgit-ai’s Vault__Crypto for the keys, the file ids and a deterministic encryption): the browser and the command line agree on all ten. Card 6, with an access key pasted and kept in memory only, checks the derived address on the vault server, creates the door by writing its one file (the master vault’s key, made at random, encrypted in the browser under the door’s read key, as a content-addressed sgit object), opens it again as a new device would, and deletes the file; every call is listed as it happens. What it is not. A feature. It does not touch the reading account, the balance or the personas, and what runs lists it as a lab. The master vault, moving the account into it, a second passkey as a door and anything that signs the reader in are not built. The door record it writes is one encrypted object, not yet a commit, so sgit’s clone of the door would show an empty history. The vault id is never destroyed, because a destroyed id can never be used again and this one is derived from the passkey. The page loads no code from anywhere else and stores one public thing, the id of a passkey it made. Checked. admin/build/test_passkey.mjs drives the page in Chromium with a virtual authenticator that has PRF: the vectors agree, a passkey is made with PRF on, the same bytes come back twice, the door is stable, the recovery code round-trips, and the server flow runs end to end against a stand-in server that checks the access-key and write-key headers; what reached it was ciphertext; the access key was not in storage; no request went to any other host. 26 checks. The real server is for a person with an access key to try; the page says what came back either way. CI now runs four test files.

The reader API mapped and reviewed, with its findings pinned by tests, and the tests in CI. Phase 0 of the move. Go slow to go fast asks, before anything moves, for a map of everything a reader does on this site: every file, capability, web control, input, place data leaves the browser, external call and configuration value, as a table and as data. The reader API: a map, and a review is that, regenerated on every build by admin/build/api_map.py, with the same map as map.json. It counts 2,872 lines of reader code in 13 files that run in a browser (and 5,697 more in 20 frozen files of earlier meter versions), 18 pages written for it, the 12 views of the one element and 56 kinds of control, 10 ways data comes in and 8 ways it goes out, and 13 contracts. Every reader file carries its SHA-256, pages with the site chrome and version stamps normalised, which is the “before” the move’s rule needs: the live site must serve the same bytes after it. The review. The meter element and core, the component base, the subscribe script, the reading-list code, the page loader, the build scripts and the gate, read line by line. Eighteen findings, with evidence and a proposed change each, among them: declining a page as “not relevant” leaves it in the persona’s reading list and pulls its topics up (R1); a restored file is trusted beyond its two checked fields (R2); a malformed payment reference fails the whole return page (R3); shares and subscriptions sent from this site are labelled sgit.ai, because the config, the subscribe script and the contact file are sgit.ai’s (R4); the live lanes and vault frames are on hosts named dev (R5); half-penny balances show as a penny more than was spent (R6); a page read as one persona is never picked for another (R7); one failed fetch of the feed is cached for the life of the page (R8); a renamed article would withdraw its number (R9); 350 pages run fetched text through eval, which stands in the way of any Content-Security-Policy (R10). Four accepted gaps are listed as accepted, with where they are said. By the brief’s rule, no behaviour was changed. Pinned, not fixed. admin/build/test_review.mjs records each bug as it is, 14 checks, so that fixing one later is a visible change to a test; a check there that fails means the behaviour moved. The review note is also at admin/notes/2026-10-11__newsroom-api-map-and-review.md, generated from the same tables. The one change: CI runs the tests. The workflow validated the site and never ran the browser tests (R11). A reader-tests job now installs Playwright’s Chromium and runs the meter test (46 checks), the reading-list test (65) and the review’s pins (14) before a release is tagged, and fails if a test skipped for want of a browser. That is the pipeline, not the product, which is why it is the one change.

Imported from sgit.ai v0.7.61: five articles and the page for publishers. The articles, all of 11 October, numbered 75 to 79 in the order sgit.ai published them: Brief the agent too, I miss it, so it is working (with the brief for the reader’s vault), The passkey opens the vault (the design and the brief for a passkey that opens it, with no server and no account), Go slow to go fast (the brief for moving everything a reader does on this site into a repository of its own, which this site’s next releases start on) and The article remains a product. That makes 79 articles and 350 pages. The passkey opens the vault was published three times on sgit.ai in the day; this is its third version, with the section on what happens in a clean browser. For publishers. sgit.ai published a page for publishers, journalists and anyone thinking about the future of news: what is live on this site, how to try it in five minutes, what is not done, and what we would like from them. It is about this site and written to be forwarded, so it is imported here at the same address, /publishers/, under the same rule as every imported page: unedited, with its links to the rest of sgit.ai made absolute. It is in the Replicate menu and the footer. It names newsroom.sgit.ai v0.7.1 as the release it describes, and says that if it and what runs disagree, that page wins. What held. All eight text rules applied, the meter is still this site’s v1.4.0 on every page including the new one, the article numbers 1 to 74 are unchanged (the gate checks), and the reading-list and meter tests pass.

Reading lists in a link, a number for every article, and a page to make and preview them. The brief. From me to you, in a link asks the newsroom for part one: a page that opens a reading list from one person to another, a stable number for every article, and a page to make a list. This is that, as written, with the pieces below. A list opens. /for/ reads the part of the address after the #, which a browser does not send to the server: from and to (two first names), r (articles to read, in order), s (worth a look), f (a persona to follow, or a collection as c:how-agents-decide), n (a note) and e (the sender’s address, which turns on a Reply button; without it there is none). It checks every part: names are letters, spaces, hyphens and apostrophes up to 40 characters, numbers must exist, a list holds 1 to 50 articles, and anything malformed is dropped and listed under “Left out”. Names and notes are drawn as text, never as markup. For the recipient the list is the page: “For Steve, from Dinis”, the note, Start reading, then each article with its number, title, teaser, date, reading time and price, and what to follow. It is also added to their personas as a visitor named “Steve’s list, from Dinis”, with the articles as its reading list, which they can keep or remove in one tap; opening it charges nothing, and opening the same link again does not add a second one. With no list in the link the page explains what a reading list is and shows an example. A page makes and previews one. /for/make.html: search the articles by title, topic or number, filter by topic or persona, put each in Read or Look, order them with the arrows or by dragging, type the two names, an optional note and reply address, tick what to follow, and copy the link. The preview is the real page: the list is turned into a link, the link is read back by the parser the recipient’s page uses, and that is drawn, so anything the page would leave out is left out and said. Open as the recipient opens it in a new tab; Edit an existing link loads a link, including one an agent built, back into the form. The list in progress is kept in the page’s own address, so it can be bookmarked, and the number at the foot of every article starts a list with that article in it. The page runs in the browser and sends nothing. A number for every article. articles/ids.json gives each of the 74 articles a number, assigned once in the order they were first published (the article’s date, then the order sgit.ai first added it) and never changed or reused; a new article takes the next. An article withdrawn would keep its number and say so. Only n and slug are the contract: title, teaser, topics, the personas whose starting list holds it and the reading time are refreshed on each build. The number is printed small at the foot of every article and its markdown twin, under “All articles · All graphs”, by a recorded rule of the import, which stops if sgit.ai changes that line. The release gate has a twelfth check: every article has a number, numbers and addresses are unique, next is above the highest, and no number that was in the last commit has moved or gone. I tried each of those by breaking the file. llms.txt describes the link format and the file for an agent. Not built, and said so. A signed list, so the sender can be proved, and paying for someone else’s reading are listed on what runs as designed. The names in a link are whatever the link says, and nothing counts who opened one. The brief also asks for a synthetic recipient, a founder called Steve on a phone and a laptop; I could not run that here, so it is not done, and the page says the tests so far are scripted. Checked. admin/build/test_lists.mjs passes 65 checks: the parser against the real numbers (valid links, each kind of malformed field, an oversized list, names with markup, unknown numbers, broken percent-encoding), then in Chromium a recipient (the example link opens, becomes a visitor persona, Keep, Remove, a second list, the reply button only with an address, a note with markup shown as text and running nothing) and a sender (the page makes the link, ordering changes it, the preview matches what the link opens, an existing link loads, the limit of 50, search and filters, Copy link), and no sideways scroll at 390px on every new page. The meter test and the release gate pass.

Imported from sgit.ai v0.7.51: From me to you, in a link, and three newsletter issues. The article. It is the brief for the next feature of this site, a reading list in a link, and it is listed under “Continued by” on the articles it builds on. That makes 74 articles and 335 pages. The newsletter. Issues 3, 4 and 5 are on 11 October (Pay after you read, Authority outside the model and No server, by design), which makes five issues; sgit.ai had split what was to be one issue into three of eight articles. The subscribe page names issue 5 as the latest. The counts on the front page, llms.txt and the design, replicate and what-runs pages are stamped from the data at build time, so they say 74 articles and 5 issues without anyone typing it. What held. Nothing here changes how the site behaves; the feature the new article describes is the next release.

One new article from sgit.ai: A model in the tab. Imported from sgit.ai v0.7.46 (v0.7.45 before). A model in the tab: Chrome now ships an LLM to capable desktops, and it is the hardest piece of the client-side puzzle, dated 11 October, which makes 73 articles and 330 pages. It continues No server, by design, which now lists it under “Continued by”. Its four figures load, checked in a browser with every image forced to load, and the page raises no script errors. Links that open the newsroom as a persona, a reading meter without Pause and Start again, and five new articles. Links to a persona. /persona/ is a picker with a card for each of the five starting personas (Morgan the founder, Rowan the journalist, Sam the security lead, Kai the AI builder, Jordan the board member), each with Read as this persona and Copy link. Each persona also has a page of its own, such as /persona/founder/, which is the link to send, and the same persona can be named after a #, as in /persona/#founder. Opening one adds the persona to the reader’s browser as a visitor and makes it the active one, and the page says “You are reading as” with Keep this persona and Remove it. Nothing is charged for opening it and the reader’s own reading is not changed. Below the banner is the reader’s newsroom for that persona: its picks, its reading list and its graph. /persona/links.json lists every link with the persona’s name, description and the articles it starts from, for whoever is writing the email, a person or an agent. This is the first step of a link to a persona, without the vault: the personas are the five in the reading meter, kept in the site. Following a persona, forking one and a persona made for one person are not built, and the what runs page says so. Pause the meter and Start again are gone. Start again cleared the balance, the history, the receipts and the personas in one tap, which is too much to sit next to Export on a live product, and pausing is not a feature of a meter that is taking payment. The account page keeps Top up and Export as JSON. A reader who paused the meter under the old version is not stuck: a stored pause is cleared when the page loads. Clearing what is kept is now the browser’s own site-data setting, and the pages that named the button say so. How. The meter is a published component and its paths never change, so the change is a new version, v1.4.0, a copy of sgit.ai’s v1.3.1 at assets/components/sg-meter/v1/v1.4/v1.4.0/ with those two removals and the landing view, and nothing else. The import points every page at it through a recorded rule, which stops the import if sgit.ai moves the component to a version this one is not based on. sgit.ai still runs v1.3.1. Where an imported page named the removed buttons (the personas page, the security model’s shared-computer row and the component documentation’s account row) a text rule changes the sentence, as before. Imported from sgit.ai v0.7.45 (v0.7.40 before): five articles, No server, by design, The agent is the reader, Where the platform draws the line, The same argument, in our words and Authority outside the model, which makes 72 articles and 328 pages. One old version page of One article, five readers that sgit.ai no longer serves went with it. Tightened. The account page said “Every page on sgit.ai has a price” and its price table named sgit.ai’s docs, vaults and network; it now names this site and the pages that carry the 1p price. The note above the top-up button is three short paragraphs and links No server, by design. The design page links the same article on its “no server” row and says “client side, for now” where it said “client side only”. The what-runs page has a row for links to a persona and, under what is designed, one for personas in a vault. The Newsroom menu has Read as a persona, and llms.txt, the sitemap and the markdown index list the new pages. Checked. admin/build/test_meter.mjs, sgit.ai’s browser test of the meter extended for this release, passes 46 checks in Chromium, among them: no Pause and no Start again, a stored pause cleared, a persona link adding one visitor and not a second on reload, Keep and Remove, a # name, an unknown name added to nothing, the picker, Copy link, links.json matching the pages, and no sideways scroll at 390px on the new pages. The release gate passes, including the figure and script checks. Not changed. The article Who will game the reading meter still says “Start again” clears a shared browser. It is an article as sgit.ai published it, and an article’s text is not edited here; it is listed in the move note for the editor to decide.

The top-up page is tidied, and what it says about your data is exact. The note above the button. It said “nothing is sent anywhere”, which is true of a reader’s reading data and reads as wider than that once a payment link exists, and it was written in a chatty register (“it never nags”, “and that is all”) on a page that now takes money. It now says where the data is kept, that the site is a client-side application of static files with what you read kept in your browser rather than on a server, that this is how it is for now and that adding encrypted vaults would be said there, and what can leave the browser when the reader chooses to: a payment, made on Stripe’s own page, a subscription, or a reading share. It links to a new section, what leaves your browser, and when, which sets out six cases in a table, including two I had not written down: that fetching any page tells its host, GitHub Pages, that you asked for it, and that the synthetic-readers study page embeds a viewer from another service, so opening it contacts that service. No absolutes. The absolutes in this wording came out, including one of my own on the design page, which said that nothing leaves the browser and that this “holds”. It did not hold for the study page, and it does not hold for a payment. That row now says what can leave and when. Removed at Dinis’s request. The paragraph under the payment button saying that the return page cannot check the payment. The limit is unchanged and is still published, on what runs and in the meter’s security model; it is only no longer on the page that takes the payment. The intro’s second sentence, which repeated what the top-up card directly beneath it says, went too. How, and what it costs. Three text rules in admin/build/newsroom-text.json, applied by the import to the account page and the top-up page and their markdown twins, so they are recorded and not hand edits. I compared the visible text of all 315 imported pages with sgit.ai’s: exactly those two differ. A rule whose text has moved on sgit.ai stops the import with a message, which I tried by changing one. When sgit.ai adopts the wording, the rules are deleted.

A reader can now top up £5 by card, on this site’s side only, and every page that said no money moves says what runs. The link. A live-mode Stripe Payment Link for £5, one payment, quantity fixed at one, that redirects to /account/topped-up.html with the payment reference in the address. The top-up page now shows one “Pay £5.00” button instead of the simulated cart and its four packs, and the account page’s top-up action goes straight to Stripe. That also removes a finding from the synthetic readers’ study: the top-up page no longer says it is simulated while asking for money. The return page was already here; I ran it in a browser on a fresh profile: it adds £5 the first time a payment reference arrives, says “Already added” when the same one comes back, adds again for a different one, and explains itself when there is none. This site only, and why that matters. The link is in admin/build/newsroom-meter.json and the import writes it into the meter config as a recorded rule, not a hand edit, so sgit.ai’s pages keep the simulated cart. A reader’s credit lives in the browser storage of the site they return to, and this link returns to newsroom.sgit.ai, so a reader who paid from an sgit.ai page would have been credited on a site they were not reading. I had said the link had to be set on sgit.ai and only at cutover; that was wrong, and this is the better way. The import and the gate both refuse anything but the live shape, buy.stripe.com/<id>, so a test-mode link, which has test_ in it, cannot reach a page. What the pages say. Four places said no money moves, and one more said the payment link was not set: the Replicate note, the Payment row on what runs, the design page, the participant card and llms.txt (twice). The top-up now sits under what runs, with its limit beside it: the page it returns to cannot check the payment, by design, and nothing is paid to the people whose facts an article uses. The participant card no longer depends on the state at all. To switch it off: set topup_link to an empty string in that file, run the import, release. The top-up page goes back to the simulated cart, and the pages that describe payment change with it. What was tested, and by whom. The return page I ran in a browser here, on a fresh profile. The payment itself I could not complete: Stripe declined the test card, correctly, because the link is live. Dinis tested the flow before this release and reports that it works; that is his report, and I did not see it.

Five invented readers tested this site, and found that 117 images were missing. They are fixed, the study and the article that came with it are here, and the gate now reads the places it was blind. What was found. Five synthetic readers drove a browser through v0.6.1, one screenshot at a time, and were interviewed: 62 steps, 51 questions the site did not answer, 56 places somebody got lost, 31 findings, six blocking. It is published on sgit.ai as a vault with a read key, and the page is now here, at the same path, with its eight images and its live embed. I opened the vault with that key and checked its headline numbers against its own run records: all of them hold, including the per-reader table. The readers are invented by a model and say so first; it is not user research. The bug was bigger than the study measured. It counted 51 missing figures in 10 articles. Forcing every figure to load in a browser, v0.6.1 had 117 figures not rendered and 2 broken card thumbnails across 13 pages; this release has 0 of 625. Two causes, one blind spot. sgit.ai’s authoring contract forbids a declarative , so a figure is a placeholder and a script builds the address from data-dir and data-shot when the page opens. The import did not treat data-dir as an address, so (1) 51 figures pointed into other vaults’ image folders that were never copied, and (2) the 66 article thumbnails on the front page at /, which I copy one level up from /articles/, still pointed at cards/. The study did not count these. The import now copies every image the moved pages point at, 52 files, to the same paths, and records which pages need each. Why the gate passed it, and what it reads now. Check 2 reads href, src and data-src, and none of this is any of them, so the gate was green on a site showing “screenshot unavailable” to every reader of ten articles. Two new checks: 2b, every figure and card thumbnail must exist, and 2c, every script a page loads at run time must exist. 2b was shown failing first on v0.6.1’s tree (119 errors, 117 figures and 2 thumbnails) and 2c on the missing embed script, and 2c was shown to see the loaders that work. Reading the study’s page turned up a third case the same way: its “See it live” section loads vault-ui-embed.js through a name built at run time, which was not here. It is copied byte for byte. It mounts the official vault viewer from dev.vault.sgraph.ai in an iframe on that one page, the first cross-origin embed on this site, so say if you would rather link out. New from sgit.ai (v0.7.40). One article, How to run synthetic users on your own site, with three figures, a card, a banner, a graph and its version page, and the study page above. Nothing else of the newsroom changed in that release but its version number; I diffed the moved tree against the last import: 11 new files, 0 removed, the rest the badge. Both are in the Replicate menu, and the Replicate page has a row for the method. Fixed because they were mine. The balance chip is on every page this site writes, as a free page: it charges nothing, and the balance no longer vanishes on the Replicate page, which the study took for lost credit. What such a page should cost is one attribute, and yours to choose. Three version numbers on one screen: the front page’s edition line now ends with this site’s own release, the number in the nav and footer, instead of “edition from sgit.ai v0.7.39”, which I had added; an article byline’s “site v0.7.36” now says “sgit.ai v0.7.36”, because that is the sgit.ai release it names and links to; the markdown twins say the same. The participant page said “Nothing here runs”, contradicting the page that says what does; the card now says most of what it argues for does not run, and names what does. /shipped/ now says who is who (Dinis Cruz holds editorial responsibility; the desk’s roles, the Editor included, are worked by agents; there is no approval step) and that there is no published way to report an error, which I checked for across the reader-facing pages before writing it. Smaller: the JSON-LD said each article was part of the website sgit.ai, and the meter recorded page titles in a reader’s history with “, sgit.ai” on the end; both now say the SGit Newsroom. Checked, and not defects. “Balance £4.49 on the card, £4.97 in the top bar” is real on the screenshot, and is the live chip against a picture of the card: pv-card.webp, a figure in the article, has the author’s own balance baked into it. In a fresh browser, and replaying the study’s reopen-and-jump pattern, chip and card agree at every depth on this site and on sgit.ai. It is still a fair point that a picture of the card is indistinguishable from the card. “Blank page after Back” is the loader’s fade-in: blank for about 0.3 seconds, not a lasting blank. The two findings the study labelled as caused by its own helper stand as labelled. Not fixed here, and why. About twenty of the 31 findings are about pages imported from sgit.ai (the meter’s install page, the top-up page, the account wording, the article layout, the unlabelled £5.00 chip, the byline); the rule is that imported pages are fixed there and re-synced, and the meter component is a published version that never changes. They are listed, with who owns each, in the move note. Two need a decision and not a fix: a contact for pilots (the one address published anywhere is the one that runs the mailing list), and whether model identifiers belong on the site: 76 imported pages name a model version, mostly in the AI-disclosure line, including this study page, while the brief says they must not appear. Caught before release: an import step crashed on a bad regex replacement and the build chain carried on, because I piped it through tail, which hides the failure; the chain now runs with pipefail. And a screenshot script wrote its output into a directory literally named $S inside the repository, found and deleted before it was committed.

The site now calls itself the SGit Newsroom, and SG Meter’s install instructions are back the way sgit.ai wrote them. The name. v0.6.0 imported the newsroom with sgit.ai’s name in every page’s metadata: the home page’s tab read “Articles, sgit.ai”, and all 312 pages declared sgit.ai as their site, which is what a search result or a link preview shows. The import now renames the site in the tab title, og:title, og:site_name and the JSON-LD, and gives the front page the newsroom’s own title and description. It is a rule in sync_newsroom.py, applied on every sync, not an edit, so the gate that refuses hand edits to imported pages still holds. A correction to v0.6.0. The import re-points links, and it reached into a code sample: on the SG Meter page the install snippet’s src="/assets/components/…" was shown as src="../assets/components/…", so a reader copying it would have copied something sgit.ai never wrote. Links are now rewritten in real tags only, never in text that merely looks like a tag. It was live for about half an hour. Why the gate let it through, and does not now. The link check had the same flaw: it read src="…" anywhere, code samples included. The snippet’s original root path does not exist as a file here, so the honest snippet would have failed the gate, and the import’s rewrite turned it into a path that did exist. The bug passed because it was a bug. The link check now reads real tags only, and was shown still failing on a real broken link beside an identical path in a code sample. Caught before release: the first version of the renaming replaced every "name" on the front page, which renamed the reader personas in the meter’s config, and the author, to “SGit Newsroom”. It now touches only the page’s own title and only inside the JSON-LD block. How it was checked, and now is: for all 312 imported pages, the visible text is compared with sgit.ai’s own copy; it is identical apart from the edition line, which deliberately names this site. The meter config is byte-identical on every page, and the markdown twins differ only in where their links point.

The newsroom moves in. newsroom.sgit.ai is now the SGit Newsroom first, and everything it said before the newsroom ran is in a dated archive. The front page is the newsroom’s. All 66 articles, the front page, the newsletter, collections, desk notes, the graphs, the backstage (six roles, their behaviour policies, the board, the log), the reader’s account and the SG Meter library now live here at the same paths they have on sgit.ai: 312 pages, 1,274 files, imported from sgit.ai v0.7.39 (commit dfd5d23), with canonical URLs pointing here. The home page looks like sgit.ai’s /articles/ because it is the same page, with this site’s navigation. The reading meter’s balance is in the top bar. Imported, not rebuilt. sgit.ai still publishes every day, from a generator that also builds the rest of sgit.ai, so admin/build/sync_newsroom.py imports the built pages and changes only what must change: links to sgit.ai pages that did not move become absolute, canonical and image URLs point here, sgit.ai’s stylesheet arrives as assets/newsroom.css because assets/site.css is this site’s own, and sgit.ai’s site chat stays behind because here it would answer questions about the wrong site. Scripts, the meter component and the subscribe lane’s public file are copied byte for byte. The record, with two SHA-256 per file, is admin/build/newsroom-sync.json, and a new gate check 11 fails the build if anyone edits an imported page here: fix it on sgit.ai and re-sync. The generator moves here at cutover. The archive: 75 pages archived in place, nothing moved, nothing deleted. The Governance Wire, Portugal Startups, the pt.newsroom designs, the brief pack, the library, the MVP specifications and seven design pages the running newsroom has overtaken keep their addresses and carry a dated note at the top saying when they were written, why they are in the archive and what overtook them. The three pages whose address now means something else (the home page, the newsroom design page, and /shipped/, which said “nothing on this site is running yet”) are copied into archive/ under the date they were written. Index: /archive/. Three new pages, in the newsroom’s look. The design, and what runs sets each idea beside what runs and what does not yet. Replicate this newsroom says what someone can copy today and what is not packaged yet. What runs, what is designed is rewritten for 10 October, and says plainly that no money moves until the payment link is set. Every count on them is read from the imported files at build time. The navigation is in the reader’s order: Newsroom, Account, How it runs, Design, Replicate, World News Day, Archive, About. The sitemap is now generated from the tree (446 pages), llms.txt leads with the newsroom and lists the archive under its own dated heading, and the front-page news strip is retired with the page it stamped: the front page now carries the newsroom’s own Latest. The gate, made precise twice. The key tripwire now also passes sgit_rk1_, the read-key prefix in sgit’s first format, which an imported article quotes and which sgit.ai’s own credential checker classifies as read-only. And an imported page meets the agent-block rule with sgit.ai’s equivalent, an llms.txt chip plus a markdown twin that exists; a page with neither still fails. Caught before release, by looking: the front page copied to / loaded its meter as import('assets/…'), a bare module specifier the browser refuses; the design page printed the whole article list where a count belonged; each archive run left one more blank line on every archived page; and the nav wrapped to two rows. All fixed, and a second build now writes nothing. Not yet: the pages that stay (the concept pages, World News Day, the site pages) still have the earlier look; the meter is not on them; /account/import.html and the meter’s browser test are the rest of the brief’s Phase 3. The plan and the full content audit are in the move note.

The gate inside the published vault was broken again, by the release that added the app. The vault’s README tells a reader to run python3 build/gates.py to re-derive every published count. v0.5.4 broke it twice over: the new published-or-private checks load data/vault-audit.json, which is a record about the vault and is deliberately not inside it; and the app was excluded from the page checks by its path, vault-app/index.html, which is where it lives in the repository and not where it lives in the vault. In the bundle it sits at the root, so the gate checked the app as if it were a page of this website and reported three failures about a file that has no business carrying site chrome. Both fixed the same way as the v0.5.1 correction: the audit checks are skippable and say so by name, and the app is now excluded by identity rather than by path — it is whatever app.json names as its entry, which is true in both layouts. Verified by cloning the published vault with the published read key and running the gate inside it: clean, with the two skips named. Third time this instruction has been caught failing, and the reason is always the same: the repository is not what was published, and only opening the published thing finds it. That check is now part of the release routine rather than something done when it occurs to us.

One vault, not two — and it opens as an app. Plus the release news on the front page, and the “design, not built” badge retired. The outreach vault should never have been published. It holds who we are contacting, through which route, and what we plan to say — ours until it is sent, and about other people before it is about us. Deleting the line from a page would not have been a remedy: revocation is not retroactive, and anyone who fetched the objects keeps them. So the vault was rekeyed with sgit vault move: every object re-encrypted under a new key, pushed under a new identity, and the old vault hard-deleted from the server. The published key now recovers zero files, which we checked by cloning with it. The correction in full. And the very next run of the publishing script re-published a key for it. Pushing a vault and publishing one are different acts and the script did not know the difference; it does now, from a table that says which vaults may carry a published key. Two new gates: a vault is PUBLISHED or PRIVATE with opposite obligations — a published one must carry a public read key the audit actually used, a private one must carry no key — and every revoked key is hunted across the whole repository, because llms-full.txt still carried this one after llms.txt had been fixed by hand. The corpus vault is now a vault app. app.json with present: true, so the SG/Send host launches index.html from inside the vault instead of showing a file tree: the finding, the twenty-one pieces, every sentence typed and anchored, and the vocabulary — read from the vault’s own encrypted files in the reader’s browser over the sg.vfs bridge, with no server, no account and no database. It follows the authoring contract to the letter (all CSS and JS inlined, nothing declarative against a vault path, an inlined fallback so it renders saved to disk, and sg-app-ready posted when it has drawn), and the build checks all of that before it ships. The vault page now carries screenshots of it, in the shape sgit.ai uses. Two site-wide changes. The design, not built badge is gone from the nav: it was written when everything here was a design, and it now undersells four sections that run, a published vault and a corrected record. The honest sentence on the front page and /shipped/ still draw that line properly, where there is room to draw it accurately. And the front page now opens with what changed lately — the newest six releases, generated from the release record so the page cannot claim an update that did not ship.

The outreach brief: what the collaborating agent is asked to do, to whom, in what order, and with what words. world-news-day/outreach/agent-brief.md, in the outreach vault beside the protocol it depends on. It carries the established findings with every figure filled from the data files rather than typed; the links to send, leading with the recipient’s own piece’s page rather than with our argument; three tiers in order, the commissioner first because a licence is theirs to name and not an author’s; the nine organisations with a role address, the nine reachable only by contact page or LinkedIn, and the nine with no route at all; three message templates; what to record after every action; and the pacing, including one follow-up per target and never a second. Two rules in it are worth naming here. A declined is final — recorded, and no other channel and no later attempt. And do not go looking for a personal address: where no route was established under the published rules, none is to be found by other means; a published organisational route can be proposed as a noted action and added at the next build. The brief is generated, so it can be rebuilt after any recapture and its numbers cannot drift from the section’s. Both vaults were re-pushed and re-audited: 14 hits in the corpus vault and 22 in the outreach vault, all cleared, none unexplained.

The two vaults listed and described the way sgit.ai lists its thirty-seven — and the live page was pointing at a vault that did not exist. The bug first. build/vault.py rewrote data/vault.json on every build and replaced the real vault id and read key with the BUNDLE's name and a null. The deployed page told readers to open wnd-2026-09-29 with an empty key. Nothing caught it because every check tested the repository rather than what the page claimed; a new gate now cross-checks the id and key on the page against the vault the audit actually opened, and fails if the page publishes the bundle id. The method is not ours. sgit.ai writes down how it publishes a vault in seven steps for another agent to follow, serving two absolute rules: read keys yes and vault keys never, and audit BEFORE the key rather than after, because revocation is not retroactive. build/vault_audit.py reimplements those checks rather than importing them, so the code that classifies a credential and the code that scans a clone can be read beside the result. What it does, all of it with the published read key and no token. Classifies both credentials; clones each vault; derives files, size, commit depth, HEAD and top-level layout from the clone rather than from the repository; scans every text file against eight patterns; and runs the negative control — an all-zeros read key, which must fail, and does, because the index address is derived from the key. 14 hits in the corpus vault and 11 in the outreach vault, every one cleared and none unexplained: they are the organisations' role addresses the contacts map publishes on purpose. Ruling a hit out is the work, so each carries the rule that cleared it, and an unexplained finding now fails the build. And the vaults now open as pages. Each carries a _page.json at its root, so opening one shows what it is and what the rules are instead of whichever file sorts first — which for the corpus vault was MANIFEST.json, a list of hashes, an accurate and useless first impression of a piece of journalism. Two more of the same family of bug. data/vault-audit.json was inside the bundle, so each audit found the previous audit's findings and the count grew from 14 to 39 in one cycle; it is now excluded, with the manifest that listed itself and the vault record that carried its own hash. The rule those three produced: a record about an artefact does not live inside it. And our own key tripwire fired on sgit clone sgit_public_read_… — the exact line a published vault page must carry. That is sgit.ai's own recorded mistake, and their rule applies: make it precise, not stricter.

Cloning our own published vault with our own published key found two defects that every internal check had missed. The vault’s README tells a reader to run python3 build/gates.py to re-derive every published count. That instruction did not work. The gate resolved its paths from the repository layout, so inside the bundle it looked for world-news-day/data/ beside the bundle and died. A published instruction that fails is worse than no instruction: it invites somebody to check us and then tells them the fault is theirs. The gate now detects which layout it is in — by the presence of the whole-site build tooling, not by data/, which exists in both — and inside the bundle it names the four checks it skips and why, because they are about this website’s pages rather than about the data. And the pushed corpus vault was two releases stale. publish_vaults.py only filled a working copy that had no vault in it yet, so every re-run pushed the same bytes: the vault was created before the fractal layer existed and silently stayed that way while its own page advertised files it did not contain. It now refreshes the contents on every run without touching .sg_vault. Both were found the same way — by cloning the published vault with the published read key and running the check the vault tells you to run. Verified end to end: a clone with the public key now re-derives all 1,070 claim classifications, re-hashes all 43 frozen files, and re-runs every licence count, from a read-only vault a stranger can open. Also: validate.js now fails on a page whose nav or footer block is empty. Pages are generated with empty chrome that chrome.py fills; skip that step and every page ships with no navigation and no version badge — and every other check still passed, because they all test what a page says rather than whether it has any furniture at all. That happened in v0.5.0 and was caught by reading a diff, which is not a control.

The fractal layer: all 1,070 sentences of the twenty-one op-eds, typed, anchored and connected — plus a page for each piece, and LinkedIn routes. Until now the section treated each op-ed as one node. This builds the level below and the level above at once. Each piece becomes its own graph of claims; the pieces connect to each other through a shared vocabulary; a term is a graph of everywhere it is used. Same shape at every zoom, which is what makes it fractal rather than merely big. 1,070 sentences, each typed by a published formula in data/claim-rules.json: 828 flat assertions, 79 hypotheses, 51 quantified observations, 41 evaluations, 31 questions, 24 attributed statements — and 16 proposals. Twenty-one of the most senior voices in news, asked what journalism is for, and sixteen sentences in twenty thousand words that propose doing anything. The rule order was deliberately set so that attributed statement is tested early, ahead of proposal and hypothesis: it is the only class that points outside the piece, and ordering it late would have undercounted attributions and flattered our own argument about evidence. How this avoids republishing anything. A claim node carries a type, an offset into the frozen prose, a length, and an anchor of at most 8 verbatim words — enough to find the sentence, far short of reproducing it. The sentence itself is stored nowhere. The gate checks every anchor is in the bytes and under the limit, and re-derives all 1,070 classifications from the frozen prose with the published rules. And the finding about meaning. 38 vocabulary terms are used, 33 by more than one piece — and there are 4 places in 1,070 sentences where anybody says what one of those words means. The vocabulary is shared; the definitions are assumed. A looser rule found 29, but read “the decline of local news is a global phenomenon” as that piece defining local news — so it was tightened to require the term to be the subject of its own sentence, both counts are published, and the 25 given up are stated as a cost. The only term stated twice is stated by the same author both times, and the gate checks that label against the bylines rather than trusting it, because calling a repetition a disagreement would manufacture a finding. Twenty-one piece pages under /world-news-day/pieces/: every sentence typed and anchored, the claim profile beside the corpus average, who wrote it with the published route to them, what it cites, the vocabulary it shares with pieces that never cite it, and a mapping to this site’s own argument by a published rule over the terms used — which claims only that the piece uses those words and that we have written about them. LinkedIn, only as an organisation offers it. 8 company pages taken from frozen bytes we already held. Personal profiles are published only where the slug is an author of this corpus, letter for letter: 12 were found and dropped and 0 passed — including a near miss, because three of the four profiles on one page belong to people with nothing to do with that newsroom, and “probably the same person” is not a standard for publishing somebody’s profile as theirs. One rule was loosened and bounded rather than quietly relaxed: each author’s role line, exactly as affiliations.json records it, joins the permission statement as an exempt quotation — because the affiliation claim is a reading of that line. The exemption is enumerated, not pattern-matched, and the gate fails if it ever grows past 400 words of the corpus’s 20,060.

Two encrypted vaults, pushed and readable — the corpus, and a second one that the agent at riskmandate.ai works in. The corpus vault (wnd-2026-09-29) holds the twenty-one op-eds as frozen bytes, every derived dataset, the build code and the gate: 107 files. It is finished on the day it was made. The outreach vault (clsc1dg4) is the opposite kind of thing — append-only, and it will move every time a message is sent or answered. It carries 27 target files, a protocol.md, a brief, an action log with a JSON schema and a closed list of verbs, and 0 actions: nothing has been sent. Its contents are generated into world-news-day/outreach/ so anyone can rebuild them and diff. Why two and not one. The first is a record of what somebody else published, safe to hand to anyone including the people it describes. The second is a record of what we do about it, and holds who we are contacting and what we plan to say. Different claims, different failure modes, different audiences — sharing a history and a hash chain between them would be a mistake in both directions. Read keys are published; vault keys are not. Both pages now carry a sgit_public_read_… key, derived one-way and granting read and only read. The vault keys were never printed, copied or written to any file by the publishing script: it derives the read key in memory and leaves the credential where sgit put it. A new gate fails the build if any private key shape reaches data/*.json. And the tripwire that would not have fired. The whole-site key-leak check had been written against a UUID-shaped vault id. When real vaults were created, sgit issued keys of the form sgit_private_vault_<…>:<id> — which that pattern does not match at all. It now matches the real prefixes by name, and the archive is no longer exempt, because a key committed into an archived copy is exactly as leaked. A tripwire satisfied by the absence of a shape nobody uses is not a tripwire. A third gate now runs over the outreach vault before it is pushed: no address in it may be anything but an organisation's role address, by the same published two-part rule the contacts map uses.

The argument, as one piece written to be sent: Free to republish is not a licence. Seventeen hundred words for the twenty-one people who wrote the corpus, and for anyone else who publishes open material without saying so in a form a machine can read. It opens by saying what is good about the act — twenty thousand words given away by people whose day job is deciding what stays behind a paywall — and then asks the question a machine asks. All twenty-one grant permission; none names a licence; the terms are stated three different ways; twenty-one of twenty-one already ship schema.org JSON-LD and none populates its license field. It carries the aggregate too: nineteen of twenty-one pieces are about truth and facts, eleven raise AI, three mention copyright or licensing at all; eleven of twenty-one offer the reader no outbound link whatsoever; and of the twenty-three domains cited between them, no two pieces point at the same one. It says plainly that the diagnosis in the corpus is shared and correct, that what is missing is a mechanism, and that we are not a neutral party — naming which parts of our own stack are designs rather than things that run. Every figure in the prose is a token filled from the data files at build time, not typed, so the article and data/*.json cannot disagree, and the build fails on an unfilled token. The markdown source ships beside it under CC BY 4.0 at world-news-day/content/ — the piece asks publishers to license their work in a form a machine can read, so it does. The last section is the one that took the longest to write: an account of this section publishing a claim about WAN-IFRA's infrastructure more strongly than the evidence supported, withdrawing it, and the gate that now fails the build if the withdrawn claim reappears without the correction beside it.

A correction about the publisher of the corpus, made in public — and a contacts map built under rules published before the looking started. What we got wrong. v0.4.0 said the World News Day announcement was “the one page in the beat a machine cannot read”, on the evidence of two refused attempts. wan-ifra.org is served through a JavaScript-challenge firewall that refuses some automated requests: going back to the same host for an unrelated reason, it answered 200, and a third attempt returned the full 59 KB page. A refusal observed twice is a fact about two attempts, not a property of a page. The announcement is now a registered, hashed source; every attempt is counted and recorded with the size and hash of what came back; and the terms it states — “All of the op-eds are free to republish with appropriate credit” — are read from the frozen bytes instead of quoted by hand. The hand-quoted sentence turned out to be verbatim, and the two-statement finding stands, now anchored on both sides. The correction in full, with the rule it produced, and a gate that fails the build if the withdrawn claim appears anywhere without the correction beside it. How to reach them. Not one of the twenty-one pages offers a way to reach its author or its publisher: no contact address, no author URL in the structured record, no press line. So the map was built by going to the organisations’ own sites, one hop each, under rules fixed in data/contact-rules.json before the fetching started: organisations and never people; a published list of role local parts; four published tests before a site counts as established; and every address re-derived from frozen bytes by the gate. Result: 20 of 27 organisations established, 14 with a contact page, 11 role addresses publishable out of 43 seen, and 15 of 23 authors with any published route — all of it via an organisation. Three pages were fetched and deliberately not kept. A page carrying ten or more addresses of named people is a staff directory; the Globe and Mail’s publishes the direct address of seventy-nine journalists. Those pages are public, so this is not secrecy — it is that freezing a staff directory into a repository and shipping it in a downloadable bundle makes it materially easier to scrape than the publisher made it. The URL, the hash and the counts are recorded so the count can be re-checked; the cost of that choice is stated rather than hidden. Organisation pages that are kept are stored gzipped with the SHA-256 of the original bytes, which the gate decompresses and re-verifies: eleven megabytes of script bundle became two, with the anchoring unchanged. The vault bundle now carries all of it: 104 files, 2.68 MB, SHA-256 02816a3dabac7085a01010d7….

The World News Day corpus as one downloadable bundle — and the section declaring its own licence in the field it says the corpus leaves empty. The vault: vault.zip, 64 files, 0.83 MB, SHA-256 72920f612e069f096f6a8e70…. Every frozen op-ed and REST record, every derived dataset, the build code and the gate that checks it, in one file. Built deterministically — the same frozen bytes produce the same zip, hash for hash — so the digest is a fact about the contents rather than a record of when the build ran. Two circular dependencies were caught getting there: the bundle contained the record of its own hash, and the section manifest listed itself. Two sets of terms, on the bundle’s own face. Our description, counts, graph, transcription and code are CC BY 4.0 — named, versioned, with a URL, and declared in licence.json. The twenty-one op-eds under sources/frozen/ are not ours and are not relicensed; the README quotes the publisher’s own sentence and says plainly that it grants the reader nothing over somebody else’s work. The bundle carries the frozen third-party pages, which departs from this publication’s standing rule that a delivered vault holds no copies of somebody else’s pages, and the reason is written into the bundle rather than left implicit. No sgit vault has been pushed, and the page says so. Creating one needs an SG/Send access token; this build environment has none, and a section about licensing does not invent a credential or publish a key. PACKAGE.sh inside the bundle carries the exact commands, and data/vault.json records "pushed": false and "read_key": null. When a vault is pushed the read key goes there — never the vault key. And the part of the argument that can only be made by doing it. Every page in the section now carries schema.org JSON-LD with license, copyrightHolder, copyrightNotice, usageInfo and isAccessibleForFree, plus a rel="license" link — the five fields the section counts as unused on all twenty-one — and a new gate fails the build if a page loses any of them, or if the notice stops saying that the licence covers our description and not the op-eds.

A new section, and the first time this publication has turned its method on somebody else’s open corpus: World News Day 2026 — twenty-one op-eds, free to republish, under no named licence. For World News Day on 28 September, WAN-IFRA and the Canadian Journalism Foundation commissioned twenty-one opinion pieces from editors, publishers and directors from Manila to Managua and made them free to republish. All twenty-one were fetched, frozen to a dated snapshot, hashed and described here — and none of the prose is republished. Forty-two frozen files: the page as served and the record from the publisher’s own undocumented WordPress REST API, for each piece. The finding, derived from the bytes by two separate implementations. All 21 carry a permission to republish. 0 carry a licence with a name — no Creative Commons, no rel="license", no copyright notice, nothing with a version and a URL. The permission exists only as a sentence at the foot of the prose, in two wordings, and the announcement states the terms a third way: the articles require republication “in full” and never mention credit; the announcement requires “appropriate credit” and never says in full. And while 21 of 21 already ship schema.org JSON-LD, generated automatically by the site’s own SEO plugin, 0 of 21 use its license field. The gap between “we want this to spread” and a statement a machine can act on is one line of JSON long. The aggregate, over twenty-one of the most senior voices in news. 19 of 21 pieces are about truth and facts; 11 raise artificial intelligence; 3 mention copyright or licensing at all. 11 of the 21 offer the reader no outbound link whatsoever — 38 links across the whole corpus, and of the 23 domains cited between them, no two pieces point at the same one. That is the measurement this publication has argued for since its first page, taken on the people making the case for trusting journalism, in the week they made it. The aggregate maps the shared diagnosis onto what we have published, and says plainly what nobody in the corpus proposes: a mechanism. And one refusal, recorded rather than tidied away. wan-ifra.org answered an automated reader with HTTP 307 and no body, from two user-agents, while rendering normally in a browser. The announcement that grants the permission is the one page in the beat a machine cannot read, and the register says so rather than quietly dropping it. The section ships with the estate’s grammar: 153 nodes and 420 edges over 8 types and 8 verbs, every verb with a distinct named inverse and a Portuguese form, 1,449 N-Triples, a published twenty-pattern lexicon as the only classification, and thirteen gates — among them one that fails the build if twelve consecutive words of any op-ed appear on any page we generate, and one that re-derives every licence count from the frozen HTML with a second implementation. agrees_with is a banned verb: shared vocabulary is not agreement, and this section does not put words in a named editor’s mouth.

The Startup Summit beat, consolidated into one archive: 160 files, each with its live URL, its repository URL and its hash. Brief 15 and the bundle (210 files, 1.5 MB, also unpacked under briefs/summit-archive/) hold everything this publication did on the beat in one place: twenty pages and seven role pages as served, twenty-two data files, twelve build scripts and viewers, three stories as prose, seven documents, and the eighty-nine frozen sources that everything else stands on. Every file was fetched from the live site and checked before the bundle was cut — all 160 returned 200 and were byte-identical to the repository, and the manifest carries the SHA-256 so a reader can repeat the check rather than take our word. Four documents carry what a file list cannot. The chronology: six days, two captures, and the release-by-release order in which the section was built. Every published number beside the file it derives from, including the four this publication refused to print — attendance, the speaker total as a fact about the event, countries, and anything about what happened in the room. The method and its eighteen gates, with the argument for why each rule is a gate rather than a habit. And three things that went wrong: the notice that should have shipped with v0.3.0, a rendered count that had become false, and the posture on biographies that changed under pressure and was nearly changed silently. The boundary is on the first page, not inferred from the last. The register stops on 13 September, four days before the doors opened; there is no capture from during or after the event, and the archive says what a successor should do first — capture again, write the fourth piece, and never backfill a dated capture.

A sibling transfer: two frozen captures go to pt.newsroom.sgit.ai, and a rule for evidence that changes hands. Memo 14, written after reading the sibling repository at its v0.3.1 and its live site. It opens with what that site built and this one does not have — a read-only JSON API with an OpenAPI document, the delivery quarantine as a build gate, and the accent and Portuguese-path gates the pack could only ask for — because the comparison is not one-way. What goes the other way is one thing that matters and several that help. Its lead story says there is only one capture of the speaker list, 70 names, nothing to report, and that it exists to say so and wait for a second. This site froze the same pages on 8 September (60 names) and 13 September (64, +5 −1). With theirs, that is three captures in six days — 60 → 64 → 70 — and the one speaker who left on the 13th has not come back. Also in the bundle: three press pages they lack, the fourth that returned 404 and is excluded with its reason, and the Guinness pitch-marathon story that two publishers report and the event’s own agenda does not list — every byte for it already frozen in their tree, and no story written. The rule the transfer forces, which neither site had written down: evidence transferred between sibling publications stays evidence only if the provenance travels with it and is published. The bundle’s manifest carries, per file, the URL, who fetched it, when, under which version, and the SHA-256 the origin register recorded — all fourteen re-verified before packaging, and meant to be verified again on arrival, because the hash is the only thing in it that requires trusting nobody. The memo proposes a register field and a gate that make the provenance impossible to lose in a refactor, and names the limits that belong on the page beside it.

v0.3.11 14 Sep 2026 Research deliveries travel as sgit vaults.
