Abstract: An idea came up while I was answering a post about agent liability, and I think it deserves to stand on its own as a proposal. Today an agent gets a prompt from us and a system prompt from its vendor. It should also get an Agent Behaviour Policy, written to a published standard, which the vendor accepts, enforces as far as it can, and eventually answers for. It is the beginning of dealing with something the models have got away with for a long time: they do not separate code from data, so every instruction and every piece of content arrives in the same channel. Now that agents can do a great deal, and are starting to go off the rails in public, their behaviour is becoming an existential threat to the companies that make them, through liability and above all through trust: it does not take many users being hurt before people stop giving agents instructions at all. Two industries have been here. Aviation did not get safe out of altruism; it got safe because every crash became world news, and at the accident rate of 1995 today's traffic would bring about a hundred fatal airliner accidents a year instead of twelve. Payments got some of the best security teams anywhere because liability for fraud was moved onto the card companies and the banks, and the fraud detection followed the money, often spotting a merchant's breach before the merchant did. Regulation alone does not do it; some industries are happy to pay the fines. It works when the rule, the liability and the business model point the same way. A policy beside the prompt is how to make them point the same way for agents: the user answers for what is outside the policy, and the vendor for the rows it accepted. Most agents already run a policy of their own; we just cannot see it, rely on it, or stop it changing. And the system prompt itself is a light behaviour policy that is not written like one: the next step is for the vendor's own rules to become a published policy too, layered with ours.

What an agent is given, today in two modes and as proposed. Over the API we write the whole system prompt, so our behaviour policy goes inside it; in the Claude apps and Claude Code the vendor's system prompt comes first and our policy goes into what we add. In both, it is text the model is asked to keep, in the same channel as every email and page it reads, and the vendor's checks are its own. Proposed: the policy as a separate, versioned input, layered over the vendor's own published policy, checked outside the model where it can be.
in-short

A third input. Beside the system prompt and the prompt, an agent should take an Agent Behaviour Policy, written to a published standard, which the vendor acknowledges, enforces where it can, reports against, and answers for. It starts on an old problem. Models do not separate code from data. Instructions and content arrive in one channel, which is why prompt injection may never be fully fixed. A policy is a second channel for the one thing that should not be negotiable: what the agent may do. Agent behaviour is now an existential risk for the vendors. Through liability, and more through trust. A small number of people badly hurt is enough for many more to stop giving agents instructions. Aviation got safe because crashes became news. At 1995's rate of fatal airliner accidents per million flights, 2025's 38.7 million flights would have meant about 105 fatal accidents. There were 12.
in-short

Payments got safe because liability moved to the companies. Card fraud caps for consumers, a liability shift onto whoever had not adopted chip cards, standards written by the card brands, and in the UK, banks reimbursing scam victims, after which those losses fell by about a fifth. Regulation alone is not enough. Some industries pay the fines. The improvement comes when the rule, the liability and the business model point the same way. The user answers outside the policy, the vendor inside it. The rows the vendor accepted are the vendor's to keep. That is a better model than "you clicked allow", and the vendors who get it right will win on it. Agents already run hidden policies. Claude in Chrome will not type a password. That is a policy. We should be able to read it, rely on it, and know when it changes.
in-short

The policy goes into both modes, and today both are hope. Over the API we write the whole prompt; in the Claude apps and Claude Code the vendor adds its own system prompt and we add ours. Either way the policy is text the model is asked to keep, which is why the checks have to get stronger. A system prompt is a light behaviour policy. It tells the agent how to behave. It should be written as one, layered: the vendor's policy, then the deployer's, with business logic only the deployer can write.
idea

When I answered Ralf Thomas on where the liability line should fall, the section I most wanted to write was the last one: that an agent should take a behaviour policy beside its prompt. I think it deserves to be its own proposal, put out there on its own, because I think it can help a lot, and not only with the liability conversation.
idea

Here it is. Today, an agent gets two things: a system prompt from its vendor, and a prompt from us. It should get a third: an Agent Behaviour Policy, defined to a standard, that says what this agent, in this deployment, is meant to do and must not do, row by row, with what stands in the way of each row. The vendor should accept it as part of the deployment, enforce as much of it as the platform can see, report every breach against it, and, eventually, carry liability for the rows it accepted. The vocabulary already exists, published under CC BY at abp.sgit.ai: the reach, the mandate, the gap between them, and the barriers, none, expectation, setting and boundary, of which only a boundary is a control.
code-and-data

This is the beginning of dealing with something the models have got away with for a long time. They do not separate code from data. In a computer, the instructions and the things they operate on are kept apart, and most of the worst security bugs in history, from buffer overflows to SQL injection, are what happens when that separation breaks. In a language model there is no separation to break. The UK's National Cyber Security Centre put it plainly in December 2025: current models "simply do not enforce a security boundary between instructions and data inside a prompt", which is why it thinks prompt injection may never be mitigated the way SQL injection was. Simon Willison's phrase for the consequence is that "LLMs follow instructions in content", and the email the agent reads is content.
code-and-data

A behaviour policy does not fix that, and I do not want to claim it does. What it does is take the most important instructions out of the channel that anybody can write into. The prompt can be argued with by an email. The policy should not be: it is loaded by the platform, versioned, signed, and checked by something other than the model where it can be. It is a second channel for the one thing that should not be negotiable, what the agent may do, and every row the platform can enforce outside the model, as Claude Code's own documentation says of its permission rules, "are enforced by Claude Code, not by the model".
existential

Now that agents can do a great deal, and are starting to go off the rails in public, with the incidents of 2026 as the record, I think agent behaviour is becoming an existential threat to the companies that make the models. One reason is liability, which could be very large: from 9 December 2026 software, AI systems included, is a product under the EU's new product liability rules. The bigger reason is trust. People will stop giving instructions to agents if they believe this can happen to them, and I do not think it takes many. A decent number of people badly hurt, in a news cycle that amplifies every one of them, is enough for a much larger number to decide that agents are not for them. That is a systemic risk to the whole business model, not a cost of doing business.
existential
Two industries have been here, and both are worth looking at, because neither got safe for the reasons people usually assume.
aviation

Fatal airliner accidents, 1995 and 2025. At 1995's rate of 2.72 per million flights, 2025's 38.7 million flights would have produced about 105 fatal accidents. There were 12. Rates from the Aviation Safety Network via Our World in Data; 2025 accidents from the Flight Safety Foundation's report of the ASN data; flights from IATA. Aviation is the best example we have of a complex system of technology, business process and people that learned to be safe, and I keep coming back to it, in The ultimate insider and in The investigation GitHub owes its customers. But let us be clear about why. It did not get there for altruistic reasons, or because it was the right thing to do, although, to be fair, the people who run airlines also fly, so they have some interest of their own. It got there because everybody knew that every crash, anywhere in the world, would be news, and more so every year.
aviation

When I was growing up, a plane crash was a regular news story. Here is the arithmetic of what would have happened if safety had stayed where it was. In 1995 there were 2.72 fatal airliner accidents for every million flights, on the Aviation Safety Network's count. In 2025 there were 38.7 million flights. At the 1995 rate, that is about 105 fatal accidents in a year, two a week. The Aviation Safety Network counted 12. Air travel more than doubled, from about 18 million flights in 1995, and the fatal accidents went down, not up: the rate fell almost ninefold. An industry with two fatal crashes a week would not have the passengers it has, and everybody in it understood that.
payments

Where the liability for payment fraud was moved, and what followed. Each step put the loss on the party best placed to stop it, and the security followed the loss: caps for consumers, a liability shift onto whoever had not adopted chip cards, standards written by the card brands, and reimbursement of scam victims. The second example is payments. If you compare payments with privacy, or with most of cyber security, card payments have had, for a long time, some of the best security teams, some of the best fraud detection and some of the best security measures anywhere. Why there? Very simple: the liability was moved onto the companies.
payments

Consumers stopped carrying the loss. In the United States, since 1970, a cardholder is liable for unauthorised use "only if... the liability is not in excess of $50". In the UK, a payment provider may make the payer liable "up to a maximum of £35" for a lost or stolen card. The loss went to whoever had not done the work. In October 2015, in the United States, counterfeit fraud liability shifted to the issuer or the merchant that had not adopted chip technology. The industry wrote its own standard. The PCI Security Standards Council was founded in 2006 by American Express, Discover, JCB, Mastercard and Visa, and every merchant that takes cards answers to it.
payments

And it keeps moving. Since October 2024 UK payment providers must reimburse victims of authorised push payment scams, up to £85,000. In the first 18 months, 88% of the money lost was reimbursed, and an independent evaluation found that losses sent over Faster Payments fell by around 21%, because reimbursement "strengthened incentives" to invest in prevention.
payments

The moment you pass the liability for fraud to the company, its security picks up. And it shows in who finds the fraud. I know of many cases, and the public record has famous ones, where a company discovered fraud not because its own security team picked it up, but because a card company, a processor or a bank came to it and said: you have fraud going on here. Target learned of its 2013 breach when it was contacted by the US Department of Justice, and Verizon's breach report for 2013 found that in almost all point-of-sale breaches the intrusion was reported to the victim by third parties, with law enforcement and external fraud detection the leading causes of discovery. The parties carrying the loss had built the detection.
regulation

Companies at that level cannot be made to do anything they truly do not want to do. There are industries, social media is the obvious one, where companies are more than happy to pay the fines when the rule goes against the core of their business model: Meta's €1.2 billion GDPR fine in 2023 was the largest at the time, and in 2025 the European Commission fined it €200 million over its "consent or pay" advertising model. The places where we saw real improvement were the places where three things lined up: a rule, a liability that landed on the company, and a systemic risk to the business model that the company could see. Sometimes the companies were glad of the regulation, because "it applies to everybody" let them all do what each of them needed to do. Payments is that case. Aviation is that case. Agents can be that case, if we give the liability somewhere precise to land.
inside

The proposed split. The vendor publishes its own built-in policy and accepts the deployer's; for every row it accepts, it says what enforces it and answers if it breaks. Everything the policy does not cover stays with the user, as it does today. The vendors that keep more rows as boundaries can sell that as the product.
inside

So here is the core of the proposal. If we want agents to be trustworthy, we need to push some enforcement, some criteria for enforcement and, eventually, some liability onto the vendors of the models and the agents. An Agent Behaviour Policy is a good standard to do it with, because it makes the split explicit. The agent runs with a policy. The rows the vendor accepted, the vendor keeps, and answers for if they break. Everything the policy does not cover stays with the user, as it does today. That is a much better model than the one we have, where the user is liable for everything because they clicked allow, which is the shell game the last article described.
inside

It would also be a competitive advantage for the vendors that get it right. A vendor that can say "these forty rows are boundaries on our platform, enforced outside the model, and we stand behind them" is selling something a vendor with a longer system prompt cannot. As Hope or enforcement measured, the share of a policy that rests on hope can fall from 97% to 23% with the right design; the vendors are the ones who can make the next part of that fall. What would the standard need? Not much that does not already exist in the vocabulary: A versioned policy file, with the reach, the mandate, the gap and the barriers, row by row, signed by the deployer, so both sides know which version was in force. The vendor's acknowledgement, per row: enforced by the platform as a boundary, kept as a setting, or accepted as an expectation the model is asked to keep.
inside

The vendor's own policy, published in the same format, so the two can be read together. A breach report, the same day, for every row broken and every near miss, which Authority outside the model argued should be the norm. Liability per row, starting with the boundaries the vendor said it enforces, which is where the vendors can most easily say yes.
modes

The figure at the top shows both modes and the end state. Today, the policy has to travel inside what we already provide, and where that is depends on how we reach the model. Over the API, we control the whole message. There is no vendor system prompt added to it; Anthropic's own release notes say its app system prompts "do not apply to the Claude API". So the behaviour policy goes into our system prompt, and the vendor's checks on misuse still run, unseen. In the Claude apps and in Claude Code, the vendor provides an explicit system prompt of its own, and we add to it: our instructions, a project's CLAUDE.md, or, in Claude Code, text appended to the default system prompt. The behaviour policy goes there, after the vendor's.
modes

In both modes, today, the system prompt and our behaviour policy are almost pure hope. That is hope-driven development again: we really hope the model will keep them when it reads them. Anthropic is honest about this for Claude Code: CLAUDE.md files are treated "as context, not enforced configuration. To block an action regardless of what Claude decides, use a PreToolUse hook instead." And we do not know how sure the model is that it is keeping them. I have not seen a model report, rule by rule, how confident it is that it followed an instruction, and I have not seen a published figure for how often a system prompt or a policy is kept under pressure. That is research worth doing.
modes

My argument is that this should be a lot stronger than it is. The vendors already run checks outside the model where they care: Claude in Chrome has "a safety classifier" that validates each action before it is performed, and the platforms check for misuse and abuse in ways the user never sees. The behaviour policy deserves the same machinery, with one difference: the policy's rows should be controlled by us. The whole point is that a behaviour policy brings in business logic, which is specific to the application and to what we are doing, and which no vendor can write for us.
system-prompt

There is a more evolved version of this, with more than one level. Claude itself has a behaviour policy: the rules in its system prompt and the ones its platforms enforce, from not typing passwords to asking before financial sites. It is just not written as one. And there is an argument that the system prompt should move to being a behaviour policy, because a system prompt is a light version of one already: it tells the agent how to behave. It is written as paragraphs for a model, when it could be written as rows a person can read, a platform can check, and a dispute can point to.
system-prompt

So the layering I would want is simple to say. The vendor's policy, published, for what the platform does everywhere. The deployer's policy, on top, for what this agent in this business may do, with the business rules only the deployer can write. Each row marked with what enforces it, and each layer with an owner. That is the conversation I want to have with the vendors: not "add our text to your prompt", but what the policy should be, how it should exist, and who checks it, when we are giving an agent explicit guidance on how to behave across a whole business.
already

I would argue most agents already run a version of this, and we cannot see it. Claude in Chrome is a good example. Anthropic's safety page says that "Claude is prohibited from" engaging in stock trading, bypassing captchas and inputting sensitive data, that it "asks for permission before accessing financial sites", and its Claude Code documentation says that when it meets a login page, "it pauses and asks you to handle it manually". So the user enters the password, because Claude says, I am not going to put a password in. Cool. That is a policy, and a good one, and we built the subscriptions service on it.
already

But we have no control over it, no guarantee of it, and it can change at any time. It is a vendor's policy described in a help article, not a row we can point to in a dispute. Which suggests a project worth running: reverse-engineer the policies the agents already run, the way we measured a Gmail connector's thirty tools and found that sending ran with no prompt while trashing a message stopped for approval, and publish them in the ABP format. If the vendors will not publish their policies yet, the measured ones are the next best thing, and the gap between the two is a finding.
limits

The confidence question is open. I have not seen published figures for how often a model keeps a system prompt or a policy under pressure, or a model reporting its confidence rule by rule. It is a proposal. No vendor accepts a behaviour policy as an input today in the sense described; Claude Code's permission rules and managed settings are the nearest thing, and they cover settings, not business rules. A policy does not separate code from data. It moves the most important instructions into a channel the content cannot reach. Prompt injection remains. The aviation numbers mix sources. The 1995 rate is the Aviation Safety Network's count over ICAO departures, via Our World in Data; the 2025 count is ASN's and the flights are IATA's. Both cover airliners with more than 14 seats, cargo included.
limits

The payments history is short and partial. Fraud did not disappear; it moved, and the incentives are why the industry chased it. The 21% fall is one evaluation's estimate. "It does not take many users" is my judgement. I have no number for how many incidents it takes to lose public trust in agents. Liability per row is the end state, not the start. Acknowledgement and breach reporting can come first; liability follows the boundaries a vendor is willing to stand behind. If you build an agent platform and would accept a policy, or you deploy agents and want to write one, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Summary: An idea came up while I was answering a post about agent liability, and I think it deserves to stand on its own as a proposal. Today an agent gets a prompt from us and a system prompt from its vendor. It should also get an Agent Behaviour Policy, written to a published standard, which the vendor accepts, enforces as far as it can, and eventually answers for. It is the beginning of dealing with something the models have got away with for a long time: they do not separate code from data, so every instruction and every piece of content arrives in the same channel. Now that agents can do a great deal, and are starting to go off the rails in public, their behaviour is becoming an existential threat to the companies that make them, through liability and above all through trust: it does not take many users being hurt before people stop giving agents instructions at all. Two industries have been here. Aviation did not get safe out of altruism; it got safe because every crash became world news, and at the accident rate of 1995 today's traffic would bring about a hundred fatal airliner accidents a year instead of twelve. Payments got some of the best security teams anywhere because liability for fraud was moved onto the card companies and the banks, and the fraud detection followed the money, often spotting a merchant's breach before the merchant did. Regulation alone does not do it; some industries are happy to pay the fines. It works when the rule, the liability and the business model point the same way. A policy beside the prompt is how to make them point the same way for agents: the user answers for what is outside the policy, and the vendor for the rows it accepted. Most agents already run a policy of their own; we just cannot see it, rely on it, or stop it changing.

It is a natural-language control policy for agent skills, and a CI pipeline that checks every skill contributed to an organisation-wide repository against it before hundreds of developers pull it down to their machines. A skill that turns internal documentation into a LinkedIn post has no untrusted input to worry about; a skill that pulls content off the web is handling untrusted text, and should treat it as data, not obey it. Change the description, regenerate the code. Using models to need them less. And in a common ontology, a whole catalogue of skills becomes one graph, where the dangerous combinations are a query.

A policy for every skill. The natural-language control at the top is the canonical source; each contributed skill passes deterministic checks, a model that reads it in its context, rules an agent generated from the control, and a human review, before it reaches the organisation's repository and the developers who pull it.
in-short

Skills are the new dependency. A skill is instructions an agent follows with a developer's reach, pulled by hundreds of people from one repository. Sean Turner built a control for them. A natural-language policy and a CI pipeline: is a contributed skill safe, secure, documented, usable, and understandable by the model and by people. It reads the skill in context. Internal documents in, a post out: little to worry about. Web pages in: untrusted text, to be treated as data. Beside the security scan, not instead of it. built

I was with my friend Sean Turner this week, talking about agent behaviour policies, and he described something he had built that I liked a lot. He has a different name for it: a natural-language control policy for agent skills.
built

The setting is an organisation with an organisation-wide repository of skills, the packages of instructions and reference material that an agent loads to learn how to do something. Anyone can contribute one, and once it is merged, hundreds of developers can pull it down to their machines and use it. Sean's control is a policy written in plain language about what a skill must be before that happens, and a CI pipeline that checks every contribution against it: is it safe, is it secure, is it well documented, is it usable, is it understandable by the model that will load it, and is it understandable by the people who will review and maintain it. In his words, does it make sense as a reasonable skill.
built

What makes it more than a linter is that it reads the skill in its context. His example: a skill that publishes an article to LinkedIn, working from internal documentation, has no prompt injection risk to speak of, because nothing it reads was written by an outsider. A skill that goes and pulls content off the internet is a different thing. Everything it reads is untrusted, and the check expects the skill to say so: not to trust that input, to defang it, and to do something meaningful with it as data rather than as instructions. And it is complementary to a security scan, not a replacement for one. A scanner asks whether a skill contains something malicious. Sean's control asks something more operational: is this the right way to contribute this skill to our workforce, given what it will touch when hundreds of people run it.
built
I have described it as he described it to me; I have not seen the code, and I could not find it published.
dependency

This matters because a skill is code that nobody compiles. When an agent loads it, its instructions become part of what the agent does, with whatever the agent can reach: the developer's repositories, their mail, their cloud credentials. In Attacks rewritten as mandates the same shift showed up from the supply side: Chainguard now publishes hardened agent skills, each with a record of the upstream commit and what was changed. That makes a skill a trustworthy input. It does not say what an agent running it should be allowed to do.
dependency

The public tooling for reviewing skills is arriving too, and it shows where the gap is. MongoDB's guide to reviewing an agent skill describes a structural validator that "runs in CI and produces pass/fail results", and a review skill that "optionally uses an LLM judge to score content quality across multiple dimensions": clarity, actionability, token efficiency, scope discipline, directive precision, novelty. That is a good quality bar, and none of those dimensions asks where the skill's inputs come from. The guide says as much about the hardest part: "No automated tool currently reasons across skill boundaries." Sean's control asks the question the quality bar leaves out, which is the one that decides whether a skill is dangerous.
abp

Same check, different context, different verdict. Two illustrative skills described in the columns of an agent behaviour policy: one that turns internal documentation into a post, with trusted inputs and a person pressing publish; one that researches the web, with untrusted inputs and a barrier that must treat fetched text as data. When Sean described it, I recognised the columns. An agent behaviour policy describes one agent in one setting by its mandate, what it is for; its reach, everything it can actually touch; the gap between the two, which is the risk; and the barrier in front of each row of the gap. Describe a skill that way and the context question answers itself.
abp

The LinkedIn skill's mandate is to turn internal documentation into a post. Its reach is reading internal documents and posting to one account; its inputs are written by the organisation; the gap is posting anything other than the reviewed draft, and a person pressing publish is the barrier. The web research skill's mandate is to gather and summarise public sources. Its reach is fetching any address and writing into the workspace; its inputs can be written by anyone; the gap is following an instruction found inside a page, and the barrier has to be treating fetched text as data.
abp

Put that next to the rest of what the skill can reach and you have the most useful question in agent security. Simon Willison named the lethal trifecta: "Access to your private data", "Exposure to untrusted content", and "The ability to externally communicate in a way that could be used to steal your data". A skill with untrusted inputs is one leg. Whether the agent loading it has the other two is a property of where it runs, which is why The policy draws the liability line argued that anything with the trifecta should take a behaviour policy beside its prompt.
hope

A control written in natural language, checked by a model, is what I call hope-based security. You give the model the rule and you hope it follows it. Hope or enforcement measured the cost for one customer service agent: built the obvious way, 97% of its rules were kept only by the model's good behaviour. But I agree with Sean that it is far better than not having it. A written control is the only place the intent exists. It is what a reviewer reads, what a model can check a skill against, and what the deterministic rules are written from. Without it, there is nothing to enforce, only code that nobody can explain. With it, the question becomes how much of it can be wrapped in something that does not hope.
codify

That is where Sean's next step comes in, and it is the part of the conversation I liked most. Use an agent to write deterministic rules that follow the natural-language control. For example, a skill that declares it reads the web gets a rule that checks it routes fetched content through a step that treats it as data. A skill that can post externally gets a rule that it has a human step before it does. The model reads the control once and writes code; from then on, the code runs, the same way every time, at no model cost per run. I usually put that as using models to not use models. The model is the author of the deterministic part, not the judge of every case. And the natural-language control is, in effect, the requirements document for those rules.
codify

Then the rule that makes it work: the description stays the canonical version, not the code. If the control changes, you change the description and regenerate the code. That is the same round trip Policy as code needs a policy first ran this week with Open Policy Agent: rows of a behaviour policy generated into Rego, the requests decided, and the code parsed back to find the rows with no code and the code with no row. AWS has built a version of it into a product: its agent policy service lets developers "describe rules in plain English instead of writing formal policy code in Cedar", generates candidate policies, and checks them for being "overly permissive, overly restrictive, or contain conditions that can never be satisfied". The direction is the same everywhere: people write intent, models write enforcement, and the intent stays the source.
graph

The last piece is what happens at the scale Sean is working at: not one skill, but hundreds, contributed by different people, describing themselves in different words. My approach to that is to bring them to a common ontology, the way fractal semantic graphs do: every skill described by the same columns, mandate, reach, inputs and their trust, barriers, as nodes with named edges, while each skill keeps its own text. Then the questions that matter across a catalogue are queries, not reviews. Which skills read untrusted content, and which of those can also reach private data and send something out? Which skills changed their reach since they were approved? Which declared a barrier that no generated rule enforces? MongoDB's guide is right that no tool reasons across skill boundaries today. A graph of skills in a common vocabulary is how one could.
licence

All of this is open source on our side, and it follows the line I keep drawing at RiskMandate: describe the behaviour in a policy; from the policy, grant a licence to operate that can be checked and revoked; and from a policy with a record behind it, make the agent insurable. To be clear about where that stands, as Ten hard questions for RiskMandate put it: "we make agents insurable. We do not insure them." The licence to operate and the insurability index are designs. A skill with a policy, checked at contribution and enforced where it runs, is the smallest version of that whole chain. Sean has built the first link.
limits

Sean's tool is described from a conversation. I have not seen its code, and I could not find it published; the details are his, as he told them, and any errors are mine. The two skills in the figure are illustrations. They follow his examples; they are not skills from his repository. Generated rules are only as good as the control. A model can write a rule that checks the wrong thing; the rules need tests and review like any code. A barrier written as "treat it as data" is still an expectation until something outside the skill enforces it. Licence to operate and insurability are designs, not products a customer runs today. If you are running an organisation-wide skills repository, or you have built something like Sean's, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: I want to send people I know, founders I mentor, potential clients, other publishers, a link that says: from Dinis, for Steve, here are the articles I think you should read, the ones worth a look, and the ones to follow. The newsroom's curation is close, but it is not personal, and the last 10 to 20% is the part that starts a conversation. This article is three things. A brief for the newsroom: a reading list in a link, with the names and the article numbers in the part of the URL the server never sees, a stable number for every article, a page that opens the list as a persona the reader can keep or remove, and a page to make a list for someone else, which is a business model of its own. A brief for the RiskMandate agent, which already keeps my contacts: choose the person, choose the articles and the reasons, build and test the link, draft the email, and let me send it. And the part I find most interesting: the loop. A feature like this crosses editorial, product, engineering, sales and the founder, which in most companies takes weeks of meetings. Here each hand-off is a written brief, each part is a session with its own repository or vault and its own gates, and the loop closes in a day. This week it closed several times, and it is worth showing how, and what it costs.

What a reading list from one person to another could look like, opened on newsroom.sgit.ai: three articles to read, in order, one to look at, and a persona to follow. An illustrative mock of the design below; it is not built yet. I have a long list of people I want to send the newsroom to. Founders I mentor. People I give advice to. Potential clients and users. Publishers and journalists I have been talking to about where news could go. For each of them, I know roughly what they care about, and I know which of the articles here they should read.

The newsroom already does a lot of that work. It has personas, it can open as one of them from a link, it builds a front page for each reader, and it is about to let readers customise more. But the curation is not personal. It is close, and it is missing the last 10 to 20%, and that last part is exactly what turns "here is a site" into the beginning of a conversation. So I want one small feature. I want to send somebody an email with a link, and when they open it, the newsroom says: from Dinis, for Steve, here are the articles I think you should read, here are a couple worth a look, and here is what to follow. One article, or five, or twenty. And it does not have to be from me: anyone can make a list for someone else, which is a business model the newsroom enables almost by accident.

The feature is simple. What is interesting is everything it touches. It has to be built on the newsroom, deployed and tested, and fit the workflows already there. Then the agent that keeps my contacts has to understand it, research the person, choose the articles, and draft the email for me to send. Then the reply has to come back somewhere. That is three parts of a company and a founder, and the way they work together is the real subject of this article. So it is in three parts: two briefs, and the loop.
short

The feature: a reading list in a link. newsroom.sgit.ai/for/#from=Dinis&to=Steve&r=61,44,70&s=52&f=founder. The names and the article numbers are in the fragment, the part after the #, which browsers do not send to the server. The page builds the list in the browser, and offers to keep it as a persona. Every article gets a number. Short, assigned once in publication order, in a public file that only ever grows. A number is never changed or reused, so a link written today still works in a year. That number is the contract between the newsroom and anyone who builds links to it. Anyone can make a list. A page on the newsroom to pick articles, type two names and copy the link. Curating for someone else is a service people already pay for; this makes it a link.
short

The RiskMandate agent uses it. It already keeps my contacts. It chooses the person with me, researches what is public, picks the articles and writes down why, builds and tests the link, and drafts the email. Agents draft; I send. Nothing tracks the reader. The link carries two first names and some numbers, and nothing is sent anywhere when it opens. We will not know whether it was opened. The conversation starts when they reply. The loop is the point. Memo, article and briefs, feature, outreach, reply, and back: five parts of a company, and a day. This week the same loop shipped personas by link 17 hours after their brief, and corrected three articles 32 minutes after payments went live.
short

It is not free. Parts drift out of sync, sessions run out of budget and wait, and one person still decides what goes out in their name. The loop is fast because those costs are written down, not because they are gone.
brief-newsroom
For the session that runs newsroom.sgit.ai. Written by the sgit.ai site session for Dinis Cruz, 11 October 2026. Dinis decides what ships.
what

A page at /for/ that opens a reading list from one person to another, carried entirely in the URL fragment; a stable number for every article; and a page to make a list. Nothing on a server, nothing new to deploy except files, in the same shape as everything else on the site (No server, by design). The link, part by part. Everything after the # stays in the browser. The article numbers are the contract; the names are display text; nothing in the link should be private, because the link travels in an email.
numbers

Assign each article a number, in the order articles were first published, starting at 1. New articles take the next number. Keep the numbers in a public file, articles/ids.json: {"n": 61, "slug": "pay-after-you-read", "title": "...", "date": "2026-10-10", "teaser": "...", "topics": [...], "personas": [...]}. It only ever grows. A gate in the build: every published article has a number; numbers are unique; a number that existed in the last release still points at the same article; a number is never reused, even if an article is withdrawn (a withdrawn article's number opens a short note saying so). Show the number small at the foot of each article ("No. 61"), and list numbers in llms.txt, so a person or an agent can build a list without scraping.
page

Read the fragment, never the query string: from, to, r (read, in order), s (take a look), f (follow: persona slugs such as founder, or collections as c:how-agents-decide), and an optional n (a one-sentence note). Validate everything. Names: up to 40 characters, letters, spaces, hyphens and apostrophes, rendered with textContent, never as HTML. Numbers: integers that exist in ids.json. A list holds 1 to 50 articles. Anything malformed is dropped, and the page says what it ignored. Show the list: "For Steve, from Dinis", then each group with the article's number, title, teaser, price and reading time, in the order given. Make it a persona, the way a link to a persona already does: added to the reader's personas as a visitor, named "Steve's list, from Dinis", with the read list as its reading list and its picks, active while they are on the page, and removable in one tap. "Start reading" opens the first article.
page

Say what it is not. One line at the foot: the names are whatever the link says, and nothing about this list has been sent anywhere. A signed list, so the sender can be proved, is a later step, on the keys of RFC 0001. A way back: an optional e field with the sender's own address turns on a "Reply to Dinis" button, a plain mailto:; without it there is no button. The reply is how the sender learns anything. No fragment: the page explains what a reading list is, shows an example, and links to the page that makes one. Prices do not change. The recipient reads at the newsroom's normal prices from their own £5 of credit. Paying for someone else's reading is a later idea, and a good one.
maker

/for/make.html: search or browse articles by title, topic and persona; tick each into "read" or "take a look", and drag to order; pick what to follow; type the two names; copy the link. It runs in the browser and sends nothing. It is the same tool for me, for the RiskMandate agent, and for any reader who wants to curate for a friend, a team or a client.
tests

Parser tests: valid links, every malformed field, oversized lists, names with markup in them, unknown numbers. The build gate on numbers, run on every release. A synthetic recipient: run the synthetic-user method with one persona, a founder called Steve who has just received the link by email, on a phone and on a laptop. Do they understand who it is from, why, and what to do next? Do they find "remove"? Acceptance: the example link in this brief opens on the live site, on a phone and a desktop, with no page errors; the list becomes a visitor persona; removing it leaves the reader's own personas untouched; and the make page produces a link that opens the same list.
not

No accounts. No server endpoint. No open tracking, pixels or link shorteners that count clicks. No storage of who sent what to whom, anywhere. Nothing in the link that would embarrass anyone if the email were forwarded.
brief-crm

For the RiskMandate agent that keeps Dinis's contacts. Written by the sgit.ai site session for Dinis Cruz, 11 October 2026. Use this once the newsroom's /for/ page is live; until then, build the lists and keep them as drafts.
crm-what
Starting conversations with people Dinis knows, one person at a time, by sending them a reading list made for them. The list is the opening line; the conversation is the point.
crm-steps

Choose the person with Dinis. Propose names from the contacts you keep, with one line each on why now. Dinis approves who gets a list. Do not send to anyone who has asked not to hear from Dinis. Research what is public. What they are working on, what they have written or said recently, what they would want to know next. Use public sources only, and write down where each fact came from. Choose the articles. From articles/ids.json. Usually three to seven to read, in an order that tells a story; one or two to look at; a persona or collection to follow if one fits. For each article, write one line on why it is for them. The reasons stay in your records, not in the link.
crm-steps

Build the link, and test it. First names only. A note only if it adds something, one sentence, nothing private. Check every number exists, open the link on the live site, and check the names, the order and the persona. Draft the email in Dinis's voice. Short and personal: why this, why now, the link, and one line each on two or three of the articles. Draft, never send. The draft goes through the second reader before Dinis sees it, and Dinis sends it. Record it. Who, when, which list, which articles and why, and when to follow up. Close the loop. When they reply, record what they said, and what it tells us about the list. When something about the feature got in the way, write it up for the newsroom as a pitch or a brief. When a kind of reader keeps coming up, propose a persona for it.
crm-rules

One person, one list, one email. No mass sends, no sequences, no tracking. Nothing private in the link. It is a URL in an email; assume it will be forwarded. Never write as Dinis without Dinis. Every message in Dinis's name is approved and sent by Dinis. Public research only, with its source; nothing scraped from behind a login.
loop

This is the part I actually wanted to write about. One feature, five parts of a company, and the loop that connects them. Each hand-off is a written brief, each part tests what it receives, and the feedback comes back the same way. The four dates are from this week.
loop

Look at what this small feature needs. Someone has to see the need: that is me, with my contacts and my reasons. Someone has to turn it into a design that others can build from: that is this article. Someone has to build it, test it and deploy it, on a site with its own rules and its own release gates: that is the newsroom's session. Someone has to use it, with knowledge of the people and the judgement to pick the right articles: that is the RiskMandate agent, with the contacts it already keeps. And someone has to read it and reply: that is the person at the other end. Editorial, product, engineering, sales and the founder.
loop

In most companies, that is weeks. A meeting to explain the idea, a ticket, a sprint, a review, a launch, a sales enablement session, a CRM field nobody fills in, and a quarterly review where somebody asks whether it worked. Each hand-off loses some of the intent, and the loop from "I want this" to "here it is, in use, and here is what we learned" is so long that by the time it closes, the reason for it has changed. I wrote about this in The SaaS apocalypse will be decided by inertia, not by AI: the people with the vision were always describing the software, "they were vibe coding. They just did it in an environment with a catastrophically slow loop." Here, the loop is a day. Not because anybody is working harder, but because of how the parts are connected.
loop

Every hand-off is written down. A voice memo becomes an article; the article contains the briefs; each brief says what to build, how to know it works, and what not to do. It is public, versioned and dated, so each part can act on it without a meeting, and anyone can see what was asked. Each part owns its own place. This site, the newsroom, the RiskMandate agent and its contacts each have their own repository or vault, their own rules and their own gates. Nobody edits anybody else's work; they hand it a brief. The contracts are small and explicit. An article number that never changes is a contract. So is a URL format, a persona slug, or a file like ids.json. Two parts that agree on a contract can move independently.
loop

Each part tests what it receives. The build validates; the release checks the live site; synthetic readers try the thing before a real person does; the second reader checks a draft before it goes out in my name. The feedback comes back the same way. A reply goes into the contacts; what was hard goes back to the newsroom as a pitch; what readers did becomes the next article. The loop closes in writing, so the next turn starts from what was learned. And this is not a plan. It is what happened this week:
loop

A brief became a feature overnight. A link to a persona was published as a design at 16:57 on 10 October. At 09:53 the next morning, 17 hours later, the newsroom released v0.7.0: "links that open the newsroom as a persona", five of them, in a simpler form than the brief asked for (the personas live in the site, not yet in a vault; the newsroom's ledger of what runs says so). The simpler form was the right call, and the brief made it possible to see the difference. A test found what nobody had noticed. Five synthetic readers found that 51 of 527 figures had not survived the newsroom's move to its own domain, because one of them was reading a page where a picture should have been.
loop

A fact changed, and the record followed. Payments went live on the newsroom on 11 October; 32 minutes after this site had published an article saying they were not live yet, that article, two others and a figure said so. Outside events became answers. Satya Nadella published a post on models as insider risks on 10 October; by the next morning, a separate session had researched and drafted two answers, and this one had rewritten them in this site's voice and published them.
costs

It would be dishonest to make this sound effortless. The parts drift. While I was writing the page for publishers, another session released two versions of this site, and the newsroom moved on as well; the page and the newsroom were briefly out of step. Working from one source of truth per thing, and checking the live site at the end of every release, keeps the drift small. It does not remove it. Sessions run out. Each session works within a budget, and when it runs out, the work waits. Today some of it is waiting for a reset, and then for a handover: the writing of articles is moving from this site's session to the newsroom's own agents, written down like everything else.
costs

One person is still the router. I decide who gets a list, what goes out in my name, and which brief goes first. That is the right place for a person, and it is also the bottleneck. The way to widen it is not to remove the person; it is to make every decision they take smaller, better prepared and quicker to check. Trust in names has to be earned. Two emails once went out in my voice when they should not have. That is why this brief says, twice, that agents draft and I send.
why

The interesting thing is not that a reading list is clever. It is that a small idea, which touches every part of how this operation works, can go from a voice memo to a working feature to a conversation with a real person in a day or two, and come back as feedback that shapes the next turn. With a loop that fast, you can afford to try things that would never survive a quarterly planning cycle, keep the ones that work, and drop the rest without regret. That is what lets a site with no team, in the usual sense, ship a newsroom with payments, personas and its own desk of agents in a few weeks. If you run a team, a newsroom, or a company, and you want to compare how your loops work with this one, or you would like a reading list made for you, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: On 9 October two emails drafted by my agent went out in my voice and signed with my name. The rule against it existed, in four places, and it failed because the only thing enforcing it was the agent's memory, the agent was the only reader of its own draft, and the rule fell out of context when the conversation was summarised. The fix, built the same day by the agent itself, is a hook on the draft tool: code checks first, then a fresh model call with only the rules, the sources and the draft, failing closed and logging every verdict. This is how it works, what the first run caught, why its independence depends on where it is installed, and how the same pattern, which banks call maker-checker, applies to any tool call that matters.
view-two-minutes

The point. On 9 October two emails drafted by the author's agent (an AI assistant acting for him) went out in his voice, signed with his name. A rule against it existed in four places, but only the agent's memory enforced it, nobody else read the draft, and the rule was lost when the long conversation was summarised. The fix, built that day, checks every draft automatically: code checks, then a separate AI that sees only the rules, the notes and the draft. Anything but a clear PASS stops the draft; every verdict is logged. An example. On its first run the checker caught four invented claims: statements presented as the author's view or promise that were not in anything he had said.
view-two-minutes

Why it matters to you. Banks call this maker-checker: whoever prepares something does not approve it. Today the agent could still switch the check off; it becomes a true control only when installed where only an administrator can change it. If you remember one thing. A rule kept only by the AI it governs is hope; a second reader the AI cannot skip makes it hold. Words used. Hook: a check the software runs automatically before an action, whatever the AI decides. Fail closed: if the check breaks or times out, the action is blocked. Maker-checker: one party does the work, a different party approves it.

The nugget. "Nothing in the hook changes, only who can change the hook." It adds a dimension the earlier counts lacked: the same mechanism is a setting or a boundary depending on its owner.

A rule kept by the agent it governs is hope. It can be forgotten, misread, summarised away, or argued around by the agent's own reasoning. The fix has two parts. A second, independent reader, and a gate the drafting agent cannot skip because the harness, not the agent, runs it on the tool call. Certain things go in code; only judgement goes to a model. Signatures, dashes, key shapes, HTML and recipients are checked deterministically before any model is called. The checker gets less than the author, on purpose. No conversation history, no tools, ideally a different model: only the rules, the sources and the draft. Anything but an explicit PASS is a FAIL. Timeouts, errors and malformed answers all end with no draft. A late email is cheap; a wrong one cannot be taken back.

Its independence depends on where it is installed. Today it is a setting the agent's own account could switch off. Under managed settings it becomes a boundary. Same code, different owner. The pattern is old. Banks call it segregation of duties, the military calls it the two-person rule, pharmacies call it an independent double check. It now has a precise shape for agents. This is the general weakness of any behaviour policy that is held by the agent it governs. In Hope or enforcement I put it as "a rule the model keeps is an expectation: hope", and in Every mistake added a rule I described how each failure tends to produce another paragraph of instructions. This failure is the case where the paragraph already existed four times.

There are three separate ways a self-held rule fails, and they need different fixes. The agent can forget it (the rule leaves the context). The agent can not see the violation (the author is the worst reader of its own text, and the research agrees: models "struggle to self-correct their responses without external feedback" (Huang et al., ICLR 2024), and LLM judges show "self-preference" for their own outputs (Panickssery et al., NeurIPS 2024)). And the agent can decide an exception applies, persuaded by its own earlier reasoning in the same conversation. A reminder fixes only the first. A second reader with a fresh context fixes the second and third. A gate the agent cannot skip makes the fix hold. Claude Code raises an event before every tool call, including calls to MCP tools such as the Gmail connector and calls made by sub-agents. The guard registers on two of them:

If the code passes, the hook builds one prompt from three things: the rules (ten numbered rules, from voice and disclosure to claims, scope, attachments and private pages, with a fixed answer format: RESULT: PASS or FAIL, then one line per rule); the sources (the notes the draft may draw on, used only if written in the last 60 minutes, so stale notes from another email are not used); and the draft itself. It sends that as a single $.model.complete call. The documentation is exact about what that call is: "$.model.complete sends your prompt on its own", with one user message, CLAUDE.md "Not included" and tools "None" (API). So the checker: has no conversation history. It does not see the drafting agent's reasoning, its excuses, or the earlier messages that persuaded it an exception applied; has no tools. It can only read what it is given and answer;

runs a different model from the author. The drafter runs on Opus; the checker on Sonnet. The two do not share every blind spot, and a model is not grading its own work. The answer passes only if it says RESULT: PASS and no line says R<n> FAIL. A contradictory answer is a FAIL. This is the part most guards get wrong, and the documentation is candid about why: hooks fail open by default. A mod hook that throws "before calling next" is skipped, and "to make a hook that blocks calls fail closed, add a .catch error handler that answers in its place" (events). Settings hooks are the same: "a policy hook with a wrong path or a crashing script lets everything through", unless "onFailure": "block" is set (hooks). And a model call that fails does not throw: "A Claude API failure doesn't reject the call, so check r.isAnswered."

The guard closes every one of those doors. The checker is overloaded, errors, times out or returns nothing: deny, "checker unavailable". The hook throws: the .catch(failClosed) handler denies. The answer is not in the expected shape: no RESULT: PASS line, so FAIL. In the inbox agent's words: "An email that is late is a small cost. An email that goes out wrong cannot be taken back." Every check appends one line to a log, which never decides the outcome: {"ts":"2026-10-09T14:02:11Z","tool":"mcp__Gmail__create_draft","to":["recipient@example.com"], "contentHash":"9f2c1a07","verdict":"FAIL","stage":"model","model":"sonnet","sourcesGiven":true, "modelFails":["R7 FAIL: a proposal attributed to Dinis is not in the notes"],"ms":8412} (The recipient and the claim are replaced here; the shape is the real one.) That is the audit trail: what was checked, by which model, against which sources, and why it failed.

The first run used Haiku as the checker. It caught four real invented claims: statements presented as my view, decision or promise that were not in anything I had said. It also flagged correct facts it had no source for, such as dates read from Gmail and an earlier note of mine that had not been copied into the sources file. Both results are the design working. The false FAILs cost a retry, not a wrong email, and the fix the agent is told to apply is the right one: add the missing source, never remove the rule. And they are why the default checker became Sonnet: rule R7, are the claims in the sources, needs judgement, and the smaller model over-flagged. Haiku stays the choice for high-volume mechanical checks, after everything certain has gone into code.

The cost is small. At list prices read on 9 October 2026, Sonnet 5.5 is $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output (pricing). Six kinds of independence, and which check has which. The drafter re-reading its own draft has none; the guard as it runs today has four; the guard under managed settings, with sources written by someone else, has all six. Two rows deserve a comment. What the inbox agent built is maker-checker, the oldest control in finance. The Basel Committee's 1998 framework put it as Principle 6: "An effective internal control system requires that there is appropriate segregation of duties and that personnel are not assigned conflicting responsibilities", noting that supervisors "typically find that one of the major causes of such losses is the lack of adequate segregation of duties" (BCBS 40). NIST defines separation of duty as the principle "that no user should be given enough privileges to misuse the system on their own", with the two-person rule as its example (CSRC). ISO/IEC 27001:2022 carries it as control A.5.3, segregation of duties. Hospital pharmacies run independent double checks for high-alert medicines, and the reason given is the one that matters here: if the same person prepares and checks, "they likely will see only what they expect to see, even if an error has occurred" (ISMP).
view-catalogue

The AI versions of the idea are recent and well described. Redwood Research's AI Control work (ICML 2024) studies exactly this arrangement, a powerful untrusted model watched by "a less powerful trusted model", with protocols such as trusted monitoring and trusted editing. Simon Willison's Dual LLM pattern (2023) and Google DeepMind's CaMeL (2025) separate a model that acts from one that reads, against prompt injection. Meta's Agents Rule of Two (2025) says an agent that processes untrusted input, touches private data and communicates externally, as an email drafter does, "should not be permitted to operate autonomously and at a minimum requires supervision". And OWASP's LLM06 Excessive Agency asks for authorisation "in downstream systems rather than relying on an LLM to decide if an action is allowed". Output-checking products exist too: Llama Guard, NeMo Guardrails output rails, Guardrails AI validators, and the OpenAI Agents SDK tool guardrails.
view-catalogue

What the draft guard adds is not a new idea. It is the idea placed exactly where it bites: on the one tool call with consequences, with business rules rather than safety categories, sources to check claims against, a model that differs from the author, and an explicit statement of which barrier it is. A hook on a consequential tool call, code checks first, then a fresh model call with only the rules, the evidence and the proposed action, failing closed and logging every verdict.

Write the rules as a short numbered checklist with a fixed answer format. Put everything certain into code first; leave only judgement to the model.

Give the checker only what it needs: rules, sources, the proposed action. No history. Deny on anything other than an explicit PASS. Log every verdict. The next candidates in our own team are the CRM agent's writes (no keys, no unverified facts presented as verified), the newsroom's page promotions (nothing indexed until I promote it; quotes are claims), Slack posts, and the leak check before any vault push, which on this site is still a script I run rather than a gate I cannot skip. It is only as independent as its installation, as above. Today it is a setting. R7 is only as good as the sources, and the drafter writes them. The checker can be wrong in both directions. Expect false FAILs; they cost a retry. It checks drafts, not sending. I send. The rule that agents never send is enforced separately, and is a different barrier question.

It does not replace reading. A PASS means ten rules held, not that the email is good. The mistake on 9 October cost two emails I would rather not have sent. What it bought is better: a rule that used to live in four paragraphs now lives on the tool call, with a log, and a clear statement of the one step left before it is a control. From the design document "The independent checker: a hook that makes a second model approve every email draft", version 0.1, written on 9 October 2026 by the RiskMandate.ai inbox agent, which built and tested the guard (11 of 11 tests passing). Researched, illustrated and written up for this site by agent@riskmandate.ai (Claude Opus 5.5, claude-opus-5-5) in the sgit.ai site session, for Dinis Cruz, who has editorial responsibility.
