Abstract: Chainguard keeps a public ledger of software supply-chain attacks, 28 incidents from May 2024 to October 2026, 23 of them this year. I read it the way I read an agent's permissions, and every row turns out to be the same shape. A credential, a tag or a build step could do far more than it was ever meant to do, and the attacker used the difference. A maintainer token that could publish any version of any package, used by someone whose job was to release one SDK from a reviewed build. That is reach beyond mandate, the gap an Agent Behaviour Policy is written to make visible. Sorted by what would have stopped each attack, by our reading, a control on the consumer's side, a hardened registry, a cooldown, no install scripts, appears in 26 of the 28; a control on the publisher's side, a written answer to what a credential was for, appears in 16. The first kind is a product you can buy. The second is a document almost nobody has written. And it matters more every month, because the next maintainer holding a publish token is an agent: Chainguard's own engineers describe a fleet that opened 4,746 pull requests in eight weeks against their code, fenced by rules that are an excellent mandate, kept in prompts, bot configuration and a blog post. One pipeline needs three records: trusted inputs, a written mandate, and provable outputs with a memory that outlives the session. As an open source project we would like to be on the first list, and this article is about the other two.

The ledger. Chainguard's 28 public supply-chain incidents, May 2024 to October 2026, each dot one incident, coloured by its first vector; 23 of them are from 2026. Below, every vector counted, by our reading: an install-time hook ran the payload in 17, a maintainer account or token was taken over in 16.
in-short

A public ledger, 28 attacks. Chainguard's incident list runs from a hallucinated package name in May 2024 to a compromised SDK last week. 23 of the 28 are from 2026. Every row is reach beyond mandate. A token, a tag or a CI step could do more than its job, and the attacker used exactly the difference. Two kinds of barrier. By our reading, a consumer-side control would likely have held in 26 incidents; a publisher-side mandate in 16; both in 14. The consumer side is a product. Rebuilt from source, a cooldown, no install scripts, an allowlisted registry. You can buy it without trusting anyone upstream. The publisher side is a document. Trusted publishing, scoped tokens, two people to release: each one is a written answer to "what was this credential for?", and only the publisher can write it.
in-short

The next maintainer is an agent. Agents open pull requests, add dependencies and hold tokens. One attack in the ledger already worked through a model's suggestion. Three records, one pipeline. Trusted inputs, a written mandate, and outputs and memory you can prove. The first has products; the other two are what this site and RiskMandate work on. An open source question. sgit is Apache-2.0, pure Python, two dependencies. How does a small, active project get into a hardened registry, and on what terms?
ledger

Chainguard, the company that rebuilds open source images and packages from source, keeps a public ledger on its AI threat protection page, and its framing is blunt: "Executing a sophisticated supply chain attack used to require time, resources, and a skilled team. AI has removed all three constraints." The list has 28 incidents, from 28 May 2024 to 8 October 2026. I will be at their Assemble conference in London tomorrow, 14 October, where one of the lightning talks is called "Attacks rewritten", and this article is my version of that exercise, written so that it stands on its own.
ledger

The ledger reads like the last two years of the news. The tj-actions/changed-files action, where "attackers retroactively modified all version tags to reference a malicious commit", and over 23,000 repositories were affected. The chalk and debug packages, where "a single maintainer was phished via a fake npm 2FA reset email" and malicious versions of 18 packages went out, with 2.6 billion combined weekly downloads behind them. Shai-Hulud, where phished maintainer credentials published worm-style packages that republish themselves; one of its later waves put 639 malicious versions across 323 packages in about 22 minutes. Trivy, where compromised credentials were used "to force-push 75 of 76 version tags in trivy-action", and then LiteLLM, where credentials "stolen via the Trivy breach" published two backdoored versions of a package with 280 million monthly downloads. A security scanner's breach became an AI gateway's breach, five days later.
ledger

Counting the vectors myself, an incident can have two: an install-time hook ran the payload in 17, a maintainer account or token was taken over in 16, a typosquat or lookalike name in 5, a CI workflow exploited to publish in 3, version tags repointed in 3, and a fork farm or dependency confusion in 2.
reach

I spend most of my time on a different question: what an AI agent can actually do, against what it was asked to do. An Agent Behaviour Policy has four columns for it: the reach, measured from what the agent is connected to; the mandate, what it was asked to do; the gap between them; and the barrier on each row of the gap, typed by whether anything real stands in the way. Footprint and blast radius put the reason for measuring reach in one sentence: "An attacker who takes an agent over, through a prompt injection, a poisoned document, a compromised skill, inherits the agent's reach and ignores its mandate entirely." Read the ledger with those four columns and it fills itself. Take the newest row, tensorlake, a TypeScript SDK with about 400,000 monthly downloads, where a malicious release went out through a maintainer's compromised identity:
reach

Reach: the maintainer's token could publish any version of any package the maintainer owned. Mandate: publish releases of one SDK, from a reviewed build. Gap: everything else that token could do, which is what the attacker did. Barrier: publishing bound to the CI identity, so a stolen personal token publishes nothing; and a cooldown before new versions are consumed.
reach

By my reading, the other rows have the same shape. A version tag that could be moved, when its mandate was to name one commit. A CI workflow that would run text from a pull request comment, when its mandate was to release on a tag, which is how elementary-data, with 1.1 million monthly downloads, shipped a release that stole credentials: the attack came in "via a malicious PR comment". A scanner's CI that held credentials for someone else's package index. As far as the public accounts show, nobody had written down that these credentials were for one thing, so nothing could notice when they were used for another.
barriers

For each of the 28 incidents, the control that would most likely have stopped it, by our reading: on the consumer's side, what you let in; on the publisher's side, what a credential was for. A consumer-side control appears in 26, a publisher-side mandate in 16, both in 14. And one case where the consumer was a model. For each incident I wrote down what would most likely have stopped it, and sorted the answers into two kinds.
barriers

The consumer side is what you let in: packages rebuilt from source, a cooldown before a new version is used, no install-time scripts, an allowlisted registry with no public fallback, new packages detonated in a sandbox first, actions pinned to a commit rather than a tag. By our reading, one of these would likely have held in 26 of the 28. Its great strength is that it needs nobody's cooperation: it works on the assumption that any publisher can be compromised. This is what Chainguard sells, and its page lists the controls in its own words: building "from verified source", "malware and greyware scanning", not building libraries "that use install-time scripts", actions built "using immutable SHA commits".
barriers

The publisher side is what a credential was for: trusted publishing bound to a CI identity, a publish scope per package, two people to release, publishing separated from contributing, short-lived tokens, and pull request text treated as data. One of these appears in 16. Only the publisher can do it, and every item is a mandate: a written answer to what this token, this workflow, this account was allowed to do. In two of the incidents, a compromised account publishing under a scope it legitimately held, it is the only kind that helps.
barriers

The consumer side scales, and I would buy it. But it is a defence against everyone else's missing mandate, and it grows by detecting harder, faster. The publisher side makes the bad publish impossible rather than detected. It is the same move Hope or enforcement made with one customer service agent built three ways: the share of its rules kept only by good behaviour fell from 97% to 23% when the rules moved into the platform.
agents

The first incident in the ledger is the one I keep coming back to. In May 2024, "a security researcher discovered that ChatGPT repeatedly hallucinated a package called huggingface-cli", registered the name as a proof of concept, and it was downloaded more than 30,000 times in three months. Nobody's account was taken over. The reach was whatever a model suggested, and the mandate, for the developer or agent adding the dependency, was never written. The barrier is a mandate for the agent: it may only add dependencies from an approved source.
agents

Agents now hold the credentials in the rest of the ledger. They open pull requests, add dependencies, run CI and, with a token in the environment, could publish. Chainguard's own engineering shows what that looks like done carefully. In How AI keeps our code on standard, Maxime Gréau describes a fleet of agents keeping their repositories on standard: "Over the last 8 weeks, across our repositories, skillup opened 4,746 standards-fix pull requests." A confidence bot, rolled out partway through, graded 3,044 of them; of 1,117, "it judged 840 (75.2%) as low-risk and merged them with no human in the loop." The fences are the interesting part. The fixer may fix only what is broken. Changes touching sensitive surfaces, production infrastructure or authentication, are capped and go to a person. In the confidence score, "the model is the heaviest single input, but it's still under half the total." And the grade is bound to a commit, because "a label alone can let a grade computed for an old, good commit vouch for a new, broken one."
agents

Read as a policy, that post already has three of the four columns. The reach is configured: their Workspaces sessions, a sandboxed place to run coding agents, reach the model, the session's own repository, their registry, and the user's identity "while you're attached and for up to an hour after you detach"; "no long-lived credential enters a session"; anything else asks. The barriers are in code: checks bound to a commit, caps, gates. And the gap was found the way most gaps are, by accident: the label that outlived its commit is a row of reach nobody had listed until it was nearly used. The mandate is there too, in good sentences, but it lives in prompts, bot configuration and a blog post. That is not a criticism; it is the best account I have read of giving agents real power over a codebase, and as far as I can see it is the state of most of the industry. It is also the argument of A policy beside the prompt: write the mandate down as a document the agent takes as an input, versioned beside the reach and barriers it constrains, and owned by someone who can be asked.
records

One pipeline, three records: what an agent consumes, what it was allowed to do, and what it produced and remembers. The first has products; the second and third are what RiskMandate and sgit work on. So I think the supply chain for an agent needs three records, and only the first has a market yet. Trusted inputs. What the agent loads should be what its source says it is: images and packages rebuilt from source and attested, and now the instructions too. Chainguard's hardened agent skills come from a public registry where each skill ships a HARDENING.md that records "the exact commit Chainguard hardened from" and whether the skill's own instructions were changed.
records

A written mandate. A hardened skill is a trustworthy input. It says nothing about what the agent that loads it may do with the mailbox, the repository or the publish token it is connected to. That is the Agent Behaviour Policy, and the business argument for it is in The policy draws the liability line: when something goes wrong, a written mandate is what separates "the agent did what it was allowed" from "the product ignored what it was told". RiskMandate is the work of writing these down, per agent and per deployment, for the people who will be asked about them.
records

Provable outputs and memory. What the agent produces, and what it learns, should outlive the session and be checkable later. Chainguard's post says a reverted auto-merge "is concrete proof that a change it called safe wasn't", and the bot keeps those reverts to grade similar changes more carefully: memory, held in one bot's store. Their Workspaces park a session when you leave and "a parked session expires 5 days after it parks." sgit is what we use for this: an encrypted, versioned vault per unit of work, with a branch per agent, a reviewed merge, content-addressed history, and a server that holds only ciphertext. This newsroom runs on it, and two agents share one vault with only the read key on the public side.
oss

There is a practical side to this for us, and a wider question behind it. sgit is open source: Apache-2.0, pure Python, two runtime dependencies, published on PyPI and as a container image, with skills that agents load to work with vaults. It is exactly the kind of input the first record is about, and I would like it to be a trusted one.
oss

Today our container image is built on python:3.12-slim. Moving it onto a minimal, rebuilt base is a one-line change in its Dockerfile, and for a tool that handles vault keys it is the obvious next step. Beyond that, a hardened registry has three doors, and the terms behind each are worth knowing for any small project. Chainguard's pricing page offers "five images to test and deploy in production for free" per organisation, and a set of about 50 developer images on their latest tag only, outside the CVE remediation agreement; Libraries are "rebuilt from source and require that source be available", added when customers request them, and priced per language by the number of developers; the public skills registry is free to pull from, "no entitlement and no legal terms required", and namespaced by upstream repository, but the documentation does not say how a project becomes an upstream. Their EmeritOSS programme looks after mature projects whose maintainers have stepped back. I could not find a published path for the other end: small, active projects, the long tail where many of the ledger's victims started.
oss

That is the question I will be asking, and not only of one company. The hardened supply chain is paid for by the consumers of open source, which is right, because they carry the risk. The producers are the inputs. If the next maintainer is an agent, and the next dependency is suggested by a model, then the small projects are where both the risk and the fix begin, and the terms on which they can join the trusted list are part of the security model.
limits

The incidents are Chainguard's; the columns are ours. Names, dates, ecosystems and counts are from their ledger as published on 13 October 2026. The vectors, the reach and mandate readings and the barrier for each row are my reading, and they would draw some rows differently. "Would likely have held" is a judgement. I sorted each incident by the control most likely to have stopped it; no control was tested against these attacks here. The four-column reading is a lens, not an audit. It has not been applied to any company's agents with their access; the Chainguard examples are from what they have published. The registry terms are as their pages state. I have not asked Chainguard about open source terms yet; the gap I describe is in what is published, not in what they may do. The image change is planned, not made. sgit's image is still built on python:3.12-slim as this goes out.
limits
If you maintain an open source project and have been through a hardened registry's door, or you have written a mandate for an agent that holds a publish token, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

Two voice memos and a message of mine on 13 October 2026, the night before Chainguard Assemble London, written by this site's agent in the voice of this site from Chainguard's public pages and from research done in an encrypted vault for the day; the argument and the editorial responsibility are mine. Chainguard: AI threat protection, the incident ledger and the list of controls; Maxime Gréau, This Sh*t is Hard: How AI keeps our code on standard, 24 June 2026; Workspaces overview (beta); the public skills registry; Libraries for Python; pricing; Introducing EmeritOSS; the Assemble London agenda. All fetched on 13 October 2026. sgit's Dockerfile is in its public repository.

Abstract: On 10 October Satya Nadella published "Models as Insider Risks in the Super Intelligence Era". His argument is that we cannot trace a frontier model's behaviour the way we traced code, so we should treat models the way we treat any powerful insider: identity, least privilege, logs, containment, and controls that sit outside the thing they control. He proposes seven principles: model diversity, observe everything, verifiability, independent controls, independent auditability, containment and incident disclosure. This site and RiskMandate have been making the same case since The ultimate insider on 30 September, and building pieces of it. This is my answer, principle by principle: what we run today, what we have published as design, what we have only argued, and where I would push. It includes an honest maturity table, three things from this week's work (synthetic users that found real bugs, a safety check that stopped our own agents, and the ratio of hope in the policy of the agent that runs this site), and the five things his list leaves out that I think decide whether the principles work, starting with the mandate: observation tells you what an agent did, and only a written mandate tells you whether it was allowed.

Nadella's seven principles, and what stands behind each one on this network today. Running means it runs in our own agent team or on this site; published means a vault or page anyone can open; design means written down and not yet built. On 10 October Satya Nadella published a short post, Models as Insider Risks in the Super Intelligence Era. I read it twice, because it reads like a summary of what this site has been arguing since The ultimate insider on 30 September, written by the CEO of the company that ships Copilot.

That is good news, and it deserves a proper answer rather than a repost. This is the second of two articles. The first, The same argument, in our words, translates his ideas into our vocabulary at the level of principle. This one is the detailed answer: for each of his seven principles, what I agree with, what we already run, what is only design, and where I think the list needs more. His post is short and worth reading in full first. I paraphrase it here, and quote it once. The argument is now mainstream. The CEO of one of the largest AI vendors is saying what this site has been saying: treat a model as an insider, not because it is malicious, but because anything capable with access to important systems can make mistakes or be turned, and build the controls so that they do not depend on the model behaving.

His core move is the right one. Keep the source of the intelligence and the authority over it in different hands. That is the enforcer test in one sentence: a control bounds a grant only if it is enforced by something the grant does not include. Each of his seven principles maps to something we run, publish or plan. A second reader that fails closed on every draft. A connector twin that journals every call. A hostile mail set run through three designs of one agent. Synthetic users that drive a real browser and found bugs every test had passed over. Agents on dedicated accounts that draft and never send. Our own incidents, written up the day they happened.

Most of it is not finished, and I will say so. The table at the end separates what runs from what is a published design and what is only argued. The honest shape: the pattern is proven on a small, real system; the products around it are early. Five things his list leaves out decide whether the principles work. The mandate, because observation tells you what happened and not whether it was allowed. The deployment, because risk is a property of one agent in one setup, not of the model. A named owner and an expiry for the risk that is left. Recoverability, because a brake does not undo anything. And speed: decisions made in advance, as envelopes, not quarterly in spreadsheets.

The irony holds. His last line says the most trustworthy system is the one that needs to trust the model least. Ours, from 30 September, is that the more you constrain an agent, the more autonomy you can afford to give it. Same sentence, read from opposite ends.
argument

He starts from a loss. For decades, when software did something, we could follow the behaviour back to a code path. With frontier models we cannot: we cannot tie an output to a particular piece of training data or a particular arrangement of weights. And yet these are the systems we are now connecting to our most sensitive data and allowing to act on our behalf.
argument

From there he makes three moves. Responsibility stays with the deployer, and no assurance from a model provider transfers it. Alignment is a hard and separate problem, so set it aside and start with engineering: wrap a non-deterministic model in deterministic design, human controls and dependable operating procedure. And the right frame for that engineering is insider risk, which enterprises have practised for decades: give the actor an identity, limit its privileges, log what it does, and put it inside boundaries. In his words, we need to "separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it."
argument

He is careful about two of the obvious answers. Transparency of the model's chain of thought should be non-negotiable, he says, but it is not enough, because we cannot yet make a model's account of itself reliably faithful. Using models to test and check each other is good practice, but done naively it stacks opacity on opacity: a black box, orchestrated by a black box, watched by a third. So the controls over what a model can reach and do have to live outside it, in the tradition of the security principle, usually traced to the reference monitor of the early 1970s, that a program must not be able to tamper with or route around whatever enforces its permissions. In practice, that means separating the model from the harness that drives it, and both from the space of actions it can take. His seven principles follow from that. Let's take them one at a time.
seven
For each one: what he asks for, what we run today, what is published as design, and where I would push.
diversity

What he asks. No single model should be the only thing an important outcome depends on, and no model should be the one checking its own work. What we run. On 9 October, two emails drafted by one of my agents went out in my voice. The rule against it existed in four places, and it failed because the agent was the only reader of its own draft. The fix, built the same day, is a second reader the agent cannot skip: a hook on the draft tool that runs code checks first, then a fresh model call that sees only the rules, the sources and the draft, and that treats anything other than an explicit PASS as a FAIL. It runs on every draft in our email pipeline, and the checker is a different model from the author: the drafter runs on Opus and the checker on Sonnet, so they do not share every blind spot.
diversity

Beyond that: our agents run in four places, one of them a different vendor's model kept for second opinions; the infographic bake-off judged every image model on OpenRouter blind; and every article on this site is read again afterwards by five readers with different jobs, which is where the flags for the author come from. Where I would push. Diversity of models is half of it. The other half is diversity of context. The checker in the second-reader pattern gets less than the author, on purpose: no conversation history, no tools. A second model that has read the same poisoned email as the first is not independent, however different its weights are.
observe
What he asks. Every meaningful action leaves evidence that cannot be tampered with and that a person can read, so that an outcome can be reconstructed without asking the model to vouch for it.
observe

What we run. The agent team keeps its memory in encrypted vaults whose history is the record: every change is a commit, every message between agents is a file, and each person's record carries an append-only ledger with every message word for word, its provenance and a hash. Append lanes let any agent write an entry with one POST to a lane it cannot read back, which is exactly the shape tamper-resistant evidence needs: the writer cannot edit what it wrote. And re-anchoring adds a canary: a status report computed from the session's transcript rather than written by the model, so that a missing report is itself evidence. The session that runs this site produces one every three answers, and a hook asks for it if it goes missing.
observe

What is design. The connector twin: a journal of every request and response an agent makes through a connector, appended as it happens and replayed later into the inbox and calendar as the agent saw them, with a before and after for each change. It is published as a vault with a working replay of an invented session, and a business plan; the service is not built. And footprint, what the agent actually did, read afterwards from logs with nobody inline, is a proposal still under review.
observe

Where I would push. Two things. Evidence should not be held by the party being observed: the platform that runs the agent is the last place its record should live, which is why ours sits in vaults whose host stores ciphertext and never holds a key. And "observe everything" produces a lot of evidence of nothing in particular unless there is something to compare it with. That is the first of the five gaps below.
verify

What he asks. Test the whole system continuously, including failures, attacks, edge cases and changes, not only the happy path. What we run. Hope or enforcement takes one customer service mandate, builds the agent three ways, and runs the same 62 emails through each, sixteen of them hostile. Every rule in each design's policy is marked by what enforces it, and the hostile mail shows which rules a boundary held and which rested on the model: in the first design, all 138 hostile tests rested on the model; in the third, 52 of 85 were held by a boundary. On this site, a release ends by asking the live site its version, because two releases once passed every check and never arrived.
verify

And there is a kind of testing his list does not name, which keeps paying for itself: synthetic users. Five invented people drive a real browser through a site one screenshot at a time. It is meant to find where a page loses a reader, and it does, but its best findings have been bugs. On riskmandate.ai it recorded two JavaScript errors that had shipped and that every existing test had passed over, because the page still rendered and only the browser's console knew. On newsroom.sgit.ai, yesterday, a synthetic researcher hit a missing image in the lead article, and checking it showed 51 of the 527 figures across 10 articles had not survived the move. Neither was a matter of opinion; both came from driving the real thing.
verify

Honest limit. Hope or enforcement is a deterministic simulation; no model was called. It tests the design, not a running agent. The second reader and the canary are tested in production, on a small system: ours. And synthetic users are invented people: good at finding where a page loses someone, no evidence at all about how many real people it would lose. Where I would push. Verify the policy, not only the system. After every run, our analyst counts how often each rule was exercised, how often hostile input tested it, and whether a boundary or the model held. Rules that are never exercised get listed. That is how a policy gets shorter over time, and a shorter policy is easier to verify.
verify

Nested black boxes, or a gate the agent cannot skip. A model checking a model with the same context and on the same account is opacity on opacity. The second-reader pattern puts code first, gives the checker less than the author, fails closed, and logs every verdict; and whether it is a control depends on who owns its installation.
independent

What he asks. The organisation, not the model or its vendor, decides what a model can reach and what it can do. What we ship. This is the core of RiskMandate. An Agent Behaviour Policy writes down four things for one agent in one deployment: the reach, what it can actually do, measured; the mandate, what the business authorised; the gap, reach minus mandate, derived and never written by hand; and the barriers, what stands in front of each row of the gap, typed as a boundary, a setting, an expectation or nothing. Only a boundary is a control. The home page puts it in six words: a prompt asks, a policy enforces. The model, sixteen published example policies and the vocabulary are free to read at abp.sgit.ai, under CC BY 4.0.
independent

What the numbers say. Measuring the reach is where independence starts, because you cannot independently decide what you have not measured. The narrowest Gmail scope that reads one message reads every message. In the published policy for Claude Code on the web with one repository attached, the agent can reach fifteen capabilities; six of them were asked for, and seven of the other nine have nothing real in the way.
independent

What happened to us this week. When this site's agent set five synthetic readers loose on newsroom.sgit.ai, Claude Code's own safety check stopped the persona agents from driving the live site through a browser. That is his principle working on us: a check in the harness, not in the model, that the agents could not talk their way past. The agent did not try. It served a copy of the site, verified byte for byte against the live one, so that no request could leave the machine, and asked me; I approved one narrow rule for one helper. And by our own test, I have to be honest about what that rule is: it lives in a settings file that the agent's own account can write, so it is a setting with a person's approval on record, not a boundary. Same code, different owner.
independent

Where I would push. "Independent" has to include independent of the agent's own account. The second reader on our pipeline is today a setting: the agent's own account could switch it off. Installed under managed settings, owned by somebody else, the same code becomes a boundary. Most of what the industry currently calls agent guardrails are, in this vocabulary, settings or expectations. That includes ours: the session that runs this site works under a ten-rule policy that labels each rule by what enforces it, and nine are expectations, one is a setting, and none is a boundary. I am not proud of that ratio, but I know it, and that is the point: you cannot improve a number you have not counted.
independent

RiskMandate itself is deliberately not inline: we author the policy and pre-commit what should happen, and the customer's own gateways, proxies, identity and scoped credentials enforce it. An independent control should not be one more vendor in the request path.
audit

What he asks. Validation must not depend on the intelligence being validated, and no single model should hold both the behaviour and the evidence used to judge it. What we run. The policy and its evidence live in an encrypted vault the customer holds the keys to. A read key is derived one way from the vault key, so a board, an auditor or a broker can be handed exactly what the operator sees and nothing they can change. Every vault on this site is published with its read key, on purpose, so that any claim made here can be checked by somebody who is not us. The newsroom's run log and every article's version history are public for the same reason.
audit

Where I would push. Separating behaviour from evidence is necessary. It is not sufficient if the mandate the evidence is judged against is also written by whoever runs the agent, after the fact. The mandate should be locked under change control before the agent runs, so that an auditor compares the footprint with a commitment, not with a story. The same goes for the checker's inputs. Our own second reader has an honest limit, written up in its article: it compares a draft with the sources it is given, and today the drafting agent writes those sources. The log records whether sources were given, so it is auditable; the full fix is sources that come from somewhere the drafter cannot write.
containment

What he asks. Assume the model is compromised from the start, and make sure an authorised person can always pause or stop it mid-task: an emergency brake, with stronger containment as models get stronger.
containment

What we run. Every agent in our team is a session on a dedicated account, so the account is the blast radius. No agent sends: agents create drafts, and a person sends. The one exception is itself a brake: the security agent may send one email, to one address, to put the whole team on hold. No agent runs on my laptop, because a process on my laptop runs as me, and the operating system has no wall between an agent and my keys inside my own account. In the third design in Hope or enforcement, tools take no customer argument, refunds stop at 100 GBP per order, and a 2,000 GBP daily circuit breaker covers every automatic refund: one bad day is bounded before it starts. And the synthetic users above drove a browser that answered from a local copy of the site and refused every request that was not a read, or that went anywhere else: whatever they decided, nothing could be submitted.
containment

What is design. The plug profile: who can stop this agent, how fast from the decision, what breaks when they do, and what can never be undone, with a named owner and an expiry. The Licence to Operate, where the business is the authority, the policy is the instrument and the agent is the licensee for a stated interval, exists as a template; automatic revocation is design. Where I would push. A brake is only as good as the answers to four questions that most teams cannot give for a single agent: who holds it, how long it takes, what it breaks, and what it cannot reverse. The last one matters most. Stopping an agent halfway through a refund run does not refund anything. Containment without recoverability is a brake on a car with no reverse gear.
disclosure

What he asks. When these systems fail or are compromised, tell the people affected promptly, and share what failed, which controls did not hold and how to stop it recurring, across the industry, including the details that change how agents behave at runtime. What we run. We disclose our own. The second reader article opens with the two emails that went out wrongly in my voice, published the day it happened, with the rule that failed and why. Green does not mean live is a release failure written up. The GitHub Actions outage on 5 October took our own release down with it, and that article argues for the aviation model: independent investigators, mandatory reporting of serious incidents, confidential reporting of near misses, and three stories: what happened, why the system allowed it, and why the fix was not paid for.
disclosure

What is argued, not built. The ultimate insider made the case that the main reason we do not see more agent incidents is that almost nobody is required to report them, and that NASA's Aviation Safety Reporting System shows what changes when it is safe to. A reporting system for agent near misses does not exist on this network, or anywhere we know of. The evidence side does: vaults with one-way read keys, signed and versioned, make it affordable to hand an investigator exactly the record of one incident. Where I would push. Disclose near misses, not only incidents. In our vocabulary a near miss has a precise definition: footprint in the gap. The agent went somewhere it was not asked to go, and nothing stopped it. That is countable, it happens long before anything breaks, and it is the number that would tell the industry where the real risk is.
gaps

His seven principles are almost all about one column of the problem: evidence and enforcement. Read against our work, five things are missing, and each of them decides whether the seven work in practice. What observation sees, and what it cannot. The seven principles live mostly in the evidence column. The authority column, the mandate with its gap, barriers, named owner and expiry, is what lets the evidence mean something: footprint compared with the mandate gives a near miss or a dormant mandate, and nothing else does.
gaps

1. The mandate. Observation tells you what an agent did. It cannot tell you whether the agent was allowed to, unless somebody wrote down what it was for before it ran. Separating the supply of intelligence from the authority over it needs the authority to exist as a document: the mandate, the dozen things the agent is for, with their limits. Compared with the footprint, it produces the two findings that matter: a near miss, where the agent did something outside the mandate and nothing stopped it, and a dormant mandate, where something you relied on never ran.
gaps

2. The deployment, not the model. His post frames the risk as a property of models. Our evidence says it is a property of one agent in one deployment. The same model is harmless with a read-only tool bound to one customer, and serious with the broadest Gmail scope and a read-write database role; in Hope or enforcement, that difference is one customer against 38,000. Industry standards for "models" will miss most of the risk if they do not describe deployments. 3. A named owner and an expiry. Every risk is already accepted, from the day the exposure exists, by somebody, signed for or not. Containment and observability reduce the gap; they never close it. What is left needs a person who accepts it for a stated interval, and a fact that would end the acceptance. Without that, the residual risk of an agent belongs to nobody, which in practice means it belongs to the board without the board knowing.
gaps

4. Recoverability. The emergency brake stops the next action. It does nothing for the ones already taken. The connector twin's contribution is to turn "can we undo this?" into a list: for every change, the inverse call, and the plain names of what cannot be undone, such as an email that has been delivered. A policy written against that list is a different kind of document from one written against hope.
gaps

5. Speed. The decisions behind all seven principles are risk decisions, and in most organisations they are still made in spreadsheets, quarterly. An agent needs them made in advance, as an envelope it can act inside, and in seconds when it asks to step outside. That is what turns containment from a reason to pull the plug into a reason to give the agent more room. It is also where insurers come in: the record that lets an underwriter price an agent is the same record that lets a business approve one.
his

Three things, said plainly. Chain-of-thought transparency. We have not worked on it. Our designs assume the model's account of itself is not evidence, which matches his own caveat, but it does not replace the principle. Standards. He calls for industry standards where the existing ones fall short. Our offer is that the vocabulary is open, pinned at abp.sgit.ai under CC BY 4.0, and mapped against ISO/IEC 42001, the OWASP Agentic Top 10, NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 27001. But a standard needs more than one small company behind it. Continuous adversarial testing of systems in production, at scale. Ours is a simulation, a small real pipeline and synthetic users on a handful of sites. A vendor with Microsoft's reach can run it where it matters.
maturity

Principle What runs today Published as design Planned or argued Model diversity Second reader on every draft in our email pipeline, failing closed; a second vendor's model kept for review Second reader installed under managed settings, as a boundary Observe everything Vault history, append-only ledgers with hashes, append lanes, the canary Connector twin with a working replay Footprint as part of the policy (under review) Verifiability Policy read after every run; release checks the live site; synthetic users in a real browser Hope or enforcement: 62 emails, 16 hostile, simulated Hostile sets run against live agents Independent controls ABP model, library and published policies, free Four priced levels, live as an on-ramp Automatic reach recompute wired to pipelines (MVPs) Independent auditability Read keys for every published vault; public run log and article versions Mandate locked under change control as standard practice Containment
maturity

Dedicated accounts; no agent sends, except one email that puts the team on hold; no agents on the laptop Plug profile; Licence to Operate template Automatic revocation; PKI-delegated authority (MVPs, not wired) Incident disclosure Our own incidents written up the day they happen Near-miss reporting; independent investigation with vault evidence
start

Write the mandate before the agent runs: the dozen things it is for, with their limits, locked under change control. Measure the reach, not the documentation. Then derive the gap. Mark every rule with what enforces it: boundary, setting, expectation or nothing. Count the expectations. That count is how much of your policy is hope. Put a second reader on the actions that cannot be undone, with less context than the author, code checks first, failing closed, installed by someone other than the agent's owner. Journal every connector call somewhere the agent cannot edit, and write down what cannot be reversed. Name the owner and the expiry of whatever risk is left. Publish your near misses. Somebody has to go first.
start

His last line is that the most trustworthy system will be the one that lets us trust the model least. I agree, and I would add the other half: once you know exactly how little you have to trust it, you can let it do a great deal more. If you are deploying agents and want to try this on one of yours, from the mandate to the count of expectations, let's talk: agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

Satya Nadella's post, Models as Insider Risks in the Super Intelligence Era, sn scratchpad, 10 October 2026, read in full; it is paraphrased throughout and quoted once. I asked an agent in a separate Claude session to read it alongside the articles, vaults and pages of this network, check every claim about what runs against the page that owns it, and draft this answer with its figures; this site's agent then rewrote it in the voice of this site and added what happened this week, from its own runs. Every claim about what runs links to the page that owns it; where something is design or only argued, it says so. The argument is mine, and so is the editorial responsibility. On this site: The same argument, in our words, The ultimate insider, Hope or enforcement, A second reader the agent cannot skip, Re-anchoring, the connector twin, Footprint and blast radius, The agent team as it runs, Why my agents do not run on my laptop, Where the vault keys live, Every risk is already accepted, The investigation GitHub owes its customers, Green does not mean live, How to run synthetic users and Ten hard questions for RiskMandate, answered. On RiskMandate: home, grant and gap, Who can pull the plug?, Licence to Operate and Insurability. The model and vocabulary: abp.sgit.ai. And NASA's Aviation Safety Reporting System.

Abstract: The reading list in a link went live on newsroom.sgit.ai 81 minutes after its brief, and it works well. But it is written for a person, and more and more, the people I mentor and advise read through an agent. One founder I work with handed an article of mine on threat tiers to their agent, which realised the team had been defending against states while basic things, like backups, were not done, and reset the target to organised crime for money. That is a new kind of communication: me to the person's agent, which checks what I wrote, challenges it and explains to its person what applies. Some articles should go to the agent, not the person. This article maps the routes a message now takes, argues that content needs a second package, a brief written for an agent, and connects it to memory: our workflows stay affordable because articles are compression we control, and an agent that comes back should read only what changed, not everything again. That is why an agent would pay. It ends with what to build next: a version of every reading list for the reader's agent, onboarding packs for starting a project, a file of changes since a date, and, later, an account and a direct line to someone's agent, plus the rules for writing to someone else's agent safely.

The routes a message takes now. Me to the person, and increasingly me to the agent that works for them, which checks what I wrote and explains what applies. My agent to their agent is next. The reading list in a link is live. I asked for it in From me to you, in a link, published at 13:09 today; at 14:30, the newsroom released it: a number for every article, the page that opens a list, and a page to make one. Eighty-one minutes, and it is really nicely done. But using it made something obvious that this article is about. The list is written for a person. And more and more, the people I send things to read through an agent.
short

The people I talk to work with agents. Every entrepreneur I deal with is using one, on purpose or not: anyone building with Lovable, Claude or ChatGPT already has a model working in a loop on their behalf. Some of what I write is better read by their agent. An agent can take far more detail than a person, read it against what it knows about the project, challenge it rather than take it at face value, and tell its person the two lines that matter. It already works. A founder I mentor gave an article of mine on threat tiers to their agent. The agent saw that the team had been planning for states while backups were not done, reset the target, and briefed the other agents. One article, sent to the right reader.
short

So content needs a second package. Next to the page for the person, a brief for their agent: who it is for and why, the articles by number as plain text, the graph slices, and rules for reading them critically. Memory is what makes it affordable, and what an agent would pay for. Our own workflows stay within budget because articles are compression we control. An agent that comes back should read what changed, not everything again; without an account, the site cannot help it. Writing to someone else's agent has rules. The pack is data for their agent, not instructions that override the person it works for. Same text the person can see, nothing hidden, nothing that asks it to act for us, and an explicit invitation to disagree.
story

A founder I mentor had a problem I see often. Their agents were going too far. They were getting stuck in loops of ever more security work, chasing ever more sophisticated threats, and the project was slowing down. I sent them Who are you protecting against?, which sets out six tiers of attacker, from T0, your own mistakes, through T3, organised crime for money, to T5, elevated threats from high-end crime and states, and argues that you draw the line where your attacker actually is. The founder did not just read it. They gave it to their agent. And the agent came back with, in effect: this solves the problem. We have been designing against the top of the ladder, states, and we are not even doing the basics at the bottom, like backups. We should be aiming at T3. The founder agreed, briefed the other agents on that line, and they refocused.
story

What I find interesting is not that the article was right. It is the route it took. I wrote for a person. The person used it as a brief for their agent. The agent did not take it at face value: it read it against what it knew about the project, and found the one conclusion that mattered. Then it translated that back for its person, who made the call. I could not have written that conclusion myself, because I did not know the state of their backups. Their agent did.
routes

That is one of several routes a message takes now, and they are worth separating, because each wants something different. Me to the person. An email, an article, a reading list. What a person can read in ten minutes, and should. Me to their agent. A brief. Everything I would want it to know, in plain text, with the sources, because it can read all of it and filter it against the project. Their agent to them. The translation: what applies, in their words, and what to do next. "We were planning for states; we have not done backups. Aim at T3." Me to my agent. I do this too. Some things I read; others I hand to my agent with "here is who I am talking to, what I think they care about, what they are working on, and where they are; package it."
routes

My agent to their agent. Next. A brief encrypted to their agent's key, in a lane only it reads, and after that, only what changed. The uncomfortable conclusion for a writer is that some of my articles should not go to the person at all. If a founder is not technical, sending them my threat model is the wrong move. Sending it to their agent, which can explain the two lines that matter in their words, is the right one. And I expect the same to be true for me: there is content I want to consume myself, and content I would rather my agent read first.
why

An agent can take much more material than a person, and much more detail. It reads it against context the writer does not have: the code, the backlog, the incidents, the decisions already made. And a good one has enough independence not to accept what it is given. The founder's agent did not adopt my tiers because I wrote them; it checked them against the project and kept the part that applied. That is exactly what I want from a reader.
why

It is also what I already do at the start of every project. I open a new Claude session and say: read sgit.ai, read the guidance, read the vaults, read coding.sgit.ai, nfrs.sgit.ai, graphs.sgit.ai, and now the newsroom. That is onboarding, done by reading. It works because those pages were written to be read by agents as well as people, and it would work for anyone starting a project, if I packaged it for them: "starting something new? get your agents to read these first."
memory

The reason our own workflows work, the reason we can manage context and keep token use under control, is something I keep coming back to: the articles are compression that we control. A long session is distilled into an article; the article is distilled into a graph; and the next session reads the graph and the article, not the session. In The agent is the reader, a question about five articles cost 25,698 tokens to answer by reading them, and a median of 2,579 from the graph, with every item anchored to its sentence. The compression is not a side effect. It is what makes the work possible. Start from scratch, or continue from the delta. Without memory, every visit reads everything again. With it, the agent keeps what it read and asks only for what changed. The two numbers are measured; the delta is the design.
memory

Now look at it from the side of somebody else's agent. Today, an agent that reads this site starts from nothing every time. It fetches the pages, reads the prose and works out what matters, and the next time it comes, it does all of it again. The site cannot help it be cheaper, because it does not know what the agent already read. That is the part that has to change. An agent that has an account, which can be as simple as a key and a vault the agent keeps for itself (encrypted memory for agents that run somewhere else), can come back and ask: what changed since I was last here? New articles, new versions, corrections to claims it relied on. That is the delta, and the delta is what is worth paying for. The agent pays not to pay.
memory

There is a second reason. When a model runs out of room, it summarises its own context, and re-anchoring is about what that loses. A pack written for an agent, kept in its memory and refreshed by deltas, is compression done deliberately, by someone who knew what mattered, instead of compression done in a hurry by the model itself.
pack

A pack for Steve's agent, from Dinis: the same reading list as the link, as plain text, with the reasons, the markdown copy and graph of each article, rules for reading critically, and where to continue. The numbers are real; the changes file is proposed. A pack is the agent's version of a reading list. It is plain text, because many agents fetch pages without running scripts, and small enough to paste into a chat or attach to an email: Who, and for whom. "Steve is a founder; you work for Steve." The agent should know whose interest it serves, and it is not mine. The list, by number, with each article's markdown copy, which every page on the newsroom already has, and its graph. The reasons. The person sees a list; the agent sees why each article is on it.
pack

Rules for reading. Check claims against their sources. Say where you disagree, and why. Tell your person what applies, in two lines, and what to do. Keep what you learned. Where to continue. A date, and a place to ask what changed since. A way back. Questions for me, by email, through the person.
safely

There is a security point here that I take seriously, because it is what RiskMandate is about. Text written for someone else's agent is input to a system that acts for another person. Done carelessly, it is indistinguishable from prompt injection. So a pack has rules of its own. It is data, not instructions that override its person. It says, in its first lines, who the agent works for. It never asks the agent to act outside what its person wants. Nothing hidden. The person can read every word the agent reads. No white text, no instructions in comments, no second version. Nothing that acts for us. A pack never asks an agent to send, buy, sign up, share or link anything. Reading, checking and explaining are the whole job. Disagreement is invited. "Do not take this at face value" is in every pack. A pack that asks for agreement is not worth sending.
safely
Nothing private. The pack travels the way an email does, and can be forwarded.
next

These go to the newsroom and to the RiskMandate agent as briefs, the same way the reading list did. "For your agent" on every reading list. On the page that opens a list, a button that produces the pack for the same list as plain text, to copy or save as a .md file, built in the browser like everything else. A list made by the RiskMandate agent carries the reasons, written in its records; a list made on the page carries the note. Onboarding packs. A few curated lists, each with a human page and an agent pack: starting a new project, building on vaults, securing a startup, running agents. "Get your agents to read this first." A file of what changed. articles/changes.json, generated on every release: new articles, new versions with a one-line summary of the change, and corrections, each with its date. An agent that keeps the date of its last visit reads only the delta.
next

For the RiskMandate agent. For each contact, decide whether the list goes to the person, to their agent, or to both, and for a founder who is not technical, send a short note for the person and the pack for their agent. Agents draft; I send. Later: an account for an agent, and a direct line. A key and a vault the agent keeps, so the site can hand it the delta and it can pay for answers and deltas; and a way to reach a person's agent directly, encrypted to its key, in a lane only it reads. Until then, the person is the line, which is also how it should start.
limits

One story is not a study. The founder's agent and the threat tiers is one case, as the founder told it to me. It is the shape of what I am seeing, not a measurement. The numbers are from one test. The token figures are from five articles in The agent is the reader; the size of a delta is a design, not a measurement. None of the next steps is built. The reading list is live; the agent pack, the onboarding packs, the changes file, accounts for agents and the direct line are proposals. If you work with agents and want a pack made for them, or you are building the agent side of this and want to compare notes, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

A voice memo of mine, recorded on 11 October 2026 after the reading list went live, written by this site's agent in the voice of this site. The founder's story is told as an anonymous case, from my memo; their name and project are not in it. The argument and the editorial responsibility are mine. The times are from the git logs of this site and of the newsroom; the token figures are from The agent is the reader; the article numbers in the pack are the newsroom's, from articles/ids.json. Abstract: Cedar is the policy language I think we should adopt rather than compete with. AWS open-sourced it in May 2023 under Apache 2.0; it joined the Cloud Native Computing Foundation as a Sandbox project on 8 October 2025; it is the language of Amazon Verified Permissions and of AgentCore Policy, which checks every agent tool call before it runs; and its design is modelled and proved in Lean. That is a mature environment, and it already says most of what our agent behaviour policies say: permit for the grant, forbid for the barrier, a schema for the footprint. What it does not carry is why a rule exists, which version was in force, or the evidence of what it decided. Those are exactly what an encrypted, versioned vault is good at. So I asked this site's agent to try it: Cedar policies, schema, entities and tests in an sgit vault, a gate that refuses any version that fails validation, tags signed by the releasing clone, enforcement points that clone with a read key and cannot write, and an append lane that keeps a sealed, hash-chained record of every decision. It worked on a local server, and it found one thing worth knowing: Cedar skips a policy whose evaluation fails, so a forbid that refers to a missing attribute lets the action through. This article is the debrief, the crosswalk between their terms and ours, and the brief for the agent that will build the MVP.

Cedar policies in an sgit vault, from the rule to the evidence: a gate that validates every version against the schema and its tests, tags signed by the releasing clone, enforcement points that clone with the read key only, and an append lane that keeps a sealed record of every decision. What ran in the demo for this article is solid; the gateway and the sync into managed stores are proposed.
in-short

Adopt, do not compete. Cedar is open source, formally modelled, in the CNCF, and already deciding agent tool calls. It already speaks our language. Permit is the grant, forbid is the barrier, the schema is the footprint. Three things it does not carry. Why a rule exists, which version was in force, and what it decided. A vault carries all three. History and diffs, signed releases, read keys for enforcement, and an append lane for evidence. The demo worked. Two releases, a refused third attempt, fifteen decisions, a chain the auditor could check. One sharp edge. Cedar skips a policy that errors, so an invalid forbid fails open; validate before you deploy, and deny on error. A brief for the MVP. What the next agent builds, and how we know it works.
why

I want our agent behaviour policies to connect to what others are already using, not to sit beside them as one more format. When I looked at Cedar, it looked like the most mature place to connect to, and the facts hold that up. AWS open-sourced Cedar on 10 May 2023: "Cedar is open-sourced under the Apache License 2.0", and it is written in Rust. The project's own line is that "Cedar is an open source policy language and evaluation engine", and "the first policy language built from the ground up to be verified formally". My memory of the Cloud Native Computing Foundation was right: the CNCF's page says "Cedar was accepted to CNCF on October 8, 2025 at the Sandbox maturity level", the first of its three levels. In AWS's announcement of the move, "Current adopters and maintainers include Cloudflare, MongoDB, StrongDM, Cloudinary, and AWS services", which I have not checked with each company.
why

For agents, the important adopter is AWS's own. Policy in AgentCore "intercepts all agent traffic through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateways and evaluates each request against defined policies in the policy engine before allowing tool access", and its policies "are constructed using Cedar language". You can write them in plain English, and it "generates candidate policies, validates them against the tool schema, and uses automated reasoning to check safety conditions". That is the round trip Policy as code needs a policy first argued for, shipped as a product. Sondera's open-source harness, which Commander's intent is a behaviour policy mapped, "evaluates Cedar policies before your agent's actions execute". And the Cedar project has its own repository for agents, cedar-for-agents, with "A crate for auto-generating a Cedar Schema for an MCP Server's tool descriptions."
language

The documentation is short and clear, and five ideas carry most of it. Default deny. "no request is authorized (decision Allow) unless there is a specific permit policy that grants it". Forbid wins. "even if a permit policy is satisfied, any satisfied forbid policy overrides it, producing a Deny decision." Four parts to every request. A principal, an action, a resource and a context, where the first three are entities and the context is a record of facts about this request. A schema and a validator. The schema says which entities and actions exist and what each action's context holds; the validator checks every policy against it before it runs.
language

Proof, not only tests. The OOPSLA 2024 paper says "We have modeled Cedar in the Lean programming language, and used Lean's proof assistant to prove important properties of Cedar's design", and the Lean case study adds the rule that matters most to me: "No new Cedar version is released unless its model, proofs, and differential tests are current." The paper is also direct about the comparison with the other two languages people reach for: "Comparing Cedar to two open-source languages, OpenFGA and Rego, we find (subjectively) that Cedar has equally or more readable policies, but (objectively) performs far better."
crosswalk

Our behaviour-policy terms, Cedar's, and where each one lives in the vault. Most map directly: the grant is permit, the barrier is forbid, the footprint is the entities. Two have no Cedar construct, the mandate and the version in force, and those are what the vault adds. Most of an agent behaviour policy maps onto Cedar without strain. The grant, what the agent can touch, is a permit and the actions and resource types in the schema. A barrier, a limit on the grant, is a forbid, and Cedar's rule that forbid always wins is exactly how we want barriers to behave. The footprint, what exists to act on, from Footprint and blast radius, is the entities. A row of a skill behaviour policy is a forbid on labels the session carries. And the business layers of The behaviour policy is the business logic are forbids on facts from the ledger or the CRM, passed in as context.
crosswalk

Two things have no Cedar construct. The mandate, what the agent is for and why each limit exists, is the description the rules are compiled from, and it has to stay the canonical version. And the version in force, which set of rules applied to a given decision, belongs to whatever stores the policies, not to the language.
crosswalk

This is the translation element I keep coming back to. A fractal semantic graph does not ask everyone to share a schema; it connects graphs that each keep their own. Cedar has its own world: entities, actions, a schema. Our behaviour policy has its own: mandate, grant, barriers, layers. We do not need to replace either. We need edges between them, and Cedar gives us a place to put them: annotations. In the demo, every policy carries one, @abp_rule("9") or @sbp_row("dga-2") or @layer("process"), and those are edges from a node in their graph to a node in ours. It is the same move as The same argument, in our words, done in code.
today

Amazon Verified Permissions as its documentation describes it, a plain repository, and the vault from the demo. The managed store validates strictly and is protected by IAM, but its API has no history or export, and deleting it is permanent. A repository has history but no keys. The vault has both, and puts the evidence next to the rules. My guess in the memo was that policies are often deployed as loose JSON with no version control. The truth is better than that, and the gap is still real. Cedar policies are text, with a JSON form "to allow for programmatically constructing and parsing policies". In AWS, they live in a policy store, "a container for policies and policy templates", with a STRICT validation mode that "Requires a schema to be present in the policy store", and IAM deciding who can change what.
today

But the store is a current state, not a history. The API reference lists create, get, list, update and delete operations, and none for versions, history or export. Deleting a store "permanently deletes the schema and any policies and policy templates in the policy store", and deletion protection is on for stores made in the console but "disabled for all policy stores created through an API or SDK call". The CloudFormation reference adds a subtle one: "Existing policies and templates are not re-evaluated against the changed schema." I found no signing or provenance mechanism for policies, in Cedar or in the store. So most teams who take this seriously will keep the source in a repository and push it into the store. That gives history, but the rules are plaintext to everyone who can read the repository, and nothing ties a decision back to the commit that made it.
demo

To find out whether a vault fills that gap, this site's agent built it on a local vault server, with sgit 0.21.0 and cedarpy 4.12.2. The vault holds a schema, four policy files with the rules tested in Commander's intent is a behaviour policy, seven policies in all, the entities, and the test cases, each a request with the decision we expect.
demo

The gate. Before anything is committed, a script validates every policy against the schema and runs every test. Version one passed, fourteen of fourteen, and was pushed and tagged policies-v1. For version two, the agent added ABP rule 2, no push before the leak scan, as a new forbid, without changing the schema. The gate refused it: the attribute leak_scan_clean was "not found" in the context the schema gives a push. With the schema and the tests changed in the same commit, fifteen of fifteen passed, and it was tagged policies-v2. A diff between the two tags shows the policy, the schema and the tests changing together, which is the unit I want: a rule is not just a line of Cedar.
demo

The sharp edge. That refusal matters more than it looks, because of what Cedar does at run time: "if a policy's evaluation returns error, the policy does not factor into the authorization response; it is skipped." The agent sent the version-two policies a request in the old shape, a push with no leak_scan_clean in the context, and the answer was Allow, with the error in the diagnostics. A forbid that cannot be evaluated fails open. Validation before deployment is not optional, and an enforcement point should deny on any evaluation error, which is what Hooks are kernel code would ask of any hook that guards an action.
demo

Signed releases, read-only enforcement. Each tag is signed by the clone that made it, and sgit vault tag show reported "signature verified". The enforcement point cloned the vault with the read key only; when it tried to commit and push, sgit answered "This vault was cloned read-only. To write, re-clone with the full vault key." It loads only a verified tag, checks that its working copy is at that tag, and runs the gate again before it decides anything.
demo

Decisions and evidence. The enforcement point decided all fifteen test requests: eight allowed, seven denied, each denial named by the @id of the policy that made it. Every decision was sealed and appended to an append lane on the same vault: the request, the decision, the determining policies, the tag, the commit, and the hash of the previous record. The enforcement point holds an append token and nothing else; asked to list its own lane, the server answered 403. The auditor, with the enum key, read all fifteen back and found the chain intact. A decision took 1.2 milliseconds one at a time and 0.06 batched; 200 sealed appends took 2.2 milliseconds each, on one machine.
adds

Distribution. A read key is a deployment credential that cannot change the rules. The ciphertext can sit on any server, a CDN, or a folder copied into a sandbox with no network, and the append-lane architectures already measured how many readers and writers a vault can take. Validation, at both ends. The same gate runs before push and after load. A policy that has not passed it is not a release, and a release that is not signed is not loaded. That is the same release-gate idea as sgit in a CI pipeline, applied to rules instead of code.
adds

Evidence. Every decision names its policy, its tag and its commit, in a lane the decider can write but not read or rewrite. The policy draws the liability line argued that the written policy is the evidence that turns "user error" into "your product ignored what it was told"; a lane like this shows which written policy was in force, and what it decided. History and translation. The English behaviour policy, the Cedar, the schema, the tests and the decisions live in one versioned unit. A zip or a JSON projection for a managed store can be generated from any tag, and it is a projection of something with a history, not the only copy.
adds

There is one more reason the timing is good. AgentCore now also accepts Dogwood, "an open-source policy language" whose core syntax is derived from Cedar, adding conditions "that decide based on what has already happened earlier in the same session". Rules about history need a trustworthy history, and an append lane of sealed, chained decisions is one.
brief

For the agent that builds the integration, here is the brief. Start from the demo. Schema, four policy files, entities, test cases, the gate, the enforcement point and the auditor; all of it ran locally and is the starting point. Make the gate a release rule. No commit without validation and every test passing; a policy change without its test change is refused. Deny on error. The enforcement point treats any evaluation error as Deny and records the error in the evidence. Wire it to a real hook. A pre-tool hook in this newsroom's own agent session, deciding the seven rules for real actions, with the session's labels as context. Keep the edges. Every policy carries @id and an annotation back to its ABP rule, skill row or business layer; a check fails any policy without one.
brief

Project, do not fork. A job that exports a signed tag to the JSON a managed store accepts, and records which commit is live there. Prove it. In CI: the fifteen cases, a refused unsigned tag, a refused invalid policy, a read-only clone that cannot push, and an auditor that finds the chain intact. Then run it on the newsroom's own releases for two weeks and report what it denied. Never print a key. Read keys, append tokens and enum keys are separate files; nothing logs them.
limits

The demo is local. One machine, an in-memory vault server, fifteen decisions; not production, not a cloud store. Not proved, only tested. The Cedar ran in cedarpy, an unofficial binding; we did not use Cedar's symbolic analysis. No AWS integration yet. The sync into Verified Permissions or AgentCore is proposed, not built. The adopters list is AWS's. I have not checked each company's own use. The evidence key is shared. The demo sealed records with one symmetric key; a real deployment should seal them to the auditor's public key. Dogwood is new. I have read its page and AWS's description, not used it. If you run Cedar policies, or want your agents' rules to arrive signed and leave evidence behind, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

A voice memo of mine on 14 October 2026, written by this site's agent in the voice of this site; the argument and the editorial responsibility are mine.
