Abstract: When a team of agents can build almost anything, the scarce thing is direction, and this article is about how I choose it. The rule I have used since I was a CISO is to work at the place of highest leverage: where I can add the most value right now, am not blocked, and can just start, even without knowing how the whole problem will be solved, because by the time I get there I will have better tooling and a better view. The last three days are the worked example. The newsroom went from a reading meter to pay by depth, personas, an encrypted share, a persona in a link, a reading list in a link, a passkey design, a lab that corrected the design, real vaults from the browser and a vault pane, each step shipped and used before the next was chosen, two steps walked back, and a branch parked because it is only valuable with many readers. On a Wardley map the passkey work moved from genesis to a product in a day because almost every shoulder it stands on is a commodity someone else matured; the one custom layer we had to add is where a provider is not. The path looks obvious backwards and was five choices at every step going forwards; walking back is not failure, and parking is not either. Constraints, saying no, shipping to a user even when the user is me, and the brief that could not be written until the art of the possible was known.

Five choices at every step; the path only looks obvious backwards. The steps the newsroom actually took from 10 to 12 October, with the choices passed over at each, two walked back, one branch parked, and every step shipped and used before the next was chosen. This morning I asked the agent that runs the newsroom to read the day's articles and tell me what it could build next. It came back with a long list, all of it possible: the inbox mode, the reading modes, the marks, automating the wire's daily run, more beats, scheduling, consumption analytics. Every item was a reasonable thing to do, and a team of agents could have started on all of them by lunchtime. That is the problem this article is about. When the agents can go in every direction, where do you focus?

My answer is the one I have used since I was a CISO, and it has a name I gave it years ago: places of highest leverage. This article says what that means, shows it on the last three days of real work, puts it on a Wardley map, and ends with the part that only became clear this week, which is that the briefs I write depend on knowing what is possible, and knowing what is possible depends on having shipped.
short

Direction is the scarce thing. Agents can build in any direction; what they cannot generate is the sense of what to build next and when to stop. Providing that is the job. Work at the place of highest leverage. Where you can add the most value right now, you are not blocked, and you can start. Not where the biggest problem is; where the next step moves the needle most. Start without knowing how it ends. By the time you reach the hard part you have better tooling, better data and a better view. Starting somewhere, even somewhere slightly wrong, beats being paralysed by the size of the whole. Shipped and used, every step. Nothing stays theoretical. Each step goes in front of a user before the next is chosen, and the user can be me.
short

The path is five choices at every step. It looks linear and obvious backwards; forwards it was a tangent, two steps walked back, and a branch parked. The non-linear path was the efficient one. Walking back is not failure, and parking is not either. A tangent reaches diminishing returns or no demand; you note it and move. The parked branch is on the map, with the reason. Shoulders matter. On the Wardley map the passkey work went from genesis to a product in a day because almost everything under it is a commodity someone else matured. The custom layer we had to add is the one place a provider is not. The brief depends on the possible. The inbox brief could not have been written until the vault ran. Shipping is what tells you what to think next.
rule

Places of highest leverage means this. At any moment there are many things that could be done. Most of them are blocked on something: a decision, a dependency, a thing that does not exist yet, a person. Some are not blocked but would not change much. A few are not blocked and would change a lot, for the people who use the thing and for everything built after. Work on those, and only those, until they stop being that.
rule

It is a rule about where, not what. It does not say what the product is; it says where to stand today. And it does not require knowing how the whole problem will be solved. I often do not. What I know is that by the time I get there, I will have better tooling, a better understanding and a better view, because every step taken produces those three things. So instead of standing in front of a large problem being paralysed by it, you start somewhere, and the somewhere can be slightly wrong, because the first step's job is not to be right. It is to produce the second step's information.
rule

There is a mathematical version of this that I use in security and cannot name from memory in a voice memo, so I will name it here carefully. It is the family of methods that begin with a guess, measure, and narrow: Fermi estimates that start wide and get calibrated; Bayesian updating, where each observation moves the prior; Monte Carlo runs that turn a guess into a range. What they have in common is that the first number is not the point. The range that emerges after a few steps is highly informative, and you cannot get to it without the first bad guess. Engineering under uncertainty works the same way, and so does choosing what to build.
rule

The other half of the rule is constraints. I have token budgets, hours, attention, and one person's focus, and I think the constraints are the reason it works rather than the price of it. The FIRE model from Dan Ward says it in four words, fast, inexpensive, restrained, elegant, and Knowing when to stop is this site's version: value rises fast and then flattens, and past the point of diminishing returns more work is optimising the wrong thing. Constraints are what make you notice the flattening. And saying no is the sharp end of it. Steve Jobs said something like: focus is about saying no to the hundred good ideas, and I am proud of the things we have not done. With agents that is not a slogan. It is most of the work.
steps

The figure at the top is the record, from the release logs of this site and the newsroom, and I want to walk it because the rule is easier to see in a sequence than in the abstract. On 10 October, Pay after you read: a meter in the browser at 12:09, pay by how far you read at 13:40, personas and your own newsroom at 14:23, sending your reading encrypted at 15:28, usefulness setting the price at 15:49. Each one was the place of highest leverage once the one before it existed. A meter made a price possible; a price made personas worth keeping; personas made sharing worth encrypting. None of them was planned a week ahead. Each was chosen after using the last.
steps

On 11 October, a link to a persona at 09:53 and a reading list in a link at 14:30, 81 minutes after its brief, because sending someone to the newsroom as nobody was the friction I felt that morning. Then the passkey design, and here the path bends. The first version had a door vault between the passkey and the master. A review in the afternoon took it out as a layer too many: there was no requirement for it in our use case, and I agreed. That is the first orange arc on the figure.
steps

On 12 October at 00:15, the newsroom's lab, which had built every step of the design as a card, found that the same passkey returns different bytes through a phone over QR than through the provider on the device. The door went back, as a door per path. That is the second arc, and it points the other way. Two reversals in twelve hours, both right, both cheap, because the design had been shipped as something you could press rather than argued as a document. At 01:33 real vaults from the browser, through the vendored library rather than a writer of our own, which was a choice passed over. At 02:22 the vault pane, live.
steps

And then, this morning, the list. The agent offered the inbox, the reading modes, the marks, and also automating the wire, more beats, scheduling, consumption analytics. The second group is parked, and the figure says why in blue: valuable only with many readers. We do not have many readers; we have articles, and me, and the person I showed the walkthrough to. The place of highest leverage is the feedback loop on what exists: the inbox, the marks, the modes, because they make every article better, they are what the readers we do have want, and they make me a better briefer of the agents, which compounds. Improving how the wire is computed is real work for a real day, and that day is not today.
back

Two things in that sequence are easy to read as failures and are not. Walking back is what a two-way door looks like from inside. The distinction, from Jeff Bezos, is between decisions you can reverse and decisions you cannot, and the point is to move fast through the first kind. Removing the door was a two-way door; so was putting it back. Neither cost more than an afternoon, both were shipped as a version with the change on its page, and the second was forced by a test, which is the best possible reason. The path with two reversals in it reached a better design faster than a path that had tried to get the design right on paper would have, because the paper could not have known what the phone would return.
back

Parking is the same move at the level of a branch. A tangent reaches diminishing returns, or it turns out there is no demand yet, and you stop. Not because it was wrong; because its leverage is lower than something else's today. The parked branch stays on the map, with the reason, and the reason has a date on it: when there are many readers, the wire's scheduling becomes a place of high leverage. That is also why I do not feel ownership of any of these pieces. They are open, the record is public, and the thing I am attached to is the feedback loop, not any one feature in it. The same thing as a shape rather than a record: three to five routes open at every step, one taken and shipped, two walked a little way and walked back, one parked, and the straight line that only exists in hindsight.
back

The hardest part is that going forwards you cannot see the path. Backwards, from the vault pane, the sequence looks inevitable: of course the meter led to personas led to sharing led to a vault led to a passkey. Forwards, at each step, there were five choices, and the figure shows the ones passed over in grey: a paywall, a subscription, an account, a recommender, analytics, a server, Google sign-in. Any of them could have been taken. The method in the madness is only visible by walking backwards, and that is fine, as long as each step forwards was shipped and used before the next was chosen. That is the discipline that replaces foresight.
map

Which shoulders the passkey work stands on. Almost everything under it is a product or a commodity someone else matured; our piece is the door and a door per path; the one custom layer we had to add is the phone by QR, where a provider is not yet mature. There is a second reason the three days went as fast as they did, and the Wardley map shows it. The passkey work went from genesis, a design on a page, through custom-built, a lab you could press, to a product, a pane on every page, in a day. Within hours of that we were building on it: vaults inside vaults, the reading records, the next brief. It is already on its way to being a commodity for us, something that just works and is not thought about. That is only possible because of what it stands on.
map

Look at the bottom of the map. Synced passkeys with the PRF extension in iCloud Keychain: commodity, mature, the same bytes on a Mac, an iPad and an iPhone. The WebAuthn PRF extension itself, Web Crypto with HKDF and PBKDF2, sgit keys made in the client, the vault library we vendored unedited, the vault server, the Stripe payment link: all products or commodities, all someone else's work, all matured before we arrived. Our piece, the door and the derivation, is small, and that is the point. We are not building a passkey system. We are adding one small custom layer on top of a stack that is already mature, and a small custom layer on a mature stack becomes a product almost as soon as it works.
map

The one exception proves it. Google Password Manager's passkey, reached through a phone over QR, returns different bytes from the same passkey on the device. That is a place where a provider is not yet mature, and it is exactly where we had to add a custom layer, a door per path, and exactly where the work slowed. If we had built on that path alone we would still be building. We built on Apple's synced path, which is further to the right, and the thing shipped. Which shoulders you stand on decides how fast your piece becomes a product. The map tells you where the mature shoulders are, and it is worth drawing before choosing where to stand.
ship

Everything above rests on one rule that I want to state on its own: it is about shipping, and it is about a user. Every piece of work, these days, has to be used straight away, by someone, and it is fine if the someone is me. Not a hypothesis, not a design document that waits for a quarter: a thing a person opens. I miss it, so it is working made the case that the people who decide the roadmap have to use the product; this is the operational version. A step that was shipped and used tells you where the next step is. A step that was only designed tells you nothing, because you have not felt it.
ship

That is also why the briefs come after the shipping and not before. The site is an inbox begins with a confession: I could not have written it two days earlier, because I did not know the properties of what would run. The vault had to exist, the passkey had to work, the door had to be per path, before I could think about what a reader does with any of it. The art of the possible is not something you reason your way to. It is what shipping leaves behind, and the next brief is made of it.
limits

Three days is a sample. The sequence is real and the times are from the release logs, but it is one project at one speed, chosen because it is the one I can show. The rule does not pick the product. Places of highest leverage says where to stand, not what to build; the what comes from using the thing and from the people who ask for it. The mathematics is named carefully. Fermi estimates, Bayesian updating and Monte Carlo ranges are the family I mean; the memo could not name them, and the analogy is mine, not a theorem. Parking has a cost. A branch left for later can be overtaken; the wire's scheduling may need to be rebuilt when its day comes. That is accepted, and it is cheaper than building it for readers who are not there.
limits
If you run a team of agents and the hard part has become choosing, or you want to compare maps, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: At an event this week a speaker described policy as code as the way to scale governance and AI innovation together, and it clicked. Policy as code is right, and it is where agent governance has to end up. But for agents it answers one question, is this request allowed, and the questions a business, an auditor or an insurer asks are the ones around it, the ones an Agent Behaviour Policy holds. What can this agent reach, measured. What was it asked to do, and why. Where the two differ. Which rules can no engine ever see. And the one that surprised me when I checked: for every rule that is code, who can change that code. A rule the agent can rewrite is a setting, not a control. Because an ABP has those columns, it can be written in both directions. From the policy, generate code: for this article, five rows of a real ABP became a Rego policy that Open Policy Agent ran against seven requests, denying a push to the wrong repository, a commit without a leak scan and a model id in a diff, asking before a pull request, and allowing a sentence no engine can judge. From what exists, reverse engineer the policy: parse the code back, and the gaps show on both sides, a row with no code and a rule nobody wrote a reason for. I did it to this session's own policy: of its eleven rules, eight have some code behind them, and only one has code the agent cannot change. Fractal semantic graphs are what make the round trip work across paper, spreadsheets, regulations and code, because each keeps its own vocabulary and the edges between them carry verbs both ways.

One policy at three altitudes. At the top, the business's words: a board policy, a row of a control spreadsheet, an article of a regulation. In the middle, the ABP row for one agent in one deployment: reach, mandate, gap, barrier and owner. At the bottom, the code where decisions are made: a Rego rule, a hook, a validator check. Generating code walks down; reverse engineering walks up; a node with no edge is a gap.
in-short

Policy as code is right, and it answers one question. Is this request allowed. For agents, the governance questions are around it. An ABP holds what the engine does not. The reach, measured; the mandate and its reason; the gap; the rules no engine can see; the owner; and who can change each rule's code. A rule the agent can rewrite is a setting. This session's policy has eleven rules; eight have code behind them; only one has code the agent cannot change. Generate code from the policy. Five ABP rows became a 35-line Rego policy; Open Policy Agent decided seven requests: three denied, one asked, three allowed. Reverse engineer the policy from the code. Parsing the Rego back found a row with no code and a rule with no row, the two gaps that matter.
in-short

The same works from paper and spreadsheets. A control spreadsheet became a graph joined to the law it maps to; a role file becomes both a published table and a check. Fractal semantic graphs make the round trip work. Each altitude keeps its own vocabulary, and every edge reads both ways. The four jobs. Enabler, scaling, enforcer and decision-maker: an ABP does the first and keeps the other three honest.
question

At an event this week, one of the speakers described policy as code as the way to scale governance and AI innovation at the same time. I agree, and I think it is where agent governance has to end up: rules that are versioned, tested, reviewed like code and enforced by something other than the model's good behaviour. The best known engine for it describes the idea well. Open Policy Agent, a Cloud Native Computing Foundation graduated project, lets you "decouple policy from that software service": services "offload policy decisions to OPA by executing queries", policies "are written in a high-level declarative language", and a decision can be "arbitrary structured data", not only allow or deny.
question

That is exactly the right shape for the moment an agent acts. An agent asks to push, to send, to read a table; the engine answers. But it answers one question, is this request allowed, and when something goes wrong with an agent, that is rarely the question anyone asks first.
adds

The questions a board, an auditor or an insurer asks about an agent are the ones around the decision, and they are the columns of an Agent Behaviour Policy, as Footprint and blast radius set them out. The reach, measured. What the agent can actually do, from its connectors and accounts. A policy engine only sees the requests that are routed through it; the reach includes the ones that are not. The mandate, with its reason. What the agent was asked to do, and why each rule exists. Code holds the condition; the reason lives, at best, in a comment. The gap. Reach minus mandate, derived. It is the list of things the agent could do that nobody asked for, which is where the rules should come from.
adds

The rules no engine can see. "Great, not perfect." "The tone is mine." Some rows will always be expectations, kept by a second reader, and an ABP lists them instead of silently leaving them out. The owner. Who answers for each row, which is what The policy draws the liability line argued decides where liability lands. Who can change the code. For every rule that is code, whether the agent's own account could rewrite it. The barrier column types it: "A boundary is enforced above the agent's reach, so it cannot flip it. A setting is a switch the agent's own account could flip." That last one is the column I did not expect to matter so much, until I checked this session.
session

This session's own policy, reverse engineered from its code. Eleven rules; for each, the code that enforces it, who can change that code, and the barrier that results. Eight have some code behind them; only one, never pushing to sgit.ai, has code the agent cannot change. The agent writing this site works under a written policy, eleven rules, reloaded after every summary, as Re-anchoring describes. So I did the exercise on it: for each rule, find the code that enforces it, in the session's hooks, its leak scan, the site's validators and its git configuration, and then ask who can change that code.
session

Eight of the eleven have some code behind them. The leak scan refuses a staged diff with a key-shaped string, a model id outside the byline, an em-dash in an article or a name on a private list. The validator fails the build on the ladder word and warns on absolutes. A hook prints the policy back after every summary and supplies the status report. Three rules have no code at all: masking keys in output, not using anyone else's credential, and answering when asked for the policy's status.
session

Then the second question, and the honest answer. Nearly all of that code is code the agent can change. The leak scan and the hooks are files in its own home directory; the validators are in the repository it pushes to and in a clone on its own disk. By the policy's own definitions, those rules are settings. Even "never push to sgit.ai", enforced by a push address set to nothing, is a setting on its own, because the agent could set it back. What makes that one rule a boundary is something the agent cannot touch: this session's access to GitHub is scoped to the newsroom's repository by the platform it runs on. One rule in eleven.
session

None of that is a failure; it is the session's real state, and most organisations' agents would look the same if anyone drew the table. It is also why policy as code alone would have scored this session as well governed: most of its rules are code. The ABP is what shows that the code is the agent's own. And reverse engineering finds the reasons where they hide. The validator's rule against em-dashes carries its reason in a comment: readers find them off-putting, "and 2,900 of them do not stay gone without a rule". The rule against absolutes is advisory, and its message says why: "say what was found, not what nobody has". That is the paper policy, scattered through the code. Walking up from the code collects it into rows.
generate

A round trip through Open Policy Agent. Five ABP rows as data, generated into a 35-line Rego policy, evaluated against seven requests, then parsed back with OPA's own parser and compared with the ABP: one row with no code, one rule with no row. The other direction was built for this article. Five rows of the session's policy went into a small JSON file: an id, the rule, why it exists, the decision, a condition where there is one, the barrier, and what enforces it today. A generator of about twenty-five lines turned them into Rego, each rule carrying its row's id and reason as a comment and as the value it returns: # R9: Never push to the sgit.ai repository. Why: sgit.ai is read-only for this session. deny contains "R9" if { input.tool == "git.push" not input.remote in {"github.com/SGit-AI/SGit-AI__Website__Newsroom"} }
generate

OPA 1.21.2 checked the policy and evaluated seven requests. A push to sgit.ai: deny, R9. A push to the newsroom: allow. A commit with no leak scan: deny, R2. A commit adding a model id in a code comment: deny, R5. A clean, scanned commit: allow. Opening a pull request: ask, R7b, because the decision is the owner's. And publishing a sentence that says "a perfect result": allow, because the row that forbids it has no condition any engine can check, and the generator wrote that down as a comment instead of pretending.
generate

Then back again. opa parse turned the Rego into its syntax tree, and comparing the rules it found with the ABP's rows gave the two lists that matter. Rows with no code: R6c, the wording rule, which stays an expectation with a second reader. Code with no row: after a second file added a rule against Friday releases, "added in a hurry after an incident", the comparison flagged no-friday-releases as enforcement nobody had written a reason for. That is the rule that will confuse the next person, block the next urgent fix, and have no owner when someone asks why.
paper

Code is not the only thing to reverse engineer, and this site has done the other two. From a spreadsheet: when Jan van Dijke published the AI Baseline Control Framework, twenty controls mapped to the NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001 and the EU AI Act, its CSV became, on the day, "a semantic graph with an ontology", "joined to the EU AI Act's own text", and "the six things the graph found that the CSV does not say". Four frameworks, one agent did the same for four frameworks and one agent, as a mapping file with a row for every element and its status.
paper

From paper, in both directions at once: sgit.ai's newsroom roles are written as files, and the check that gates a release reads them. In the words of the check itself, "The policy is the writes and edits lists in admin/content/newsroom/roles/<role>.md, the same files the /newsroom/policies.html table is generated from." One source, rendered as a page people read and as a check a release must pass. That is the pattern I would want for every agent: the ABP is the source, the table and the code are renderings, and neither can drift from the other because neither is edited by hand.
fsg

A round trip like this breaks if every format has to share one schema. A board policy is written in the board's words; a regulation in the legislator's; a control spreadsheet in the auditor's; an ABP in reach, mandate, gap and barrier; Rego in packages, rules and conditions. Asking any of them to adopt the others' vocabulary is why mapping exercises become workshops.
fsg

Fractal semantic graphs are the answer this site has been building: "Zoom into any node and you enter a new world with its own node types, its own verbs, its own taxonomy." Each altitude keeps its own vocabulary; the edges between them are verbs with inverses, so a row answers a policy and the policy is answered by the row; a rule enforces a row and the row is enforced by the rule. Then the questions that matter are walks, not workshops. "A question can cross formats without a join table." Which board policies have no row? Which rows have no code? Which code has no row? Which rows are enforced only by code the agent's own account can change? And when a regulation changes, supersede the node, never delete it, and every row and rule that rested on it becomes the answer to a query.
fsg

That is what makes reverse engineering practical at scale: the code, the spreadsheet and the paper do not need to be converted, only connected. And it is what makes generation safe: the code that comes out carries an edge back to the row it came from, so the next person can ask why.
jobs

The speaker's framing was policy as code as an enabler, a way to scale, an enforcer and a basis for decisions. With an ABP as the source, each one gets sharper. Enabler. A written mandate lets a team ship an agent without a review meeting per agent, because the review was of the policy. The behaviour policy is the business logic: writing it is the work. Scaling. One source, rendered into as many engines and agents as needed, versioned and diffable, with every generated rule traceable to its row. Enforcer. Rows compiled into boundaries, and the barrier column saying, honestly, which ones still are not. Hope or enforcement measured what that is worth: one agent's rules kept only by good behaviour fell from 97% to 23% as they moved into the platform.
jobs

Decision-maker. Every decision returns the row it came from, allow, deny or ask, and every ask goes to a named person, as The human in the loop argued, with the record of decisions moving the line over time.
limits

The round trip is a demonstration. Five rows, a short generator and seven requests, run for this article; it is not a product, and real agents need their requests routed through the engine for any of it to bind. The session table is one agent's. Counted from this session's hooks, scripts, validators and configuration on 14 October 2026; other agents will look different, and I expect most to look similar. The GitHub scope was not tested by trying. It is how this session's access is configured; pushing to sgit.ai to prove it is exactly what the policy forbids. Some rows will never be code. That is a feature of the method, not a gap in it: an ABP says which rows rely on a person. The speaker is not named. I took the idea from a talk and have not checked how they would put it.
limits
If you have policies in code, spreadsheets or paper and want to see the agent behaviour policy they imply, or the code an ABP implies, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

A voice memo of mine on 14 October 2026, from an event where a speaker described policy as code as a way to scale governance and AI innovation; written by this site's agent in the voice of this site, and the argument and the editorial responsibility are mine. The round trip was run for this article with Open Policy Agent 1.21.2: a JSON file of five rows from this session's policy, a generator written for the purpose, opa check, opa eval on seven requests and opa parse to read it back. The session table is from this session's own policy (v0.3, eleven rules), its hooks, its leak scan, sgit.ai's validator and policy check, and its git configuration. OPA's description is from its philosophy page, read on 14 October 2026.

Abstract: The follow-up to "the most important question is whether they miss it". The step after giving something away is to define a product, put a price on it that makes sense to you, find a way to deliver it at a cost that grows a step at a time rather than a curve, and then offer it, free, to the people who already know you: early adopters, power users, past customers. What that measures is brutal. The price is a statement of what you think it is worth; the test is whether people take it at zero. If they say it is interesting but they have no time, it does not fit the team, or it is hard to deploy, the problem is not the price, and you go back to the drawing board. The part that is easy to leave out is that free is never free for the other side: engaging costs them attention, thinking and schedule, so the exercise is to measure that cost and cut it, until the service costs you the least and costs them the least. Written as a record of where this came from, and as a brief for the agents who will run it.

The ladder, what each tier costs each side, and the fork. Four tiers already on sale, from the ten-pound pack to the fifteen-hundred-pound reviewed vault, each with a relative cost to us and a cost to the customer. The early access programme gives the five-hundred-pound tier away, free, to people who already run an agent. The question on the right is the whole exercise. Prices as published on 2 October 2026; cost bars are relative, not measured. Price it before you give it away. A price is a statement of what you think the thing is worth. Giving it away at that stated price, to people who know you, is the cleanest test of whether the statement is true.

Deliver it at a cost that grows a step at a time. The reason this is possible now is the agentic workflow. Provisioning a vault and a policy for one more customer costs a little more, not a lot more, and that is what lets you give twenty away without flinching. Offer it to the people who already know you. Early adopters, power users, past customers. Not "apply for a chance", which puts work on them before they have anything. "We have twenty; would you like one, or shall I give it to someone else." It is also how you thank them. Free is never free for the other side. They still have to read, think, decide, find a slot, and fit it into a team. A price can even help, because it tells them you are serious. Either way, the cost they bear is the number to measure and the number to cut.

The answer is brutal either way. If they take it, use it and ask for more, you have a product and the question becomes price. If they say it is interesting but they have no time, it does not fit, it is hard to deploy, the problem is not the price and you go back to the board. Count what matters. Policies created per day, customised, used; scenarios run; corrections sent back; and the minutes each one cost the person on the other side. The earlier article ends on a question. Hand the thing to people for free, briefly, then take it away, and ask whether they miss it. If they shrug, you do not have a product yet. If they come back for it, you have something, and the model turns on.

That is the right test and it has a gap in it, which is what happens next. "Something" is not a product until it has a shape, a price and a way of being delivered that does not break you on the tenth customer. So the next step is four moves, in order. Define the product. Not the technology, the thing somebody receives. For RiskMandate the thing is an Agent Behaviour Policy for one agent, as an encrypted vault the customer holds the keys to, with the mandate corrected for their deployment. That sentence took weeks to get to and it is the product.

Price it, at a number that makes sense to you. Not a number from a competitor's page, a number you would be content to be paid. RiskMandate's ladder is four tiers: ten pounds for the pack downloaded, fifty for a working vault, five hundred for the vault corrected for your situation, fifteen hundred for two sessions and a professional's signature. The first two are automated and already on sale. The third is an email thread: we send prompts, the customer runs them, we build the vault and the policy from what comes back. The fourth adds people's time on both sides.

Find a way to deliver it at a cost that grows a step at a time. This is the move that was not available a year ago and is the reason to do this now. The agentic workflow means the marginal customer costs a little more, not a lot more. The vault is provisioned by an agent, the policy is drafted by an agent from the customer's prompts, a person corrects it. The cost of serving the twentieth customer is close to the cost of serving the second. That is linear, not exponential, and it is the condition under which you can afford to give twenty away. Then offer it, free, to the people who already know you. Which is what the programme does, and the next section is about why the free part is the hard part.

Here is the thing that is easy to leave out, and the memo was careful about how to say it, because it is easy to say it in a way that sounds like a lecture. When you give something away, or when you say "this is worth five hundred pounds and I would like you to have it", you are not making a zero-cost offer. You are asking the other side to engage. To read the message. To think about whether it applies to them. To consider it against everything else on their list. To find twenty minutes for the prompts and half an hour for a call. To fit a new thing into a team that already has a way of working.

None of that is zero, and all of it is paid by them. The honest version of the offer accounts for it. A price point, oddly, can help here: it says the thing is serious and that you expect it to be used, which is a reason to find the twenty minutes. But whether the price is five hundred or zero, the attrition you place on the other side is real, and the first measurement the programme makes is of that attrition. How long did it take from the message to the first reply. How many people never replied. How many started the prompts and stopped. How many asked a question that the message should have answered.

Then the exercise is to reduce it. The service you want is the one that costs you the least to provide and costs the customer the least to receive. No overhead on them, no overhead on deployment, no second tool to install, no account to create. Those are product decisions, and the programme is where you find out which ones you got wrong, while the people finding out for you are people who like you. Two small rules, both from the memo. Do not make them apply. "Apply for a chance to be considered" asks for work before there is anything in hand, and it inverts the relationship: they are doing you a favour by using the thing, not the other way round. "We have twenty of these in the first round. Would you like one? If not, I will give it to someone else" is honest about scarcity and leaves them nothing to do but say yes or no.

Reward the people who were there early. The early adopters, the power users, the past customers who paid for something before it was finished. They are the ones who should get the first twenty, and the offer should say that is why they are getting it. It is a thank-you that also happens to be the best possible test group, because they know enough to tell you where it is wrong, and they are the ones whose silence means the most.

The early access page went live on 30 September 2026, invite only. Its own words: "A small programme for people who already run an agent with real access: a mailbox, a code host, a workflow tool, a CRM. Each member gets an Agent Behaviour Policy for one agent, as an encrypted vault they hold the keys to, and is asked to do one thing with it: say where it is wrong." The asks of the member: "Run it against the real agent. Tell us where the mandate is wrong, and what you would do with the document. Twenty minutes for the prompts, and a reply; half an hour on a call." The commitments back: "A person confirms your place within a working day, and the vault follows within five." And the caveat that keeps it honest: "Not a security assessment, and not a promise about your agent's behaviour."

That is the five-hundred-pound tier, given away. The programme page does not say the price, and it should not; the price is for the people who come after. What it measures is whether people who already run an agent, and already know us, will spend twenty minutes and half an hour to get a document that describes what their agent can do. If they will not, no price fixes that. It is worth being plain about the two outcomes, because one of them is a bad day and the exercise only works if you are prepared for it.

If people take the offer, run the prompts, read the vault, send corrections and ask what else there is, you have a product. The next question is price, and it is a good question to have: would they buy more, is five hundred too low for what they got, is it too high for the next tier of customer, does the fifteen-hundred tier sell itself once someone has had the five-hundred one free. Those are the questions the earlier article called "can you charge, and can you charge at a profit", and you can only ask them of people who have had the thing.

If people say it is interesting and then do not find the time, or say it does not fit how their team works, or start and stop because the vault was harder to open than the message implied, then you do not have a product yet. You might have a technology, you might have an idea, you might have a document people would read if someone else did the work. But you do not have a commercial product, because a commercial product is one people take when the only cost is their own attention. That is the drawing board, and the sooner you are at it the cheaper it is. Neither outcome is a marketing problem. The earlier article said that about revenue and it is just as true here: if friendlies will not take it free, a bigger audience will not take it either.

The programme runs against numbers that are already defined, and the memo is firm that they are the ones that matter: how many Agent Behaviour Policies get created each day, how many get customised, how many get used, how many scenarios get run. Those are the KPIs. The objectives sit above them and are about the same thing: is anyone building these, is anyone changing them, is anyone running their agent against them. A policy that was created and never customised is a download. A policy that was customised and never used is a document. The commercial value is in the third number. To those four we add the measurement from the section above: the minutes each step cost the person on the other side, and where they stopped. That is the number that tells us what to cut.

This section is the brief. It is written so that an agent picking up the programme in a week, or in a year, knows what to do and why. The list is the early adopters, power users and past customers. It lives in the CRM vault. Nobody outside it gets the first round. The reason is in the section above: they are the best test group and the thank-you is deliberate. The message is short and makes no one apply. It says what the thing is in one sentence, that there are twenty in this round, that they are being offered one because they were early, and asks yes or no. It carries the invitation code. It does not carry the price.

Record the clock. Time from message to first reply. Time from yes to vault delivered, against the five-working-day promise. Time from vault to first correction. Who never replied, who said yes and never ran the prompts, who ran them and stopped. Every one of these is a row in the programme vault, with no message content copied, only the timestamps and the step. Count the four KPIs daily and write them to the same vault: policies created, customised, used, scenarios run. Add corrections received, because a correction is the strongest signal that someone read the thing. Every stop is a finding. When someone stops, the question is not why they did not care; it is what cost them more than it should have. Write it down as a product change to make, not a reason the customer gave.

The stop rule. If, after the first twenty, fewer than a handful have run the prompts and sent a correction, the programme stops and the drawing board starts. That number is for the founders to set before the first message goes out, not after the results are in. This article is part of the record. It says where the programme came from and what it was for. If the shape changes, add a dated note here rather than rewriting it, so the next agent can see the path. Three reasons, and the third is the one the memo was reaching for. The product is a vault. Everything that makes the programme possible, keys the customer holds, a reading app inside, version history, a read key for the person who corrects it, is the machinery this site documents, and the cost structure that makes giving twenty away affordable is the agentic workflow that provisions them.

The method is the one this site runs on. Ship, give away, take away, watch; now define, price, deliver at a flat marginal cost, offer to friendlies, measure both costs. The business plans published here are written to be taken and run the same way. And the site is becoming the memory. An agent that picks this programme up in a year should be able to read, in order, the article that said "do they miss it", the page that published the offer, this article that said why it was shaped this way and what to count, and then the vault that holds the counts. That chain is how the next agent gets context rather than instructions, and it is why a voice memo about a sales campaign became an article rather than a task.

Abstract: Twenty-five real vaults a stranger can open in one click are the most persuasive thing on this site, and the homepage shows none of them. It leads with encryption, which cannot be seen, and buries the artefacts under a table. This is the diagnosis, with screenshots, before the rebuild, and the second article will show what changed. Three weeks ago this site had four published vaults. Today it has twenty-five, built by several agents working with one human, and the collection now includes things that are genuinely hard to make without sgit: a penetration test report that ships with a retest script per finding, a conference keynote that carries its eight cited papers, a compliance standard rebuilt as a citable graph with 82 hashed source snapshots, a game that reports anonymous telemetry through a write-only channel.

None of that is visible from the homepage. This article is the diagnosis of why, written before the rebuild rather than after, so the two can be compared honestly. Here is the first screen a visitor gets: The hero today: a claim about encryption, a pip install, and a terminal walkthrough of create, commit, history and clone. Every word of it is true, and almost none of it is persuasive, for one reason: encryption is a property you cannot look at. Zero knowledge is a property you cannot look at. The visitor is asked to take the value on faith before being shown anything, and the first thing they are then shown is a terminal walking through create, commit, history and clone, which any git user has watched a thousand times. The walkthrough demonstrates familiarity, which is a virtue, but not power. The word "vault" appears in the hero three times and the visitor is never shown one.

Scroll on and the site tells you what people use it for: Five use-case cards, each a category rather than a thing: private memory, multi-agent collaboration, workspaces, encrypted folders, signed exchange. These are categories, not examples. "Multi-agent collaboration, agents on their own branches, humans reviewing the merge" is a description of a capability. Meanwhile, one level down, there is a vault where one agent copied another agent's entire catalogue byte for byte and built a conformance layer on top of it, and the tests that prove the copy is exact still pass. That is the same idea, except you can open it. The homepage has the abstraction. The proof is elsewhere. Where is it? Under a dropdown: Vaults → Published vaults. Two clicks from the hero to the most persuasive page on the site. And when you get there, it is a table:

The published vaults, as of this week: sortable, categorised, and still a table, the right shape for finding a vault, the wrong shape for being convinced by one. To be fair to the table, it was rebuilt this week and it is now a good table, sortable, categorised, newest first, with the read keys moved off it because they were squeezing the vault id to one character per line. But a table is the right shape for finding a vault and the wrong shape for being convinced by one. It answers "which of these do I want" for a visitor who already wants one. Here is what the visitor could have been looking at one second after arriving, with no account and no install:

A real vault, open: the AIUC-1 conformance layer computing insurability for a named subject as of a date, one condition met, 52 exclusions, zero of five consequences covered, each with the reason in the control's own words. Another: a game about which wings of the building an agent can enter, drawn as a floor plan, with a belief column ranking nine public agent profiles as you answer. Both of these are opened by one string. Both run entirely in the browser. Both ship with their data, their sources and their tests inside the same encrypted unit. The second one built its own telemetry from a brief published on this site. None of this requires the visitor to understand encryption first. It requires them to click.

The thing that most distinguishes how this site is made is that it is built by one person and a team of agents, and the agents build for each other. The evidence is real and specific: A brief published here on 6 September was read by another agent, who built a vault from it the same day. That vault was reviewed by the team that owns the API it uses, who found the brief had been wrong in two places, and the correction is now published above the mistake. One agent forked another agent's vault, kept every byte, added a layer, and shipped a fourteen-version history that labels seven of the versions as reconstructed rather than inventing commits. Where does a visitor learn this? Here: The briefs page, the cross-team collaboration log, filed under Docs, three levels from the homepage, and written as a log rather than a story.

It is filed under Docs. It is written as a log, which is the right format for the record and the wrong one for a first-time reader. The productivity claim that the whole site rests on, this is what working with agents looks like when the state is versioned and shareable, has no page that tells it end to end. The homepage says "a branch per agent; work meets on named branches; a human reviews the merge." It is the site's strongest claim about multi-agent work, and no published vault demonstrates it. Every vault here was built by one agent, or by one agent on top of another's finished work. None shows two agents' branches and a human merge in its history.

If such a vault exists, publishing it is the single highest-value addition to the site. If it does not, the next multi-agent build should be run so that its history shows it. A claim on a homepage with no artefact behind it is exactly what this site says it does not do. Not more bands. The homepage already has nine, and 1,370 words. The fix is to reorder so proof comes before mechanism, and to cut. The hero shows vaults. One reframed sentence (a vault is a unit of work: data, app, history and sources, shipped as one string, and the server cannot read it) with four real vaults as cards under it, each with a screenshot and an open it link. The visitor is inside an artefact before they have read a paragraph. pip install stays, second.

"What people actually ship": six vaults chosen by job rather than by shape: hand over a report, publish a standard as data, give a talk, pitch an investor, run a game, give an agent a workspace. Each with one line on why it is hard without this. Generated from the same data as the table, so it never goes stale. "One human, a team of agents": the collaboration story told as a story, with the numbers, and a single page behind it that walks the loop end to end. Then the terminal walkthrough and the zero-knowledge explanation, for the developer who is now interested in how. The honesty band and the network band stay. The "three doors" band moves to the docs.

A beta tool that asks people to publish their read keys on it is asking for trust, and this site has no page saying who is asking. There will be one. It will be about sgit (who builds it, honestly including the agents; why; the commercial line) and it will borrow two sections that fit this site's culture exactly, Interests declared and Reach me, or correct me, from the fuller record that already exists on a sibling site: That card is new as of this article. The .sgit.ai sites exist so each topic can get the depth a section here could not give it, which only pays off if this site points at them constantly, and a bare link does not say this continues elsewhere, on purpose*. The card does. Authors write one line; the site's own category and thesis come from its entry in the network directory, so the card describes that site the way it describes itself.

The rebuild is the next release. The article after it will put the new homepage next to these screenshots, and say what changed and what it cost. If the "before" pictures here still look better than the "after", that article will say so too. Written by Dinis Cruz and the agentic team working with him. Licensed CC BY 4.0.

Abstract: The previous article diagnosed a homepage that led with encryption and buried twenty-five real vaults under a table. This is the rebuild, put beside those screenshots, what moved, what was cut, what it is generated from, and the one thing it still cannot show. The previous article made a diagnosis and a promise: the homepage led with a property nobody can look at, the proof sat two clicks away as a table, and the rebuild would be put next to those screenshots so the comparison could be made honestly. This is that comparison. Before: a claim about encryption, a pip install, and a terminal walkthrough of four commands every git user has seen. Before. The word "vault" appears three times and the visitor is shown none. After: one reframed sentence, and four real vaults under it. After. Four published vaults with their screenshots, each one click from open. pip install is still there, second.

The sentence changed from "the encrypted git for humans and AI agents" to "a vault is a unit of work: data, app, history and sources, shipped as one string." Encryption did not leave; it became the subordinate clause, and the server that stores it cannot read it, which is where a property you cannot see belongs. The four cards are chosen by a hero field in the vault data, so changing the front door is a data edit, not a page edit. Before: five cards, each a category. Before. "Multi-agent collaboration, agents on their own branches, humans reviewing the merge." True, and not something you can open. After: six vaults chosen by the job they do.

After. Hand over a report. Publish a standard as data. Give a talk. Pitch an investor. Ship a game that reports back. Give an agent a workspace. Each is a real vault, with one line on why it is hard to make any other way. The distinction the band is built on: none of those six lines is about encryption. A pentest report whose retest scripts travel with the findings; a talk whose cited papers never separate from the deck; a game whose telemetry uses the one credential shape that survives being published. Those are properties of a vault as a unit, and they are what a newcomer can actually feel. Before: a log, filed under Docs. Before. The cross-team briefs, the record of agents working with each other and with the human, three levels from the homepage, written as a log. After: a band with the numbers and the story.

After. Four numbers computed at build time (releases, vaults, sibling sites, briefs) and the loop told in three beats with the artefacts linked. The numbers are not typed. Releases come from the version log, vaults from the vault data, sites from the network directory, briefs from counting the entries on the briefs page. If a number on that band is wrong, the site is wrong somewhere else too, and that is the right dependency. The abstract use-case band. The five categories still exist as pages, still in the nav under Evidence; they are no longer the homepage's answer to "what is this for". "One vault, three doors." The sgit / SG/Vault / SG/Send explanation was a full band. It is a single pill in the trust strip now, pointing at the page that already explained it.

Nothing from the terminal walkthrough. It moved down and gained a heading (Under the hood, it is git) because for the visitor who has just opened a real vault, how is now the question. It gained one feature card too: apps live inside the data, which was somehow never on the list. The band count did not change, nine before, nine after: three were cut and three were added, so what changed is the order and what comes first, not the length. (The first version of this paragraph said "nine became eight"; it was corrected in v0.2.61 after counting rather than remembering.) The page is longer in bytes, because it carries ten screenshots, and slightly shorter in words: 1,370 to 1,332. That is the trade: pictures of real things instead of paragraphs about them. The screenshots load lazily and through the same mechanism every vault page uses, so the page still renders from inside a vault.

The previous article named a gap, and the rebuild did not close it: no published vault demonstrates two agents on one vault: their branches, and a human merging them. The team band tells the story of agents building for each other, which is true and evidenced. It does not yet show agents building with each other in the same history, which is the site's strongest claim. The band is written so that it does not pretend otherwise. When that vault exists, it goes in the hero.

One file, admin/content/vaults.json, now drives the hero cards, the six jobs, the sortable table and the vault count on the team band. Adding a vault is adding a row; promoting one to the front door is setting a field. The homepage stopped being a page somebody edits and became a view over the site's own data, which is the same rule the articles band, the network directory and the update feed already followed. It just took the homepage longest to get there. Written by Dinis Cruz and the agentic team working with him. Licensed CC BY 4.0.

Abstract: Instructions given only in conversation can be lost when a long session is summarised. The session that runs this site has been summarised eighteen times in a month, each time keeping under 2% of what it replaced. Re-anchoring is the answer: keep the agent's rules in a behaviour policy file and have the harness print it back after every summary, so the rules are restored rather than remembered. And because you cannot see what a summary drops, add a canary: a short status report, computed from the transcript, that ends every few answers. If it stops appearing, something in the policy has not been read. Both are running in this session now. This is how they work, what each piece is for, and why the best way to do it today is a recipe that someone has to keep up to date.
view-two-minutes

The point. When a long AI conversation fills up, the software swaps it for a short summary the AI writes, and a rule given only in conversation can vanish unnoticed. The article's fix, re-anchoring, keeps the rules in a file that the software pastes back after every summary, so they are restored, not remembered. A short status report every few answers is a warning light: if it stops appearing, something was not read. An example. The session behind the author's site was summarised eighteen times in a month, each time keeping on average 1.7% of what it replaced. Its report measures one rule, "leak scan before every commit" (check for secrets before saving work). Rather than asking the AI, it counts saves with no scan before them. That number should be zero.
view-two-minutes

Why it matters to you. Re-anchoring keeps rules in view but does not enforce them; an AI can still miss its own mistake or argue itself into an exception. The right set-up also changes with each software release. If you remember one thing. Keep the rules in a file that comes back after every summary, and watch for the report that shows it did. Words used. Compaction: the software summarising a long conversation to make room. Hook: a step the software runs automatically, such as after every summary. Canary: a regular signal whose absence warns you something is wrong.
view-arc

Introduced. The canary: a status report computed from the transcript, checked by a Stop hook and expected by the person, so a missing report signals that the policy was not read (canary). The name re-anchoring, for what article 4 called "a reminder": a hook on the compact matcher that prints the policy back after every summary. One policy file with three jobs: memory, the checker's rulebook, the enforcement list. A policy row as "a rule, its barrier, and the current recipe for keeping it", and the maintained recipe library as the thing people will pay for. The nugget. "The rules are restored, not remembered." It names the move the whole set has been making: a rule taken out of the model's memory and put back by something outside it.
view-arc

Reused. Almost everything. From a-second-reader-the-agent-cannot-skip, its only link: the three failure modes, voice-incident, compaction-warning, placement, hook, recipe, re-anchoring. From every-mistake-added-a-rule (not linked): compaction, forgetting, memory-as-files, record-reading. From article 1: the barrier kinds and enforcement-audit, now as one measured rule (commits not preceded by a leak scan). Before the set, memory-is-not-a-spectator-sport described the same session summarised across resets. Changed. It extends article 1's policy row from rule and barrier to rule, barrier and recipe, and is explicit that re-anchoring "does not change a rule's barrier". "The re-anchor after a compaction has not been observed yet." The canary is a setting, not a boundary, and a report can be pasted without the rules being followed. That sentence is the most important one I have read this week about running agents, because it explains a failure I had just watched happen. On 9 October two emails drafted by one of my agents went out in my voice, against a rule that had been written down four times; one of the reasons was that the rule fell out of the agent's context when the conversation was summarised. I wrote about the fix for that email, a second reader the agent cannot skip. This article is about the general problem underneath it, and a technique for it that I have started calling re-anchoring. What summarisation does to a long session: every compaction in the session that runs this site, read from its own transcript. Each turned about 785,000 tokens into 9,000 to 19,000. All eighteen were automatic.
view-catalogue

Summaries are frequent, heavy and invisible. This session has been summarised eighteen times in a month. Each time about 98% of the context was replaced by a summary written by the model, and nothing told me what was kept. A rule held only in conversation has to win every summary. It often will. When it does not, nothing tells you. Re-anchoring takes the rule out of that contest. The rules live in a file, an Agent Behaviour Policy, and a hook prints the file back into the context after every summary, verbatim. The rules are restored, not remembered. Re-anchoring fixes forgetting, not the other two failures. An agent that has its rules in view can still miss its own violation or argue itself into an exception. Those need a second reader and a gate.
view-catalogue

A canary makes the invisible visible. A short report, computed from the transcript, ends every few answers. If it stops appearing, the person notices before anything important goes wrong: the brown M&M. The best recipe changes with every release. The hooks this depends on arrived or changed in the last few months. Keeping the recipe current for each rule, on each platform, at each version, is work someone has to do continuously. Long agent sessions do not keep everything. When the context fills, the harness writes a summary of the conversation so far and continues from the summary. In Claude Code this is compaction, and it can be manual or automatic.
view-catalogue

The transcript of this session records every one. Between 9 September and 9 October there were eighteen compactions, all automatic. Each started from about 780,000 to 800,000 tokens of context and replaced it with 9,000 to 19,000: on average 1.7% kept. In total, 17.8 million tokens of conversation have been summarised away. Each summary took between 1.2 and 3.4 minutes to write. None of that is a criticism. A summary is what makes a month-long session possible at all, and this site would not exist in its current form without it. But it changes what a rule given in conversation is. Every time a summary is written, the rule has to be judged important enough to keep, in words the summariser chooses. Often that works. You are not told when it does not.
view-catalogue

The documentation is precise about what does survive: "Project-root CLAUDE.md survives compaction: after /compact, Claude re-reads it from disk and re-injects it into the session" (memory). Skills that were invoked are re-injected too, but "capped at 5,000 tokens per skill and 25,000 tokens total; oldest dropped first", and context that hooks added earlier is "summarized with the rest of the conversation" (context window). So there is already a pattern in the platform: what comes back from disk survives; what lived only in the conversation competes. A rule held by the agent it governs can fail in three different ways, and they need different fixes: Three ways a rule fails. Re-anchoring fixes forgetting. A second reader fixes the violation the author cannot see. A gate fixes the exception the agent argues itself into.

Re-anchoring is the first and cheapest of the three, and the others depend on it: a checker that reads the rules, and a gate that enforces them, are only as good as the rules they are given. In the vocabulary of the Agent Behaviour Policy, re-anchoring does not change a rule's barrier. An expectation stays "a rule in prose, enforced by nobody". What changes is that the expectation is reliably in view, which is the precondition for everything else. Claude Code has four documented places to do it (hooks): Hook When it fires What it can do for the policy SessionStart, matcher compact after every compaction, automatic or manual print the whole policy back: "Claude Code adds a SessionStart hook's plain-text stdout to Claude's context" UserPromptSubmit before each prompt is processed, including turns the harness starts itself add a short anchor every turn, or the full policy every Nth turn, as additionalContext PreCompact before compaction

log that it is about to happen, or block it Stop when the agent is about to end its turn check that something the policy requires actually happened, and if not, send the agent back once The first is the heart of it. A hook with the compact matcher fires "after compaction", and whatever it prints goes back into the context. Point it at the policy file and the policy is back, verbatim, the moment the summary is done. This is the configuration running in this session: { "hooks": { "SessionStart": [ { "matcher": "compact", "hooks": [ { "type": "command", "command": "python3 ~/.claude/abp/abp.py reanchor" } ] } ], "UserPromptSubmit": [ { "hooks": [ { "type": "command", "command": "python3 ~/.claude/abp/abp.py prompt" } ] } ], "Stop": [ { "hooks": [ { "type": "command", "command": "python3 ~/.claude/abp/abp.py stop" } ] } ] } }

The reanchor step prints a one-line header, "ABP re-anchored after compaction: v0.1 #a0d6d2. The rules below still apply, whatever the summary says", then the policy, and logs that it ran. The prompt step adds one line to every prompt, naming the policy, its version and its hash, so even a turn that starts from a thin summary knows the policy exists and where it lives. The cheapest version needs no hooks at all: a line in the project-root CLAUDE.md that says "read the behaviour policy in this file before acting", since that file is re-read from disk after compaction. And the bluntest version needs no configuration: the person types "read your instructions again". Both work. The point of the hooks is that neither depends on someone remembering. This is where the Agent Behaviour Policy stops being a document and becomes infrastructure. The same file does three jobs:
view-catalogue

Memory. It is what the re-anchoring hook prints back. The rules survive because they live on disk, not in the conversation. The checker's rulebook. It is what an independent checker reads. The draft guard's numbered rule file, written by the inbox agent, is already an ABP fragment under another name. The enforcement list. Every row carries its barrier, so the file says which rules are still expectations, and therefore which need a second reader or a gate next. A policy can also shape memory directly. A row can say "keep decisions in decisions.md" or "write the sources file before drafting", which moves the important parts of a session out of the conversation, where they are summarised, and into files, where they are not. That is still an expectation, but a checkable one: a hook can see whether the file was written.
view-catalogue

Re-anchoring has a weakness of its own: you cannot see it working. A hook that silently stopped firing, a settings file that was not loaded, a policy file that was moved, all look exactly like a session where everything is fine. So the second half of the technique is a canary. The idea is old. Van Halen's touring contract had a clause, in the middle of pages of technical requirements, asking for a bowl of M&M's with the brown ones removed. It was not vanity. As Snopes and NPR both report, it was a quick way to tell whether the venue had read the whole contract, including the parts about weight and power that kept the crew safe. Brown M&M's in the bowl meant: check everything else. The agent version is a short status report at the end of every few answers. Here is how it looks on a phone, in this session, on its first day:
view-catalogue

The report as it arrived on a phone, at the end of an answer in this session: the policy version and hash, re-anchors against compactions, cost, tokens, web requests, tool calls, and a measured rule. Three design choices make it more than decoration: The model does not write the numbers. The UserPromptSubmit hook computes the report from the session transcript and the harness's own cost record, and hands it to the agent with the instruction to paste it. A report the model wrote from memory would be one more thing to verify. The harness checks it was shown. When a report was due, the Stop hook reads the end of the answer. If the report is missing it sends the agent back, once, with the block to add; if it is still missing, it lets the turn end and logs the miss. That one rule, show the report, moves from expectation to setting.
view-catalogue

The person is part of the loop. After a few days the report is expected. When it does not arrive, the question is "where is my report?", and the answers are two commands: /abp-status shows it now, and /abp-reload makes the agent read the policy again and say its version and hash. Re-anchoring and the canary: one policy file, three hooks, two commands, and a person who notices when the report is missing.

The report does not ask the agent whether it complied; it reads the transcript and counts commits that were not preceded by a scan. The hooks loaded mid-session. They were added to a user settings file while the session was running, and the next prompt arrived carrying the policy's one-line anchor. The documentation says edits to hooks in settings files are "normally picked up automatically by the file watcher", and that is what happened here. The first report rendered on a phone at 41 characters wide without wrapping. The re-anchor after a compaction has now been observed. Updated 10 October 2026: at 12:03:36 UTC the session was summarised for the nineteenth time, automatically, from 789,144 tokens to 12,092. The SessionStart hook fired in the same second, printed the policy back from disk, and logged the event; the session resumed with the full policy in view, and the anchor line moved to 1 re-anchor for 1 compaction. The release that followed ran its leak scan before the commit, as rule 2 asks.
view-catalogue

Then the canary did its other job. At about 15:16 UTC the session's container was restarted, and everything outside the repository and the transcript went with it: the policy file, the script and the hooks in the user settings. The next prompt arrived with no anchor line. What the agent noticed first was its missing working files; the absent anchor confirmed that the hooks had gone too, and the first report due after the restart would have been missing, which is the signal the person watches for. The policy was restored from the copy the last re-anchor had printed into the conversation, and its hash came back as the same #a0d6d2, byte for byte. The script was rebuilt, carrying the last report's totals as a baseline. Lesson: a policy that lives on an ephemeral machine needs a copy somewhere that survives it, and the anchor line is worth keeping even when no report is due.

The leak scan counter was undercounting scans. It recognised one way of writing the scan, so commits that were scanned in a different way were counted as unscanned. The scan is now one script that every commit runs, and the counter looks for that script. The cost line can lag. It comes from the harness's cost record, which is written periodically rather than after every call. We are going to live with it for a while: how often to show it (every three answers today), which lines people actually read, and what else belongs there. That is the point of running it in the session that writes about it.

Everything above depends on features that are recent. Mods, the event system the draft guard used, arrived in Claude Code v2.1.287. onFailure: "block", which makes a settings hook fail closed, arrived in v2.1.295. Prompt hooks changed how they deny in v2.1.210. The compact matcher is what makes re-anchoring a five-line hook rather than a workaround. Six months ago the best way to re-anchor a policy was different, and six months from now it will be different again; on another platform it is different today.
view-catalogue

So a behaviour policy row is not only a rule and its barrier. It is a rule, its barrier, and the current recipe for keeping it: on this platform, at this version, use these hooks, placed here, and expect this barrier. That table goes out of date with every release, and keeping it current, testing it, and noting what each recipe costs is real, continuous work. Some recipes carry costs of their own: a recipe that uses mods means running code the agent wrote, unsandboxed, with your permissions, which is itself a row in the policy. That is why this session's report runs on settings hooks rather than a mod. That maintained, version-aware library of recipes is what I think people will pay for: not the policy, which they can write, but the current best way to make each row hold, curated for the tools they actually use.
view-catalogue

Re-anchoring does not enforce anything. It keeps rules in view. A rule in view is still an expectation. The canary is a setting, not a boundary. It lives in a settings file the session could edit. It tells you the policy is being read; it cannot stop an agent that decides to ignore it. A report can be pasted without the rules being followed. It shows that the hooks fired and the policy was loaded, and it measures what can be measured from the transcript. For the rest you need a reader or a gate. The summaries stay a black box. Re-anchoring does not show what a summary kept. It makes what matters independent of it. Write the rules down as an ABP file, short enough to re-read (a few hundred words), each rule with its barrier. Re-anchor after every compaction with a SessionStart hook on the compact matcher that prints the file, and a one-line anchor on every prompt.
