Abstract: I wanted one presentation from SlideShare and was offered a 30-day trial and then £10.99 a month. The author of the deck receives nothing from that subscription, under an uploader agreement that grants the platform a royalty-free licence to monetise, charge for, sublicense and train models on the work, and I am one of those authors, with 69 decks uploaded over fifteen years. This article does three things. It says what happened to SlideShare, from a 2006 start through LinkedIn and Scribd to the September 2021 paywall, and why a service with a PDF viewer and a file store has not been replaced: fifteen years of embeds and links, which is inertia in Wardley's sense. It sets out what an author can ask the old platform for today, under the right of access and, in the EU, the copyright transparency duty, including the two questions platforms do not expect, how many downloads and what revenue. And it designs the service the author would have chosen, on the primitives this site already publishes: every author's decks in a vault the host cannot read, access decided by keys rather than settings, a read key for what is free, a receipt turned into a ten-minute key for what is paid once, a revocable grant for what is private, decryption in the browser, an attested enclave for the one step that needs plaintext, seven roles that no single company holds, and a split of 85% to the author on a ledger the author can recompute. The plan is published as a vault with a working mock, the Deck Vault, with its economics worked for one author and its risks as an acceptance register. The marginal cost is storage and bandwidth, which are near zero; the hard row is the fixed part of a card fee, which the plan says so about rather than hides. Somebody should build it. The author will build the first step for their own decks.

The screen that started this, as shown to a reader on 6 October 2026, with the deck and its author left out of the crop. One download offered as a subscription; the author of the deck receives nothing from it. The three complaints, and the one that is not: the licence the author signed allows all of it. One download, one subscription decision. The reader is offered a 30-day trial and then £10.99 a month, $11.99 in the US. There is no one-off option unless the author switched one on, and the setting was reported as off by default when the paywall arrived in September 2021.

The author receives nothing, by agreement. The uploader agreement of August 2024 says it "does not entitle You to any payment, royalties, remuneration, or other compensation", and grants a royalty-free, sublicensable licence to "monetize, charge money for, restrict access to view, restrict access to download, advertise against, create derivative works from, train machine learning, large language, or other statistical or data models" the work. The same company forbids its users from training models on the same content. Why it has not been replaced. Fifteen years of embeds, backlinks and search ranking point at one domain, and about forty million visits a month still arrive, most from search. That is inertia, and it is a stronger moat than the technology.

What an author can ask today. A right-of-access request for the counts and the recipients, with the European Data Protection Board's guidance that derived data counts and the Court of Justice's ruling that recipients must be named; and, in EU states that implemented it without a payment condition, the copyright transparency duty on "all revenues generated". The UK did not implement that duty. The design. Every author's decks in a vault the host cannot read. Keys decide access: a read key for what is free, a receipt turned into a ten-minute key for what is paid once, a revocable grant for what is private. Decryption in the browser. Seven roles, no single owner. The author takes 85%, on a ledger in their own vault.

The economics. Serving one author's whole shelf for a month costs less than the incumbent charges one reader for one download. The hard row is the card fee, 1.5% plus 20p with a 30p minimum, which eats a fifth of a one-pound download; wallets, batching and an open payments protocol are how the plan gets under it. Status. A plan and a mock, published as a vault with a read key. Nothing in the build order beyond the vault exists. The author will build the first step for their own 69 decks.

SlideShare was founded in October 2006 as a place to upload a deck, embed it anywhere and link to it, and it spread because it worked. LinkedIn bought it in May 2012 for about $119 million. Microsoft bought LinkedIn in 2016. In August 2020 LinkedIn announced that Scribd was acquiring SlideShare, with operations moving over on 24 September 2020 and forty million presentations cited. Scribd's own help page from that month said that users would not need a subscription to access or upload, but that "for full access, including the ability to download content directly to your device, a subscription is required" from September 2021. When the paywall arrived, authors found an account-level checkbox, "Allow users to read and download your slideshows without a subscription", which one writer who documented it in October 2021 reported as off by default. The checkbox still exists in Scribd's 2025 help pages, with a per-upload toggle beside it. Scribd's corporate site in 2026 describes SlideShare as twenty-five million presentations, which is fifteen million fewer than the number cited at the sale; the company has not explained the difference publicly.
Twenty years of one service. The owner changed twice and the terms changed once; the links did not change at all. In Wardley's terms this is inertia, and it is also the opening.

Why nothing replaced it. Third-party traffic estimates put slideshare.net at thirty-six to forty-three million visits a month across 2025 and 2026, with seventy to eighty per cent arriving from search and India the largest country. The service persists as a search artefact: every public deck is indexed, embedded on conference pages and blogs, and linked from the decks that cite it. Simon Wardley's observation is the right one: "Past success breeds inertia." For years the balance was good enough that few authors thought about the terms, and a service people feel good about linking to is shared; the sharing built the moat before the terms moved. A replacement needs the authors to move, and the authors' links are the thing the incumbent holds. None of the alternatives I looked at pays authors per download; the only author-payment model among them is a pooled royalty with an unpublished rate.

I want to be precise here because the complaint is easy to overstate. The uploader keeps copyright. The licence is non-exclusive. I uploaded most of my decks under a Creative Commons licence and I am content for them to be shared. What the author grants, in the agreement last updated on 1 August 2024, is "a worldwide, non-exclusive, transferable, assignable, fully paid-up, royalty-free license (with the right to grant and authorize sublicenses)" to, among other things, "monetize, charge money for, restrict access to view, restrict access to download, advertise against, create derivative works from, train machine learning, large language, or other statistical or data models, and otherwise exploit Your Content", and the agreement says it "does not entitle You to any payment, royalties, remuneration, or other compensation in exchange for posting Your Content." The general terms, updated in September 2026, forbid users from using "any content made available through the Services for the purpose of training, fine-tuning, or otherwise developing a large language model". The right the platform reserves for itself it withholds from its users. Whether the right has been exercised, I could not find out; no public report of a licensing deal or of the corpus in a named training set turned up, and the dashboard does not say.

So the three complaints are these. The reader is sold a subscription for one file that the author would have given away or sold for a pound. The author has no say and no share, and cannot change the terms for their own work except by deleting it. And the author does not know where the work went. The licence allows all three, which is why the complaint is not that anyone broke a rule. It is that the service an author would have chosen does not exist, and in 2026 it could. Before designing anything, there is the question of what an author can do with the platform they are already on. Three things. Switch the setting on. Readers can then download without a subscription. It is per account, with a per-upload override, and it is the reason my decks can be downloaded and the deck I wanted could not.

Send a right-of-access request, under GDPR Article 15 or its UK equivalent, asking the ordinary things and two unusual ones. First, the view and download counts recorded against each upload, by month. The platform's likely answer is that these are statistics about content, not personal data. The author's answer is that a count held against a named author's upload, in that author's account, relates to an identifiable person: the European Data Protection Board's guidelines on the right of access say it "includes both inferred and derived data, including personal data created by a service provider", and the Court of Justice has held that information relates to a person where "by reason of its content, purpose or effect, it is linked" to them. Second, the recipients: whether the uploads or text from them have been licensed to third parties, including for training, and to whom. The Court of Justice ruled in January 2023 that a controller must name the actual recipients where it can, not only categories. The deadline is one month, extendable by two with notice. A revenue figure is harder to compel, because the access right discloses data that is processed rather than creating a new statistic, and a subscription platform may not attribute revenue to authors at all; but "we do not compute it" is an answer worth having in writing. The letter is in the vault, as a template.

In the EU, ask under copyright law. Article 19 of the 2019 Copyright Directive gives authors the right to receive, at least once a year, "up to date, relevant and comprehensive information on the exploitation of their works ... in particular as regards modes of exploitation, all revenues generated and remuneration due" from those they licensed. Whether a royalty-free upload licence falls within it is untested: Germany's implementation applies only to licences granted for payment, France's has no such condition, and no case on a user-generated-content platform was found. The UK said in January 2020 it would not implement the Directive, so a UK author has the access right and the terms, and nothing else. I will send the request for my own 69 decks, and the answer goes in the first article the ledger below is built for.

Now the service I would have chosen. It is built from things this site already documents, and the vault at the end of this article is the plan with a working mock. Every author gets a vault the host cannot read. Who may open a deck is decided by which key a device holds: a publishing key for the author, a content key per deck, a read key for what is free, a receipt turned into a ten-minute key for what is paid once, and a revocable grant for what is private. Design sketch; proposal.

Every author gets a vault. An encrypted, versioned store of their own files, on any host, that nobody who does not hold a key can read, including the host. The author's device encrypts a deck before it leaves; the host receives ciphertext and a size. That one decision carries the rest, because a service that cannot read the content cannot sell it, index it for someone else, or change the terms under which it is read. This is the sgit vault model, which the security page describes and which the team in the previous articles runs on.

Keys, not settings. The author's publishing key is bound to a passkey on their device and signs every decision: access rules, grants, revocations, content credentials, licences. Each deck is encrypted under its own content key, wrapped to the publishing key, so re-keying one deck touches nothing else. A read key per deck, derived one way from the content key as vault credentials describes, is published for decks the author marks read-free; it cannot write and cannot be turned back. A grant is the content key wrapped to a recipient's public key with an expiry, signed by the author; revocation is a signed statement and a re-key. And a receipt from the payments service, for a one-off payment, is turned by an attested enclave into the content key wrapped to the reader's device for ten minutes. A setting lives on a server and changes when the server's owner changes. A key lives with the author and is verified by anyone.

Decryption on the client. The reader's browser fetches ciphertext and decrypts it in the tab, as every vault page on this site does today. No account to read what is free. The one bounded exception is the unlock service, an attested enclave that handles one deck's plaintext in memory for one request, to wrap a key, render a preview or build an index, and whose operator cannot read it; the device checks the attestation before trusting it, in the way the personal agent design set out this morning.

The incumbent is one company holding the files, the keys, the payments, the identities and the front page, which is what lets the terms change for everyone at once and what makes it one thing to buy and sell. The plan separates the roles so that no party holds more than one of the content, the keys and the money, and so that each can be provided by several parties the author chooses between. Seven roles: storage host, key service, unlock service, payments, identity and provenance, the front, and add-ons. What each does, what each sees, who could run it, and which exist today. Sovereignty by construction: an archive can hold a nation's authors' ciphertext without reading it.

The storage host stores the vault and serves ciphertext to key-holders; it sees sizes and timings, and it can be any object store, a national archive, a university, or the author's own bucket. The key service publishes public keys and bindings and records grants and revocations as signed statements; it never holds a private key. The unlock service is the enclave. The payments service takes a one-off payment, issues a signed receipt the enclave accepts, settles to the author and publishes a statement the author can recompute. The identity service binds the publishing key to a person in tiers, from key-only through a domain or ORCID binding to a verified identity or an institution's signature, and signs content credentials. The front is the website people see, and because it works from a read key alone, several fronts can list the same vaults; the mock in the vault is one. Add-ons, a semantic graph of a deck, an infographic, question answering, a translation, run inside the enclave on the plaintext, are approved by the author before they are sold, and pay the author the same share.

The sovereignty follows from the separation. Each role can be provided per country, per profession or per company. An archive can hold its authors' ciphertext without being able to read it, which is a role archives already understand. A professional body can verify identities without touching the files. A cooperative of authors can run the payments. An author moves between providers by changing a key binding, not by migrating content, which is the shape the supply chain of vaults argued for one domain over. Pay once and download the original. The payments service sees a payment, the enclave sees a receipt, the host sees a read; none sees all three. The ledger line goes into the author's vault, and the month's statement is computed from lines like it.

Read for free. The reader opens the deck on any front. The browser fetches ciphertext with the deck's read key and decrypts it. The front appends a read to the author's ledger through a write-only lane: a count, not a person.

Pay once and download the original. The reader presses Download original and sees the price the author set, the author's 85% and the platform's 15%. The payments service takes the payment and issues a signed receipt naming the deck's hash, valid for minutes. The enclave checks the receipt and the author's access rule and wraps the content key to the reader's device for ten minutes. The browser downloads the ciphertext and decrypts the original locally. The ledger line names the deck, the amount, the split, the receipt and the hash served. No subscription is offered for a single file; a subscription is allowed for a reader who wants thirty a month, and its revenue is split to authors by downloads on the same statement.

Share privately, and take it back. For a deck marked by grant only, the author wraps the content key to a recipient's public key with an expiry and signs the grant. To revoke, the author signs a revocation; the enclave stops honouring the grant at once and the deck is re-keyed on the next commit. A file already downloaded is the reader's, and the plan says so on every grant rather than pretending otherwise. Publish, and migrate. The author drops a file; the browser hashes and encrypts it and commits the ciphertext; the identity service signs a content credential; the enclave produces a preview and an index. Migration from the incumbent is downloading one's own decks, for authors who switched the setting on, and publishing them with permanent per-deck addresses and an embed that works from a read key, so the links that pointed at the old domain can be updated once.

Serving an author's whole shelf for a month costs less than the incumbent charges one reader for one download. Where a one-off price goes by card, from 50p to the incumbent's subscription for scale: under a pound the rail eats the price. Illustrative figures with list prices as inputs. Take my own case: 69 decks, about 5 MB each, 345 MB in all. Object storage at list price is about $0.015 per gigabyte-month on a provider that charges nothing for egress, and up to $0.09 per gigabyte of egress on one that does. Serving 400 downloads and 9,000 reads a month, with a 1 MB preview per read, costs between nothing and under a pound. Two seconds of enclave time per unlock adds less than a penny. The whole month's infrastructure for an author's shelf costs less than the incumbent charges one reader for one download. For one author, a month Decks 69, about 5 MB each Storage under 1p
Bandwidth 0p to 77p, depending on the host's egress price Enclave time under 1p The incumbent's price for one download £10.99 a month after a 30-day trial

The thing that does not scale down is the payment. A UK card through a mainstream processor costs 1.5% plus 20p with a 30p minimum, so a 50p download loses two fifths of its price to the rail, a £1 download loses about a fifth, and the plan's default of £1.50 loses about fifteen per cent. The plan's answer is to state this rather than hide it. The split is 85% to the author and 15% to the platform, and the platform pays the card fee out of its 15%, which at the default price leaves it almost nothing on a card payment. The platform's margin is in wallet top-ups, where one card fee covers several downloads, in batching settlements, and in add-ons at a 70% author share; it is not in the author's share. An open payments protocol moved to a foundation in 2026 with card networks and processors among its members and is settling machine-to-machine payments at fractions of a cent, so the first readers to pay per download cheaply may be agents; a person still needs a wallet, and the plan's first open question is which rail a UK or EU front can offer a person at under five pence a transaction.

The positive loop the plan bets on: authors who are paid publish more and publish here first; readers who are not sold a subscription for one file come back; fronts compete on discovery and on the share they take, because the content is not theirs to lock.

Strip the storage and payments away and what remains is the thing a reader cannot get anywhere else: assurance that this file, with this hash, was published by this person, who is who they say they are. Every deck already carries a signature over its hash from a key bound to an identity, so the assurance is cheap to produce. A conference wants to know the decks on its page are the speakers'. An employer wants to know a candidate's deck is theirs. A journalist wants a date that cannot move. A reader wants to know the version they are reading is the one that was published and the forty copies elsewhere are copies. On the incumbent, an upload is bound to an account and an account to an email; here it is bound to a key, and the key to a person in tiers the badge names. This is the argument the news articles on this site made about selling provenance and trust, applied to presentations.

The plan is published as a vault, Deck Vault, with a read key on its page. It holds ten plan documents, the data behind them, the right-of-access letter, a register of ten risks written as acceptances with a holder and a date, and a working mock: the shelf of a fictional author with twelve decks, a deck page with pay-once and the split, the author's own view with a statement they can recompute from the ledger, the seven roles, the five flows, the economics and the rights. The app is built as web components in the shape coding.sgit.ai documents, three files per component on one base, bundled into one file for the vault host by a script in the vault; the source stays split so the tool can be reviewed as code, as the review brief asks. Press the pay button on a deck and the ledger line appears on the author's view.

A deck page in the mock, after the pay button: the content credential, the hash, read free in the browser, pay once with the split shown, and the ledger line the payment would write. Vaults with client-side encryption, one-way read keys, write-only lanes and decryption in the browser exist and are documented with their limits on this site. Confidential compute with attested key release is sold by three cloud vendors. Payment processors issue receipts; identity verifiers charge a few dollars a check; content credentials ship in cameras and phones; the EU's identity wallets are due by the end of 2026. The Agent Behaviour Policy for the platform's agents is written in the vault.

What does not exist: the unlock enclave for decks, the per-task key release, grants and revocation as a service, the receipt that becomes a key, a front that lists a vault from a read key alone, the migration tool, and any payment rail that gets a person under five pence a transaction in the UK. The vault's build order has nine steps, and step zero is one author's shelf as a vault with per-deck read keys and an embed per deck. I will build step zero for my own decks, because I want a home for them that I hold the keys to. The rest is for whoever takes the plan; what they may not do and still call it this is written in the vault's last chapter. The agent team as it runs and A personal agent that keeps your secrets: the vault properties, the three classes of information, and the enclave with per-task key release this plan reuses.

A supply chain of vaults: one vault per party, lanes between them, no platform in the middle. The future of news is the story vault, not the paywall and The reader was always the product: selling provenance rather than access, and what platforms did to the people who made the content. The SaaS apocalypse will be decided by inertia, not by AI: the same Wardley point, applied to the incumbents of software. Vault credentials, the security model and append-lane messaging: the read key, what the host sees, and the write-only lane the ledger uses. Abstract: For as long as I have worked in security there has been no clear winner between open source and proprietary software. Open source had the code in view, and fixes that sweep a bug's variants; it also had very few people and almost no budget for the slow, expensive reviews that find the hard bugs. Proprietary software had the budget, and the cover of being hidden, and got away with a lot. That balance just moved. Models can now run deep security reviews over and over, on every project, at a cost that used to buy one consultant for a day. The thing open source lacked was paid attention, and that is the thing that just became abundant. I thought Chainguard had started publishing the projects where its AI found nothing; I could not find that. What I found is better: the maintainer of curl writing about a year in which AI review first drowned his project in noise, then produced hundreds of real fixes, then a frontier scan that found a single low-severity bug, and then, today, deeper tools finding more. That is what a project getting harder to break looks like. Put it next to two things I have argued before, that sovereignty needs open code and open schemas, and that the business is maintaining the version each customer actually runs, and three forces meet at one place: the least amount of code in production.

Open source against proprietary: the balance that just moved. Open source had the source in view and paid for few reviews; proprietary had the budget and the cover of being hidden. Cheap, deep, model-driven security review changes one side of that balance far more than the other.
in-short

No clear winner, until now. Open source had visibility and few reviewers; proprietary had budget and cover. The eyeballs get cheap. Deep security review by models, repeated on every change, is the attention open source could never pay for. curl shows the shape. Noise, then hundreds of real fixes, then a frontier scan that found one bug, then deeper tools finding more. The scale is real. Over a thousand projects scanned by one lab; thousands of patches by one coalition; maintainers asking for it to slow down. Higher bars, fewer and better projects. Low-hanging fruit disappears; contributions need proof; provenance matters. Three forces meet. Secure, sovereign and paid for, all pointing at the same place. The least code in production. What the maintainer sells, what the customer runs, and what security wants.
balance

The argument for open source security has always been Eric Raymond's, from The Cathedral and the Bazaar: "Given enough eyeballs, all bugs are shallow." The argument against it has always been that the eyeballs were not there. Most open source is understaffed and unpaid; in Tidelift's 2024 survey, as The Register reported, "The portion of respondents who reported they are unpaid hobbyists remains at 60 percent". Projects used by companies with thousands of developers are maintained by a handful of people with almost no revenue. Nobody pays for the slow security review that takes weeks, the kind I have done many times, where finding the bug, proving it and documenting it is work you cannot do in five minutes. The low-hanging fruit was eaten fast; the deep work often never happened.
balance

Proprietary software had the opposite profile. It had budget for security teams and paid reviews. It also had cover: code nobody outside could read, fewer attackers looking, products hidden behind other environments. A lot of software got away with things that would not have survived being public. If the source of some of the major SaaS products were exposed tomorrow, a lot would be found. What open source did have was efficiency. Anyone can read the code, and when a serious bug is reported publicly, the fix rarely stops at the one bug: the variations get hunted down too. We know how to build secure systems; the proof is the number that survive very motivated attackers. The question was always who could afford the attention.
cheap

That is what changed. I now run security reviews with models on the products I work on, and the depth is remarkable: it finds real issues, I can point it at particular areas, we argue about what it found, and we fix it. That used to take a specialist weeks. It now takes an afternoon, and it can run again on the next change. The thing open source lacked was paid attention, and that is the thing that just became abundant. The thing proprietary software had, being hidden, is worth less every month, because the same reviews run on whatever ships, leaks or can be reverse engineered. That is the move: open source on steroids.
cheap

The numbers are already large. Anthropic's update on its Project Glasswing in May reported scanning "more than 1,000 open-source projects" and estimated "6,202 high- or critical-severity vulnerabilities" among the findings; the bottleneck, it said, is now "how quickly we can verify, disclose, and patch", and "some have even asked us to slow down" the rate of disclosures. Chainguard's Athena coalition reported, at its launch in June, "2,000 patches across 500 projects", and its harness, which Chainguard, mapped described, has been run "against over 65 projects and validated over 680 findings". In DARPA's AI Cyber Challenge final in 2025, the systems "discovered 54 unique synthetic vulnerabilities" and also found "18 real, non-synthetic vulnerabilities".
curl

One project, one year of machine eyeballs: curl, from its maintainer's own posts. A bug bounty that found 87 vulnerabilities; a year of reports that were mostly noise; a first wave of AI-assisted reports that triggered hundreds of fixes; the end of the bounty; a frontier scan that found one bug; and, in October, deeper tools finding more. I went looking for something I thought I had seen, Chainguard publishing the projects where its AI hunting found nothing, with curl among them. I could not find it, from Chainguard or anyone else. What I found tells the story better, in the words of curl's maintainer, Daniel Stenberg. First the noise. curl ended its bug bounty on 31 January 2026. Over its life it had found "87 confirmed vulnerabilities", but by 2025 "Not even one in twenty was real." Low-effort, machine-written reports were swamping a small team.
curl

Then the real wave. In the autumn of 2025, AI-assisted reports from careful researchers and tools started landing real bugs, and by May he counted that earlier tools had "triggered somewhere between two and three hundred bugfixes". Then the quiet scan. In May, a frontier model's scan of curl found one vulnerability, "yes, as in singular one", of low severity, and its report said "Zero memory-safety vulnerabilities found." His conclusion was the right one: "Any project that has not scanned their source code with AI powered tooling will likely find huge number of flaws". And then, today, more. An audit with AI tooling produced "no less than thirty-five published curl vulnerabilities", a high-severity bug was found by Anthropic "using their new OSS Scanner", and curl 8.23.0 shipped with 24 security fixes.
curl

That is not a project failing. It is a project getting harder to break, wave by wave, with each better tool finding what the last one could not, and the fixes sweeping the variants. The cost has moved from paying for attention to judging it: the maintainers' time is now the bottleneck, which is why curl's contribution rules now say that "If you asked an AI tool to find problems in curl, you must make sure to reveal this fact in your report."
changes

So I expect the bar to rise everywhere. More findings, with more proof. Contributions held to a much higher standard, because the small fixes a newcomer used to send can now be done by anyone with a model, and should be. Fewer projects, and better ones. The long tail of tiny packages and single-purpose libraries, the dependency trees with hundreds of entries, will shrink, because a lot of very specific little APIs can now be written in place, better.
changes

What will not go away is security research by people motivated to find what the tools miss, domain experts who understand what a project is for, and maintainers who keep it working. And provenance will matter more: where a piece of code came from, who wrote it, who reviewed it. In Simon Wardley's terms, you do not want mission-critical code written at explorer speed; you want it industrialised. In his words, "Town Planners are brilliant people. They are able to take something and industrialise it". Accountable code, reviewed up to the line, is what makes all of this scale, and it is the same graph from story to line that code review as a fractal semantic graph draws.
forces

Three forces meeting at the least code in production: open source becoming very secure, open source becoming required for sovereignty, and open source with commercial models that pay for maintenance. Where they meet is the customer running exactly the code they need, maintained by the people who know it best. Put this next to two things I have argued before, and they line up. Secure. The eyeballs open source never had, at last, and a higher bar for everything that goes in. Sovereign. You cannot have sovereignty without open source and open schemas. Sovereignty is the ability to move: move the data, the compute and the applications. You can only move what you can read and run elsewhere, and with competition on service rather than lock-in, the bigger companies should win because they serve better, not because the customer cannot leave.
forces

Paid for. The business model I already run in my sgit environments, in vaults and in RiskMandate: the customer gets a private repository with their deployment, their configuration and only the features they actually use, and pays for it to be maintained. They could do it themselves, and then they would have to keep doing it. The SaaS apocalypse made the same point from the other side: what people really bought was never the features, it was that the thing is maintained, and the future is companies that take what was built and run it. This is not a free-for-all; open source is a licence, as What open source is, and is not explained, and Open source is not free measured how little of its value comes back to it. Maintenance as the product is how more of it can.
least-code

Here is the irony where the three meet. The customer wants only the features they use. The maintainer who sells the customised version wants as little as possible to maintain. Security wants as little as possible to review, patch and attack. Everyone ends up aligned on running the least amount of code in production, which is the argument of The minimum code below, where removing what a use case never runs took one real tool from 1,500 files to 428. For the first time, the incentives of the people who write open source, the people who sell it and the people who secure it point the same way. That is the intersection I think we are at: open source that is more secure because the eyeballs finally got cheap, required because sovereignty needs it, and paid for because maintaining exactly what each customer runs is a business.
limits

No list of clean projects. I could not find Chainguard or anyone else publishing the projects where AI hunting found nothing; curl's story is the evidence instead. curl is not clean. It is a well-run project being found harder to break, and still having bugs found, as of today. The counts are the reporters' own. Anthropic's, Chainguard's and DARPA's figures are as they published them. The cost and depth of model review are my experience. On the products I work on; others will see different results. The future part is an argument. Fewer and better projects, a shrinking long tail, and maintenance as the business are predictions. If you maintain an open source project and want help with review at this new scale, or you want your version of one maintained for you, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.

Abstract: The homepage of this site has to be fresh every day, and today it changes only when someone releases the site. I want a job that runs every morning at about 05:45, reads the latest articles, the wires and what is happening in the industry, and writes a new edition of the homepage. And I want that homepage to be a vault. Every edition a commit with a signed tag and its own version line; every edition carrying the links it showed and why, a screenshot of itself and the release note that explains it; any past homepage one commit id away; variants side by side for A/B tests; and anyone who wants their own homepage, in another language or for another audience, forks the vault. The encrypted objects can be served as plain files from S3, a CDN or GitHub Pages, read in the browser with a published read key. I had two facts wrong: this site is not served by a Lambda, it is on GitHub Pages; the Lambda is the vault API the wire reads through, and that is where the time goes, at 317 milliseconds a request against 44 for a static file. This site's agent built the homepage vault locally: three editions, three signed tags, a static export, and a browser that rendered today's edition in four requests, yesterday's in three, and nothing at all inside two minutes. A stats lane took 300 page-load beacons. This is the design, the measurements, and the brief.

The homepage as a vault: a morning job writes an edition and tags it, the encrypted objects go to plain static hosting, a small shell on GitHub Pages carries the read key and a snapshot for search engines, and the browser reads the edition. A stats lane and a daily run of synthetic users feed the next morning's edition. Dashed boxes are proposed.
in-short

Fresh every morning. A scheduled job writes a new homepage edition at about 05:45, or every hour if we want. The homepage is a vault. Every edition a commit, a signed tag and a version of its own. Every past homepage, one commit away. With its links, its screenshot and its release note. Plain files, not a function. The encrypted objects can sit on S3, a CDN or GitHub Pages. Where the time goes. 317 ms a request through the vault API, 44 ms from GitHub Pages. Measured locally. Today's edition in 4 requests, yesterday's in 3, nothing at all inside two minutes. Variants, stats and synthetic users. A/B variants in one commit, a stats lane for page loads, a daily run of readers who do not exist. Fork it. A homepage for another language, culture or publisher is a fork of the vault.
why

The homepage is the page that most needs to be fresh and the one that changes least. Today it is generated when the site is released, so it moves when I publish and stands still when I do not. What I want is an edition: every morning, a job that looks at the latest articles, the wires, and what is happening in the industry we write about, and decides what leads, what follows and what rotates out. The structure, the highlights and the selections are the edition. Parts of the page can stay dynamic: the wire and the full list of articles load live, from their own sources, as they do now.
correction

I had two facts wrong. This site is not served by a Lambda function: newsroom.sgit.ai is on GitHub Pages, whose responses say server: GitHub.com. The Lambda is the vault API, behind CloudFront, that the Industry Wire reads its vaults through. And the wire is half of what I described: it does read encrypted vaults in the browser with a published read key, as Two agents, one vault explained, but through that API, not from plain files.
correction

That is where the time goes. On one cold load of the wire from this sandbox, the browser made eight requests to the API, one after the other, each taking between 360 and 810 milliseconds, and the last one ended 3.9 seconds after the page itself had loaded. On a warm connection, one request to the vault API took a median of 317 milliseconds; one request to GitHub Pages for a small file took 44. The API also sent no cache header for an immutable object, which sgit.ai's own measurements noted in September: "the read endpoint returned no Cache-Control header at all for an immutable object".
static

The good news is that sgit already reads from plain files. sgit.ai's update Take the API out of the path cloned the same vault in 65.4 seconds through the serverless API and in 2.63 seconds from plain GETs: "Twenty five times faster, with nothing about the vault changed." It was honest that the static host was on the same machine, so a real CDN adds its own latency. Its conclusion is the one that matters: the API is "a convenience over a store, not a requirement of it".
static

The browser side is documented in Static hosting: the same reader runs against the API or a folder of files laid out as api/vault/read/<vault id>/bare/, where content-addressed objects can be cached for ever and the one ref, the pointer to the latest commit, must never be. It also names the limit: "Read-only and frozen." A static copy changes only when it is exported again, which is not a problem for a homepage that is released once a day. It is exactly the model.
demo

Three editions of the demo homepage vault, each a commit with a signed tag, carrying its page, the links it showed and why, both variants, its release note and a screenshot of itself. Any edition opens again from its commit id. This site's agent built the homepage vault on a local vault server with sgit 0.21.0. A small script, the edition job, reads the articles and their graphs and writes one edition: index.html with the structure, edition.json with the lead, the picks, the topics and every link shown with the reason it was chosen, variants/a.html and variants/b.html, a release note in releases/, and a screenshot in shots/. It ran three times, for 13 October, the morning of 14 October and the evening of 14 October, and each run was committed, pushed and tagged: home-v0.1.0, home-v0.1.1, home-v0.1.2, each "signed by this clone". The homepage now has its own version line, separate from the site's.
demo

Then the agent exported the vault as plain files with sgit publish, put the objects in the documented layout, and served them from a plain static server with the cache headers S3 or a CDN would send. A reader cloned it with --transport static in 0.38 seconds, against 0.33 through the local API: on one machine, the network costs nothing either way. In a browser, using the same reader the wire uses, the results were these. Today's edition, cold. 4 requests and 4.7 KB: the ref, the commit, the tree and the page. The same reader inside two minutes. No requests at all: the ref is reused for 120 seconds and the objects come from the browser's cache. Yesterday's edition. 3 requests, by commit id; no ref is needed, because history is just another object. The other variant. 2 requests, for the variants folder and the page.
demo

Those are counts, not network times. With 44 milliseconds a request, four chained requests are about 0.2 seconds from static files; at 317, about 1.3 seconds through the API. The live vault docs on sgit.ai found the same shape in production: a cold load of 18 objects, then "one 69-byte request per reader per two minutes".
sequence

One page load: the shell from GitHub Pages, then four chained requests to the static host for the ref, the commit, the tree and the page, decrypted in the browser; the dynamic slots load from their own vaults; a beacon goes to the stats lane. Each step waits for the one before, so where the bytes come from decides the time.
sequence

The order matters because each step needs the one before it. The shell comes from GitHub Pages, with the read key and the reader. The ref says which commit is today's edition; the commit names the tree; the tree names the page. Only the ref can change, so it is never cached; everything else is named by its own hash and can be cached by every layer in between for ever. The browser decrypts with the read key, renders, and records which variant it showed. The read key is public on purpose: sgit.ai's credentials page says it is "derived from the vault key by a one-way function, so a read key can never be turned back into write access."
history

Version control of the homepage is the feature I like most. Every edition is a commit, so any day's homepage can be opened again exactly as it was, with the links it showed, the screenshot of how it looked, and the release note that says why it changed. That also means we can rotate: the job can see every link that has led the page and give the rest a turn. Variants sit in the same commit, so an A/B test is a choice the page makes, not a second deployment. And a fork is a whole homepage: another language, another culture, another publisher, or one reader who wants their own front page, takes the vault, changes the edition rules and publishes their own.
stats

What the measurements say: the live numbers from this sandbox to newsroom.sgit.ai and its vault API, and the vault numbers from a local static server and a local vault server, which count requests and bytes, not network time.
stats

For the test to mean anything, we need to know what happened. An append lane is "A write-only channel attached to a vault, gated by a token the writer holds and nothing else", and sgit.ai already has a brief for telemetry through one. The agent configured a lane on the homepage vault and sent it 300 synthetic page-load beacons, each with the edition, the variant, a load time and whether a link was clicked: 2.6 milliseconds each on the local server, and all 300 read back with the enum key. The click rates in that test were invented by the script, so they show the plumbing, not a result. Two limits apply. A static host cannot take writes, so the beacons still go to the API; and the cap is "1000 pending files per token → 507", so the morning job has to collect and clear the lane every day, writing the totals into a stats vault.
stats

The other daily input is the synthetic readers. How to run synthetic users describes five to ten invented readers who drive a real browser and report what they saw; run every morning against the live page, with their findings and timings in their own vault, they tell us when something has broken or slowed down before a reader does.
handled

Search engines. sgit.ai's case study is plain about it: "Search engines and agents see an empty shell." The shell on GitHub Pages should therefore carry a plain snapshot of today's edition, generated from the same commit and naming it. Surfaces gives the rule for that: "What must never be duplicated is the content itself"; the snapshot is a projection of the edition, not a second copy to edit. Revocation. sgit publish warns that bytes deployed into a git repository "stay in its history after any later deletion, so rotation cannot revoke access to what you publish now", and suggests object storage when that matters. For a public homepage it does not, but it is a reason to put the static objects on S3 rather than in this repository.
handled

A mirror needs a reader. sgit.ai learnt this the hard way when it removed its own vault mirror: "give a mirror a reader before giving it a remote". The homepage vault has a reader from the first day: the homepage.
brief

Start on a separate page. Build /front/ from the homepage vault and leave the homepage alone until the numbers say it is better. The edition job. Every morning at 05:45 UK time, read the articles, the wires and the stats, write one edition, commit it, tag it home-vX.Y.Z and add its screenshot and release note. Plain files. Export each edition to S3 behind a CDN, with immutable objects cached for a year and the ref never cached; keep the vault API as the writer's path only. A shell with a snapshot. A small page on GitHub Pages with the read key, the reader, and a plain snapshot of the edition for search engines, naming its commit. Every edition reachable. A "this page on another day" link that opens any tag by its commit id.
brief

Variants and stats. Two variants per edition, assigned in the browser; a beacon per load to a stats lane; the morning job collects, totals and clears it, and writes the totals to a stats vault. Synthetic users daily. Five readers against /front/ and the homepage, findings and timings in their own vault. Prove it. Time the live cold and warm loads of /front/ against the current homepage, every day for two weeks, and report; move the homepage only if /front/ is at least as fast and the variants show which works better. Move the wire too. The same export for the wire's vaults would take its eight API requests off the reader's path.
limits

The demo is local. A local vault server and a local static server; the vault numbers count requests and bytes, not network time. The live timings are from this sandbox. One location, medians of ten requests; readers elsewhere will see other numbers. The beacons and clicks were synthetic. They show the lane works, not which variant is better. Nothing is scheduled yet. The morning job, the S3 export and /front/ are proposed. A/B tests need readers. With this site's traffic, a difference between variants may take weeks to show. If you want your own homepage to be a vault, or want to fork ours, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

A voice memo of mine on 14 October 2026, written by this site's agent in the voice of this site; the argument and the editorial responsibility are mine. The demo and the timings were run by this site's agent on 14 October 2026; a research agent read sgit.ai's documentation, and the quotes were checked against it.
