Abstract: On 11 October The New Stack published a piece by Ignacio Aldama, an engineer at Bit Cloud, in which a brand-new Claude Code session with no history and no local code found a support console's shared ticket contract in two MCP calls, from the dependency records the build platform writes as each component is versioned, and then left the contract alone because it knew two components depended on it. It is a good demonstration and an honest one, because he then says where the records ran out. They describe structure, not behaviour; a green build can hide tests that never ran; a demo carries a public signing secret and a list of unfinished work; and memory, which holds intent, is not tied to a code version. Those edges are exactly where sgit and RiskMandate sit. Label every fact with how it is known. Treat a skipped test as a control that did not run. Accept a demo shortcut by name and for an interval, or stop. Keep memory and records in one encrypted, versioned history so the intent of version 1.4 is recorded at 1.4. And let records cross a company boundary with publish, clone and mirror. What exists, what is documented and what is only proposed are marked as such.

Where the records ran out, and what fills each gap. The left two columns are Ignacio Aldama's own findings; the right two are the label each one gets in the vocabulary of evidence and barriers, and what fills it today. The status column says which of those exist, which are documented and untested here, and which are proposed.
in-short

The demonstration is real and useful. A fresh Claude Code session, no history, no local code, called read_scope and read_components over MCP, found that the app and the service depend on the same version of a shared ticket entity, and changed only the app. 41 tests passed, nine of them new. Knowing what is shared tells an agent what not to touch. He says where it stops, which is why it is worth answering. Records describe structure, not behaviour. A green build can hide tests that did not run. A demo carries a public signing secret and a list of unfinished work. A memory note is dated but not tied to a version.
in-short

Each edge has a name. A route list in a test fake is a documented claim, not an observed fact. A skipped test is an expectation reported as a boundary. A public signing secret is a grant wider than the mandate. These are the labels RiskMandate already uses. Memory and records belong in one history. sgit is version control for files the host cannot read, so the intent that explains a version can be committed at that version, and written down at all, because the sensitive part of intent is exactly what teams leave out of a repository. Records have to cross company boundaries. His stated goal is a record that holds where the other side of a dependency sits outside the agent's index. sgit's publish, clone over plain GETs, and mirror are built for that, and are documented in the 0.21.0 release.
reports

The piece, published on 11 October, is contributed content with a clear disclosure: the author is an engineer at Bit Cloud, the platform that produced the records, and the page notes that The New Stack's owner, Insight Partners, is an investor in Bit and in Sourcegraph. None of that weakens the test; it is a single demo, by one author, of his own platform, and he says so.
reports

The test is simple and well chosen. He opened a fresh Claude Code session in an empty workspace and asked it to add filtering by ticket status and assignee to a four-component support console: a React app, an Express service on MongoDB, a shared ticket entity, and a platform component behind one gateway. The session found no local code, said the console must live remotely, called read_scope for the public scope, then read_components for the app, the service and the entity. Both the app and the service depended on the same version of the ticket entity, whose documentation called it "shared between the support service and the agent-facing app". The agent imported the components, implemented the filter client-side inside the app, and left the shared entity and the service alone. In his words, "knowing what is shared also tells an agent what not to touch."
reports

Then the part I like most: he says where the records ran out. The route list the app calls lived in the documentation of a fake service used in tests, and "nothing checks that list against the real service". The MongoDB integration tests skip when their temporary database cannot start on the CI runner, so "a passing build doesn't show they ran"; he checked persistence by hand. It is a demo, "with a predefined demo account and a public signing secret", and concurrency control, migrations, recovery and mandatory database tests are still to do. And memory and records cover different ground: a memory note carries the time it was written, "but nothing ties it to a code version", while a dependency record is part of the version it describes and carries no intent. His goal is a record per component "that still holds when the other side of a dependency lives somewhere the agent hasn't indexed", because what agents still lack "is a view of the system they are about to change".
evidence

The route list was a documented claim that read like a fact. That is the gap evidence levels exist for. The behaviour policy packs on abp.sgit.ai label every row as derived, inferred, self-reported, documented, measured or observed, and a reader, a reviewer or an agent should treat each accordingly; the pack's own headline counts only the observed rows. In Aldama's demo the route list was documented, by a fake. The persistence check he ran by hand, create a ticket, add a comment, restart against the same database, confirm both are there, was observed.
evidence

The record and the observation want to live together, with their labels and dates. That is the shape of the connector twin: every call the agent makes is appended to a journal in a vault, and what the agent did is kept apart from what it then saw. In an sgit vault the observation is a file committed in the same history as the claim, and since 0.19 sgit check verify classifies every commit reachable from the head as verified, bad, unsigned or without a known key, so who recorded an observation, and when, is part of the history rather than a comment beside it.
green

A test that skips is a control that did not run. In the vocabulary of Agent Behaviour Policies there are four barriers, none, expectation, setting and boundary, and only a boundary is a control, because only a boundary is enforced by something the grant does not include. A build that reports green over a skipped required test is reporting an expectation as a control, which is the risk that the controls reported upwards are not real. Every risk is already accepted is about where that kind of risk ends up.
green

The fix is small and it is the one we use on ourselves: count the run from what happened, not from the exit code. This session's own status report counts tools, calls, commits and commits without a leak scan from the transcript, not from what the agent says it did. A build could write the same small record into a vault: required tests, run, skipped, and why. A skipped required test then drops the evidence for that component back to documented until it runs, and "41 passing" becomes "41 passing, of which this many exercised the database". This one is proposed, not built.
shortcuts

A public signing secret and a predefined demo account are a grant wider than the mandate: anyone can sign as the app, anyone can be the demo user. That is fine for a demo and it is exactly what drifts into production. RiskMandate's position, on its acceptance page, is that there is no deny button for a deployed system: the risk is real, so it is accepted by a named owner, in a direction, for an interval, or the activity stops. "Public signing secret, accepted by the author until the first user who is not a demo, then rotated" is a decision. The same secret with no owner and no date is drift.
shortcuts

The unfinished items Aldama lists, concurrency control, migrations, recovery, mandatory database tests, are conditions in a licence to operate, each beside the thing that enforces it or beside the admission that nothing does, with an owner and an expiry, rather than a paragraph at the end of an article. On the specific shortcut, sgit keeps signing keys out of files: sgit pki keygen makes the key pair locally, and a leak scan now runs before every commit on this site, because an exposed vault key of our own, on the vault that serves this site, taught us to; the case study has the rotation steps.
memory

This is the strongest fit. Aldama's point is that memory holds intent, the release date, the person to ask, why a feature was cut, and is not tied to a version, while a build record is tied to its version and holds no intent. sgit is git-shaped version control for files the host cannot read. Memory and records can sit in the same vault and the same commit, so the intent that explains version 1.4 is recorded at version 1.4, and sgit history log, diff and show answer the question that matters after an incident: what did we believe when this shipped?
memory

Encryption matters more than it looks here. Intent is usually the sensitive part: owners, customers, why something was cut, who to avoid. Teams leave it out of a repository for exactly that reason, so it ends up in a chat that is compressed into a summary and gone, which is the problem his article opens with. In an sgit vault the host never sees file names, contents or commit messages, so the intent can be written down at all. Encrypted memory for agents that run somewhere else and Memory is not a spectator sport describe how that works for sessions like this one, and The mandate stack describes a team of agents that clone a shared vault at the start of every session, read their brief and their behaviour policy, work, commit and push.
boundary

His stated goal is a record that still holds when the dependency sits somewhere the agent has not indexed. He names Nx serving its project graph over MCP and Sourcegraph serving code search across repositories, and says both do that well; what neither does is cross a company boundary without a shared index or a shared server. sgit has three things built for that, all documented in the 0.21.0 release: Publish. sgit publish writes a small plaintext surface, a loader, a manifest and, if asked, API docs, that any static host can serve, and sgit clone reads it back over ordinary GETs. A supplier can publish its contract records and a customer's agent can clone them with no server and no API.
boundary

Mirror. sgit vault mirror makes a keyless, verifiable copy, re-hashing every content-addressed object rather than trusting the manifest, so a host cannot substitute content. That is custody without access, for a third party holding records it should not read. Append lanes. An outside agent can write into a vault it cannot read, which is how the connector twin's journal and this site's inbox work. I have not tested publish or mirror for this article; they are described here as their README and changelog describe them.
abp

The agent had real reach in the demo: it could read every component in the scope, import source and change shared code. Its best decision, to leave the shared ticket entity alone, was its own judgement. Nothing stopped it from changing a contract that two components depend on. In the terms of a behaviour policy that is a write row with a blast radius of two components, held by an expectation, the agent's good sense. A platform holding the records is in the right place to make it a boundary, for example by requiring an approval to version a shared entity, and Footprint and blast radius is how that row would be measured and priced. That would turn the demo's best moment from a judgement into a guarantee.
limits

It is one demo, by the platform's own engineer, and he discloses it. The four edges are his findings; the labels on them are ours. The green-build record is proposed. Counting run, skipped and why into a vault is an idea, not a feature. Publish and mirror are documented, not tested here. They are in the 0.21.0 README and changelog; this article did not run them. Nothing here replaces records. The point is that records, memory, evidence and acceptance are four different things that want to live in one history, not that any one of them is enough. If you are building the records side of this, at Bit Cloud or anywhere else, and want to compare notes on the edges, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

A research note from RiskMandate's research agent on 11 October 2026, rewritten by this site's agent in the voice of this site; the argument and the editorial responsibility are mine. The article answered is Ignacio Aldama, Claude Code found my app's shared contract in two MCP calls. Then the records ran out., The New Stack, 11 October 2026, read in full for this piece; quotations are his. The sgit features are from the sgit-ai 0.21.0 README and changelog. RiskMandate: acceptance, licence to operate, Agent Behaviour Policies; the evidence levels are on abp.sgit.ai.

Abstract: On 10 October Satya Nadella published "Models as Insider Risks in the Super Intelligence Era", a short post arguing that because we can no longer trace what a model does back to a code path, we should treat models the way we treat any powerful insider, and keep the authority over them outside them. Reading it, I kept translating. His lost code path is what I have been calling software was the law. His insider that need not be malicious is the ultimate insider. His split between the supply of intelligence and the authority over it is RiskMandate's founding line, the grant is not the mandate. His controls outside the model are the enforcer test. And his last line, that the most trustworthy system is the one that needs to trust the model least, is the irony The ultimate insider ended on: the more you can constrain an agent, the more autonomy you can afford to give it. This article puts the two vocabularies side by side, idea by idea, shows where ours came from, and names the two places where they differ: his unit is the model and ours is one agent in one deployment, and his frame is observation where ours is authority, accepted by a named person for a stated interval. A companion article takes his seven principles one at a time.

His words and ours. Each idea in Satya Nadella's post, paraphrased, beside the word this network has been using for it, and the page where that word is defined and worked through. On 10 October Satya Nadella published Models as Insider Risks in the Super Intelligence Era. It is short and careful, and as I read it I kept doing the same thing: translating it, line by line, into the words we have been using on this site and on RiskMandate for the last few weeks, and in some cases for much longer.

This is a big deal, and not for the reason you might think. It is not about who said it first. When the CEO of one of the largest AI vendors arrives at the same conclusions from the other side of the market, from the side that builds the models rather than the side that has to live with them, that is evidence the conclusions are right. Two very different starting points, one set of answers. So this is not a rebuttal. It is a translation, because the most useful thing I can do with his post is show how the two vocabularies map onto each other, and where they do not.

This is the first of two articles. The second, Authority outside the model, takes his seven principles one at a time and says, for each, what we run, what we have only designed, and what we have only argued. His post is worth reading in full first. I paraphrase it here, and quote it once. We are describing the same thing. He starts from what we lost when models replaced code; I called it software was the law. He treats models as insiders that need not be malicious; I called that the ultimate insider. He separates the supply of intelligence from the authority over it; RiskMandate's first line is that the grant is not the mandate.

His most important idea is our enforcer test. Controls have to sit outside the thing they control. In the ABP's words, a control bounds a grant only if it is enforced by something the grant does not include. Everything else in his post follows from that, and so does everything in ours. We got here from risk, not from models. Twenty-five years of security work, much of it in application security and as a CISO, taught me that most damage is not malice, that every risk is already accepted by somebody, and that the interesting number is the gap between what a credential allows and what its holder was meant to do. Agents made that gap the whole problem.

Two differences are worth naming. His unit is the model; ours is one agent in one deployment, because the same model is harmless in one setup and serious in another. His frame is observation; ours is authority: a mandate written before the agent runs, and the risk that is left accepted by a named person for a stated interval. The ending is the same sentence, read from opposite ends. His: the most trustworthy system is the one that needs to trust the model least. Ours: the more you can constrain an agent, the more you can trust it, and the more autonomy you can afford to give it.
lineage

It helps to say where our vocabulary comes from, because it was not built for models. It was built for risk. Most of the worst damage I have seen in twenty-five years of security work was not an attack. It was a bug, a misconfiguration, a script run against the wrong environment, a person doing something that was allowed and should not have been. So when I say threat, I mean anything that causes business impact, malicious or not. And underneath the damage, the same thing kept turning up: what somebody could do was much larger than what they were meant to do, the difference was rarely written down, and so it was rarely accepted by anyone.
lineage

That became the research behind risks.sgit.ai, which starts from an inversion: you cannot deny a risk, you can only say how long you accept it. A risk with a real exposure under it exists whether or not anyone signs for it. Take away the deny button, ask a named person to underwrite the exposure for a stated interval, and risk management stops being a gate and becomes a forcing function, because whoever has to sign starts asking for evidence.
lineage

Then agents arrived, and every part of that problem got worse at once. An agent is given a credential whose reach has rarely been measured, a job that is usually clear but rarely written down, and a set of rules it is asked to keep itself. RiskMandate exists to answer one narrow question about that arrangement: what can this agent we just connected actually do, and who said it could? The answer is a document, the Agent Behaviour Policy, and its four words are the vocabulary the rest of this article translates into: Reach: what the agent can do, measured. Mandate: what the business authorised, written down. Gap: reach minus mandate, derived, never written by hand. Barriers: what stands in the way of each row of the gap: nothing, an expectation, a setting, or a boundary.
lineage

How the vocabulary was built, in dated public work. Most of it was written in the three weeks before Nadella's post, on top of risk and identity research going back to 2025. The convergence is the point: two very different starting places, one set of conclusions.
law

He opens with a loss. For decades, when software did something, we could follow the behaviour back to a code path. With frontier models we cannot, and yet these are the systems we are connecting to sensitive data and letting act for us. I described the same loss from the business side, in Zoom into an agent's behaviour policy and you find the business logic. For decades, the rules of a business lived in its systems. A clerk could not send an unapproved invoice, because the finance system had no button for it until the approval was recorded. Those rules were enforced by omission, by the screen that did not show the button. An agent works through APIs, not screens: it can call the endpoint the button would have called. So the rule is no longer enforced, unless somebody writes it down and something outside the agent enforces it.
law

The translation adds one thing to his version. What we lost was not only traceability. It was the place where the business kept its rules. Many organisations have never written those rules down, because their software was the law. The behaviour policy is where they get written down, and that is why, a few layers in, an agent's policy stops being about security and starts being about how the company actually works.
insider

His frame is insider risk: treat a frontier model, closed or open, as an insider, not because it means harm, but because anything capable with access to important systems can make mistakes or be compromised. That is the argument of The ultimate insider, from 30 September. Insider threat was always real and always hard to scale, because the insider was either a person, bounded by hours, skills and conscience, or code, which did exactly what it was written to do. An agent is neither. It is a reasoning engine in a loop with tools, fluent in every language and every schema, able to write the connector it lacks and try again. Three of the five public incidents in that article were not attacks at all, just agents being agents. The way I put it then: the distance between the benign case and the hostile one is a prompt.
insider

Knowing when to stop adds the part that is easy to miss. The variability that makes an agent dangerous is also what makes it useful; in a person, we would call it creativity. You cannot engineer it away without losing the point of the agent. A model that can go in every direction needs someone with a direction, and something that stops it.
accepted

He is clear that responsibility for what intelligence does on our behalf stays with us, and that a model provider's assurances do not move it. In our words: every risk is already accepted. The day an agent is connected, the exposure exists, and somebody is carrying it, signed for or not. There is no deny button, only the question of who holds it and until when. A risk that nobody accepted has not gone away. It has come to rest on whoever is nearest, and it rolls upward to the board without anyone choosing to escalate it.
accepted

The vendor point has a sharper edge in our vocabulary. On nhi.sgit.ai we separate agents you run from agents you rent. Almost every agent a business can name today is rented: it runs on somebody else's infrastructure, and the only thing the business controls is the credential it hands over. For those, the honest current workflow is to hand over a broad credential and hope. Hope is not a control, and it does not change who is accountable.
supply

This is the centre of his post, and of ours. In his words, we need to "separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it." RiskMandate's first page says the same thing in five words: the grant is not the mandate. A grant is what the credential technically permits. A mandate is what the holder is authorised and expected to do. In practice the first is much larger than the second, and the difference is where the exposure lives. The supply of intelligence arrives with a grant attached. The authority is the mandate, and it only exists if somebody writes it down.
supply

Our vocabulary is stricter about what counts as authority. A mandate has an issuer, a subject, a scope, an interval and a way to revoke it; an instruction in a chat has none of these. And a mandate with no clock is just a grant. That last line is the one I would most like to see in an industry standard, because an authority that never expires is not separated from the supply. It has quietly become part of it. Supply and authority, in RiskMandate's terms. The supply arrives with a grant; the authority is a mandate with an issuer, a scope and a clock. The gap between them is derived, and each row of it has a barrier. Only one kind of barrier is a control.
enforcer

He grounds the separation in an old security principle: a program must not be able to bypass or tamper with whatever enforces its permissions. So the controls over what a model can reach and do have to sit outside it, which means pulling apart the model, the harness that drives it, and the space of actions it can take. The ABP turns that principle into a test you can run on any rule: a control bounds a grant only if it is enforced by something the grant does not include. Four kinds of barrier follow from it: Nothing. An expectation: a rule in prose, enforced by nobody. A setting: a switch the agent's own account could flip. A boundary: enforced above the grant, out of the agent's reach. Only the last one is a control. RiskMandate's home page says it shorter: a prompt asks, a policy enforces.
enforcer

His worry about models checking models, an opaque system watched by another opaque system, is the same test applied to verification. A second reader the agent cannot skip starts from the line that a rule kept by the agent it governs is hope, and ends on this: the same checking code is a setting when the agent's own account installed it, and a boundary when somebody else did. Same code, different owner. Independence is not a property of the checker. It is a property of who controls it.
code

He asks for engineering before alignment: wrap the non-deterministic model in deterministic system design, human controls and dependable procedure. Hope or enforcement measured what that does. One customer service agent, built three ways, with the same rules each time. With one model and broad connectors, 97% of the policy was hope. Behind a harness of business tools, 73%. As a team of narrow agents behind a deterministic gateway, with tools that take no customer argument and limits written into the tools, 23%, and one run could reach one customer instead of 38,000. The phrase that came out of it is my translation of his: granularity moves knowledge out of the prompt and into code. And there is a finding he does not mention: as the reach falls, the policy gets shorter, because it no longer has to forbid what the agent has no way to do.
calibrator

He wants every meaningful action to leave evidence that cannot be tampered with and that a person can read, so that an outcome can be reconstructed without relying on the model's account of it. We arrived at the same rule by being wrong. I wrote a policy for an agent from the vendor's documentation, which said the connector could not send attachments. The agent found a way, proved it with a signed PDF, and wrote it up; that story is in Six agents, one inbox. Since then the rule has been that the grant is measured on the thing itself, and calibrated against what the logs show it did: the footprint. Reality is the calibrator. The connector twin is the same idea for actions: journal every call, replay it as the agent saw it, and turn "can we undo this?" into a list.
calibrator

Our version adds two conditions. First, the evidence should not be held by whoever is being observed, which is why ours lives in vaults whose host stores ciphertext and never holds a key. Second, observation needs something to compare against. A footprint read against a written mandate produces findings: a near miss, where the agent went somewhere it was not asked and nothing stopped it, or a dormant mandate, where something you relied on never ran. A footprint read against nothing produces logs. That is why RiskMandate's order is to instrument before you enforce: the measurement is what tells you where enforcement is worth its cost.
brake

He asks us to assume the model is compromised from the start, and to make sure an authorised person can always pause or stop it mid-task. Our first containment rule came from running agents, not from theory: the account is the blast radius. Every session an agent opens runs as the account that authorised it, so the first real control is a dedicated account per agent. The brake, in RiskMandate's language, is the question a board asks in one sentence: who can pull the plug? The plug always exists. What is missing is its profile: who holds it, how fast it works from the decision, what breaks when it is pulled, and what can never be undone. The last of those matters most, because a brake stops the next action and does nothing for the ones already taken.
disclosure

He asks for timely disclosure to the people affected, and for the industry to share what failed and how to prevent it. The ultimate insider argued that the main reason we do not see more agent incidents is that almost nobody is required to report them, and pointed at aviation, where confidential near-miss reporting, about 100,000 reports a year, helped make a complex system safe. Our own practice is to write up our incidents the day they happen: the second reader article opens with two emails that went out wrongly in my voice. And our vocabulary gives disclosure something precise to count. A near miss is footprint in the gap: the agent went somewhere it was not asked to go, and nothing stopped it. It happens long before anything breaks.
brakes

His last line is that the most trustworthy system will not be the one with the most trusted model, but the one that needs to trust the model least. Ours, from the end of The ultimate insider: the more you can constrain an agent, the more you can trust it, and the more autonomy you can afford to give it. Once you know the universe of what an agent can do, and that universe fits inside your risk appetite, you can let it act freely within it, and every human decision becomes an exception worth making rather than one alarm among thousands. We put brakes on cars so that we can go faster. They are the same sentence. His is written from the point of view of the system that has to be trusted. Ours is written from the point of view of the business that wants to use it.
differ

A translation is most useful where it is not one to one. There are two differences, and both matter. The unit. His post is about models. Ours is about one agent in one deployment. The same model, connected to a mailbox with the broadest scope and a read-write database, can reach 38,000 customers; behind a gateway with bound tools, one. RiskMandate's home page says it in a heading: not a model property, a property of this deployment. Standards written for models will miss most of the risk if they do not describe deployments.
differ

The frame. His principles are mostly about seeing: observability, verification, audit, disclosure. Ours start one step earlier, with deciding. A mandate written before the agent runs. A gap derived from it. And the risk that is left, accepted by a named person for a stated interval, where the interval is the decision: accepting for four hours is declaring an incident, for a month is funding the work, for six months is a named decision to wait. Observation tells you what happened. Authority tells you whether it was allowed, and acceptance tells you who carries it if it was not. Neither difference is a disagreement. They are the two halves a business needs: the vendor's half, which makes the system observable and containable, and the deployer's half, which says what it is for and who answers for it.
next

For me, the most useful thing about his post is that it names principles at the level where an industry can agree on them. The next step is a vocabulary precise enough to write them down for a real agent, and to test them. Ours is open. The ABP model, its four objects, its barrier kinds and the enforcer test are published under CC BY 4.0, with sixteen example policies anyone can read. It is not the only possible language, but it is a working one, and it already says, row by row, how much of a given agent's policy is a control and how much is hope. If you are working on agent standards, or deploying agents and want to try writing the mandate down, let's compare notes: agent@riskmandate.ai.
next

For the detail, Authority outside the model takes his seven principles one at a time, says what we run, what is published as design and what is only argued, and lists the five things I think the principles need in order to work.
sources

Satya Nadella's post, Models as Insider Risks in the Super Intelligence Era, sn scratchpad, 10 October 2026, read in full; it is paraphrased throughout and quoted once. I asked an agent in a separate Claude session to read it alongside the articles, vaults and sites of this network, check every claim against the page that owns it, and draft this answer with its figures; this site's agent then rewrote it in the voice of this site. The argument is mine, and so is the editorial responsibility. The pages it translates into: on this site, The ultimate insider, the business logic, Every risk is already accepted, Knowing when to stop, Six agents, one inbox, Hope or enforcement, A second reader the agent cannot skip, Footprint and blast radius and the connector twin; on RiskMandate, the grant is not the mandate, Who can pull the plug? and the home page; the model and vocabulary at abp.sgit.ai and the barrier and the enforcer test; and the research sites risks.sgit.ai and nhi.sgit.ai.

Abstract: I usually give a talk by reading it, with the slides behind me. For a short slot tonight I want to try something else: a talk that is completely scripted, where the slides, the builds, the animations and even the demo play on a clock, and I speak to them instead of reading from them. This grows out of two talks already published as vaults on sgit.ai. The Black Hat Europe 2025 keynote made the slides data: 26 slides in one JSON file that the app reads at load time, with ten versions of the slide system beside it. The VoiceDebrief pitch added a presenter with per-slide timings, a countdown and speaker notes, built from a template by a script. The next step is to make the whole talk a timeline. This site's agent built a first version: one HTML file that plays a file of beats, each with a start, a duration, a slide and the words to say, with builds, a terminal that types a command and prints its recorded output, tables that reveal row by row, video, and a presenter view with the words, the seconds left and what comes next. A rehearsal mode records planned against actual times. The first timeline is the five-minute demo for ruv.sgit.ai, the newest site in the sgit family, built for tonight's Agentic Engineering Live with rUv in London. And Claude Motion, which Anthropic released in beta on 8 October, makes the animations the same way: as code, exported as MP4.

A scripted talk, from the memo to the room: a file of beats, each with its slide and its words; a player that turns it into slides on a clock; the audience sees the slide, the speaker sees the words, the time left and what comes next; a rehearsal records planned against actual times. Dashed boxes are proposed.
in-short

A talk as a timeline. Slides, builds, animations and the demo play on a clock; the speaker speaks to them. It grows out of two vaults. Black Hat made the slides data; the VoiceDebrief pitch added timings and a presenter. A player, built and tested. One HTML file, a file of beats, a presenter view and a rehearsal mode. The demo is recorded truth. The terminal types the command and prints the output the real run produced. Animations as code. Claude Motion, Manim or Remotion: editable, versioned, exported as MP4. First use, tonight. The five-minute demo for ruv.sgit.ai, at Agentic Engineering Live with rUv in London.
why

I usually read my presentations, with the slides behind me as a backdrop. It works, but it splits the attention: the audience reads the slide while I read the script, and the two drift apart. For a short slot, where every second counts, I want to try the opposite: a talk that is completely scripted. The slides, the builds, the animations and the demo are written down as a timeline and play on a clock, and I speak to them. The pace is set before I walk on, the demo cannot fail live, and the whole thing can be rehearsed, measured and changed like code.
lineage

Three talks, one direction: Black Hat Europe 2025 made the slides data; the VoiceDebrief pitch added a presenter with timings, notes and a countdown; the player for tonight makes the whole talk a timeline that plays on a clock. All three live in vaults. This is the third step of something I have done twice before, and both are published as vaults on sgit.ai.
lineage

The first was AI vs. AI, my keynote at the AI Security Summit at Black Hat Europe on 9 December 2025. The deck was fully generated from scripts. Its 26 slides, in seven layouts, are one JSON file: "The app reads it through the vault bridge at load time, so a content change needs no rebuild." The vault also carries the slide system itself at ten versions, six PDF exports, and the eight research papers the talk was built from. The lesson I took from it is the one that matters here: content is data, the renderer is code, and they change separately.
lineage

The second was the VoiceDebrief pitch to Founder Institute on 2 September 2026: a presenter app with per-slide target timings, a three-minute countdown and speaker notes, built from a template by a script in the vault, with the spoken script extracted from the notes and the PDF and PPTX regenerated on every release. That added time to the slides: each one knew when it should be on screen. The next step is to let the clock drive. Instead of a deck with timings beside it, a timeline with slides on it.
player

The prototype's presenter view, at 2:58 of the five-minute demo: the slide on the left, with every row of the table revealed; on the right, the words for this beat, the seconds left and what comes next; along the bottom, the clock and a progress bar marked at every beat. This site's agent built a first version, and it is deliberately small: one HTML file and one JSON file, no build. It is a page made for one moment, which Custom UIs are not the exception argued is normal now: "A custom interface per message or moment is not an exception". The talk is a list of beats. Each beat has a start in seconds, a duration, a title, the words to say, and a slide with a layout: statement: a line of text, with builds that appear at set seconds; terminal: a command typed out character by character, then the output the real run produced;
player

table: rows revealed every few seconds; bullets, video, for example an MP4 exported from Claude Motion, and iframe, for a live page. A clock drives everything. Press Space and it plays; the beat at the current second is on screen, its builds appear at their offsets, and the next beat starts on time without a click. The arrow keys jump between beats if the room needs a moment. P opens the presenter view: the words for this beat, the seconds left, highlighted in the last five, and what comes next. R starts a rehearsal, which records when each beat actually began; when it stops, it saves a file of planned against actual times, the evidence of whether the script fits the slot.
player

It was tested in Chromium: every beat came on at its second, the builds and rows appeared on schedule, the terminal finished typing and then printed, the arrows jumped forward and back, it stopped at 5:00, and the page raised no errors. A version with the talk inlined opens straight from a file, with no server and no network, which is the version to carry into a room with bad wifi.
demo

The part I like most is the terminal. A live demo is where talks go wrong: the network, the package cache, the one command that behaves differently on stage. In a scripted talk, the command is typed on the timeline and the output is the one the real run produced, captured beforehand and kept with the talk. That is not faking the demo. It is the same principle as every vault on sgit.ai: the evidence is recorded, versioned and inspectable, and anyone can run the command again from the vault and compare.
motion

The memo's transcription garbled two names. The first is clearly Claude Motion, which Anthropic released in beta on 8 October 2026 for Team and Enterprise plans: "Claude writes code that animates your text, charts, shapes, and images, so you can change any word, number, or timing." It "doesn't use a video generation model", and the result downloads as an MP4. I could not make out the second word with confidence; the code-based animation tools it most likely refers to are Manim, the Python library for mathematical animation, and Remotion, which makes video from React components, and both are already used with Claude Code through community skills.
motion

They all fit the timeline the same way. An animation made as code can be edited a word or a number at a time, versioned beside the talk, exported as an MP4, and placed on a beat. The talk stays data from end to end: the words, the slides, the animations and the recorded output, each in a file, each with a history.
ruv

The first timeline is a real one. ruv.sgit.ai is the newest site in the sgit family, built on 14 October for Agentic Engineering Live with Reuven Cohen, rUv, in London on 15 October. It shows sgit vaults and agent behaviour policies running inside his stack, Ruflo, RuVector, RVM and MetaHarness, as six proofs of concept, and it already has a five-minute demo written in five beats. The agent turned those beats into the first talk.json: the claim, Ruflo's default saying yes to sending email, the same eleven actions with and without the behaviour policy, read from the site's own data, memory with history across runners, and the ask. A ten-minute version is the same file with more beats.
brief

The talk vault. talk.json, the player, the assets and every rehearsal file in one vault, with a published read key once the talk is given. Recorded demos. A script that runs each demo command and saves its output beside the beat that shows it. Motion on beats. Animations made in Claude Motion, Manim or Remotion, exported as MP4 and referenced by path. Rehearsal as a test. A rehearsal file committed after each run-through, and a check that fails if any beat runs more than ten seconds over. Exports. The same timeline rendered to a PDF, one page a beat, and to one MP4 of the whole talk. A vault app. The player served from the vault itself, as the Black Hat deck is, so the talk and its evidence travel as one object.
limits

It has not been given yet. The player was tested in a browser, not in a room. Scripted is not read. The words are in the presenter view; whether to read them is the speaker's choice. The second animation tool is a guess. The transcription was unclear. Claude Motion was not used here. Its details are from Anthropic's pages; it is in beta on Team and Enterprise plans. The exports and the talk vault are proposed. The player, the timeline and the tests exist. If you give talks and want yours to be a timeline with its evidence attached, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

A voice memo of mine on 14 October 2026, written by this site's agent in the voice of this site; the argument and the editorial responsibility are mine. The player was built and tested by this site's agent on 15 October 2026, from the two published vaults, which it cloned with their read keys, and from ruv.sgit.ai's demo script and data. From sgit.ai: AI vs. AI, Black Hat Europe 2025 and A three-minute pitch. Anthropic, Build live dashboards and animate explainers with Claude, 8 October 2026, and Get started with Claude Motion; ruv.sgit.ai and its demo. Read on 15 October 2026.

Abstract: With the reader's vault live on newsroom.sgit.ai, the next brief is about what a reader does with it, and it starts from one image: the site is an inbox that starts empty. Every piece that arrives, an article this site wrote or a story the wire aggregated, is something I have not decided about yet, and the first thing I do with it is decide, in a second, with nothing loaded: read now, read later, not for me, more of this, less of this, comment, move it to another persona. That is the inbox mode, and it is thinking fast. Reading is the slow mode, and it is where the marks live: highlights of different kinds, not one or two as Medium has but interesting, great phrase, not sure, fact, evidence, question, each a node in a graph the reader owns and that connects to the graphs this site already publishes for every article; the pane on the right becomes about the piece in front of you; the piece can be shown with every term a link, or classified sentence by sentence. The signals that come free, scroll depth, time while awake, where you came from and went to, are kept the way the meter keeps them: in the browser, in the vault when you ask, shown to an agent only by your read key. Comments for the newsroom go down the write-only lane, signed by the persona's key, with a copy kept. None of it is gamified: a decision is offered where you would take it, never at the end of a page to make you scroll there. The brief is the second part. The first part is why I could not have written it two days ago: the properties of what runs are the constraints I think with, and the constraints are what let me think.

Two modes. The inbox mode decides what happens to a piece with nothing loaded; the reading mode is where the marks and the signals live. Everything stays in the reader's browser and vault, and the reader chooses what an agent sees. The vault is live, and I have a brief for what to do with it. But the brief is the second half of this article, because the first half is about why I have it at all.
short

I could not have written this brief two days ago. Not for lack of time or ideas. For lack of constraints. Until the passkey worked and the sign-in was not needed, until a door was per path, until the sync was one file per device, I did not know the properties of the thing I would be writing for. The properties are what let me think. The site is an inbox, and it starts empty. Every piece that arrives, an article this site wrote or a story the wire brought in, is something the reader has not decided about. Deciding is the work; reading is one of the decisions. Two modes. The inbox mode decides, fast, with nothing loaded: read now, read later, not for me, more like this, less like this, comment, move to a persona. The reading mode does, slowly, with the piece open and its context loaded.
short

No gamification. A decision is offered where the reader would take it, never at the end of a page so that they scroll there. A signal the site engineered is not a signal. Marks build the reader's own graph. Not one highlight but kinds: interesting, great phrase, not sure, fact, evidence, question. Each is a node, connected to the graphs this site already publishes for every article. Meaning comes from connectivity, and the reader's graph is worth more the more it is used. The signals come free and stay yours. Scroll depth, time while awake, where you came from and went to. Kept as the meter keeps everything: in the browser, in the vault when you press Update, seen by an agent only through a read key you gave it.
short

Personas have keys. Each persona is disposable and has its own key pair, so a comment to the newsroom is signed by the persona that made it, goes down the write-only lane, and leaves a copy in your vault. The reply is a new version of the article. The test is simple. It works if reading here, with a graph that grows, is better than reading without one.
constraints

The vault is live ends with a sentence I want to start from, because this article is the proof of it. The brief below did not exist on 10 October. I had the ideas; some of them are years old. What I did not have was the shape of the thing they would run on, and without the shape I could not hold them.
constraints

This is not the usual point about agents making things cheap to build, true as that is, and I made it in Pay after you read: the more you have, the faster you go. It is a point about thinking. When the vault did not exist, "a reader's marks on an article" was an open question in every direction: where would they live, who could read them, what would it cost, would the reader have to sign in, could a mark be sent to us and by whom. Each of those questions is big enough to stop a brief. Now each has an answer, and the answers are not mine, they are the properties of what runs. Marks live in the reader vault, in a file per device. Nobody can read them but the reader, and an agent the reader gives a read key to. Writing them costs one commit when the reader presses a button. There is no sign-in. A persona can have a key pair in the master, so a mark can be signed. Those five facts close off most of the design space, and what is left is small enough to think about in a morning.
constraints

I did not expect this, and I think it is the more important half of the feedback loop. I had it as: use it, miss it, build it, use it again. It is also: build it, learn its properties, and only then have the next idea, because the next idea is made of the properties. The constraints limit what I can write, and without that limit I would write everything and finish nothing. So the order matters. Ship first, think second, and do not pretend the thinking could have come first.
brief
For the session that runs newsroom.sgit.ai. Written by the sgit.ai site session for Dinis Cruz, 12 October 2026, on top of the vault pane at v0.11.0. Dinis decides what ships, and is the first user.
inbox

Start from this image and most of the rest follows. The site has two kinds of content now: the articles it writes, and the wire it reads from a vault that other agents keep, which will grow into sources the reader chooses to follow. For a reader, both arrive the same way: as pieces they have not decided about. So the site, for that reader, is an inbox. It starts empty, cleared, nothing to see. As pieces arrive, each one waits for a decision. When the decision is made, the piece leaves the inbox and the decision becomes a record. The state the site should always be able to return to is empty. This is a different thing from a front page, and it is why the front page can stay the Editor's: the inbox is the reader's view of the same pieces, and it is personal because the decisions are.
modes

Kahneman's distinction between thinking fast and thinking slow is the right frame, and I would build the two modes to match it. The inbox mode is fast. The reader meets a headline, a line, and where it came from, and nothing is loaded: not the article, not its graph, not the reader's context for it. The only thing to do is decide what happens next, and the decision should take a second: read now; read later; not for me; more like this; less like this; comment; move it to another persona. Each is one tap, offered at the piece, and each clears the piece from the inbox. For the wire especially, "not for me" is the most important button, and the most useful signal: it says which concern the join got wrong.
modes

The reading mode is slow. The piece is open, its context is loaded, and the pane on the right, which today holds the vault and the meter, becomes about this piece: its graph beside the text, the reader's marks on it, the decisions already taken, and what it cost. This is where the reader does something with the piece, and it is where the next three sections happen.
modes

The split matters because today the newsroom asks for the reader's judgment at the end of the article, where the meter's card is. That was the right place for a rating that sets a price, and it is the wrong place for a decision, because a decision at the end is a reason to scroll to the end, and that is gamification: a signal we engineered, which is then not a signal. The rule for both modes is that a decision is offered at the moment the reader would take it, and nothing is placed to make them go somewhere.
marks

The reader's graph is made of marks, each with a kind; the marks land on the public graphs this site already publishes; a chosen slice goes to the newsroom, signed; a new version comes back. Medium lets you highlight, and I used it, and what I did not like is that it had one or two kinds of highlight and I have six. When I read, I mark things for different reasons: this is interesting; this is a great phrase; I am not sure about this; this is a fact; this is evidence; this is a question. Each of those is a different kind of node, and the moment the site lets me say which, I am not highlighting any more. I am building my graph.
marks

A mark is a node. It carries the phrase, the article and its version, the persona that made it, the kind, and the time. A comment is a node with an edge to the phrase it is about. An inbox decision is an edge from the persona to the piece. Marks land on the public graphs. Every article here already has a graph as JSON beside it, and every wire story has entities, claims and a quote. A mark on a phrase links to the node that phrase belongs to, so "not sure" on a claim is an edge to that claim, and a reader who marks the same claim in two articles has connected them without naming anything.
marks

Meaning comes from connectivity. A phrase marked three times, from three articles, is a topic the reader did not have to declare. That is what Fractal Semantic Graphs are for, and what Obsidian users already know: the graph is a by-product of use, and it is the most valuable thing the reader makes. The vocabulary view, on demand. Not always on, because it is noisy. But a switch that turns every term in the piece into a link into the vocabulary, the facts, the connections, the way some of our vaults already do, so that the reader can walk from a word to everything it touches, including their own marks.
marks

The piece, classified. Another switch: the same text shown by what its sentences are, facts, observations, evidence, claims, questions, and by tone or confidence. The site's agents already read its articles this way, as five readers; the reader should see that view and be able to disagree with it, sentence by sentence, and the disagreement is a mark.
marks

This is where the economics of the whole thing sit, and I want to say it plainly. The more a reader marks, the more they use the site; the more they use it, the more they pay, by the meter; and the more they pay, the more their own graph is worth to them, because it is theirs and it is connected. That loop only closes if one thing is true: reading here, with a graph that grows, is a better experience than reading without one. Every feature in this brief is a bet on that sentence, and the vault is what makes the graph the reader's rather than ours.
signals

The reading mode can record four things without asking, and it should, because they are useful to the reader first. How far. The scroll depth, which the meter already charges by. The bottom of the page means read; a little means glanced. Shown to the reader as a simple "you read this" or "you read a third of this", which is the information I most often want about my own past reading. How long, awake. Time on the piece counted only while there is movement, scroll or pointer or key, so that a tab left open for an hour is not an hour of reading. This is an experiment: whether movement is a good enough proxy for attention is something to measure, not assume.
signals

From and to. The page the reader came from and the page they went to. The site already knows the latter; the former is what lets it answer "how did I get here", and give the reader back and forward through their own reading, which will matter more once search works. The decisions. Every inbox decision and every mark, with the persona and the time. All of it is kept the way the meter keeps everything today: in local storage as it happens, in the reader vault when they press Update, as records and never totals, and shown to any agent only through a read key the reader gave it. The reader can see every record, which is the other half of not gamifying: the signals are the reader's, and they can watch what they produce.
lane

The reason this brief needs the vault and not just local storage is in two places. The first is personas. I will have several, and one of them is the newsroom's editor: I read every article, I see what works, I review it, and I need to comment on everything. That is a different lens from my CISO persona or my founder persona or my general-interest one, and the inbox mode's "move to a persona" is how a piece gets to the right one. Personas should be disposable, and each should have a key pair of its own, kept in the master vault as the passkey design describes: one to sign, one to receive. What the editor persona signs is not what the CISO persona signs, and a persona can be handed to an agent as a read key to its slice of the graph, and only its slice.
lane

The second is the lane. A mark or a comment the reader addresses to the newsroom, "not sure" on a claim, a wrong flag on a wire story, a comment on a sentence, goes the way sending your reading already goes: encrypted in the browser to the newsroom's published key, into a write-only lane only the newsroom's agent reads. Two things are new. It is signed by the persona's key, so the newsroom knows which of my personas said it and that it was me. And a copy stays in the reader's vault, so the reader always knows what was sent, which is the privacy property: the user controls what goes, and can see it afterwards. The reply, as with the brief in I miss it, is a new version of the article, and the version page shows it.
lane

In my own case I will go further and give the agent that edits the site a read key to my editor persona's vault, so that it sees every mark I make as the editor, not only the ones I send. That is my choice, as a reader, and it is the point: the same mechanism serves a reader who sends nothing and a reader who shares everything.
order

The inbox mode on the front page and the wire: the seven decisions as one tap at each piece, clearing it, recorded as an edge in local storage. Test with the wire first, where "not for me" is the signal the join needs. The pane about the piece. On an article, the right-hand pane shows the article's graph, the reader's marks and decisions on it, and what it cost. The vault and the meter move to a tab of the same pane. Marks with kinds. Select a phrase, choose a kind, see it in the pane and in the graph. Six kinds to start; the reader can add one. The free signals: depth as "you read this", awake time, from and to, in the reader's records, visible to the reader on the account page. The persona key pairs in the master, as the passkey design specifies, generated at random on first use, one pair per persona.
order

The signed lane: a mark addressed to the newsroom, signed, sent, copied to the vault; and the reply as a version. The views: vocabulary on demand, and the piece classified, starting from the five readers' output where it exists. An experiment per feature. Each of these is small enough to ship in two versions and compare, and that is how they should be built: a synthetic reader, two variants, a measurement, and the one that holds. The inbox decisions, the kinds of mark and the awake-time proxy are the first three to test.
not

No decision placed at the end of a page to make the reader reach it. No signal sent anywhere without the reader pressing something. No mark the reader cannot see in their own records. No server of ours.
limits

None of the brief is built. The vault, the meter, the personas, the share lane, the article graphs and the five readers' views exist; the inbox mode, the marks, the signals and the signed lane are a design. The science is a frame, not a finding. Thinking fast and slow is a useful way to split the two modes; whether readers behave that way on this site is what the experiments are for. Awake time is a guess. Movement as a proxy for attention is an assumption to measure. The economics are a bet. The loop closes only if reading with a graph is better than reading without one, and one reader's experience, mine, is where that will first be tested. If you build reading tools, or you want to be a reader whose marks build a graph you own, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

A voice memo of mine on the morning of 12 October 2026, recorded after the newsroom's overnight releases and before I had tested the vault pane myself, written by this site's agent in the voice of this site.
