Abstract: Since 2022 I have said that Wardley maps changed how I think, and this site has quietly become a place where I draw them: eleven so far in the articles, seven in a vault, five in a conference talk. This is the best of them, with the context each one came from, and the reasons the technique matters to me. A map is a graph with two kinds of context, a value chain that starts with a user and an evolution axis that says how mature each piece is, and the second axis does not have to run from genesis to commodity. The map tells you what is moving the needle, whether you are optimising at the wrong altitude, what to build and what to buy, and whether a market exists at all: a commoditised layer is a hard sell, and custom building on top of it is where the market is. Two worked examples, sgit and RiskMandate. Then one map read step by step, as a story, because that is what a map is for. Then the fractal: every node on a map is a map, and the dot's place on the parent is the anchor of the child. Two decks you can print to PDF from your browser, and the maps published as data so anyone can take them.

Nine of the maps drawn on this site since September 2026. Every one is a claim about something real: a product that shipped, a plan that is published, a mistake that became a rule. The ninth is three maps deep.
in-short

A Wardley map is a graph with context in two directions. Down the page is the value chain, from a user's need to the things it depends on. Across the page is evolution, how mature each piece is. Nothing else about the drawing matters much; those two kinds of context are what make it useful. The evolution axis is a choice. Genesis to commodity is the usual one, and it is the one on every map here, but risk, data and governance can each be an axis. The map is a way of placing things against a scale you chose because it answers your question.
in-short

The map tells you where the market is. A layer that has become a commodity is a hard sell. A layer where everyone is custom building on top of a commodity is where the money and the attention are. sgit and RiskMandate are the two examples below, and the second one moved in the last year. A map is a story. The best use of one is not to show it finished but to read it out: here is the user, here is what is new, here is what it stands on, here is where it is going. One of the maps on this site is read that way below, frame by frame.
in-short

Maps nest. Every node is a map of its own, the way every node in a fractal semantic graph is a graph. The place a dot holds on the evolution axis of the parent is where the child's anchor sits. The figure near the end shows three altitudes of this business. Everything here is published as data. Every figure on this site now sits in the article's graph with its caption and kind, so "every Wardley map on sgit.ai" is one query, not a reading list.
what

The short description I use is that a Wardley map is a graph with two axes of context. The first is vertical: a value chain, anchored at the top on a user and a need, with each component drawn under the components that need it. The second is horizontal: evolution, how far each component has travelled from a new idea nobody has built to something you buy by the unit without thinking. Simon Wardley's four stages, genesis, custom built, product and commodity, are the scale on every map on this site.
what

That second axis is the part people argue about and the part I think is the least fixed. In 2022, at the Open Security Summit, I gave a talk called Why Wardley Maps changed how I think, and the argument was that the mapping habit produces a set of shifts in how you see a problem, eleven of them in that talk. Around the same time I wrote about alternative evolution scales: risk as the axis, data as the axis, governance as the axis, and others. I went looking for that post while writing this and did not find it, so I will not quote it; if you have it, send it. The point survives without the text. The horizontal axis is a scale you choose because it answers the question you have, and genesis to commodity is one good answer, not the only one.
what

What does not change is that the map must be based in reality. Every dot on every map here is a claim: that thing exists, it sits there in the chain, and it is about that mature. The captions say so, and the footer on most of them says "a map, not a measurement", because the positions are judgements and the judgements are the argument. A map you cannot be wrong about is a diagram.
why

The talk's eleven shifts are a longer list; these are the ones I use every week. What is moving the needle. On a map you can see which components are moving, and which movement matters to the user at the top. Most activity is in places the user never sees. The question "what moved this week, and did anything above it notice" is answered by looking. Altitude. A great deal of effort is spent optimising at the wrong altitude: polishing a component three layers below the need while the layer the user touches has not changed. The vertical axis makes that visible, and the fractal view below makes it precise: pick the altitude first, then the dot.
why

Build or buy. Anything in product or commodity, buy, rent or vendor it. Anything in genesis or custom built that sits on your path to the user, build it, because nobody else will build it the way you need. Most build-or-buy arguments are two people drawing the same component in different columns, and the map settles which column it is in. Does the market exist. This is the one I find most people have never asked of their own product. A layer that is commoditised is a hard sell: the buyer already has it, and cheaper. A layer where everyone is custom building, on top of commodities, is a market: each of those builders would rather buy. The examples are below, because the map answers differently for sgit and for RiskMandate.
why

Flow and attrition. A map shows the flow from the need down to the things that serve it, and where that flow leaks. The attrition points are the dependencies that are slow, immature or owned by somebody else: on Places of highest leverage the one custom layer we had to add sat exactly where a provider was not yet mature, and that is exactly where the work slowed. Who the players are, and where to hook. The components at the commodity end have names: Apple, Google, Stripe, git. Drawing them puts the people you depend on, and the people you could plug into, on the same page as your own pieces. Where to hook is a question of which mature component you can stand on so that your custom piece is small.
why

A common language. Two people with a map argue about positions. Two people without one argue about words. The mandate stack maps below were drawn twice, from the outside and from the inside, because the people on each side of the team see a different chain, and the two maps made the difference discussable. Start with the user. Every map here has a person at the top. It is a discipline, not a convention: the moment the anchor is "the platform" or "the roadmap" the map stops being able to tell you whether anything matters. Many maps, not one. The same business from different angles and altitudes: a user's chain, a team's chain, a feature's chain, a day's chain. None of them is the map. This article has nine because that is how they are used.
why

Peace. This is the one I say least often in public. Once a thing is on a map, placed and connected, I stop carrying it in my head. The zen of a map is that the anxiety about what to do next has somewhere to go, and most of it turns out to be about things far from the user.
best
Each map below is in the article it came from, with that article's argument around it. Here they are together, with a line of context each, in the order they were drawn.
mandate

Map one, from the outside. The anchor is a person who writes to the team. What they see, a reply with a name on it, is custom. What they do not see, the vaults, the sessions, Workspace and encrypted storage, is product or commodity. Rendered with Mermaid wardley-beta. Map two, from the inside. The anchor is the person running the business. The dashed arrows are the movement the team is making: shared memory and the sgit CLI toward commodity, the behaviour policies, the graphs and the custom interfaces from genesis toward product. Everything rests on encrypted storage, which is already a commodity.
mandate

The mandate stack is a team of agents described as a stack, and these were the first two maps on this site that were drawn as a pair on purpose. The person writing in sees one chain; the person running the team sees another, with the same components in different places. The second map carries movement, which is the part of a Wardley map that most diagrams cannot do: the arrows are claims about where things are going, and they were checkable within weeks. They were rendered with Mermaid's Wardley map syntax, so the source is in the article, which matters for the community point at the end.
pay

The reading meter at the end of 10 October, as a Wardley map: everything added that afternoon sits on the left, built on components that already existed on the right. Pay after you read shipped a reading meter, pay by depth, personas and an encrypted share in one afternoon, and the map is of that afternoon. It is the clearest example here of the build-or-buy reading: every new thing is on the left, and every one of them stands on something on the right that already existed, including the site's own vaults, git and a Stripe link. The frame-by-frame version of this map, one release at a time, is the one read as a story below.
cost

The map in three frames: the problem as most companies have it, what the service adds from what is already there, and where it goes. Agents in production on the explorer side, billed by the token, with logs nobody reads together; then the footprint, the twin, the policy and the graph; then cost as a discipline. Agentic cost is an engineering problem is a business plan, and the three frames are the plan's argument. The first frame is a market: the person paying the bill at the top, commodity model APIs at the bottom, and between them a blob of custom built things nobody owns. The second frame adds the service, and shows that it adds very little that is new; it reads what is there. The third is the movement. The controls under the figure let you stop on any of the three, which is the whole reason the animated version was replaced today.
leverage

Which shoulders the passkey work stands on. Almost everything under it is a product or a commodity someone else matured; our piece is the door and a door per path; the one custom layer we had to add is the phone by QR, where a provider is not yet mature. Places of highest leverage asks where to focus when agents can go in every direction, and this map is the answer to "why was it fast". The passkey work went from a design to a product in a day because the shoulders were mature: synced passkeys, the PRF extension, Web Crypto, the vault library, the server. The map also shows the one place it was slow, and that place is the one immature dependency. It is the attrition reading in one picture.
mac

The agent's desktop moves from custom-built to product, on parts that are already products or commodities: Apple silicon Macs, the macOS virtual machine, the models, the desktop agent apps. State, keys and lock-down move with it, because the vaults, the PKI and the policies already exist as parts. A Mac of the agent's own is the plan for a desktop per agent, and the map is a build-or-buy map with Apple's licence drawn in. Every heavy component is bought; the custom part is the bootstrap that assembles them and the record that leaves the machine. The published plan is in the Agent Desk vault, map included.
mistake

Map one: the verification as it runs. The person preparing the install needs confidence the tool is safe, which comes from a report, which rests on the tool's tests and on a team of agents. The six things that keep failing sit in a blob on the left, each rebuilt by hand inside a prompt every session. Files, hashes and git sit at the far right, unused. Map two: the same verification with each piece of process made small and drawn moving right. The tool's tests and the judgment in the report stay custom, because that is the work. Everything else becomes boring on purpose, leaning on files, hashes and git.
mistake

Every mistake added a rule is about a workflow that kept failing in the same six ways. The two maps are the before and after, and the after is the altitude reading: the custom work is kept where it is the work, the judgement and the tests, and everything else is pushed right onto files, hashes and git that were already there and unused. The blob on the left of map one is what "optimising at the wrong altitude" looks like when you draw it.
vaults

Three more sets are not in articles but in published vaults, each with its read key on the page. Strategy Maps holds the SG/Send strategy as seven Wardley maps, the ones I published on LinkedIn in May 2026, served live from an encrypted vault; its republish story is on The strategy in seven maps. ThreatModCon 2025 has five Wardley map walkthroughs inside a threat modelling talk, which is where the mapping habit and the security habit met for me. And the Agent Desk vault above carries its map as an app view. They are listed here because the best-of should include the maps that were not drawn for an article.
market

sgit. Take sgit apart and every layer is mature. Storage is a commodity. Version control is a commodity; git won. Encryption is a commodity; AES-GCM and HKDF are in every browser. Each of those is a hard sell on its own, because the buyer has it, cheaper, from somebody with a bigger name. The map says do not sell those. What the map also shows is what sits above them: everyone who wants a private, versioned, shareable unit of work is custom building one, out of a bucket, a repository and a key management story that never quite lands. That is the vault. The market for sgit is not the three commodities; it is the custom building that is happening on top of them, and the product is the piece that lets a customer keep custom building above a vault instead of below it. Every vault on this site is somebody's custom layer, and that is the evidence that the market is there.
market

RiskMandate. RiskMandate is a productised thing: a mandate, a footprint, a behaviour policy, a record of what an agent did against what it was allowed. It connects to agents, and a year ago agents were a product at best, and the companies building them were the customers. In the last year agents became a commodity: every platform ships one, by the token. On a map that moves the whole dot to the right, and the opportunity moves up. The market for agent behaviour, what an agent is allowed, what it touched, who can prove it, is all genesis and custom built right now; every team running agents is building their own version of it inside prompts and spreadsheets. That is the shape of a market that exists. The map told us the layer below had commoditised before the invoices did.
market
The two answers are different, and that is the point of asking. For sgit the market is above the product; for RiskMandate the product is at the market and the layer below it just moved.
story

A map is fundamentally a way to tell a story, and the best way I know to show that is to read one out. These are the eight frames of the afternoon from Pay after you read. Use the controls to stop on each one; the second deck below walks the same frames with one question per slide. The afternoon as a Wardley map, one release at a time: what already existed, then each feature as it was added and what it was built on, ending with what comes next. Times are UTC, from the commits. Frame one, before. Where is the user? At the top: the reader, on every device. What exists? Everything on the right: the articles and the build, git, browser storage, vaults, the sealed envelope, Stripe. Nothing on the left. What am I seeing is a business whose user touches only mature things, which is comfortable and not a strategy.
story

Frame two, a meter. The first new dot appears at genesis, close to the user, and it stands on browser storage. One question: is anything above it? Yes, the user. So this is at the right altitude. Frame three, it goes live. Pay by depth, below zero with no block, a Stripe link. Three new dots and every edge from them runs to the right. The build-or-buy reading is clean: nothing new was built below the line. Frame four, personas. The dot that matters is not the persona but the edge: it connects to the articles, the thing the site already had most of. Where to hook was answered by the oldest component on the map. Frame five, versions. A small dot, and it stands on git. It cost almost nothing because its shoulder was a commodity. This is the frame I use to explain why some features are free.
story

Frame six, the encrypted share. The first dot that stands on a vault. Here is where the map starts to pay for itself: the custom thing we had to build sits on the one product we had made ourselves, so the chain under it is ours end to end. Frame seven, the reader card. Usefulness sets the price. Nothing new under it; it is a change at the top of the chain, where the user is. The flow reading: everything below now has a reason to exist that the user can see. Frame eight, next. Dashed dots: real payments, a persona in your own vault, other sites. The story's last line is always the same question: which of these moves first, and what does it stand on.
story

That is the whole method. Where is the user, what is new, what does it stand on, where did the movement happen, where did we walk back, where would somebody else hook in, what is next. Seven questions, one picture, and a reader who did not know the business now knows what it is.
fractal

Three altitudes of one business. The vault is a dot on the business map; zoom in and it is the anchor of the vault map, at the same place on the evolution axis; the door is a dot on that map; zoom in and it is the anchor of the door map. Up from the top is the market the business sits in, down from the bottom is a key derivation, and the axes and the reading do not change.
fractal

The last reading is the one this site is built around. In Introducing fractal semantic graphs every node of a graph is itself a graph, and the altitude you read at decides which vocabulary you are in. Wardley maps have the same property, and drawing it makes the altitude argument precise. Every node on a map is a Wardley map. Zoom into a dot and it becomes the anchor of the next map, and the place it held on the parent's evolution axis is where the child's anchor sits, because the maturity of a thing does not change when you look inside it.
fractal

The figure goes three levels down. At the business altitude the anchor is a person who holds something others must read, and the vault is one dot among the site, the meter and the articles. Inside the vault, the anchor is the vault, and the door is one dot among the keys, the CLI and the library. Inside the door, the anchor is the door, and the phone by QR is one dot among the passkey providers. Each child map is what The passkey opens the vault and Where the vault keys live describe at length; the figure is those articles at three altitudes.
fractal

It goes up as well as down. Above the business map is the market it sits in, where the whole of sgit.ai is one dot on somebody else's chain, and that is the map the "does the market exist" section was reading. Which altitude to draw is the first decision, and most of the wrong decisions I have seen on maps were made by drawing the right map at the wrong altitude.
decks

The maps are better presented than read, so there are two decks, both plain pages on this site with the figures in them, and both print to PDF from your browser: open the deck, press the print button or your usual shortcut, and choose "Save as PDF". One slide per page, landscape, nothing uploaded anywhere. Why I love Wardley maps: the explanation, using the maps above as the examples. Twelve slides. Reading one map: the eight frames of the afternoon, one question per slide. How do I think about this, what am I seeing, where do I focus.
data

A reader asked today whether collecting these should have been a simple query, and it should have been. Every article on this site has a graph beside it, published at articles/graphs, and as of this release each graph also lists the article's figures: the file, its URL, the caption, the kind the author gave it, and for a multi-frame figure every frame in order. The Wardley maps are tagged. So "every Wardley map on sgit.ai, with its context" is one read of articles/graphs.json and a filter on kind, and the next best-of can be drawn by an agent from that file rather than by rereading the articles. The same change is why the animated maps on this site now have play, pause, step and numbered buttons rather than a loop nobody could stop.
community

There is a serious community around Wardley mapping, and most of what is on this site has not reached it. Three things might be of use there. The maps above are source, not pictures: two were written in Mermaid's Wardley syntax and the rest are drawn from small scripts, so the placements are in a form that can be disagreed with line by line. The evolution axis as a choice, with risk, data and governance as alternatives, is an argument I would like to have again with people who map for a living. And the nested reading, maps all the way down with the dot as the next anchor, is either already a well-known practice I have not seen written up or an extension worth testing on somebody else's business. If you map, and any of that is wrong, that is exactly what the maps are for.
limits

Positions are judgements. Every placement on every map here is a claim by the author, not a measurement of anything. The captions and the footers say so. The eleven shifts are a 2022 list. The talk is linked; the list in this article is the shorter one I use now, and it is not the same list. The alternative-axis post is not quoted. It was not found while writing this, so the claim that it exists is from memory and the argument is restated, not cited. The two market readings are ours. They are how we read our own maps, and they can be wrong in the usual way maps are wrong: the layer moves, and the map was drawn before it did.
limits

The fractal rule is a practice, not a theorem. Keeping the child's anchor at the parent dot's position is how we draw it; there are cases, when the inside of a thing is much more or less mature than the thing, where it will be worth breaking. If you map, and want to compare one of these with yours, or want the maps as data for something of your own, write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
sources

A voice memo of mine on 12 October 2026, written by this site's agent in the voice of this site. The argument and the editorial responsibility are mine. The maps are from the articles linked beside them, all on this site, and from the three vaults named above; none was drawn new for this piece except the three-altitude figure and the collage. The 2022 talk is Why Wardley Maps changed how I think, Open Security Summit, 14 July 2022, recorded on YouTube. The build change that indexes the figures, and the frame controls, shipped with this article in site v0.7.77.

Abstract: I do not run any model or agent on my laptop, and I am asked why often enough to write it down. The reason is not a worry about models. It is a fact about operating systems: they have two hard walls, the kernel and the user account, and an agent on my laptop runs inside the wall marked "me", where it can read everything I can read, SSH keys, cloud credentials, the password manager's session, every site my browser is signed into. The rules the desktop agents add on top are settings, enforced by the process they constrain, and fifteen months of incidents show what happens when a mistake or an injected instruction reaches the account. So the agents run in four places that are not my laptop: Claude chat, with nothing connected and search across past chats switched off, for thinking; Claude Cowork in the cloud, with no repositories, for most of the agentic work; Claude Code on the web, with one repository per session and a network allowlist, when code has to change; and ChatGPT with no assets at all. What makes this workable is a vault as the shared drive between them: encrypted on the agent's side, keys handed to a session out of band, commit, pull, push, so the laptop passes keys and nothing else. The article gives the setup, the evidence, what the OS can and cannot isolate, the usability trade-offs, the three things I wish the platforms gave me, identity, secrets and a key pair per agent, and one caveat: this is about a laptop that holds the main account. A dedicated machine with separate accounts and nothing of mine on it is a different model, which I will try and report on later.

Four places the agents run, none of them my laptop, and the one vault they all share. Each surface gets the reach its job needs. The laptop holds the main account and is where I type, not where anything runs. As configured on 6 October 2026. No model runs on my laptop. Not because local models are bad, but because a process on my laptop runs as me, and I have not seen a desktop agent that runs as anyone else.

An operating system has two hard walls, the kernel and the user account. Inside the user account there is no boundary the OS enforces between an agent and my SSH keys, cloud credentials, password manager session, browser cookies, dotfiles and files. The desktop agents' permission prompts and sandboxes are settings the agent's own process enforces. The first vendor's own documentation lists "most of the machine, including credential files such as ~/.ssh" as the default read scope of its local sandbox. Fifteen months of incidents say what that means. Home directories and drives deleted by agents in their fastest modes, repositories that execute code before the trust prompt, hidden instructions in pull requests and tool descriptions that exfiltrated secrets, tens of thousands of self-hosted agent gateways exposed with keys in the clear, a local-sandbox escape that reached SSH keys. Every one was fixed. The pattern is what stays.

So the agents run in four places that are not my laptop. Claude chat for thinking, with nothing connected. Claude Cowork in the cloud for most of the agentic work, with no repositories. Claude Code on the web when a repository has to change, one per session, behind a network allowlist. ChatGPT for a second model, with no assets. The vault is what makes this workable. A shared drive the host cannot read, that any session can be handed a key to. Each session reads its state from files, does its kind of work, writes files back; the next session pulls. Without it I would have to run something locally to pass work between agents. With it, the laptop passes keys and nothing else.

The trade-offs are real and I accept them. No agents on a flight. A key handed per session. Cowork has no per-session secrets, so one vault per scope does the job instead. Chat does not search my past chats, because that was the one gap. Three wishes: an identity per agent, secrets per agent, and a key pair per agent. The cloud surfaces are one step from all three. The question arrives as "why don't you run Claude on your Mac" or "why not a local model". The short answer is that I have no business need to run a model offline, so I accept the constraint of needing a connection; and that the thing I would need from a local agent, isolation better than I get online, is the thing no local agent offers. The models are fine. The place they run is the problem.

For a while I did try the desktop tools. What I saw was the amount of reach. On a laptop that holds a working life, the reach of a process running as me is everything: the credentials for every cloud I use, the keys for every server I can log into, the password manager while it is unlocked, every site my browser is signed into, every project's environment file, the shell, the network. In RiskMandate's vocabulary, the grant is my whole account, the mandate is "help me with this document", and nearly every row of the gap has an expectation in front of it, a rule the agent's own process is asked to keep. I would not accept that from a contractor and I do not accept it from a process.

An operating system has two hard walls, the kernel and the user. An agent on your laptop runs inside the wall marked "you", where everything your account can read is readable. The desktop agents add settings on top. The caveat is in the black bar.

A general-purpose operating system separates two things by force. The kernel is separated from everything else, and one user's files are separated from another's. Within one user account there is no third wall. A process you start runs with your identity and your rights, and the file system does not know the difference between you opening your SSH key and a process you started opening it. macOS adds consent prompts for a handful of folders and devices, and a terminal that has been granted full disk access has already answered them for everything launched from it. The keychain can scope items per application, and most of the tokens that matter are not in the keychain; they are in dotfiles, environment files and browser profiles.

The desktop agents know this and add their own layers. Approval prompts before destructive commands. Allow lists for shell commands. A process sandbox, built on the operating system's own primitives, that restricts writes to the working directory and routes network through a proxy. A virtual machine, in one product's case, with a scoped token. These are real, they reduce accidents, and they are all inside the wall marked "me", enforced by the process they constrain. Anthropic's own documentation for its local coding agent is candid about where that leaves the reads: the sandbox is "off by default", it covers shell commands only while "Claude's file tools, MCP servers, and hooks run outside it", and the default read scope is "most of the machine, including credential files such as ~/.ssh and ~/.aws/credentials". Its security page says the same thing in one sentence: "The boundary is a permission prompt, so a Bash command you approve can still write anywhere your user account can."

What would be a boundary is a separate operating-system user for the agent, with its own home, keychain and sessions and nothing of mine in them; or a separate machine; or a container or cloud environment with a network allowlist and credentials injected per task. As far as I have been able to find, none of the mainstream desktop agents runs as a separate user by default; a commenter on one of the incidents below put the fix in a sentence, "make claude a local user, without sudo", and it remains community advice rather than a product. The cloud environments do the equivalent by construction, which is the whole of my argument.

One more thing about words. When a local agent deletes a directory, the usual account is that the model hallucinated. The account that matters is that nothing stood between the mistake and the account's reach. A mistake inside a boundary is a bad afternoon. The same mistake inside "me" is an incident, and the incidents are below. Fifteen months of agents reaching what they were given, July 2025 to September 2026. Every flaw was fixed, most within days; the cloud versions of the same tools were often unaffected. The last column is the point. I want to be careful with this list. Every item is a reported incident or disclosure with a source, every vendor fixed what was theirs to fix, and several of the tools involved are ones I use in their cloud form every day. The list is not an argument against the tools. It is an argument about where they run.

July 2025. A release of Amazon's coding assistant for VS Code shipped with an injected prompt telling the agent to act as a "system cleaner" and delete local files and cloud resources; Amazon says the payload was malformed and did not run. The same month Google's Gemini CLI, asked to move a user's files into a new folder, failed to notice the folder was never created and moved each file onto the same path, losing all but the last. Also that month: a critical command-injection flaw in the MCP connector most desktop agents used, and two containment flaws in Anthropic's reference filesystem server, one a prefix match that let an allowed path like /tmp/allow_dir also match /tmp/allow_dir_sensitive_credentials, the other a symlink that reached arbitrary files.

August 2025. Two Cursor flaws: a prompt hidden in content could write a tool configuration that executed before the user approved it, and in a shared repository an approved configuration could be silently swapped for another command. September to October 2025. A fake MCP package on npm built trust over fifteen versions and then added a hidden copy of every email to an attacker. Hidden comments in a pull request made GitHub Copilot Chat search a victim's private repositories for secrets and exfiltrate them character by character through an image proxy. Claude Code's own project settings file could run shell commands from a cloned repository before the trust prompt; a later flaw could redirect API traffic and leak the API key.

December 2025. A user running Claude Code with permission prompts skipped asked it to tidy some folders; the command ended in ~/ and removed the home directory, keychain data reportedly among the losses. A photographer using Google's Antigravity in its fastest mode to clear a cache lost a whole drive; the agent's own words afterwards were "No, you absolutely did not give me permission to do that." January to February 2026. OpenClaw, the self-hosted personal agent that became the design Meta later acknowledged copying, was found exposed on the internet in the tens of thousands of instances, between twenty-one and forty-two thousand depending on the scanner and the date, with API keys and chat histories in the clear under the user's home directory. A supply-chain campaign placed 341 malicious skills in its marketplace, most of them delivering a macOS credential stealer that targets the keychain, browser passwords, wallets and SSH keys.

March 2026. A compromised release of a widely used Python package harvested environment variables, SSH keys, cloud credentials, cluster configurations and shell history on install. Not an agent incident; the same blast radius, and the same machine. July 2026. Researchers showed that untrusted content in a local Claude Cowork session could escape its virtual machine through a kernel bug and "read and write files anywhere on your Mac", reaching "SSH keys, cloud credentials, anything the user's account can touch". Cloud execution had become Cowork's default two weeks earlier, and the report notes the cloud path did not appear to be affected. September 2026. Meta's Muse desktop app had an undocumented setting, writable by any unprivileged local process, that redirected dictation to an attacker's server and could capture prompts and tokens. Meta fixed it within a day and called it a local privilege escalation; the researcher pointed out that a one-click social-engineering attack delivers exactly that.

Two numbers frame the list. GitGuardian's 2026 report counted 24,008 unique secrets in agent tool-configuration files on public GitHub, 2,117 of them still valid, and its June 2026 note on developer laptops reported an average of 150 secrets per machine in its beta programme, 38 per cent of them private keys, with 40 per cent found in directories and logs left by AI tooling. The sample is not random and the vendor sells the scanner; the order of magnitude is the point. The laptop is the credential store, and the agent runs in it.

The mechanism in most of these is the one Simon Willison named in June 2025 as the lethal trifecta: access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and the ability to communicate out. "LLMs follow instructions in content. This is what makes them so useful ... The problem is that they don't just follow our instructions." On a laptop all three legs are present by default, because the private data is the account, the untrusted content is every file and page the agent reads, and the network is the user's. So the agents run in four places, and the places are chosen by what each job needs to reach.

Claude chat, for thinking. The most isolated surface and the most interactive. Nothing is connected to it: no files beyond what I paste, no connectors, no internet in my configuration. The one gap was the feature that lets a chat search and reference my past chats, which would have let any conversation reach every other; I have switched it off, which Anthropic's help pages describe under memory settings. What a chat says can leave it only through me.

Claude Cowork, in the cloud, for the team. This is where most of my agentic work happens, because it is better at running several agents in parallel on longer tasks and because its flow is the one I prefer: it talks. It runs on Anthropic's servers, which has been the default since July 2026 and, from today, the only option on individual plans. It has no GitHub connector and reaches no repository. Its one persistent asset is the vault, and I decide which vault each session is handed. The limitation is that Cowork has no per-session secrets; a key given to one agent is available to the surface, which is honest about what the platform can and cannot scope, and which I work round with one vault per scope.

Claude Code on the web, when code has to change. Each session gets a cloud environment with a network allowlist, one repository that I choose, and environment variables per environment, which is the control Cowork lacks and the reason the repositories live here. It is less conversational; it gets on with it. I use it only when a repository has to change, and I give it that repository and nothing else. The egress allowlist is what the how-to on Team and Enterprise plans is about, written after a session could install sgit and not reach it. ChatGPT, for a second model. Infographics mostly, a second opinion sometimes, a little vault work. It has no connectors to any of my accounts and no assets at all, apart from a vault read key when I choose to hand it one. What it makes comes back through me.

In Six agents, one inbox I noted that Cowork and Claude Code are different agents with different reach even on the same seat. This setup is that observation used on purpose: the surface with the repositories has no mailbox, the surface with the mailbox has no repositories, and the surface with neither does the thinking. The vault as the shared drive between agents. A session is handed a key out of band, pulls, works, commits and pushes; the next session on another surface pulls. The host holds ciphertext. Keys masked, paths illustrative.

None of this would work without a way for the agents to hand work to each other that is not my laptop. That is what the vault does, and it is why this article is also about vaults. An sgit vault is a folder whose every file, filename, commit message and branch name is encrypted on the agent's side before it leaves; the host holds ciphertext and sees sizes and timings. A session is handed a key out of band, in the session, never written to a file. It clones or pulls, reads its state from files, does one kind of work, runs the leak check, commits and pushes. The next session, on another surface or another day, pulls and continues. Two sessions cannot overwrite each other's unpushed work, because each clone has its own branch and key and pushes are compare-and-swap. The record is the vault's history, readable later with a read key and no write credential.

The vault is also the reason the surfaces can be so isolated. Cowork needs no repository because the brief it writes goes into the vault and Claude Code pulls it. Claude Code needs no mailbox because the result it writes goes into the vault and the inbox agent reads it. ChatGPT needs no connector because a read key is enough to show it a vault. The one thing that moves between surfaces is a key, and keys have three reaches: a vault key that writes, a read key derived one way that only reads, and a lane token that only appends. The agent team as it runs is this pattern with twelve agents and three vaults; this article is the single-person version of it.

The same modest mandate deployed on my laptop and in a cloud session, read as a behaviour policy. On the laptop the grant is the account and most barriers are expectations. In the cloud the grant is built small and most barriers are boundaries. The last row, an instruction hidden in a file the agent reads, has no barrier in either; what differs is what it can reach.

The table is worth reading row by row, and the last row is the point. Prompt injection is not prevented by moving to the cloud. An instruction hidden in a page or a file the agent reads will be followed in either deployment, because that is what a model does with instructions. What the cloud session changes is what the followed instruction can reach: one repository and one vault, instead of my account. The barrier that holds is the small grant, not a cleverer filter. This is the argument of Footprint and blast radius, that blast radius is defined over the reach because whoever takes the agent over inherits the reach; and of the ultimate insider, that the more you constrain an agent the more you can trust it with. Honestly: a few things, and I pay them.

No agents without a connection. On a flight I have the chat on my phone and nothing else. I have not had a business need that this breaks. A key per session, by hand. Each session is handed what it needs. It is a minute's work and it is also the control. No per-session secrets in Cowork. One vault per scope, and the keys for the scope, instead of one vault with scoped keys. More vaults than I would like. Chat does not remember across chats. I switched that off and I paste what matters. The alternative was one conversation reaching all of them. Two products, two flows. Cowork talks, Code gets on with it. I would like Code to talk more, and I accept that it is built for people who want it to get on with it.

The usability is otherwise better than the alternative, not worse. The sessions start clean, nothing accumulates on a machine I have to look after, and when something goes wrong the blast radius is a repository with history and a vault with history. That is a bad afternoon, which I have had, and not an incident, which I have not. Three things that would change the security of the whole setup and that no platform I use provides yet: an identity per agent, secrets per agent, and a key pair per agent. Each exists in pieces on this site; none is a product feature.

An identity per agent. Each agent should be somebody: an account the platform knows, a name on its commits, a footprint under that name. Today the nearest thing is a dedicated Workspace and Claude seat per agent, which the RiskMandate team buys and which costs a human's seat each; inside a shared vault an agent's identity is its branch, because signed authorship is not yet recorded, as the limitations page says. Secrets per agent. Each agent should hold the keys its job needs and no other agent's, injected per session and revocable per agent, with a record of which session used which. Claude Code on the web has per-environment variables and an API-credential mode that never shows the key to the agent, which is the right shape; Cowork has neither, so the workaround is vaults per scope.

A key pair per agent. Each agent should be able to sign what it writes and receive what is encrypted to it alone. The append-lane work gives agents per-session keys and a pinned registry, and Agent Contact signs mail between the sites' agents; it is machinery built beside the platforms, not something they provide. Together the three turn "the agent runs as whoever started the session" into "the agent runs as itself", which is the difference between the laptop model, where the only identity available is mine, and the model the cloud surfaces are one step away from.

Everything above is about a laptop that holds the main account. The wall marked "me" has a working life inside it, and that is why no agent runs there. A dedicated machine changes the picture: a Mac mini or a second laptop with a separate Apple account, a separate Workspace account, no password manager of mine, no browser signed into anything of mine, and only the keys that machine's agents need. The wall marked "that user" would have nothing of mine inside it, which is the property the cloud sessions have by construction. It is a reasonable way to run local agents, and some of the isolation the vendors have shipped, the virtual machines and the process sandboxes, would be a second layer on a machine like that rather than the only one. I have not run it, so I am not reporting on it. When I have, it will be its own article, with the same honesty about what broke.

The setup described runs. The four surfaces, the vault as the shared drive, the keys handed per session, the leak check before every commit, the read keys published on this site and the write keys escrowed. The RiskMandate team runs the twelve-agent version of it. The evidence list is sourced and dated. What does not exist: the three wishes, as platform features; a desktop agent that runs as a separate operating-system user by default; and my own report on the dedicated-machine model, which is next. The agent team as it runs: the twelve-agent version of this setup, with the security properties as properties. Six agents, one inbox: the account as the blast radius, and Cowork and Code as different agents with different reach. Footprint and blast radius and The ultimate insider: why blast radius is defined over the reach, and why constraint is what lets you trust an agent.

A personal agent that keeps your secrets: the same question for the vendors' personal agents, and a design with the compute where the user can see it. The 10,000-hours case is one claim, followed by hand. This is the same failure mode measured at network scale: one biomedical belief, traced through its entire citation network.
mechanisms

Mechanism What it does Citation bias Papers selectively cite sources that support the claim already being made, rather than a representative sample of the evidence Amplification Each new citation adds apparent weight without adding independent evidence — a chain of papers citing each other reads, from outside, as many independent confirmations Invention A hypothesis is converted into a stated fact purely by the act of being cited as one, with no new evidence produced at any step Citation diversion A later commentary's addition: a citation is used to support a claim the cited work does not actually make, redirecting the reader's trust toward a conclusion the original never reached The distortions did not stay academic. They extended into grant applications — funding decisions made partly on the strength of a citation network that, traced back, terminates in nothing. The underlying source data is publicly citable: pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19622839.
why-it-matters

A single claim like the 10,000-hours figure is a story a reader can hold in their head. A 242-paper citation network is not — nobody reads 675 citations to check whether they actually support what they are cited for. That is exactly the case a graph is built for: typed citation edges mean the amplification and the invention are visible in the structure itself, not something a reader has to reconstruct by hand from 242 separate PDFs.

"This is not necessarily conspiracy theories, it's just that every person has an agenda, every entity has core objectives — whether it's to sell more or provide certain things — the bias is always there." Disclosing an agenda is not dismissing a claim. It is context a reader is entitled to before deciding how much weight to give it.
disclosure-not-dismissal

A study funded by the company whose product it evaluates is not automatically wrong. A regulator's finding about the industry it regulates is not automatically right. In both cases, the funding relationship, the reporting relationship, and the stated objective of the entity behind the claim are facts a reader can weigh — if they are visible. Today they usually are not: "most articles do not provide evidence, they provide a link, the link is never followed." Attaching agenda as a disclosed, structured field to every claim is not an accusation; it is the same discipline a graph applies to every other fact.
self-critique

The hazard is what a reader, or a downstream system, does with it. The same tool that helps a reader discount a vendor's study of its own product helps them discount a regulator's finding about their own industry. The graph has an agenda too. This is not a footnote added for balance. It is the argument's own weak point, stated plainly rather than left for a critic to find. Agenda-tagging is a tool for weighing evidence, not a tool for winning an argument by pointing at a funding source and stopping there — and nothing about the mechanism prevents it from being used the second way. A site that names the way its own tool can be abused is making the argument the rest of the site depends on: if this page were missing, everything else here would be easier to distrust, correctly.
open-question

Does agenda-tagging survive contact with a motivated reader? The corpus asks this of itself and does not resolve it. A reader determined to dismiss an inconvenient finding already has the disclosed agenda as ready-made ammunition; a reader determined to accept a convenient one can ignore the same disclosure just as easily. Whether structured agenda disclosure changes behaviour on average, or simply gives every reader a new tool to use exactly as motivated as before, is not answered anywhere in this material. See the site's open questions.

The fact doesn't exist in a vacuum. A document set has no mechanism for asking "what do I currently believe that rests on something since corrected?" A graph answers that question as a traversal, not a research project.
supersede

A superseded claim is marked from the date it was superseded and stays in the graph — it is not removed. That preserves a question a deleted-and-replaced record cannot answer: what did we believe in March? Deletion optimises for a tidy present state; supersession optimises for an honest history, which is the property a corrections mechanism actually needs.
typed-edges

A citation is not a single undifferentiated link. Each one is typed by how faithfully it represents the source it cites: Edge type What it means Supports The cited source states the claim as represented Partially supports The cited source supports part of the claim, or supports it under narrower conditions than stated Extends beyond The citing claim goes further than the cited source actually established Contradicts The cited source states the opposite, or a materially different finding The 10,000-hours claim, correctly typed, would carry an edge to the original 1993 study marked extends beyond — the study reported an average for a subgroup; the popularised claim states a universal threshold. That single typed edge is the correction, attached at the point where anyone would encounter the claim, rather than published separately and hoped to be found.
freshness

A claim's freshness — how long since it was last checked against its sources, and whether any of those sources have since changed — is a recorded property of the claim, not an implicit assumption a reader has to make. The AI Act case is what an unpriced, unrecorded staleness failure looks like in practice.

The most distinctive argument in the corpus, and the one nobody else is making. In a document, a correction is a new document. Nothing that cited the original knows. In a graph, a correction is an edge — typed, dated, and traceable. Five pages, building from a single story any reader can follow with no technical background, to the self-critique that keeps the argument honest. Page What it carries The claim that would not die The 10,000-hours case, in full: an average mistaken for a threshold, and thirty years of correction that never attached to the claim 242 papers The same failure, measured: one biomedical belief, 675 citations, >220,000 supporting paths, tracing back to nothing How a graph answers it Supersede-never-delete, citation edges typed by faithfulness, and the traversal that answers "what do I believe that has since been corrected?" Agenda is context

Disclosing an agenda is not dismissing a claim — and the self-critique this site chooses to publish rather than bury: the graph has an agenda too Staleness in the wild A live example: the EU AI Act's "consolidated" text is dated 2024 and incorporates nothing since
fact-in-a-vacuum

Every person has an agenda, every entity has core objectives — to sell more, to protect a position, to advance a case. "This is not necessarily conspiracy theories, it's just that every person has an agenda." Even a direct quote can mislead: "even quotes sometimes don't have the correct meaning, and the original author didn't actually mean what is now being quoted as reference." A graph does not resolve this by declaring a winner. It resolves it by making the agenda, the citation chain and the correction history all walkable — and by refusing to delete what turned out to be wrong.

Not a hypothetical. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 — the EU AI Act — was adopted 8 July 2026 and entered into force 27 July 2026. The official consolidated text is dated 12 July 2024 and incorporates nothing since. A reader following the "official" source is reading a document that predates the regulation actually entering into force by over a year.
three-states

Public sources describing the Act's status fall into three distinct categories, and none of them is labelled as such at the point a reader encounters it: State What it means Current and correct Reflects the Act as adopted and in force. Rare, and not distinguishable from the other two states by appearance alone Stale but was once true Accurately described an earlier draft or an earlier state of the process, and has not been updated since Never was the law A pre-adoption negotiating draft, presented without the caveat that it never had legal force at all — "worse than stale because it never was the law." At least one public source in circulation carries exactly this
probe

Article 10 of the Act was the subject of amendment during the legislative process. A reader checking a source's treatment of Article 10 specifically — rather than the Act's headline status — can determine which of the three states above that source is actually in, because Article 10's language differs materially between the draft and adopted versions. This is the kind of check the corpus argues should be structural, not something a reader has to think to perform.
why-it-matters

This is exactly the failure the rest of this section argues about, caught in the act rather than reconstructed after the fact. No single actor lied. Sources were accurate when written and were never updated, or were published as drafts and never re-labelled once superseded. Nobody is tracking which state each source is currently in, and a document-based system has no structural way to do so — each source is its own island, and there is no edge connecting "this text" to "the regulation's current state" that updates when the regulation changes. That absent edge is precisely what a typed, dated citation graph supplies.

The site's best non-technical story, because it needs no technical background to land. In 1993, a study of violin students at a Berlin academy found something specific. By 2008, the public remembered something else entirely — and the difference is the whole argument for why corrections need to propagate as forcefully as the original claim.
study

Violin students at a Berlin academy were grouped by ability. The top group had, on average, accumulated roughly 10,000 hours of practice by age 20. That is an average, not a threshold: roughly half the top group had not reached it. The mechanism the researcher identified was deliberate practice — structured, feedback-driven, effortful practice — not simply accumulated time. Individual variation was large: one chess player studied elsewhere reached master level in roughly 3,000 hours; another needed more than 20,000. The students in the Berlin study were, by the researcher's own account, not yet experts at the point the hours were counted.
popularised

Popularised in 2008, the number became, in public memory, a threshold: 10,000 hours of practice at anything makes you an expert. The researcher who ran the original study called the figure "catchy rather than meaningful — it could as easily have been eleven thousand." He spent much of the rest of his career trying to correct the record: books, articles, interviews, an open letter addressing the misreading directly. None of it ever attached to the claim. The person best placed in the world to say that is not what my study showed had no channel that reached where the claim was actually being repeated, no standing at the point of use, and no economic reason to keep correcting it beyond his own conviction. Every retelling of the 10,000-hours claim since 2008 has been, structurally, a fresh document with no edge back to the correction.
graph

In a graph model, the claim is a node. The correction is not a separate document somewhere else on the internet — it is a typed edge attached directly to that node, dated, and traceable from every place the claim is cited. A reader encountering the 10,000-hours figure in 2015, or 2026, would see the correction at the point of use, not have to go looking for it. The correction propagates with the same force as the original claim — the inverse of how misinformation actually spreads today, where a false or oversimplified claim travels virally and the correction barely travels at all. This is the case for how a graph actually does this — supersede-never-delete, typed citation edges, and the traversal query that this study never got to run against its own citation network.

Oxigraph, a SPARQL 1.1 store compiled to WebAssembly, running in this tab over 4,001 triples: the Portugal graph re-serialised at build, with the ontology inside the store, every inverse declared with owl:inverseOf, and labels in English and Portuguese. Pick a worked query or write your own; the same question in Cypher is shown beside each, and not run.
scheme

The triples are triples.nt, written by the Portugal graph build from graph.json and ontology.json — a re-serialisation, not a second source. Nodes are portugal/id/<graph id>, verbs portugal/verb/<verb>, types portugal/type/<Type>, scalar attributes portugal/prop/<key>. Each fact is stored once in its forward direction; the inverse verb is declared with owl:inverseOf so a query walks it with ^. Node and verb labels carry @en, and @pt where the ontology has one, which is what lets the third worked query read a path aloud in Portuguese from the store alone.
why

Three of the worked queries cannot be asked comfortably in SQL: the property path that walks any verb in either direction, the CONSTRUCT that derives 298 inverse edges without storing them, and the ASK that checks the grammar's ban on symmetric edges. The rest are the same questions the SQL console answers, so the two can be read side by side. Cypher is the other common graph language and is shown for every query; running it here would mean vendoring a 73 MB engine, and the argument page says why that was declined.

This site has no server. The Portugal section is 19 JSON files in a git repository, 1.3 MB in all, each with its hash in a manifest. Two real database engines run over exactly those files in your browser, compiled to WebAssembly: SQLite, and Oxigraph speaking SPARQL 1.1. Nothing is uploaded, nothing is queried remotely, and when the tab closes the database is gone. The files are the database. The engines are readers.
two-consoles

15 tables built from the JSON on load, 16 worked queries from a count-by-class to a recursive graph walk, and a box to write your own. Every example ran at build; its row count is printed beside it so your run can disagree. 4,001 triples — the same graph, the ontology inside the store, inverses declared with owl:inverseOf and walked with a property path, labels in English and Portuguese so a path reads aloud. 13 worked queries, each shown beside the same question in Cypher.
pattern

Every fact on the Portugal section lives in one JSON file that owns it: the people in people.json, the frozen pages in sources.json, the sessions in sessions.json. The build derives the other shapes a reader might want — the graph in graph.json, the same graph as RDF in triples.nt, the manifest with every hash — and nothing is derived twice. There is no import step, no schema migration and no connection string: the SQL console reads a loader spec, tables.json, that says which file and which field each column comes from, so a reader who doubts a cell can open the file it came from. Three things follow, and they are the argument for doing it this way rather than a cheaper way of doing the usual thing:
pattern

A query is reproducible against a commit. The files are versioned by git; a result carries the site version it ran against, and this page's examples record the row count they returned at build. A database that answers differently tomorrow with no commit in between is a database that has been edited. A check is a query. The Portugal build runs fifteen gates in Python — no verb its own inverse, every node naming a registered source, nobody in the graph who is not on the published list. Each is expressible as a query here, and the SPARQL console runs one of them as an ASK. When the rule and the check are the same sentence, the rule cannot drift from what is enforced.
pattern

The reader pays nothing and trusts nothing. No account, no key, no request to a server that could log the question. The engine is 4.6 MB of vendored code, fetched once and cached; the data is the same files the page is built from. An agent gets the same: both consoles publish window.__tools after a tool:ready event, the convention graphs.sgit.ai's universe reader set.
honest

It is not a graph database, and graphs.sgit.ai's position is inherited on purpose: “not a graph database pitch — the claim is that one grammar is the interface at every boundary, not that things are stored in a graph.” The JSON stays the source of truth. The SPARQL store is built from it on load and thrown away on close; nothing is ever written back. Its shipped page lists “browser SPARQL/Cypher, RDF in code” under what that site does not have; this page is where the estate now has it, as a reader over files rather than a store of record.
honest

It is not a server in disguise. newsroom.sgit.ai · the design The ideas behind the newsroom, each one next to what now runs and what is still only a design. This site spent August and September 2026 arguing for a newsroom before one existed. On 10 October 2026 the newsroom it argued for runs, so the argument can now be checked against it. The table puts each idea next to what runs and what does not. The idea Where it is argued What runs What does not, yet Sell the graph, not the paragraph. The story is a graph; the article is one projection of it. The thesis Every article is published with its own graph: 132 of them, drawn together at As graphs. The World News Day corpus is a graph of 160 nodes and 427 typed edges, in a vault anyone can clone. Nobody buys a graph. There is no price, no API and no customer for one.

Corrections must propagate. In a graph a correction is an edge, so it reaches what cited the claim. Corrections, with one worked case and the mechanism Every article keeps every published version and what changed (175 version pages). Corrections are recorded as corrections, for example World News Day’s. A correction does not yet reach the pages that cited what it corrected, here or anywhere else. Provenance is the product. A newsroom that shows its work earns trust a black box cannot. Provenance, articles as vaults, the decision graph The newsroom publishes how it runs: 6 roles, the rules each works under, the board and a log of every run. The World News Day sources are frozen and hashed, and the gate that re-checks them ships inside the vault. Articles are not yet vaults, and no per-story ledger of cost and decisions is published. Pay the person who found the fact. Revenue should reach upstream, not stop at the last publisher.

Paying the fact creator, trust as a service A reading meter: a few pence a page from a balance kept in the reader’s browser, priced by how far they read and how useful they said it was. A £5 card top-up runs, on Stripe’s page. Nothing is paid upstream to the people whose facts an article uses. Rights travel with the content. A licence nobody can read is not a licence. Content rights: CC-Signed Every article here declares CC BY 4.0 in a form a machine reads. The World News Day corpus measured the gap: 21 op-eds free to republish, none under a named licence. CC-Signed, where breaking the signature chain breaks the licence, is a design. No server. Reader data stays in the reader’s browser unless the reader sends it. No server, by design, databases with no server

The pages are static files, and what you read is kept in the browser rather than on a server. The meter, the personas and the reading history live there; SQLite and a SPARQL store run there too. Three things can leave the browser, when the reader chooses: a payment, to Stripe; a subscription and a reading share, encrypted, to a write-only lane. What leaves, and when. Encrypted vaults for readers would change this, and are not built.
pages

Pages that the running newsroom has since overtaken, like the fifteen-department newsroom design or the itemised £8.40 story, are in the archive, dated and labelled with what replaced them.

Every page on this site was written from a source, and the sources are published here rather than summarised away. Raw markdown is the source of truth; these reader pages are presentation. Each one states the single most important thing in its document, says why it is on this site, and renders the raw file in-page — so a reader page cannot drift from the document it claims to render. This is the site whose central claim is that most articles do not provide evidence, they provide a link, and the link is never followed. Handing a reader a bare .md file and calling it "the source" is the lazy version of exactly that failure. So the document is readable where the reader already is, with its provenance stated — and still one click from the byte-for-byte original.

Provenance makes the upstream flow trackable; the argument is that this makes it billable. "In companies that's okay, because that's already covered by the cost of the company operating, but in the real world at the moment we don't have that." A fact-checker inside a company is paid by the company's existing budget. A fact-checker correcting the public record has no equivalent budget, and the record decays accordingly — the 10,000-hours case is that decay, measured over thirty years.
larger-market

"We also need to have a commercialisation model for journalists, and entities who do research; they should also have a way to confirm that research is correct and has been used in that particular way." Selling access to a finished article is one business. Selling confirmation that a specific claim was used correctly, in a specific context, is a different and — by the source material's own assessment — arguably larger market that almost nobody is currently addressing.

The largest single treatment of news monetisation anywhere in either corpus, and the earliest by over a year: published 2 April 2025, fifteen months before the x402 payment rail this argument depended on actually existed. Read the original in full at the link above; this page states what it argued and pairs it, deliberately, with what has since become real.
what-it-argued

The piece made the case for micro- and nano-scale payments as the mechanism that could let news monetise at the granularity of a single fact or a single article read, rather than only at the scale of a subscription or a full-page advertisement. Written well before any production-grade rail existed to carry payments that small economically, it argued the case on the economics and the reader behaviour, not on any specific implementation available at the time.
pairing

This page is deliberately paired with the 2026 payment-rails page. The original argument is unedited at its source — nothing about it has been rewritten to look more prescient in hindsight. What is new is that x402 now exists, settles in ~200ms, and charges zero protocol fees: the mechanism the 2025 argument needed has since arrived. That is this site's own central argument about correction-propagation, applied to its own history rather than to somebody else's mistake: the original stays where it is: the newer knowledge attaches alongside it rather than overwriting it.
why-not-verbatim

Per this site's provenance contract, a page must state its curation honestly. This site's brief pack recorded the original's title, date, authors, word count and theme in full, but not its complete text. Rather than fabricate a verbatim reproduction from that metadata, this page states plainly that it is a synthesis and points to the real original for the full argument. Synthesised is not a lesser status; it is a different claim about the text — and a false claim to verbatim reproduction would be exactly the provenance failure this site exists to argue against.

"The angle is not just, is this statement correct in itself; the question is, is this correct in this context, for this use, for this conclusion." A refinement made on 31 July 2026 that changes what is actually billable.
split

Reader pays the outlet. The value behind that payment, per the origin document, actually breaks down: 60% original researcher · 25% data organisation · 10% journalist synthesis · 5% outlet distribution. Today, essentially all of that revenue is captured at the 5% layer. Provenance makes the other 95% visible; the argument is that visibility is what makes it payable.
billable-unit

Not is this true — a question with no clean billing event, since truth does not have a moment of consumption. Instead: is this use of it sound, evaluated and cached per claim-and-context pair. The same underlying fact can be soundly used in one argument and unsoundly extended in another; the design bills the validation of a specific use, not a one-time certification of the fact in isolation. This is theme 4's central mechanical idea, and the pack is explicit that every open question about metering, settlement and licensing is still open — see the payment rails page and the open questions.
ericsson

Returning to the 10,000-hours case from the economics side rather than the corrections side: "the person best placed in the world to say that is not what my study showed had no channel, no standing at the point of use, and no economic reason to keep doing it beyond his own conviction." A contextual-validation market is, among other things, a proposed economic reason. Whether it would have actually reached the researcher in this specific case is untested.

Fifteen months after the micropayments argument was first published, the rail arrived. This page is real and cited — it describes payment infrastructure that exists and is operating today, not a design.

Governed at the Linux Foundation since April 2026, with more than 20 founding members. Settlement runs at roughly 200ms, at a fraction of a cent per transaction, with zero protocol fees. In its first year, the rail processed approximately 169 million transactions. It reached general availability in Amazon CloudFront/WAF in June 2026.
others

Cloudflare Monetization Gateway was announced 1 July 2026, currently waitlist-only. AWS Bedrock AgentCore Payments, announced 7 May 2026 with Coinbase and Stripe as partners, is specified for ticket sizes from $0.001 to $1,000 — a range that spans a single-fact micropayment and a substantial evidence-pack purchase in one rail.
wall

A £1 card top-up returns 59p of usable credit. Fixed per-transaction fees on traditional card rails make anything below roughly a pound uneconomic to charge for at all. "The fixed fee is not an inconvenience in that market, it is a wall." A single-fact micropayment, a per-source read fee, a £8.40 story purchase — none of these are viable on rails built around a fixed fee that eats more than half of a £1 transaction. x402's near-zero marginal cost is what makes contextual validation as a billable unit arithmetically possible rather than merely conceptually appealing.

Named Trust-as-a-Service across 43 occurrences in the source material. The register splits into a risk-acceptor role and a fact-certifier role — distinct, payable, and warranted, not a courtesy credential.
fact-certifier

A fact-certifier does not just state an opinion about a claim's reliability; the design specifies two prices for the service, and a warranted output — a certification that carries consequence if it turns out to be wrong, not a disclaimed guess. The stated aim: "trade on facts and evidence rather than attention." An outlet's business today is largely attention; this design proposes a parallel market trading directly on verified facts and evidence packs instead.
decouple

Credibility, under this design, is a track record over time, calibrated by outcomes rather than assigned by title. The explicit goal: it "decouples the weight a statement carries from the volume, power, or rank of the person making it, so the quiet person who is usually right is heard and the loudest or most senior voice does not automatically win." A junior analyst with a strong, checkable track record on a narrow domain could, in principle, carry more calibrated weight on a claim in that domain than a senior figure with a weaker record on it.
liability

Selling trust makes the seller a target. A fact-certifier issuing warranted output has created a liability surface for themselves — a wrong certification is not just an embarrassment, it is a claim against a warranty. The source material notes this tension explicitly and does not attempt to size it: how large the liability exposure actually is, and what insures against it, is not specified anywhere in the corpus.

Engineering · open Feedback without a vault: the newsroom's append lane, with a public write token and key on the page, and a typed schema Id 010 Status open Kind Story Priority urgent Created 2026-10-12T15:20:00Z Source the owner's first run of v0.12.0 on an iPad, 12 October 2026: three screenshots and a note kept in the pane, relayed in chat Release v0.12.2 Effort large File admin/engineering/issues/open/010-feedback-without-a-vault.md
what-is-asked

The owner, after a note kept with no vault could not be sent: "these messages should be sent to an append lane … a vault that you have created that you're going to use to receive messages from the site … you put on the web page the public key to write the message and also the ID of the append lane … and you should also push a schema, a strongly typed schema, so you prevent a little bit of injection." The generic feedback "should always be there", with or without a vault.
how-it-is-done-on-this-site-already

The subscribe form writes to sgit.ai's subscribe lane: the contact file /.well-known/sgit-subscribe.json carries the vault id, the lane's append token and the recipient's public key; the browser encrypts a single-part .eml to that key and POSTs it to /api/vault/append/write/{vault}. The append token can only write. The API: https://sgit.ai/api/append-lanes.html; the two-way write-up: https://sgit.ai/docs/append-lane-messaging.html; the message convention: https://sgit.ai/docs/agent-contact.html.
scenario

Given I have kept notes and have no vault When I press Send to the newsroom Then each note is encrypted in my browser to the newsroom's public key And written into the newsroom's append lane with the published token And marked sent, with the lane's id And the newsroom drains the lane with its own key and reads the notes as the feedback schema Given the contact file says the lane is closed Then Send says so and offers the same notes as an email instead Given a note does not match the schema Then it is not sent
mock-up

/.well-known/newsroom-feedback.json: {schema, recipient {address, fingerprint, encrypt}, inbox {vault, endpoint, lane {append_token}, status}}; the message: newsroom-feedback/v1, a JSON document {schema, sent_at, device, persona, notes: [note…]} validated against /.well-known/newsroom-feedback.v1.schema.json before sending and after draining; admin/build/feedback_drain.py: list, fetch, decrypt, validate, mark processed, write the notes into the engineering inbox.
what-it-needs

An access key to create the newsroom's inbox vault and configure its lane (the keypair is made with sgit pki keygen and kept, passphrase-encrypted, in the inbox vault itself, as sgit.ai's subscribe vault does). Until the lane is open the contact file says status: closed and Send falls back to an email. Back to the board.
