Engineering · open The early-access key first, checked against the server, before a passkey or a vault is made Id 012 Status open Kind Story Priority high Created 2026-10-12T15:20:00Z Source the owner's first run of v0.12.0 on an iPad, 12 October 2026: three screenshots and a note kept in the pane, relayed in chat Release v0.12.2 Effort medium File admin/engineering/issues/open/012-early-access-key-first.md
what-is-asked

The owner: use the access key as an early-access token; "you should not even attempt to create a vault or even attempt to create a passkey until you have been given a valid [key], which you should also be able to check"; the key should be easy to enter, once.
scenario

Given I open the Vault tab for the first time on a device with no account Then the first thing asked is the early-access key, with a Check button When I paste it and press Check Then the pane asks the vault server with it, without creating anything, and says valid or not And only then are Make a passkey and Create the account offered Given the key is invalid Then nothing else is offered, and the pane says where a key comes from
how-to-check-a-key-without-side-effects

POST /api/vault/append/configure/{any vault id} with the key and a wrong write key: the server answers 401 to a bad or missing key and 404 to a good one (https://sgit.ai/api/append-lanes.html, checked 12 October against dev.send.sgraph.ai). The server also has GET /api/transfers/check-token/{token}, which answers {valid, status, remaining}; whether it takes an access key is not yet known.
on-the-question-of-hiding-the-key-on-the-page

A hash of the key on the page cannot be used to open anything, so it cannot replace typing the key; the key itself is the credential the server checks. A hash would only let the page say "that is not the key" before asking the server, and a published hash of a short key invites guessing. The early-access flow above is the answer: the key is typed once and kept in the master. Back to the board.

what-is-asked

On an iPhone, in a browser that could not reach the passkeys, the Vault button said sixteen changes existed only in that browser. The owner wanted them, and the recovery code is too much power to type into a browser that is not trusted, for a job that only needs to add. The brief, in six steps: a key pair for the reader, the private half in the master; an append lane on the reader vault, its token in the master; the link three ways (URL, text, QR) carrying the lane address, the append token and the public key, nothing else; the sender's side, which encrypts the pending records and appends them; the drain, on unlock, which says what arrived and from which browser and merges it on one press, keeping the sender as the author; and tests. With care for: a rotatable token, the drain showing what arrived before it merges, and a link that can expire.
scenario

Given my vault is open with my passkey When I press "Make a link for another browser" in the Vault tab Then a key pair is made in this browser, an append lane is configured on my reader vault, and both are recorded in my master And the link is shown as a URL, as text and as a QR code, carrying the lane, the append token and the public key, and nothing else Given a browser with no passkey opens the link Then it keeps the link, takes it out of the address, and says which vault and key it will send to and what it holds that the vault does not When I press "Send to my vault" Then its own records are written as one device file, sealed to the key in the link, and appended to the lane And the count of what is only in this browser goes to zero, and nothing is removed from it And on any page after that, the strip above the pane offers "Send to my vault" Given messages are waiting in the lane When I open my vault Then the Vault tab lists them: from which browser, when, and what each carries And a message sealed to another key, changed on the way, or not a newsroom inbox message is refused, with its reason When I press "Bring them in" Then each browser's records are written into the reader vault as its device file, the lane is marked, and they are merged here with that browser as their author When I press "Make a new link" Then the lane takes the new token only, and the old link can no longer write
mock-up

In the Vault tab, under Across your devices: Send from another browser, with what is waiting in the lane first, then the link (shortened, with Copy), the text (with Copy), the key's fingerprint, the QR code, and two buttons, Look in the lane and Make a new link. The sending page, vault/send.html: the vault and key, what is only in this browser, a name for it, Send to my vault and Forget the link.
outcome

Shipped in v0.12.26. The cryptography is the one this site already uses to write to sgit.ai's subscribe lane: sgit's hybrid envelope v2, AES-256-GCM wrapped with RSA-OAEP, here to a 3072-bit key made in the reader's browser (assets/vault-pane/inbox.js). 3072 rather than the CLI's 4096 keeps the link at about 650 characters and the QR code at 89 modules, which a phone camera reads off a screen. The lane is on the reader vault, configured with its write key and the access key from the master (POST /api/vault/append/configure). The enum key is a random value kept in the master; the server keeps its hash. The message is a device file, in the format the vault already uses (assets/vault-pane/sync.js), so the drain writes it into the reader vault as that browser's file (combined with any earlier one, combine()) and the usual merge brings it in. The sending browser is a device like any other, a row across the devices.
outcome

Refused, not merged: a message sealed to another key, one whose ciphertext was changed (AES-GCM fails), one that opens but is not a newsroom inbox message for this key, one whose browser id is not a file name or whose notes claim another browser. They are listed with the reason and can be discarded. The sender (vault/send.html, assets/vault-pane/send.js) needs no passkey and no vault library: it keeps the link in local storage, takes it out of the address, and only ever calls the lane's write route. A new link keeps the key and changes the token; configure replaces the anchors, so the old token is refused. It waits until the lane is empty, so no message is stranded in an old lane.
outcome

Not built: expiry. The append routes have no expiry on a token, so a date in the link would only be advisory, honoured by this page and by no one else; a new link is the revocation that the server enforces. Signatures: anyone holding the link can write, as the brief says; the drain shows what arrived, from which browser, before it is brought in. Purge of processed files, which needs the write key and the access key and is left to a later release. The reply lane (card 015) can use the same machinery.

The wireThe floorWorkflowThe graphSourcesResearchMethodThe teamAbout & limits The Governance Wire is a beta. It is produced end to end by software agents, it has had no legal review, and the verification layer that gives it its reason to exist is specified but not running. This page is the list of everything a reader should hold against it.
what

A publication covering risk, governance and accountability in autonomous systems. It originates no facts. Everything it carries was published by another organisation — regulators, supervisory bodies, standards bodies, and for now the sibling sites of this network. What it adds is a graph, verification and linking layer: typed structure over other people's material, a path back to the original, and a record of whether anybody read that original.
limits

Deliberate for this release. Seven agent roles run the pipeline; a named human reads the output afterwards, as a reader, and can pull anything that has gone off. That is a real safety model but it is a detection model, not a prevention one: a mistake is public before it is caught. Every fact is secondary. No primary artefact has been fetched, frozen or hashed, so no quote is pinned to a byte range and the staleness detector described in the method cannot run. The verification layer is the product, and in this release it is a design. There is none. The publication therefore does not assess, score or characterise any named organisation, and the editor role refuses it structurally rather than case by case. Reporting what a body itself published, with a link, is the whole permitted surface.
limits

19 nodes drawn from 5 sources, none of them a regulator. It is enough to prove the structure and nothing like enough to cover a beat. A publication about the governance of autonomous systems, written by autonomous systems. Either the strongest demonstration available or the most obvious conflict, depending entirely on whether it holds itself to what it reports against — which is why the agent roles, their refusals and this limits page are public from the first release.
disclaimer

Not legal, compliance or professional advice. Nothing here is advice of any kind, and no reader should act on it. Regulatory obligations depend on facts and jurisdiction that this publication does not know. Machine-generated, unreviewed. Every page is written by software agents without human review before publication. Errors of fact, reading and emphasis should be assumed present rather than exceptional. No claim of currency. Sources go stale, and detecting that is precisely the capability this release does not yet have. A page may describe a text that has since changed and give no sign of it. Verify before relying. Follow the source link on any node and read the original. Where this publication and a primary source disagree, the primary source is right.
where

Inside newsroom.sgit.ai for now, as a self-contained folder that can be lifted out whole — its own data, prose, templates, generator and gate, with no dependency on the rest of the site beyond the shared stylesheet and chrome. The intended destination is its own domain, and the publisher role refuses to move it until the ingestion path exists: a publication that cannot reach a primary source should not look like a going concern. It is built from the commissioning brief, which is the document to read for why any of this is shaped the way it is.

Every node names a source, and every source in the register was fetched with its status recorded. Nothing is asserted without somewhere to go and check it. A statement becomes a Fact with edges to the Provision it sits in and the Questions it raises. Structure is what lets a correction find everything downstream of it. pipeline

One role per step, each with its own centre of gravity and its own refusals. Nobody in this list is a person. The same seven steps are the route drawn through the newsroom floor, and a gate compares the two so the room cannot draw a workflow the publication does not run. Step 1 · librarianRegisters a source and its ingestion state. Step 2 · researcherFetches and freezes the artefact; records the hash and retrieval time. Step 3 · extractorTypes nodes and edges against the ontology; runs the formulas. Step 4 · writerProjects a subgraph into prose, listing the nodes it rests on. Step 5 · editorApplies the refusal list; cuts rather than softens. Step 6 · qaRuns the gates. A failure is answered, never silenced. Step 7 · publisherBumps the version, writes what changed and what is still missing.

Where two retention periods appear in the same instrument — a 30-day window at one provision and a six-month minimum elsewhere — the text does not state which governs. That is not a drafting quibble. A library · v1.3.1 One web component that charges readers a few pence a page from a balance kept in their own browser, by how far down the page they read. It never blocks a page, it lets the balance go below zero, it lets a reader decline to pay for a page and say why, and it turns what they read into personas: named, drawn as a graph, curated by the reader, and as many as they want. No server, no account, no cookies, no third-party script. It is what runs on this site: the balance in the top bar is it.
install

Copy two folders into your site, keeping their paths: the component and the base class it extends (it imports the base by a relative path). assets/components/base/v1/v1.0/v1.0.0/sg-component.js assets/components/sg-meter/v1/v1.3/v1.3.1/sg-meter.js assets/components/sg-meter/v1/v1.3/v1.3.1/sg-meter-core.js assets/components/sg-meter/v1/v1.3/v1.3.1/sg-meter.tpl assets/components/sg-meter/v1/v1.3/v1.3.1/sg-meter.css The paths are versioned and immutable, as in the estate's JavaScript guidance: a fix is a new path, so a page that works today keeps loading the same files. Read them first; they are short: the rules (no rendering), the element, its styles, the base class. Then, on every page, load the module once, give it a config, and say what the page is:
install

<!-- in the top bar --> <sg-meter view="balance"></sg-meter> <!-- at the end of the text: charges this page, shows what it cost and the "don't charge me" choice --> <sg-meter view="page" kind="article" date="2026-10-10" topics="news pricing" title="The page's title"></sg-meter> <script type="application/json" id="sg-meter-config"> { "storageKey": "mysite.meter.v1", "start": 500, "prices": { "article_new": 10, "article": 5, "page": 1, "free": 0 }, "topup": { "amount": 500, "link": "https://buy.stripe.com/your-link" }, "picks": { "feed": "articles/feed.json", "base": "articles/" } } </script> <script type="module" src="/assets/components/sg-meter/v1/v1.3/v1.3.1/sg-meter.js"></script> Every key has a default, so an empty config works. Put data-root on <html> (for example data-root="../") if your pages are not all at the top level; links the component writes are prefixed with it. This site loads the module with a dynamic import() from an inline script instead of a src, because its own build forbids script tags that point at files; either works.
views

One element, one shared meter: an ES module is evaluated once per page, so however many <sg-meter> elements a page has, it is charged once. view What it shows Attributes balance The balance as a small link to the account. Shown in a warmer colour below zero, with a tooltip that says nothing is blocked. Nothing else: no banner, no count of articles read. page Opens this page on the meter and charges it by scroll depth. At the foot of the text, a reader card (v1.3): what the page has cost, the share read, the reading list, three five-step ratings (how useful, more like this, level of detail), and last, as the exception, "Don't charge me" with a reason. kind, date (YYYY-MM-DD), topics (space separated), title, quiet (charge, show nothing) account
views

Balance, pages opened, spend, what was declined, picks, spend by topic, the history with the depth read, top-ups; the top-up button and export as JSON. Version 1.3 also had pause and start again; version 1.4.0, which this site runs, does not. topup With topup.link set, one button to the payment page. Without, a simulated cart (packs, cart, review, receipt) that says it is simulated. topped-up The page a payment link returns to. Adds topup.amount once per session_id in the URL. It does not verify the payment; see the security model. picks Unread pages for the active persona. Hidden until there is something to pick from. count (default 4) newsroom The reader's own front page (v1.1): their personas as chips, the active one's name and description, its picks with Keep and Not for this persona on each, what was kept in it or put out, and its graph. count (default 9) personas
views

Rename, switch and remove personas, and add one from a preset or a blank one (v1.1). graph A persona drawn as an SVG graph (v1.1): the persona in the middle, its topics sized by weight, the pages behind each topic, and the citations between those pages, from the feed's links_out. Each page is a link, with its title and depth read as a tooltip. persona (default the active one) link One line linking to the newsroom, named for the active persona (v1.1). share Shows the reader exactly what their reading looks like as text (a summary, then the same data as JSON), copies it to the clipboard, or sends it with their name and email, encrypted in the browser to the public key in share.contact and written to that file's append lane (v1.2). Sends nothing until the reader asks and ticks consent; never includes payment references.
rules

By depth. A page costs its price times the deepest point the reader has scrolled to, measured on the page's main element and rounded to 5%, never less than minDepth (default a tenth), so opening a page is not free. Read half, pay half. Once per page per session. Scrolling further later in the same browser session tops the same charge up; coming back does not start a second one. Below zero is allowed. Nothing is blocked and nothing nags. The balance is shown, that is all.
rules

Usefulness sets the price (v1.3). The reader rates how useful the page was from 1 to 5, starting in the middle: 1 is free, 2 half, 3 the price, 4 one and a half times, 5 double (rating.price). "More like this" (1 to 5) moves the page's topics and tags in the active persona (rating.more); "level of detail" is kept as the persona's preference and shown in the newsroom. The scales start in the middle, drawn as an outline until the reader touches them. The reading list (v1.3). An article opened for the first time joins the active persona's reading list (autoKeep), unless the reader put it out of that persona; one tap removes it.
rules

Declining is allowed. A reader can refuse to pay for a page, with a reason: the headline promised more than the page gave, not relevant to me, I did not really read it, another reason. The charge is refunded and the reason kept in their history; "not relevant" counts against that page's topics in the picks. New costs more. An article whose date is within newDays is priced at article_new, judged in the reader's browser, so prices age without a rebuild. Any other kind is looked up in prices, falling back to page. Storage may fail. In a browser that blocks storage the page still works, and the account says it cannot keep a balance.
personas

A reader has one or more personas and one is active. They are a way to manage focus: the same reader reads differently as a founder and as a security lead, and wants different picks for each. "me" always exists. It is built from everything the reader reads, weighted by what each page cost them (so by depth), and named from the topics it reads most until the reader names it: with names set to {"agents-and-policy": "The Policy Architect", …}, a reader of agents and graphs becomes The Policy Architect, with a streak of the Cartographer. Presets. A site can offer starting personas in personas.presets: a name, a label, a colour, a description, a few topic weights and a handful of articles. Adding one makes it active. Reading counts towards the active persona. Each page opened records the persona that was active; a persona's profile is its preset, plus what was read while it was active, plus its curation.
personas

Curation. Any article can be kept in a persona (its topics and tags +5) or put out of it (−3, and never picked). The page view has "Keep in your persona"; the newsroom has Keep and Not for this persona on every pick. Picks score unread articles by the persona's topic weights plus twice its tag weights, so two personas on the same topics still differ. Moving them. The account view exports everything as JSON and restores it in another browser. Nothing syncs on its own yet.

Add your own kinds. newDays 7 How long an article is new. depth true Charge by scroll depth. false charges the whole price on opening. minDepth 0.1 The least share of a page that is charged. topup {"amount": 500, "link": ""} The payment link and what it adds. config

A JSON feed of {"articles": [{slug, title, date, teaser, topics}], "topics": [{id, label}]}, and the folder an article's slug + ".html" is in. Empty feed: no picks. This site uses articles/graphs.json.
events

Dispatched on document, bubbling and composed, named <namespace>:<noun>.<verb>. Event names are API: renaming one is a major version. Event detail sg:meter.charged {path, depth, cost, balance}, each time a charge grows sg:meter.declined {path, reason, balance} sg:meter.toppedup {credit, source, balance}; source is simulated or link sg:meter.reset {} sg:meter.persona {active, what}; what is active, added, renamed, removed or curated (v1.1) sg:meter.rated {path, field, value, cost, balance}; field is useful, more or detail (v1.3) sg:meter.shared {how, pages}; how is copied or sent (v1.2) sg:meter.restored {reads}, after a restore from an export (v1.1) sg:meter.changed {balance}, on any saved change; the elements repaint on it sg-meter:error {why}, if the component's markup or styles failed to load; the element also gets data-state="error"
storage

One JSON value under storageKey in localStorage, and a map of this session's pages under storageKey + ".seen" in sessionStorage. The reader can export it from the account page. { "v": 3, "created": "2026-10-10T09:00:00.000Z", "balance": -12.5, "spent": 512.5, "reads": 91, "declined": 14, "paused": false, "log": [ { "id": "…", "at": "…", "path": "/articles/x.html", "title": "…", "kind": "article", "topics": ["news"], "price": 10, "depth": 0.55, "cost": 5.5, "persona": "me", "rating": { "useful": 4, "more": 5, "detail": 4 }, "declined": { "reason": "clickbait", "at": "…", "refunded": 4 } } ], "topups": [ { "ref": "cs_…", "at": "…", "credit": 500, "source": "link" } ], "sessions": [ "cs_…" ], "cart": [], "active": "security-mv2h4bb2", "personas": [ { "id": "me", "name": "", "on": [], "off": [] }, { "id": "security-mv2h4bb2", "preset": "security", "name": "", "on": ["footprint-and-blast-radius"], "off": ["a-mac-of-the-agents-own"] } ] }
theme

The component draws in a shadow root, so your stylesheet cannot reach in, but CSS custom properties cross the boundary and every colour reads one first: --fg, --dim, --line, --line2, --panel, --accent, --accent-dk, --warm (the colour of a negative balance), --mono, --serif, --sans. Each has a neutral fallback, so a site with none of them still gets a readable meter. The host element is yours to place and size: sg-meter { display: block }, and the root is exposed as ::part(root).
stripe

In Stripe, create a product (for example "£5 of reading") and a Payment Link for it. In the link's After payment settings, choose not to show Stripe's confirmation page and to redirect to your site, with this URL (Stripe fills in the placeholder):https://your.site/account/topped-up.html?session_id={CHECKOUT_SESSION_ID} Put the link in the config as topup.link, and the credit it buys as topup.amount. Make a page at that path with <sg-meter view="topped-up"></sg-meter> on it. Stripe's own guidance is that fulfilment should come from the checkout.session.completed webhook, not from the redirect, because a redirect can be skipped or faked. A static site has nowhere to receive a webhook, so this library credits on the redirect and says so. On a £5 payment with a standard UK card Stripe's listed fee is 1.5% + 20p, about 27.5p, or 5.5%; premium and international cards cost more. The arithmetic for this site is in going live with the reading meter.
principles

The first version ran on pt.newsroom.sgit.ai as its wallet: says up front what it is, never blocks, one charge per page per session, storage allowed to fail. Its code follows coding.sgit.ai's JavaScript guidance: ES modules, native web components on a shared base class, markup and styles in sibling files, page data set only as text, events as API. And two carried over from the NFRs, whose rule is "generate or date every number": the balance and the spend are running totals, but the log of every charge that made them sits beside them in the same export (the last 500), so a reader can check one against the other; and "a restore that has never been performed is not a backup", so the export is plain JSON a reader can open and read, the only copy of their history there is.

SG Meter · security model Everything the meter knows is in the reader's browser, so the reader controls it completely. This page lists what that lets them do, what it costs the site, and what it costs them. The short version: every way of cheating changes a number only the cheater can see, and costs the site a payment it was never going to get.
asset

Not money. The meter never blocks a page, so there is nothing behind it to steal: a reader who never pays reads exactly what a reader who pays reads. What it protects is narrower: the reader's own history (what they read, what they declined and why) from other people, and the site's honesty about what it records. The first question of who are you protecting against applies, and the answer here is "a reader's flatmate, and our own mistakes", not "a determined attacker", because a determined attacker gains nothing. Who might try anyway, and how many of them there are, is in who will game the reading meter.
known

# What a reader can do Effort What it costs the site What it costs the reader 1 Edit their balance in the browser's developer tools (Application → Local Storage) A minute, for someone who knows devtools exist Nothing it would otherwise have had Nothing 2 Open a private window or another browser and start again at £5.00 One keystroke Nothing Their history and picks, which stay behind 3 Open the topped-up page with any session_id and get £5 of credit, once per id Read this page, type a URL Nothing: no money moves, and the credit is only on their screen Nothing 4 Replay the same topped-up URL none Blocked: each id is credited once per browser (but a new id is trivial, see 3) none 5 Clear site data to wipe a negative balance Two clicks Nothing; there was never a debt Their history 6 Read as an agent: fetch the markdown twin or the newsroom wire
known

None; it is the intended route for agents Unmetered by design, for now none 7 Someone else on a shared computer opens the account or newsroom and sees what was read and declined, and the reader's personas Sit down at it none Privacy. Mitigations: clearing this site's data in the browser removes it; a private window keeps nothing 8 A script injected into the site (XSS) reads the history Needs a hole in the site first Reputation Privacy. Mitigations: the meter sets page data only as text; the only third-party code on this origin is the in-browser Python on the try page, loaded from a pinned version, so that page shares the same storage and the same trust 9 Card testing, fraud or chargebacks against the Stripe link Ordinary payment fraud Fees and disputes, held by Stripe's own controls (Radar) none
why

Because protecting it would need a server, and the one thing a server would protect is a number on a reader's own screen that unlocks nothing. Stripe's recommended way to know a payment happened is a webhook from Stripe to a server you run, and the honest alternative to building one is to say plainly that the return page trusts its URL. So it does, and here it is said. What we did do is keep the default route the real one: every top-up button goes to the payment page, the return URL is not linked as a way to get credit, and the page adds nothing when opened without a reference.
what-would-change

If the balance unlocked something (a page, a download, a reply from an agent), it would have to be held by a server or a signed receipt, and gaps 1, 3 and 5 would stop being acceptable. If the history synced between devices, it would be kept in an encrypted vault whose key only the reader holds, so the site would still not be able to read it. If cheating showed up in the one place we can see (the Stripe dashboard: payments, amounts, repeat payers), we would know the honesty box was not working, and the hypotheses in going live with the reading meter say in advance what number would mean that.

The newsroom was never specified as one product. Between April and May 2026 the design material names a series of small, concrete, replicable publication instances — a bilingual country publication, an agentic newsroom to run it, a rebuilt live property, an evidence-backed report tool, and a set of open-sourced business templates. Each is scoped to ship on its own, and an eighth was commissioned here in August 2026. This page is the index of that programme, and the decisions it left open. None of it has been built — see /shipped/.
shape

The rest of this site argues a thesis: sell the graph, not the paragraph, corrections must propagate, provenance is the product. The material on this page is the other half — the part that asks what would you actually launch first, and by when. The answer it reaches is consistent across the cluster: not a newsroom platform sold to publishers, but a small number of real publications run in the open, each one a working demonstration of the argument. The generalisation is stated plainly in the 12 May index for that day's work: “Publishing infrastructure becomes a fully productisable category. The same platform that supports the medical partner's POC supports the friend's CV site, supports a bilingual news publication, supports a future Spanish or Brazilian publication.” That sentence is the programme in one line. The instances below are the news-shaped members of that family.
instances

Every row is a dated document linked to its source. The first seven are from the project's own brief corpus; the eighth was commissioned on this site and lives in its own brief pack. report-tool

The April tool predates the May cluster by a month and is worth separating out, because it is the only member of the family that is a tool rather than a publication — and correspondingly the only one that could be built in days rather than weeks. The pipeline is four stages. A live-data model with web access answers a topic query and returns source URLs with the response; a second stage organises the findings into sections and maps evidence to claims; a third generates one infographic per section; a fourth packages report, infographics and citations together as a shareable unit.
report-tool

The design note that matters is where the provenance lives: citation extraction is treated as the load-bearing technical piece, not a nicety. Each claim is mapped to its backing sources, and the chain — claim → source URL → date accessed — is stored as structured data alongside the report rather than being rendered into prose and lost. That is the typed-citation-edge argument in miniature, and it is the one piece of this whole page that a small team could put into production without any of the rest existing.
repeatable

The instances are only a programme rather than a list if the second one is cheaper than the first. The May architecture work names the separation intended to do that: the vault (the unit of publishable content — an article, a briefing, an investigation), the storage substrate (where that vault happens to live, interchangeable per vault), and the management layer (a vault-of-vaults holding keys, metadata and editorial workflow state for every published artefact). The substrate mechanics are not this site's story — they belong to sgit.ai, which builds and runs that layer, and this site deliberately spends no words re-explaining them. What is news-shaped in that design, and does belong here, is the third primitive: the management layer is where editorial state lives. Draft, in review, signed off, published, archived — each transition a commit, each with an owner and a timestamp. That is the decision graph given a place to actually be stored.
repeatable

The same brief puts the review conversation inside the artefact: reviewers send messages to an inbox held in the article's own vault, approvals are first-class structured messages, and the audit trail is that inbox plus the article's commit history. An external reviewer — an expert, a subject, an editor outside the organisation — submits a signed response that verifies against a published key. The article carries its own editorial provenance as part of its content, which is the whole argument of /provenance/ arriving as a file layout.
eighth

The seven instances above are all dated April–May 2026 and were read out of the source corpus. An eighth was commissioned here, in August 2026, and it is the first to be written with the rest of the network already built underneath it. Its argument is the one this page has been circling. Portugal's acceptance criteria required ≥200 entities in its knowledge graph before it could report competently on its beat; that graph was never built and the publication never launched. A risk-and-governance beat inverts that constraint, because the graph is already public: 1,523 nodes and 1,944 edges of EU AI Act parsed from official Formex XML on graphs.sgit.ai, three worked risk graphs, and a 42-concept published ontology on risks.sgit.ai. The publication starts where Portugal was still trying to get to.
eighth

The commercial claim is a division of the grounding ladder rather than a marketing funnel: the publication owns Evidence and Fact for the public regulatory world, the customer owns Reality, Twin and Measure inside their own vault, and a Vulnerability — by the published formula, a Fact with an upward path to a Risk — exists only where the two meet. A risk product cannot compute anything without a supply of grounded public facts, and that supply is currently a person reading a PDF.
eighth

The inversion is held. This site's most important boundary says risk management is one customer of the future-of-news stack, not its parent. The brief is written that way round — a news operation whose first customer is a risk product, not a risk product with a blog — and it carries a hard editorial rule to keep it that way: no severity assessment of a named third party publishes without that party's right of reply recorded as a node in the same vault, at the same altitude, reachable from the same place. A declining to reply is recorded as an absence fact, which is both fairer and more informative than “did not respond to a request for comment”.
eighth

It is also the only instance on this page that now exists. A first MVP ships at /governance/ — a typed graph, a published vocabulary, a source register and a build gate, produced by seven agent roles with no human review. What it does not have is the ingestion path that would let it reach a primary text, so every fact in it is second-hand and nothing is anchored; its limits page leads with that. It also half-answers the question Portugal left open. Combining signed identity-and-mandate statements with acceptance-by-interval makes a by-line into a dated act rather than a title: the editor of record is whoever's signature is on the current interval. The legal half — who is answerable in a jurisdiction — stays open, and the brief says so rather than letting a signature stand in for a defence. Read the brief →
honest

None of these instances launched. The dates above are the dates the designs were written, not the dates anything shipped. The Portugal publication has no domain; the newsroom has no roles running; the report tool has no deployment. This site's shipped page is the authority on that line and this page does not move it. One property in this family does exist. myfeeds.ai runs as a personalised-news pipeline — this site lists it among the things that actually run. Its eight-phase rebuild did not happen, and what it does commercially — its pricing, its clients, its corporate detail — is deliberately not published here. The ideas in its rebuild brief are publishable and are what appears above; the commercial specifics are Tier 3 and are withheld. That omission is recorded rather than hidden: see the transparency note.
open

The source material carries a numbered open-decisions register, and three entries from it belong to this programme. They are reproduced here unresolved, in keeping with how this site publishes open questions: # Decision State as recorded 51 Which domain the first country publication launches on needed by end of week — and, more than a year later, still unregistered 52 Which 8 of the 15 newsroom departments are operational for the first MVP active scoping 53 Design specification for the reader contribution and validation system new work item — never specified Decision 52 is the interesting one for this site specifically. Fifteen public departments is the design; eight is what the first instance was scoped to actually run. The gap between those two numbers is the honest distance between the argument and a launchable product, and it was recorded at the time rather than discovered later.

The flagship MVP, and the only one with a date attached. A bilingual daily publication mapping one country's generative-AI ecosystem — companies, funding, policy, academia, diaspora — on a knowledge-graph backbone, produced by an eleven-role agentic newsroom on a daily clock. A trip supplied the deadline. Designed 12 May 2026 across two briefs; never launched.

Update, 13 September 2026 — a first instance is running, and it is much smaller than this. Portugal Startups is live on this site. It takes this design's scoping sentence and its ontology, and it takes almost nothing else: one beat rather than a country, one event rather than a daily clock, seven agent roles rather than eleven, and no personalisation layer at all. The design below is still a design and is still unlaunched — the ≥200-entity graph, the daily rhythm, the fifteen departments and the bilingual publication have none of them been built. What the instance does have is the thing this design never got to: the sources are primary, frozen and hashed, so a claim walks back to bytes rather than to a URL. That is the step The Governance Wire specifies and cannot run. And question 5 below is answered. See the note against it.
why

The scoping argument is the most transferable thing in the whole document, and it is one sentence: That is the actual MVP criterion. Not “a smaller version of a news site” but a beat whose entity graph can be closed — where you can plausibly name every company, every funder, every institution, every relevant researcher, and then keep that map current. A publication that has mapped its whole domain can answer questions no general outlet can, and that completeness is reachable in a small market and unreachable in a large one. Three secondary reasons are given, and they are honest about self-interest: the coverage gap (most reporting on the market happens in English, from outside it), the relationship value (people written about seriously tend to talk to you), and the platform demonstration (bilingual publishing shown rather than asserted).
surface

Eight sections define what the publication covers. Each item becomes one or more articles, an entry in the knowledge graph, and a node in the ecosystem map — so the section list doubles as the graph's top-level schema. Section What it holds The companies Startups, their funding, their teams, their products The players Founders, researchers, investors, advisors The institutions Government bodies, universities, accelerators, foundations The policies EU AI Act implementation nationally, strategies, public funding The use cases Real deployments in companies and the public sector The open source National contributions to open-source AI projects The diaspora Talent abroad and the work they are doing The events Conferences, meetups, hackathons, public consultations
graph

Each article sits in a graph of entities, relationships and sources rather than standing alone. The graph captures every company, person, funding round, product launch, policy document, event and open-source contribution mentioned — and then earns its keep by powering things an article list cannot: This company, this person — every piece of coverage in one place, assembled rather than authored. Who invested in whom; who works with whom. The relationships are the story as often as the events are. How funding evolved; how policy changed. Queryable, because the dates are structured rather than prose. Read about a company in one language, click through to the coverage in the other. Entities carry labels in both. Every article mentioning a given entity — by identity, not by string match.
graph

The design note is that the graph is language-agnostic: entities have labels in both languages and cross-language entity resolution happens at the graph layer, not the article layer. That is what makes the bilingual property structural rather than a translation pipeline bolted on the end.
bilingual

The brief is explicit that this is not “English with translations”: content is created with both audiences in mind, sometimes from the same source material with different angles per language. Storage is one markdown file per language per article; routing is by URL or an explicit reader choice; each version cross-links to its counterpart; and a reviewer fluent in the second language reviews that version specifically rather than trusting the generation. That last point is the one that costs real money and is the easiest to quietly drop, which is presumably why it is written into the acceptance criteria as a named human review pass rather than left as an aspiration.
newsroom

The companion brief of the same date specifies the operating model. It opens by asking what a modern editorial operation would look like if built from scratch with agents in mind, and answers with a mapping from traditional roles rather than an invention: Function Traditional role Agentic equivalent Editorial direction Editor-in-chief, managing editor Conductor — sets daily priorities, allocates stories Story sourcing Reporters with beats Researcher agents — continuous monitoring of named sources Investigation Investigative reporter Deep-research agent — multi-day stories, evidence accumulation Fact-checking Fact-checking desk Verifier agents — cross-reference sources, flag uncertainty Writing Reporters, feature writers Writer agents — multiple voices, tunable per story Copy editing Sub-editors Editor agent — style, tone, length, clarity Localisation Multilingual desk Translator agents Visual production Photo desk, graphics Visual agent — infographics, headers Personalisation Did not exist traditionally Briefing agent — tailored views per reader Publication Production team Publishing pipeline — vault to website, social, briefings Audience engagement Community team
newsroom
Community agent — responses, follow-ups, reader signal The line the brief draws under that table is the doctrinal one, and it is the same commitment the newsroom section of this site is built on:
clock

06:00Researcher agents finish overnight scans of national news sources, official feeds and social signals; candidate stories surface with summaries written to the newsroom's shared vault. 07:00The conductor reviews the overnight surfacing, picks the day's priority stories, and allocates each to a writer and a verifier. 08:00Writer and verifier work in parallel, not in sequence — the verifier builds the evidence set while the writer drafts against it, citing as they go. 10:00The editor agent returns notes on clarity, tone, length and missing context; the writer revises. 11:00The visual agent produces headers and infographics from the story's own graph. 12:00Final review, with a human spot-check. Publication. Personalisation agents fan out to generate the sector- and audience-specific versions. 13:00Distribution: social posts, briefing emails. 14:00 onwardThe community agent monitors response and surfaces follow-up signals; researchers begin scanning for tomorrow; investigative agents continue multi-day pieces.
clock

The parallelism at 08:00 is the structural claim worth noticing. In a conventional newsroom fact-checking follows writing, which is why it is the step that gets cut under deadline pressure. Here the evidence set is built alongside the draft and the draft cites into it, so a story that skipped verification would be visibly missing its evidence rather than merely unchecked.
story-vault

Every story that moves from “watched” to “active” gets its own vault. The layout is the data model: story-{date}-{slug}/ ├── brief.md what this story is, why it matters ├── sources/ │ ├── primary/ original documents, statements, releases │ ├── coverage/ how other outlets reported it │ └── interviews/ ├── evidence/ │ ├── facts.json verified facts, with source attribution │ ├── disputed.json claims under dispute, with both sides │ └── contradictions.md where sources disagree ├── drafts/ v1 research → v2 writer → v3 edited → v4 published ├── personalisation/ general, business-leader, per-sector, regional ├── graph/ │ ├── entities.json people, companies, places mentioned │ ├── relationships.json what connects to what │ └── semantic.json the knowledge graph for this story └── _page.json how this story renders
story-vault

Two folders in that tree are the ones a conventional CMS has no place for. evidence/disputed.json and evidence/contradictions.md mean disagreement between sources is stored rather than resolved away — the published article makes a call, but the record of what did not reconcile survives it. That is the same commitment the agenda-is-context argument makes, arriving here as two filenames.
personalisation

The personalisation layer generates per-audience projections from the same source material after publication: a general version, a business-executive version, a technology-leader version, per-sector versions, an investor version, a version tailored to a named subscriber's declared interests, and a version translated and contextualised for readers outside the country. Each is generated by a personalisation agent from the same evidence, which is what stops them from drifting into seven differently-wrong stories.
personalisation

This generalises a pattern from an earlier personalised-briefing product built by the same team for a security audience: take a domain's news, project it for a specific reader based on their role and concerns, deliver it as a briefing. The newsroom brief's claim is that the pattern is domain-independent — that if it works for general news it works for any structured-information-projection product. The brief also notes the reader can supply their own model key and generate a projection nobody designed for them, which is the part that makes it a graph being sold rather than an article.
launch

Three phases, each with an explicit decision point — the detail that separates this from a wish-list: One story per day. Human conductor. Low-stakes subject matter. The question being answered is whether the vault structure holds, the personalisation generates sensibly and the pipeline ships — not whether the journalism is good yet. Two or three stories per day. A community agent joins to monitor response. Traction tracking starts, per story and per personalisation. Five or more stories per day. The conductor role passes to an agent under human oversight. Personalised briefings go to a small pilot subscriber set.
launch

The publication brief adds a separate and more demanding set of ten acceptance criteria, of which two are worth quoting because they are the ones a demo would fail: at least three articles reviewed and approved by a fluent human reader in the second language, and the publication surviving the trip ending — a cadence that continues without the project lead running it manually. The second is the real test. An intensive burst of content around a trip proves nothing about a publication; what it proves is that a person was available for two weeks.
replication

The publication brief closes by naming the generalisation: Spain, Brazil, Italy, Germany — each with its own publication on the same infrastructure, same workflow, different domain, different language pair. The stated strategic value is that a platform visibly running several national AI publications has a presence in each of those markets that a publishing tool cannot buy. The source labels this speculative, and so does this page. The brief's own words are that the pattern is revisited only “if this works as a publication and as a case study” — the first instance is the precondition, and the first instance did not launch. Reproduced here because the replication argument is the reason the first instance was scoped the way it was, not as a roadmap.
open

The newsroom brief ends with six questions it declines to answer, and they are published here in the same state. Three are ordinary product questions; three are the ones that make this a news organisation rather than a content pipeline. # Question Why it is not a detail 1 Editorial voice — bold or restrained, opinionated or neutral, analytical or narrative Named as needing to be decided before the agents are tuned. House style is a configuration input here, not a culture that emerges. 2 Primary language only, or bilingual from day one Determines whether translation is a parallel output or a second-tier feature. The companion brief assumes bilingual; this one leaves it open. The two briefs of the same date disagree. 3 Funding model — free with paid personalisation tiers, sponsor-funded, or no revenue model initially The rest of this site argues a specific answer to this. The launch plan does not adopt it. 4
open

Distribution — own site only, or also third-party platforms Effort allocation, and a dependency question for a publication whose whole point is owning its chain. 5 Editorial accountability — who is the editor of record, and who carries legal responsibility for published content The unanswered question that matters most. An agentic newsroom publishing daily in a jurisdiction needs a named human who is legally answerable. No candidate is named. 6 Pace — is daily too ambitious to start The brief asks whether twice-weekly is the sensible opening. The phased plan assumes daily anyway. Question 5 is the one this site should be most uncomfortable about. A publication built to make provenance walkable, that has not decided who is accountable for what it publishes, has an unclosed chain at exactly the point where the chain has to terminate in a person. It is recorded as open in the source and it stays open there.
open

Answered on 13 September 2026, four months after it was asked. Dinis Cruz is the named editor of record for the running instance, and reads every page before it publishes. The answer arrived with a constraint the design did not anticipate: the journalistic route is not available. Article 24(3) of Portugal's Lei 58/2019 conditions processing for journalistic purposes on the national rules governing access to and exercise of the profession, which an unaccredited publication does not satisfy. So the instance runs on legitimate interests instead, with a published notice, a written balancing test and an unconditional removal route. That is an answer, not a clearance. No lawyer has reviewed it, and the statutory article was returned truncated to the research that found it. It is recorded here because the alternative — leaving the question open while publishing the names of 64 people — is worse.

The last MVP in the family is not a publication at all — it is the business idea itself, given away. Seven fully-formed, Creative Commons-licensed company descriptions, published so that somebody else can pick one up and build it. One of the seven is an evidence-research company aimed squarely at journalists and investigators, which is why this page is on a news site. Designed 17 May 2026; none of the seven was ever published.
what

The source brief spends its first section on getting the category right, and the distinction it lands on is load-bearing: The brief records that it tried “fake company” first and rejected it, on the grounds that the phrase implies deception. What it settles on is a genuinely unusual artefact defined by three properties held at once: fully-formed (market analysis, product, pricing, operating model, technology stack, investment ask — not a paragraph), Creative Commons-licensed (so it can be taken and built without asking), and platform-aware (the economics assume a specific substrate, which is what makes it viable at small scale).
what

Each of those exists on its own — business plans get written, CC licensing is ordinary, platform-dependent businesses are everywhere. The combination is the thing. And the brief insists on a fourth property that is really an editorial standard: open about its own status, so a reader is never in any doubt they are looking at a proposal rather than a going concern.
seven

# Seed What the company would do 1 CV / job search Vault-grounded CV, portfolio and application workflow; agents tailor per application; the candidate owns and controls the artefact. 2 Pitch creation A firm helping founders build investor pitches — human pitch coaches using the platform as their working substrate rather than documents and slides. 3 Health score Individual health data held in the person's own vault; the company sells the analysis layer, the user keeps the data. Named as the most validated seed, with the most prior material behind it. 4 Evidence researchthe one that belongs to this site Gathering and presenting evidence on a specific question, for people who are not a large institution — journalists running investigations, expert witnesses, researchers, advocacy groups. Detail ↓ 5 Accountant workflow A small accountancy delivering strategic-partner service at SME prices via platform-grounded workflows. Empower the existing small firms rather than displace them. 6 Lawyer workflow
seven

The same shape applied to law — client communication, documents, case tracking, evidence handling. Encrypted storage and a free audit trail map unusually well onto privilege requirements. 7 Local AI enablement Connecting local small businesses with local people who can teach them to use these tools well. Short engagements, per-task pricing. Community-rooted rather than platform-rooted, and flagged in the source as the odd one out.
evidence

This is the seed that belongs to this site, and it is the commercial form of the argument the rest of the site makes abstractly. The company sells the evidence work rather than the article: the vault as an evidence locker, agents doing source-checking, citation management and document analysis, cross-document linking as the deliverable. The economic claim is the interesting part, and it is a claim about who gets served rather than about margin: That is the same argument as paying the fact creator approached from the buying side. This site argues that near-zero-cost settlement makes it possible to pay for a single fact; the evidence-research seed argues that near-zero-cost evidence assembly makes it possible to commission an investigation that no newsroom would fund and no law firm would quote for. Local accountability reporting, a single-issue campaign group, an expert witness working alone — these are the buyers that currently fall below the floor.
evidence

The brief also names, in one line, the relationship between this seed and the one property in the family that actually runs: myfeeds.ai is the live instance of the evidence-research seed. The seed is the generalised business; the property is one person's version of it, already operating. What that property charges and who it serves is deliberately not published here — see the note on the MVP index.
why

Six reasons are given. Five are ordinary strategy — it demonstrates capability without a sales pitch, it seeds an ecosystem, it is cheap to produce relative to building each one, it generates publishable content, it forces the authors to articulate what the platform actually enables. The sixth is the one with an edge on it: For a news site there is a sharper version of that, and it is the reason this page is not merely adjacent to the argument. This site's whole thesis is that the value is in the graph rather than the paragraph — that the assembled, evidenced, structured thing is what is worth paying for, and the readable projection on top of it is nearly free. A publisher who believes that should be entirely comfortable publishing their business plan, because the plan is a paragraph and the operation is a graph. Giving away the seven seeds is the thesis being tested on its authors.
structure

Each seed is one vault with a consistent layout — the investor-pack template filled in, plus the working detail a builder would need: seed-{name}/ ├── pack.md the investor pack, against the shared template ├── operating-model.md how the company runs day to day ├── product.md what it builds ├── financials/ projections · unit economics · assumptions ├── go-to-market/ strategy · pricing · partnerships ├── technology/ architecture · platform leverage · build vs buy ├── examples/ sample customer flow, sample output ├── license.md Creative Commons └── readme.md front matter; how to use this vault
structure

Underneath the seven sits a reusable investor-pack template — the same thirteen sections any company would present, held as a vault rather than a slide deck. The brief argues the vault form buys four things a PDF cannot: the reader can change the financial assumptions and see the model move, every market claim links to the source behind it, each reader can annotate their own copy without affecting anyone else's, and when the pack is updated the reader sees what changed rather than receiving a new file. That last one is supersede-never-delete applied to fundraising.
risks

A seed that is obviously hype rather than a real model damages the thing it is meant to demonstrate. The stated mitigation is to write each one as if genuinely pitching it, with financials validated against real market data rather than chosen to look good. Creative Commons means no control over who picks a seed up or what they ship under it. The mitigation is framing rather than enforcement: these are templates, not endorsements, and no builder is presented as a partner without review. Open-sourcing a business you may later want to build yourself is awkward. The stated resolution is deliberate: publish only the seeds you are confident you will not build, and say which ones are being held back.
risks

Risk 3 has a consequence the brief accepts explicitly — a numbered task requiring a documented decision per seed: published, internal-only, or deferred. Whether the evidence-research seed would have survived that filter, given that myfeeds.ai already occupies exactly that space, is not recorded. A cluster of the source material's strongest documents — the evidence-economy briefs, credibility calibration, the fact-creator payment mechanism — were originally written for a corporate risk-management product, framing news as the evidence supply for risk graphs. A client-side-assembled vault page, served the way sgit.ai serves one, can be invisible to a crawler. Measured and documented as a known limitation of the delivery substrate this site cites rather than re-explains. For most sites that is a nice-to-have fix. For a news site it is close to existential — almost all of a news site's reach depends on being findable by search and by other agents, and a site that argues for provenance while being unreadable by the tools that would check it has undermined its own case before a reader ever arrives. Decide rendering before content; this is flagged here rather than left implicit.

tensions

Provenance is the product — and provenance is expensive. The £8.40 story cost is the argument and the objection in the same number. Corrections propagating is a feature until it is a liability. A graph that can answer "what rests on claims since corrected" can also be subpoenaed for the answer. "More humans, not fewer" is a design principle, not an economic result. Nothing in this material tests whether it actually holds once real budgets are involved. Selling trust makes the seller a target. A warranted fact-certifier has created a liability surface the material notes but does not size — see trust as a service. This site inherits sgit.ai's crawler-invisibility problem — see above. For a news site, existential rather than cosmetic. Two licences over one thread. docs.diniscruz.ai is CC0; *.sgit.ai is CC BY 4.0. The resolution this site argues for, stated on the disclosure page.

Create anywhere, edit your own. Any role adds files; only a file's author edits it. The one exception is a pitch's status line, which is how the Editor answers. One owner for each shared surface. The front is the Editor's, collections are the Historian's, the build is the Developer's. Ownership is what stops two agents rewriting the same thing in turn. Flag, do not fix. Write one log entry, admin/content/newsroom/log/YYYY/MM/DD/HHMM__editor__<slug>.md: what changed on the front and why, what was declined, what the desk should do next. Build, validate, run admin/build/policy_check.py --role editor, release. Live first, placed second. An unplaced article is still published. The front is a recommendation, not a gate. Say why. Every lead and highlight carries a why the reader can see. A placement nobody can explain is a habit.
policy

Prefer the evidence. Between two articles, lead with the one that shows its data: the graph, the figures, the vault behind it. Flag, do not fix. A factual problem in another agent's article goes to its author as a pitch or a board card, or into a correction note, never as a silent edit. You are the Editor of the sgit.ai newsroom. Read /newsroom/index.md, /newsroom/roles/editor.md and /newsroom/policies.md, then run python3 admin/build/desk.py from the repository root and work through its findings. You may write only the files in your policy. Finish with a log entry and a release.

SGit Newsroom · how it runs Reads across the articles for what none of them says alone. The line in the middle of one piece that turns out to be the thesis of five, the rule learned twice, the pattern on its third appearance, and publishes each as a short note or a collection with the evidence linked. Owns the nuggets and threads in admin/content/newsroom/notes/, and every collection in admin/content/newsroom/collections/ Never edit an article; write front.json; editorialise past what the articles say, a note quotes and connects, it does not add claims the articles do not make Cadence after each batch of articles; a collection whenever three or more articles share a method, a map or a question
policy

admin/content/newsroom/notes/* admin/content/newsroom/collections/* admin/content/newsroom/pitches/* admin/content/newsroom/log/* This is not a logging role. Logs record everything; historians find what mattered. The definition comes from the SG/Send team's Historian: "Flag patterns. When you see the third scope expansion decision in a row, name the pattern." Here the record is the articles, and the patterns are ideas rather than decisions. Three outputs: Nugget (kind: nugget): one line from an article, quoted exactly with !quote <slug> <n> from the article's graph, and a paragraph on why it matters beyond the article it is in. The example that defined the form: a model that can go in every direction needs someone with a direction, a sentence in the middle of a measurement article that is the answer to a question half the site asks. Thread (kind: thread): a connection across articles, with every article it rests on in cites, so the note appears on the front beside them and the subscriber agents can follow the links.
policy

Collection: a curated set with an introduction that says what the set shows together, for example every article that thinks with a Wardley map. Collections are the Historian's; which ones are featured on the front is the Editor's. Quote, do not paraphrase. A nugget uses the article's own words, through the graph's quotes, so a changed article changes the note. Contradictions are signals. Two articles that disagree are a finding: publish it as a thread, and file a board card for the authors. Edges are the output. A note with one citation is a nugget; a thread needs at least two. You are the Historian of the sgit.ai newsroom. Read /newsroom/index.md and /newsroom/roles/historian.md, then read articles/graphs.json: the teasers, core ideas, quotes and links of every article. Find one idea that recurs across articles and nobody has named, and publish it as a thread note citing every article it rests on. Then check whether any three articles now form a collection.

SGit Newsroom · how it runs Writes the long pieces and the short ones. Articles that argue one point with the evidence attached, the weekly summary of what was published and what it adds up to, and the brief that turns the data behind the articles into something a subscriber can read in a minute. Owns every article file in admin/content/articles/ and the graph beside it, the weekly notes, the briefs, the article images and cards Never write front.json or a collection; edit another role's note; publish a number that was remembered rather than counted Cadence an article when there is an argument worth making; a weekly note every week; a pitch whenever an article deserves more than Latest
policy

admin/content/articles/* articles/images/* articles/cards/* articles/data/* og/* admin/content/updates/* admin/content/newsroom/notes/* admin/content/newsroom/pitches/* admin/content/newsroom/log/* admin/content/newsroom/newsletter/* articles/banners/* The articles are the site's main output, and the direction set for them now is more evidence, not more words: every article carries its graph (admin/content/articles/graphs/<slug>.json), its figures, its links, and wherever possible the data or the vault it was written from. The longer the article, the more it should be standing on. Then the short forms, which only exist because the long ones are data-rich: The week (kind: weekly): what was published in the last seven days, rendered from the articles themselves with !articles FROM..TO, and two or three paragraphs on what it adds up to.
policy

The newsletter (admin/content/newsroom/newsletter/NNN-YYYY-MM-DD.md): the regular issue, due a week after the last or once five articles have been published since it (desk.py says when). Written with the same directives, cross-posted as a LinkedIn article: render the cover with node admin/build/make_banners.mjs, upload it, paste the title, select and copy the body from the page; group the issue's article list by theme with !list, and promise completeness with !covers, then add the post's URL as linkedin: in the issue file. Brief (kind: brief): one finding from the data behind the articles, a count from articles/graphs.json or a dataset in articles/data/, said in under three hundred words. Publishing needs nothing from anyone: add the file, build, release, and it is live and at the top of Latest. To ask for the lead, a highlight, the homepage or a collection, add a pitch:

admin/content/newsroom/pitches/2026-10-07__the-mandate-stack.md --- date: 2026-10-07 from: journalist ask: lead article: the-mandate-stack status: open --- One paragraph: why this article, why now, and what it shows that the current lead does not. A lab: the passkey opens the vault Each step of the design, as a thing you can press in your own browser: a passkey, its PRF bytes, the door derived from them, a recovery code, and the door created on a vault server. The design is in The passkey opens the vault: a passkey, through the WebAuthn PRF extension, gives the browser 32 bytes that only your authenticator can produce for this site; from those bytes the browser computes the key and the address of a small door vault, so nothing has to be stored to be found; the door holds the master vault’s key. Each card below is one step of that, as a thing you can press.
poc0
WebAuthn, the platform authenticator, and whether the browser says it supports the PRF extension. Nothing to press: it is read when the page opens.
poc1

navigator.credentials.create() with rp.id set to this host, a resident key, user verification required, and the prf extension. The passkey is stored by your provider (Google Password Manager, iCloud Keychain, Windows Hello, a hardware key, or the browser’s own store); the page learns a credential id, a public key and whether PRF is on. It never learns who you are.
poc1-ladder

Sign in to a passkey provider (Google Password Manager in Chrome, iCloud Keychain in Safari), so the passkey syncs and PRF is available. Use your phone by QR: a passkey on the phone, one scan at a time. Plug in a hardware key. Stay on this device: the browser’s own copy of the reading account keeps working, and the recovery code (4) is the way back.
poc2

navigator.credentials.get() with the fixed input, the SHA-256 of a public string. The authenticator returns 32 bytes computed from a secret it keeps for this site and this passkey. The same passkey gives the same bytes on every device it syncs to, through the same kind of path; that is the whole trick. Through a different path (a phone over QR, instead of the provider on the device) the same passkey can give different bytes, which a test here found on 12 October 2026; the result shows which path answered, and the design gives each path its own door: one door per passkey path.
poc3

The article’s derivation, made exact: HKDF to a seed, a passphrase and an 8-character vault id; then sgit’s own derivation of the read key and the write key, PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 at 600,000 iterations each, timed on this device. The door’s key is not stored anywhere: it comes out the same every time.
poc4
26 characters of base32, 128 bits, made by the page and in the real flow shown once. In place of the PRF bytes it derives a second door to the same master, for the day every passkey is gone.
poc5

The same derivation from a fixed, fake PRF output, compared value by value with what sgit’s own Python produced (vectors.json, from admin/build/passkey_vectors.py). Runs when the page opens. If any line is wrong, the browser and the command line would open different vaults.
poc6

With the door from 3 (or the recovery code from 4, or the test vector), the vault library that runs dev.vault.sgraph.ai, vendored here and loaded from this origin, creates and opens real sgit vaults: the door at its derived address, holding the master’s key and a record of where it came from (kind, provider, path, credential id, device, date); the master, made at random, holding the reader vault’s key and the list of doors; the reader vault, where a note is written and read back. Every vault made here is one sgit clone opens, with write access, from the key shown behind each reveal. Writing needs an access key for the server, which is the thing a reader will buy; opening and reading need nothing.
poc6

An address with no door says so; it is not an error. A vault id is never destroyed, because a destroyed id can never be used again and a door’s is derived. The test vector’s door has the same address for everyone, so on the real server only the first person can create it. Moving the reading account into the reader vault is the next step and is not built.
notes

The relying party id is this host. On newsroom.sgit.ai a passkey made here is for newsroom.sgit.ai exactly, as the article’s trust boundary asks; it does not work on sgit.ai or on any other site. The derivation’s constants name newsroom.sgit.ai whichever host runs the page, so the test vectors are the same everywhere. Where the passkey lives decides what you get. Card 1 shows whether the passkey is backup-eligible, which is the browser’s word for synced. A clean browser with no provider may make a passkey that signs and returns no PRF bytes; card 2 says so if it happens, and card 1 shows the ladder.
notes

A door per path, not per passkey. On 12 October 2026 one Google Password Manager passkey gave one set of bytes through the provider on a Mac and on an iPhone, and a different set, consistently, when a phone answered a QR code from a Mac or an iPad: same credential id, same user handle, same input. Apple’s developer forums carry the same symptom for iCloud Keychain passkeys since late 2024, with a fix announced and a tester reporting it persisting. A second passkey in iCloud Keychain gave the same bytes on a Mac, a current iPad and a current iPhone, in Safari and in Chrome, which is the common case; an older iPad that could not use it locally offered only the QR path. The design therefore treats every distinct set of bytes as its own door to the same master, adds a door while unlocked on a device where both paths run (a Mac with Chrome runs both in one session), and uses the recovery code to bring a new path in where no door opens. The finding, the bug and the revised design are written out in one door per passkey path.
notes

Not built here: the master vault, the newsroom vault, moving the reading account into it, adding a second path or passkey as a door, retiring a door, and anything that signs the reader in. The brief’s phase five is where those land, after the move. The door record this lab writes is one sgit object (obj-cas-imm-…, content-addressed), encrypted the way sgit encrypts, so sgit’s own code can decrypt it; it is not yet a commit in a tree, so sgit clone of the door would show an empty history. The real door will be a vault with one committed file. Tests: admin/build/test_passkey.mjs drives the page in Chromium with a virtual authenticator that has PRF, checks the derivation against the vectors, and runs the server flow against a stand-in server; the real server is tried by a person with an access key.

The wireThe graphThe filesConnectionsThe SummitWho is speakingThe organisationsWhat changedSourcesMethodThe teamYour dataAbout & limits Portugal Startups is a beta with one beat and no registry behind it. It does the thing this network argues for — primary sources, frozen and hashed — and it does it over a very small piece of the world. This page is the list of everything a reader should hold against it.
what

A publication mapping the Portuguese startup ecosystem, beginning with one event. It originates no facts. Everything it carries was published by somebody else; what it adds is a typed graph over that material, a path back to it, and a hashed copy of what it said on the day we read it.
limits

88 frozen files: the event’s own pages, and 7 pages by other publishers about the event. That is enough to report what the event says about itself and what the press says about it, and to notice where they differ. It is nowhere near enough to report on an ecosystem: there is no company registry, no funding record and no institutional source, and every third-party page here is about the event rather than about anything the event does not itself describe. The original brief scoped a country. This is a conference. The scoping argument holds — a closeable graph — but a publication that stops when the doors close on 2026-09-18 has proved nothing except that somebody was available for a week. The real test is whether this is still running in October.
limits

The original brief asked for both languages, and its two source briefs disagreed with each other about whether that was a day-one property. Nothing here is published in Portuguese. Section labels carry a pt alongside the en in the generator, so the second language is a projection to switch on rather than a retrofit — but the switch has not been thrown, and a structural capability is not a translation. There is a named editor of record, which is a person taking responsibility. It is not a legal opinion. The publication therefore does not assess, rank or characterise any named person or company, and the editor role refuses it structurally rather than case by case. It is one organiser’s selection for one event. Several of the organisations are not Portuguese and several are not startups. Treating it as a map of the ecosystem would be the most obvious mistake available here.
disclaimer

Not advice of any kind. Nothing here is investment, business, travel or professional advice, and no reader should act on it. Agent-produced. Research, extraction and drafting are done by software agents. Dinis Cruz reviews every page before publication, which catches what a person catches and not more. Errors of fact and emphasis should be assumed present rather than exceptional. Ticket prices, dates and venues change. Everything here is as published on the frozen copy named beside it. Check the event’s own site before buying anything or travelling anywhere. We do not explain absences. Where a name has left a published list, that is recorded without a reason. Do not read one in.
where

Inside newsroom.sgit.ai as a self-contained folder that can be lifted out whole — its own data, frozen sources, generator and gate. It is built from the 12 May 2026 briefs, which are the documents to read for why any of this is shaped the way it is, and which this section is the first attempt to actually run. The commissioning brief for what comes next — a natively Portuguese newsroom at pt.newsroom.sgit.ai, written for the agent that will build it — is here. WITH ground AS ( SELECT DISTINCT p.org AS org, t.type AS kind, t.tag AS what FROM person_tags t JOIN people p ON p.id = t.person WHERE t.type IN ('Industry', 'Technology', 'Idea') AND p.org NOT IN (SELECT name FROM orgs WHERE placeholder = 1) UNION SELECT DISTINCT p.org, 'Topic', pt.topic FROM person_topics pt JOIN people p ON p.id = pt.person WHERE p.org NOT IN (SELECT name FROM orgs WHERE placeholder = 1) ), offers AS ( SELECT DISTINCT p.org AS org, t.tag AS service FROM person_tags t JOIN people p ON p.id = t.person WHERE t.type = 'Service' AND p.org NOT IN (SELECT name FROM orgs WHERE placeholder = 1) ), founder_led AS ( SELECT DISTINCT n.org AS org FROM nodes n WHERE n.type = 'Person' AND n.role_class = 'founder' AND n.org IS NOT NULL AND n.org NOT IN (SELECT name FROM orgs WHERE placeholder = 1) ) SELECT a.org AS org_a, b.org AS org_b, COUNT(*) AS shared, GROUP_CONCAT(a.kind || ':' || a.what, ' · ') AS on_what FROM ground a JOIN ground b ON a.kind = b.kind AND a.what = b.what AND a.org < b.org GROUP BY a.org, b.org HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3 ORDER BY shared DESC, org_a, org_b LIMIT 40;

WITH ground AS ( SELECT DISTINCT p.org AS org, t.type AS kind, t.tag AS what FROM person_tags t JOIN people p ON p.id = t.person WHERE t.type IN ('Industry', 'Technology', 'Idea') AND p.org NOT IN (SELECT name FROM orgs WHERE placeholder = 1) UNION SELECT DISTINCT p.org, 'Topic', pt.topic FROM person_topics pt JOIN people p ON p.id = pt.person WHERE p.org NOT IN (SELECT name FROM orgs WHERE placeholder = 1) ), offers AS ( SELECT DISTINCT p.org AS org, t.tag AS service FROM person_tags t JOIN people p ON p.id = t.person WHERE t.type = 'Service' AND p.org NOT IN (SELECT name FROM orgs WHERE placeholder = 1) ), founder_led AS ( SELECT DISTINCT n.org AS org FROM nodes n WHERE n.type = 'Person' AND n.role_class = 'founder' AND n.org IS NOT NULL AND n.org NOT IN (SELECT name FROM orgs WHERE placeholder = 1) ) SELECT o.org AS provider, o.service AS offer, f.org AS founder_led, COUNT(g2.what) AS shared, GROUP_CONCAT(g2.kind || ':' || g2.what, ' · ') AS on_what FROM offers o JOIN founder_led f ON f.org <> o.org JOIN ground g1 ON g1.org = o.org JOIN ground g2 ON g2.org = f.org AND g2.kind = g1.kind AND g2.what = g1.what WHERE o.service IN ('investment', 'incubation', 'compute-support', 'advisory', 'coaching') GROUP BY o.org, o.service, f.org HAVING COUNT(g2.what) >= 2 ORDER BY shared DESC, provider, founder_led LIMIT 40;
