Date: 12 October 2026. Status: a finding from the passkey lab, and the design change it forces. The lab shows the finding; nothing beyond the lab is built. Related: The passkey opens the vault (the design), the passkey lab (where the finding was made), admin/build/testpasskey.mjs (what is checked).
in-one-paragraph

The design derives a small door vault from a passkey's PRF bytes and keeps the master vault's key inside the door. It rests on one claim: the same passkey gives the same bytes wherever it is used. A test on 12 October with one Google Password Manager passkey found that the claim holds along one path and not across paths. Used by the provider on the device (a Mac, then an iPhone), the passkey gave one set of bytes. Used through the cross-device flow, where a phone answers a QR code from a Mac or an iPad, the same passkey gave a different set, and gave it consistently. Same credential id, same user handle, same input, different bytes. A second test with an iCloud Keychain passkey gave the same bytes on a Mac, a current iPad and a current iPhone, in Safari and in Chrome, which is the main scenario the design is for; an older iPad that could not use the passkey locally offered only the QR path, which is a different path. The unit of the design is therefore not the passkey but the path: a door per set of bytes, every door pointing at the same master and recording where it came from. The article already has most of this (every passkey is a door, so is a recovery code, a door is added while unlocked, the master lists its doors), so what changes is small and sharp: the middle layer stays because it cannot be removed, adding a door becomes a normal first-week step rather than an edge case, and the page must treat an unknown door address as "no door here yet", never as a failure.
tested-first-a-google-password-manager-passkey

One passkey, made on newsroom.sgit.ai by card 1 of the lab with the PRF extension, stored in Google Password Manager and synced. Card 2 asks the authenticator for the PRF bytes with the fixed input, the SHA-256 of newsroom.sgit.ai/door/v1, and shows a fingerprint of the result. Four runs: In all four the page showed the same credential id, the same user handle and the same flags (user present, user verified, backup eligible, backed up). The input hash was the same. Runs 3 and 4 share a client-side path, the hybrid transport, and share a result. Runs 1 and 2 share the other path and share the other result. Nothing else distinguishes them: run 1 and run 4 are the same browser on the same machine, minutes apart, differing only in which way the phone's provider was reached.
tested-first-a-google-password-manager-passkey

The fingerprints quoted are those the lab showed on the day. The lab's fingerprint was then the first four bytes of the PRF output itself, which is a careless thing to put on a screen and in a chat; since v0.9.1 it is the first four bytes of the SHA-256 of the output, so the values above are no longer what the page would show, and they remain valid as evidence that the outputs differed.
tested-second-an-icloud-keychain-passkey

A second passkey, made by card 1 and stored in iCloud Keychain instead, on the same day: Runs 5 to 8 are the scenario the design is for: one person, their own devices, one provider, and the same bytes everywhere through the platform path, in both browsers. Chrome on the Mac matches Safari because it reaches iCloud Keychain passkeys through the same system provider, so the bytes are computed in the same place. Run 9 is the boundary: a device that cannot use the passkey locally, because its operating system predates the support, offers only the cross-device path, and by the first test's result that path should be expected to give its own bytes and therefore its own door. It was not completed, so whether an iCloud Keychain passkey over QR matches its local bytes on these versions is unknown; the lab's path row would tell, and the design does not depend on the answer.
tested-second-an-icloud-keychain-passkey

Two conclusions follow. The claim in the article is right for the common case and needs the qualifier "through the same kind of path", not a retraction. And the product should steer a reader to the provider on the device first, and present the QR route as a path that gets its own door, rather than as the same thing done remotely.
what-the-extension-is-supposed-to-do

The WebAuthn PRF extension is defined over the CTAP2 hmac-secret extension. An authenticator keeps a random value per credential (CTAP calls it CredRandom, and keeps two: one used when the user was verified, one when not) and returns HMAC-SHA-256 of that value over a salt the client supplies. The WebAuthn specification asks the client to hash the site's input first, as SHA-256 of the string WebAuthn PRF, a zero byte and the input, so that a site's chosen bytes never reach the authenticator raw, and asks platform authenticators that answer PRF directly to apply the same hashing, so that the result is the same whichever way the credential is reached. The intent is explicit: one credential, one input, one output.
what-the-extension-is-supposed-to-do

Two layers can break that intent without either being obviously wrong on its own. If one path applies the prefix hash and the other does not, or one applies it twice, the HMAC is over different salts. If one path selects the "with user verification" seed and the other the "without" seed, the HMAC uses different keys even over the same salt. The second is the one Apple's engineers pointed at (below). From outside the authenticator the two cannot be told apart, and neither output can be checked against the specification, because both need the credential's secret. What can be said is that each path is deterministic: the device-local path gave the same bytes on two devices and two operating systems, and the hybrid path gave the same bytes from two clients.
this-is-a-known-class-of-bug

Apple's developer forums carry the same symptom for iCloud Keychain passkeys, reported from late 2024: one PRF value when the passkey is used on the device, another when an iPhone or iPad scans a QR code shown by a Mac, for the same credential and the same salt. In one thread an Apple engineer called it a bug, said the hybrid value should match the local one provided user verification is handled the same way on both paths, noted that the extension uses different seeds depending on whether user verification was performed, and said a fix was in the iOS 18.4 and macOS 15.4 betas. A later tester in another thread reported the mismatch persisting on a Safari 18.4 beta. A third thread records a Chrome-on-Mac user seeing exactly runs 1 and 4 of the table above.
this-is-a-known-class-of-bug

Our passkey lives in Google Password Manager, not iCloud Keychain, and is served to the QR flow through iOS's cross-device role for third-party providers. So either the bridge that hands a hybrid request to a third-party provider still carries the bug, or the provider itself behaves differently when reached that way. Both are plausible; the lab cannot tell them apart. What the lab can tell, now, is which path a result came from: the browser reports whether the authenticator was platform or cross-platform, and card 2 shows it.
this-is-a-known-class-of-bug

The thing to notice is how long this sat. PRF reached Safari in 2024 and the hybrid path later still; the forum threads are months apart and unresolved on the page. A defect in the one property that makes PRF useful for encryption, visible to anyone who tries two paths, would not survive long under real load. The reasonable inference is that few people are deriving encryption keys from passkeys across the hybrid path in production. That is not a reason to avoid the technique; it is a reason to design as if the bytes are a key a provider lends for one path, on one day, and to keep every door replaceable.
the-unit-is-the-path

A door is a function of the bytes. Whatever produced a distinct set of bytes gets a distinct door: a passkey through its provider on the device, the same passkey through a phone over the hybrid link, a hardware key, a second passkey, the recovery code. The article's sentence "the same passkey gives the same bytes on every device it syncs to" becomes "the same passkey gives the same bytes on every device it syncs to, through the same kind of path; a different path can give different bytes, and gets its own door". The lab's card 2 and the hub pages now say the narrower thing.
the-middle-layer-stays-and-this-is-why

An earlier draft of the design had a stored first vault that pointed at the main vault, and it was simplified to a door computed from the passkey with nothing stored. The door that remained is still a middle layer, one small vault between the passkey and the master, and this finding is the reason it has to remain. If the master's key were derived from the PRF bytes directly, a path that gives other bytes would derive another master, and nothing could join the two. With the door in between, a second path is one more small vault holding the same master key, written once. The layer costs one vault per path and one derivation on unlock, and buys independence from how any provider computes its bytes.
every-door-says-where-it-came-from

A door holds the master vault's key and a small record: the kind of door (a passkey, the recovery code), the provider as the browser named it, the path (platform or cross-platform), the credential id (public; it is what any site sees at sign-in), a device label the reader types, and the date. The master vault keeps the list of its doors with each door's own vault key, so that from any open door the page can read, rewrite or delete every other door. That list is what makes retiring a door possible without the passkey that made it.
adding-a-door-moves-no-key-through-a-person

The step the article describes as "while unlocked on one, register the other" is the whole mechanism, and it does not involve typing or pasting a vault key. The page is unlocked, so the master key is in its memory. The reader asks for the PRF bytes again by the other path. The page derives the new door from those bytes, encrypts the master key under the new door's read key, writes the door's one file with the reader's access key, and adds the door to the master's list. The provider that answered sees a PRF evaluation request and returns bytes; it never sees the master key, a vault key or a passphrase. Nothing is copied, nothing is pasted, nothing public carries a key.
adding-a-door-moves-no-key-through-a-person

A Mac with Chrome is where both paths run in one session, as run 4 showed: the provider on the Mac answers locally, and "use a phone, tablet or security key" reaches the same passkey over the hybrid link. So the one-off setup for the phone-by-QR path is two gestures on the Mac: open the door you have, then add the QR path as a door. Afterwards the iPad, or any browser that reaches the phone by QR, derives that door and finds the master.
where-no-device-has-both-paths-the-recovery-code-is-the-boot

On a device that cannot reach an existing door (a new tablet whose only route is the QR path, before that path has a door), the reader types the recovery code once. It derives the recovery door, which holds the master key; the page is now unlocked; the new path's door is written as above. The recovery code is the one secret a person ever types, and only on a device where no door opens. It is already in the design as the second door; this makes it also the way a new path joins.
providers-without-prf-hold-the-recovery-code-and-are-not-doo

A provider that returns no PRF bytes (Chrome's own store today, and any password manager whose passkeys do not support the extension) cannot be a door, because there are no bytes to derive one from. It can still hold the recovery code as a secure note. That makes it a holder of a door's passphrase, which is a different and weaker thing: whoever can read the note can open the recovery door. It is a fair place for the code for a reader who trusts that manager with their passwords already, and it should be described as what it is, not as a passkey door.
what-a-lost-device-needs

Deleting a lost device's door file stops that path from finding the master, from the next unlock on. It does not stop a copy of the master key that the lost device may have had in memory. The full answer is to rotate the master vault's key and rewrite the doors that are kept, which is a larger operation on the master vault and is designed, not built. The door list in the master is what makes the smaller step possible from any remaining door.
what-a-provider-s-fix-does-to-a-door

If Apple or Google changes one path so its bytes match the other, the door for the path that moved stops opening and the door for the other path takes over, with no loss. If a change moves a path's bytes to something new, that path finds no door, says so, and the reader adds one from an open door or with the recovery code. The design never has to guess which output was correct; it only has to keep every door replaceable and never treat an unknown address as an error.
the-flow-written-out

1. First device. Make a passkey. Get its bytes. Derive the door. Create the door, the master, the newsroom vault and the recovery door, with the access key. Show the recovery code once. The master records one passkey door and the recovery door. 2. Second path, same device. Unlocked. Ask for the bytes by the other path (on a Mac: the phone by QR). Derive. Write a second door with the same master key. The master now records three doors. 3. A new device that can reach an existing path. Ask for the bytes, derive, open the door, read the master. Nothing to set up. 4. A new device that reaches only a path with no door. The page derives an address, finds nothing, and says "no door here for this path yet". Type the recovery code. The recovery door opens the master. Add this path as a door. From now on this device opens without the code. 5. A lost device. From any open door, delete the lost door from the master's list and the server. Rotate the master's key when that is built.
what-the-lab-shows-now-and-what-it-does-not

Card 2 shows the path (platform or cross-platform) with each result and says that a different path can give different bytes. Its fingerprint is a hash of the bytes rather than a prefix of them. The comparison box names "another path" among the reasons two fingerprints differ. Card 1 already showed the attachment and the transports at creation. Not built: adding a path as a door (a card that takes an open door and the other path's bytes and writes the second door), the master vault, its door list, retiring a door, rotating the master. Those are the article's phase five. The lab's card 6 writes one door; the add-a-door card is that same write with the master key taken from memory instead of made at random.
field-notes-from-the-two-days
Smaller things seen while testing, for whoever updates the article or builds the next step:
field-notes-from-the-two-days

- Chrome's first attempt to create a Google Password Manager passkey showed "Can't reach Google Password Manager. Try again in a few minutes"; the second attempt worked. That is Chrome's side, transient, and the page should say "try again" rather than treat it as a failure of the design. - Card 0's PRF capability reads null in some browsers rather than true or false, through getClientCapabilities(). The lab now says "the browser does not say" in that case; card 1's prf.enabled is the answer that counts. - Safari's QR dialog names the registrable domain ("sign in to sgit.ai") where Chrome's names the host (newsroom.sgit.ai). The relying party id is newsroom.sgit.ai on both create and get; the dialogs word it differently. - The flags were the same on every path: user present, user verified, backup eligible, backed up. The flags do not reveal the path; authenticatorAttachment does, and card 2 now shows it. - The credential id and the user handle were identical across every path and provider path, which is how the page can be sure that the differing bytes came from one passkey. - The lab's fingerprint was the first four bytes of the PRF output until v0.9.1, which put 32 bits of the secret on screen and in chat; it is now a hash of the output. The door derivation was never weakened in practice (the seed is a 256-bit HKDF output), and it was still the wrong thing to show. - PBKDF2 at 600,000 iterations for the read and write keys took on the order of a tenth of a second each on a laptop and several times that on a phone, as the article estimated; the lab shows the time with each key. - Chrome's own store (no provider signed in) signs and returns no PRF bytes, as the article says; the lab shows the ladder in that case.
reporting-it

The symptom is reproducible with the lab in a few minutes: one Google Password Manager passkey, card 2 on the device, then card 2 through "use a phone" from the same browser. It is worth filing with Apple through Feedback Assistant, with logs from both devices as their engineers asked in the forum threads, and with Google against Password Manager's PRF handling on iOS, so that whichever side owns the bridge sees it.
sources

- Apple Developer Forums, "Different PRF output when using platform or cross-platform authentication attachment": https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/764730 - Apple Developer Forums, "Passkey PRF inconsistency between Apple devices": https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/774111 - Apple Developer Forums, "PRF extension not supported in Safari's cross-device WebAuthn flow": https://developer.apple.com/forums/thread/774112 - W3C Web Authentication Level 3, the PRF extension (prf), and the FIDO CTAP2 hmac-secret extension it is defined over. - Yubico, the PRF extension: https://developers.yubico.com/WebAuthn/Concepts/PRFExtension/

Date: 12 October 2026. Status: the design, and a first build (the vault pane, v0.11.0); what the pane gained since is at the end, before the experiments. The experiments it calls for are listed at the end; the design will move as they are run. Related: The passkey opens the vault (the account with no server), one door per passkey path (why the doors are per path), the passkey lab (every piece, as a thing you can press), the vault pane (where this runs), assets/vault-pane/sync.js (the logic, as pure functions), admin/build/testsync.mjs and testpane.mjs (what is checked).
what-this-is-for

The reading account lives in one browser's local storage: what was read and how far, what it cost, what was declined and why, the top-ups, the personas and their lists. It is updated as the reader reads, and it goes nowhere. The vault gives it a second home that the reader owns and that every device of theirs can reach through a passkey. The loop to close is short to state: enable the account on one device, read, press Update the vault; open another device, enable it, and see the same reads, the same spend, the same balance.
the-principles

1. Local storage stays primary. It is written in real time by the meter, as today, and nothing about the meter changes. The vault is a copy that the reader keeps current. 2. The reader chooses when to sync. One button. Nothing commits on its own, so the number of commits is the number of times a person pressed the button, and the cost of a sync (a few key derivations, one commit, one publish) is paid when they want it. A timer or a quiet-moment sync can come later, as a setting, once the shape of a sync is understood. 3. The vault holds records, never totals. Reads, top-ups and personas go in raw. Reads, spend, declined, credit and balance are recomputed from the records every time they are shown, with one starting credit for the account. A total copied from a device would be wrong the moment a second device existed. 4. One file per device, written only by that device. Each device is fingerprinted once (the id it already uses as its clone branch, nr- and eight characters, kept in local storage) and writes everything it originated to its own file, whole, on every sync. Two devices never write the same file, so there is nothing to merge at the file level and no conflict by construction; the compare-and-swap on publish still guards the ref, and a race there is merged by the library at file level, which keeps both files. 5. The consolidated view is computed, not stored. Opening the vault reads every device's file and builds one view: per device, and in total. Bringing other devices' activity into a browser adds their records to its local storage, tagged with the device they came from, and recomputes the totals; the next sync from that browser writes only its own records back, so a record has exactly one author for ever. 6. Keys never leave the device unencrypted and nothing is typed twice. The passkey derives the door; the door holds the master's key; the master holds the reader vault's key and the access key. The access key is pasted once, on the first device, and lives in the master from then on; a second device gets it by opening the master, which it can do with its passkey once it has a door, or with the recovery code once.
the-data

In the reader vault: A device file: Every record is the meter's own, unchanged, plus the device that originated it (the notes are assets/vault-pane/notes.js's own records, kept apart from the meter's state, and travel in the same file; the stories seen are assets/vault-pane/wire-state.js's). A read's id is made on one device and only that device's meter changes it afterwards (its depth grows while the page is read; a rating or a decline is added), so the device's next sync carries the latest version and the rule "the version that knows most wins" (declined over rated over deeper) is a safety net, not the mechanism. The totals, recomputed:
the-data

start is the account's one starting credit, written to account.json by the device that created the account; every device's meter begins with the same starting credit locally, and the vault counts it once. Payment references make top-ups unique across devices, which matters because a merged top-up is also added to the device's list of credited references, so a return page opened again on another device cannot credit the same payment twice.
the-flow

1. First device. Open the pane, Enable with your passkey. The passkey gives the bytes, the bytes give the door, the door is not there: no door here for this path yet. Paste the access key, Create the account: the door, the master and the reader vault are made; the access key goes into the master; a recovery code is shown once and its door is added. Read some pages. Update the vault: this device's file is written, one commit, published. 2. Second device. Open the pane, Enable with your passkey. The door is there; the master opens and brings the access key; the reader vault opens. Across your devices lists the first device with its reads and spend. Bring that device's activity here: the records are added to this browser's local storage and the meter now shows the consolidated balance. Read, Update the vault: the second file is written. The first device, on its next open, sees two. 3. A device whose passkey cannot be a door, or a path that gives other bytes: no door here for this path yet, then Add this device with the code: the recovery door opens the master, the access key comes with it, and this path gets a door of its own; the code is not needed on that device again. 4. Forget on this device clears the session; the vault is unchanged.
the-flow

The keys for an unlocked session are kept in memory and, for the life of the tab, in session storage, so that moving from page to page does not ask for the passkey each time. This is a choice for the beta, written here so it can be revisited: the article's final shape may keep them in memory only and ask again on each page, or hold them behind a lock screen in the pane.
what-is-not-synced-and-why

- The active persona and the reading position are a device's own. - Shares (what the reader sent to the newsroom) are not in the vault yet; they are a record of something that already left the browser. - The simulated cart is unused with a live payment link. - Local pruning. The intent is that local storage holds what the vault does not have yet, and no more. That is not done in this build: the meter keeps its own window of 500 reads regardless, and the vault keeps everything. Pruning needs the meter to read from the consolidated view rather than from its own log, which is phase five of the article's plan. - Retiring a device and rotating the master's key are designed, not built, as before.
what-is-built-in-v0-11-0

- assets/vault-pane/vault-pane.js and .css: the pane on the right of every page that carries the meter, opened by the Vault button beside the balance; the page moves left while it is open and the pane overlays at phone width. Enable, create, join with the code, update the vault, the table across devices, bring their activity here, forget on this device, and every call to the vault server listed. - assets/vault-pane/sync.js: extract, consolidate, mergeInto, accountFile, as pure functions, checked by admin/build/testsync.mjs with two devices' states. - assets/door.js: the door derivation, moved out of the lab so the pane and the lab derive the same door from the same bytes; the lab re-exports it. - admin/build/testpane.mjs: the loop in Chromium against the mock of the vault API, with a virtual authenticator standing in for one synced passkey: device A reads, enables, creates, updates; device B (the same passkey, a cleared browser) enables, sees A, brings A's activity in and shows the consolidated balance, reads, updates; a third opens with the recovery code. - /vault/index.html: the page that explains this and opens the pane.
what-the-pane-gained-after-v0-11-0

- v0.12.0: a This page tab before the vault's, with the notes and the lane to the newsroom, and a Keys tab with every vault's key behind Reveal (the feedback loop). A device's file carries its notes beside its reads. - v0.12.1: the pane stays open from page to page (the open state and the tab in session storage); a Reading tab, every page read here with its decision and the done ones folded away; what the browser knows about the page above the chips; the three steps with the next one in bold; an account made without an access key in its master asks for it once; a send rewrites the device's file (cards 001 to 009). - v0.12.6: what only this browser holds, counted on the Vault button and named in a strip above the tabs with Update the vault one press away (assets/vault-pane/pending.js); the wire's seen stories in the device file as wire.seen, so New is right on every device; two window events, sgit-vault-open and sgit-vault-update, so the wire can ask for the pane and for an update (cards 027, 028). - v0.12.8: Write to the newsroom, with Save and send (card 034). - v0.12.14: more than one wire, so a seen story's id carries the wire's scope in the device file (owasp:sec-01); the Industry Wire's stay bare. - v0.12.26: the inbox, an append lane on the reader vault that a browser without the passkey writes into with a link; what arrives is written as that browser's device file (combine() in sync.js when it already has one) and brought in by the same merge (send to my vault from any browser, card 049). - v0.12.58: two ways in, Open with your passkey and Connect with a link, nothing named first; after an explicit open the pane asks which device this browser is when the vault knows devices (an existing one is adopted with its records) and brings in what the vault holds on its own; both directions counted above the tabs; every write combine(prev, extract(local)), so two browsers may share a device; a sent batch filed under a device of the reader's choosing (open, or connect, card 059). Principle 4 above now reads: one file per device, and a device is a bucket the reader names.
the-experiments-to-run-next

1. Two real devices, your own. iPad and laptop with the same iCloud Keychain passkey: the loop above, watching the number of calls per sync and per open in the pane's log. The question is whether a sync is one commit (it should be: one file) and whether an open is cheap enough to do on every page. 2. A page read on both devices. Open the same article on both after a merge: two read ids for one page, charged twice, which is the meter's rule today (a page is charged once per session per device). Decide whether the consolidated view should show it once. 3. Ratings and declines after a merge. Rate a page on the device that read it after the other device has merged it; sync both; check the other device's copy updates on its next bring-in (it should: the author's version wins). 4. A top-up on one device, a return page on the other. The merged payment reference should stop a second credit. 5. Pruning. Once the meter can read the consolidated view, drop local records that a device's file already holds, and measure what the meter loses (nothing, if the view is complete). 6. Automatic sync. A timer, or a sync when the tab goes to the background, as a setting the reader turns on, once the per-sync cost is known from experiment 1.

12 October 2026, built in newsroom.sgit.ai v0.12.0. Status: a beta, against dev.send.sgraph.ai, with one reader. The pieces it stands on: the activity vault (the pane, the device files, the consolidated view) and one door per passkey path. The brief it answers is the first item of The site is an inbox, read in what the new articles ask, narrowed to what one reader and the agent that runs the site need to learn from each other before anything is automated.
in-short

- A note is one tap at a piece: done, read later, follow up, not for me, more like this, liked, wrong, fix this, idea; with words if the reader adds them and the phrase they had selected on the page. Or a message: words alone, written under Write to the newsroom (since v0.12.8, after the first lane read asked where to write to the newsroom's agent), sent with Save and send in one press. It is a record, like a read in the meter: kept in local storage the moment it is made. - The vault carries it, when the reader asks. Update the vault writes this device's notes in the same file as its reads; another device brings them in, tagged. Nothing new in the sync model. - The lane carries what the reader chooses to send. Send to the newsroom puts the notes not yet sent into a vault of their own, one file per note. The reader keeps the write key in their master; the newsroom gets the read key, once, in the open, and reads with sgit clone or admin/build/lane.py. Nothing else of the reader's is in the lane, so the reader never shares the reading account to be heard. - The keys are the reader's. A Keys tab lists every vault of the account with its key behind Reveal: the doors, the master, the reader vault, the lane. Any of them opens on its own, in sgit or in the vault app. - On the wire, the decision is at the story: four of the brief's seven at each card; a decided story folds to its headline, with undo. "Not for me" is the signal the wire's desk asked for, and it is a note like any other.
why-this-and-not-the-news-automation-first

The wire's next turns (a pitched story becoming an article, placement on the front page, the weekly newsletter) are worth building when there are readers to place for. Today the site has one reader who is also its owner, and what is missing is not output but the return path: a way for that reader to say, at the moment of reading, what is wrong, what to do next, what to drop, and for the agent that runs the site to read that without being handed the whole account. The vault was the right kind of experiment: small, real, and it was known to work by the next morning. This is the same kind.
the-record

Kept in localStorage under sgit.notes.v1, apart from the meter's state, so the meter's own writes never touch it (assets/vault-pane/notes.js). In the reader vault: inside activity/devices/<device.json, as notes[] beside reads[], written whole by that device and only by it (assets/vault-pane/sync.js). In the lane: notes/<id.json, one file per note, with device and sentat added; a note sent twice rewrites its file.
the-lane

A vault of its own, made the first time the reader sends, by the pane, with the access key the master holds. Its record in the master, lane.json: the vault key, the read key, when and by which device it was made. The read key is the library's own derivation exported in the form the CLI clones with, sgitpublicread<64 hex:<id; it opens the vault for reading and carries no write capability, which is a separate derivation it does not hold. The test proves both: the CLI clones the lane with the read key alone and reads every note, and a push from that clone is refused. What the lane is not: a channel the newsroom can write back on. A reply goes the way replies go on this site, as a new version of an article or a note on a page, and a reply lane is the next thing to design if that proves too slow.
the-loop-step-by-step
The reader.
the-loop-step-by-step

1. Read. On any page, open the pane (the Vault button beside the balance; it opens on This page). Select a phrase if one is the point. Tap a kind. Write under Write to the newsroom if there is more to say: Save and send keeps the message and sends it in one press, Save, send later keeps it for the next send (since v0.12.8; before that the box was unnamed and its button read Keep the words). On the wire, tap the decision at the story. 2. Now and then, Update the vault, from the strip above the tabs, the Vault tab or the wire's bar: the notes travel with the reads to the other devices. Until then the Vault button counts what is only in this browser (since v0.12.6). 3. When there is something for the newsroom, Send to the newsroom. The first send makes the lane and shows its read key; hand that key to the agent once. Later sends go to the same lane and need nothing handed over. A send also rewrites this device's file in the reader vault, so the other devices see the notes as sent (since v0.12.1, card 009). 4. In Keys, any vault's key, to open it elsewhere.
the-loop-step-by-step

The newsroom. 1. With the read key in the environment, never in a file of the repository: NEWSROOMLANEKEY=sgitpublicread…:… python3 admin/build/lane.py clones the lane the first time and pulls after that, then prints the notes grouped by page, newest first, with the article number, the kind, the quote and the words. --json gives the records; --dir names the clone. A vault key is refused: the newsroom is not to hold write access to a reader's vault. 2. Act on them in the open: a fix in a release, a version of an article, a line in a note. The version row says which notes it answers, by page and kind, never by quoting a note the reader did not make public. 3. Nothing is sent back through the lane.
what-is-not-built

- Three of the seven decisions: read now, comment (words are a note; a comment addressed to a sentence is a mark, which is item 3 of the brief), move to a persona. - The pane about the piece (item 2 of the brief): the article's graph, the marks and the cost in the pane. The pane now has tabs, which is where that goes. - Signing. A note in the lane is not signed; the lane's existence in the reader's master is what says whose it is. Persona key pairs are item 5 of the brief. - A reply lane from the newsroom to the reader. - The front page. It is imported, so the decisions are on the wire and on article pages, not on the front page's cards. - A second device does not send another device's notes: only this device's own unsent notes go to the lane. (Sent marks reached other devices only with the next Update in v0.12.0; since v0.12.1 a send rewrites the device's file too.) - Pruning, as before: local storage keeps every note.
what-the-first-run-changed-v0-12-1

The owner's first run on an iPad, the same afternoon, is on the engineering board as cards 001 to 018. Fixed at once: the pane stays open from page to page; an account made in the lab before the pane existed takes its access key once, in the Vault tab; a stray null. Added at once: Done as the first decision, what the browser knows about the page from the meter's records, a Reading tab with done pages folded away, the three steps, and a send that updates the device file. Filed for the next releases: feedback without a vault through the newsroom's own append lane with a typed schema (010), screenshots (011), the early-access key first (012), first-time guidance (018).
the-experiments

1. A week of use by one reader: notes per day, which kinds, how many led to a change in a release. The honest measure is whether the reader keeps doing it. 2. The morning read on the wire with the lens set to the named reader: "not for me" and "more like this" at each story, and whether the desk's weekly pass can propose persona edits from the lane alone. 3. Two devices: notes made on a phone, updated, brought into a laptop, sent from there; the "sent" marks after the next update. 4. The agent reading the lane at the start of a session and acting before anything else is asked: whether that changes what the sessions do. 5. Which chips are never pressed. Seven is a guess; the brief said six kinds of mark and seven decisions. The ones not used in a month go.
the-first-lane-read-13-october-2026-v0-12-8

The owner's first send arrived whole: seven notes, five decisions on wire stories, a Done on article No. 10, and one message asking where to write to the newsroom's agent, and calling Keep these words a weird button. Both were right: the box had no heading and the button described the browser, not the destination. v0.12.8 heads the box Write to the newsroom and adds Save and send; lane.py now prints messages first. The lane is one-way: the reader writes, the newsroom reads with the published read key and cannot write. Replies need a vault on the newsroom's side (card 035).

For: https://github.com/the-cyber-boardroom/SGraph-AIAppSend, the vault UI library at sgraphaiappsenduivault/v0/v0.2/v0.2.3/common/js/lib/sg-vault/sg-vault.js. From: newsroom.sgit.ai, 12 October 2026. Local patch until it ships: assets/vendor/sg-vault/local/sg-vault--create-with-id.js in SGit-AIWebsiteNewsroom. Also listed as item 4 of "What the library needs" on https://sgit.ai/docs/vault/vault-from-javascript.html.
the-ask

Let SGVault.create(sgSend, passphrase, options) take options.vaultId. When it is given, use it in place of the random 8-character id drawn at step 1, validate it as parseVaultKey does (^[a-z0-9]{4,24}$), and refuse to create when a vault already exists at that address.
why

The passkey design (https://sgit.ai/articles/the-passkey-opens-the-vault.html) computes a small door vault's id and passphrase from a passkey's PRF bytes, so that nothing has to be stored to find it: the browser derives the address, opens the door, and finds the master vault's key inside. Such a vault can be opened by the library today (SGVault.open takes any passphrase:vaultid) and cannot be created by it, because create always draws its own id. newsroom.sgit.ai had to add a static method to make doors as real vaults instead of raw objects.
the-shape-we-are-running

Before writing anything it makes the two reads open makes before it loads a tree: the branch index, then the named ref it names (or the derived one). If either exists, or either exists and cannot be decrypted, it throws with code: 'EEXISTS'; "HEAD ref missing" is the one answer that means free. It then resets the ref manager's raw-ref cache, so that the first pushIfMatch after creation arms the compare-and-swap exactly as it does after create(). Suggested upstream form:
two-things-seen-while-doing-this-for-the-same-change

- create hard-codes the clone branch 'web-ui'; open takes options.cloneBranch. Letting create take it too keeps one client's clone ref apart from every other browser's from the first commit. - The random draw in create is alphabet[b % 36] over 8 random bytes, which favours the first 4 characters of the alphabet slightly (256 is not a multiple of 36). Rejection sampling (b < 252) is what sgit's own generatevaultkey does and what the newsroom's randomPassphrase does.
tests-that-would-show-it

In the newsroom's admin/build/testvault.mjs, against a mock of the vault API: a door created at a derived id is a vault with a named ref, a branch index and content-addressed objects; sgit clone of it from the prefixed key reads every file; a second createWithId at the same address is refused with EEXISTS; open of an address nobody has used fails with "HEAD ref missing" and nothing else.

12 October 2026, written for newsroom.sgit.ai v0.11.1, the release that imports sgit.ai v0.7.70. Status: an analysis and a proposed order; nothing in it is built unless a version row says so. sgit.ai published five articles on 12 October and revised the passkey article twice. Three of the five are briefs addressed to the session that runs this site. This note reads them against what runs here at v0.11.0, sorts their items into done, ours to build, and sgit.ai's to build, and proposes an order.
in-short

- The briefs assume v0.11.0. They are written on top of the vault pane, the reading records in the reader vault, the door per path and the wire read from a vault. Each of those is a property they rely on, and none of them asks for those to change. - The next thing is the inbox mode on the wire: seven one-tap decisions at each story, recorded as edges in local storage and carried by the sync. It is the smallest item, it is first in the brief's own order, and "not for me" is the feedback the wire's desk is waiting for. - The second is the pane about the piece: the right-hand pane becomes about the article in front of the reader, with tabs, and the ways into the article (headlines, facts, relationships, what is new) are computed from files this site already publishes. - Several items are not this site's. The fold under the abstract, the newsletter cut by the reader's default, the Editor placing wire stories on the front page and a pitched wire story becoming an article are sgit.ai's pages and roles; the imported pages are never edited here, so those go to the sgit.ai session as asks. - One item is cheap and honest and no brief orders it: the five counts of Firing journalists, run on this site from its own files and published.
the-vault-is-live-81

A description of v0.11.0 as it stands, drawn: the layers, the key chain, the sync model, the tests, the timeline. It asks for nothing new. Its value for the next steps is its list of what is not built, which is the same list as the activity vault note: pruning local storage once the vault holds it, retiring a device, rotating the master's key, automatic sync, the key pairs for signing, the persona vault, the notes lane to the newsroom. It marks the keys of an unlocked session living in the tab's session storage as a choice to revisit, and that stands. Its argument matters more than its list: the brief that follows could not be written until the properties of what runs were known. The order below keeps to that. Each step ships a property, the version row and the note record it, and the next brief is written against it.
two-agents-one-vault-80
The wire as it runs, from both git logs. The next turns it names:
the-site-is-an-inbox-82

The brief for what a reader does with the vault, with its own order. Read against v0.11.0: What not to build, and what it changes here: no decision placed at the end of a page, so the seven decisions go at the piece, in the inbox and at the top of an open article, and the meter's rating card at the end stays what it is, a price; no signal sent anywhere without a press, which the pane already keeps to; no mark the reader cannot see in their records, which the device file and the consolidated view already give; no server of ours.
ways-to-read-one-article-84

The modes in the pane about the piece, on top of item 2 above. The ones that can be computed today, from files this site already publishes: The brief's other items: a default mode per persona, kept with the persona; the mode in the address, so a reading list can say "the slides of this one"; on the phone the pane as a sheet from the bottom, where today it overlays; the email cut by default is sgit.ai's newsletter; a figure drawn for this reader, later. firing-journalists-83

An argument about publishers, with five counts that read one from outside: original share, sourcing, corrections, roles, the metric reported. It does: the articles and their graphs for the first two, with a check that the source links still resolve; the corrections page and the version pages for the third; the newsroom's roles for the fourth; the meter for the fifth. the-passkey-opens-the-vault-v1-4-0

Revised twice after this site's lab. what-belongs-to-sgit-ai-not-here

the-order-proposed

the-order-proposed
