13 October 2026, by newsroom.ux. A review of the handover from the Claude session that ran the Newsroom Design Lab on 11 October (the UX review, the kit, four published vaults, 162 screenshots), judged against the site as it is today, not the v0.6.4 to v0.7.1 it was built on. What is there, what has already been overtaken, what to take, and in what order.
what-the-lab-is

Another agent session, 11 to 13 October, did three things in order: a UX review of newsroom.sgit.ai from the point of view of a contact arriving from a link (six roles, measured on the live site at v0.6.4); a brief for prototypes in SGit vaults, three design directions of everything, explored before anything touched the live site; and the prototypes themselves, built with a shared kit by a dev and an architect, each gated and published with a read key.
what-the-lab-is

The three directions, in every vault: A Broadsheet (a serious paper, serif, warm), B Briefing (answers first, labelled blocks, phone-first), C Your desk (the reader's own newsroom: persona, board, notes). A top-bar switch and a Compare view at phone width. All four vaults open read-only in the SG/App host today (https://dev.vault.sgraph.ai/#<read key with %3A), and sgit clone <read key works with sgit-ai 0.21.0. The write keys were delivered separately and must not enter this repository; the gate's key-leak tripwire would refuse them.
the-quality-of-the-work

High, and honest about itself. Every vault carries a REALITY file checked by a test, a BRIEF-CORRECTIONS file naming each deviation and deferral, and a sources file with the SHA-256 of the newsroom data it was built on. Nothing is lorem ipsum: it runs on the real wire.json, persona/links.json and the markdown twins, and everything the site does not have yet is labelled Proposal in the interface and kept in data/proposals/.json so an editor can change it without code. The kit has an escaping template that refuses raw HTML, a gate that renders every route in every direction at 390 and 1280 with zero page errors and no sideways scroll, a contrast test over every theme block, and a budget on the bundle. The architect's review of the kit (lab/reviews/architect-kit.md) is a real review: 22 checks, defects reproduced before and after, and the open risks named. Three things it measured that this repository should know and not re-discover:
the-quality-of-the-work

- The vault host's CSP is connect-src blob: data:: fetch() to newsroom.sgit.ai is refused inside a vault app even though the newsroom sends access-control-allow-origin: . Images and classic scripts from other origins do load. So a vault app carries a byte-faithful snapshot and reads live only when opened standalone. - localStorage throws in the app frame; sg.state works and survives reload. - Never assign location.hash in the host; the srcdoc frame re-navigates. Routes live in a variable, filters in the route path.
what-the-site-has-done-since-without-the-lab
The lab was built on v0.7.1. The site is at v0.12.13 and several of the review's asks arrived by another road, which changes what to take: Of the review's ten bugs, checked today on the built tree:
what-to-take-in-order

1. The data, this week, not the code. This is the lab's own advice and it is right. Four files in the findability vault are editorial work that does not exist anywhere else and would take the Librarian days to redo:
what-to-take-in-order

- desks.json: five desks by audience with a scoring rule, a start-here list of five per desk, and every one of 73 articles assigned (one primary, at most one secondary). Today one topic holds 38 of 73; the largest desk holds 18. - tags.json: 339 raw tags reduced to 42 controlled ones in five groups, each with a scope sentence and the raw tags it absorbs; 40 rejected with a reason (format, product, too broad, one-off). Median tags per article from 11 to 4. - series.json: 11 series found from Builds on chains and the desk notes, each with its order and dek (the reading meter in five, behaviour policy from argument to gate in four, where agents run in four). - formats.json: a format label per article (field report, explainer, analysis, RFC, answer, how-to) with the rule that derived it.
what-to-take-in-order

Where they go: the newsroom's authoring side is sgit.ai's generator, so the honest target is admin/content/ on sgit.ai (the catalogue and the wire are built there), or, until the generator moves here, a derived index this site builds and renders as pages: /desks/, /tags/<id.html, /series/<id.html, reading time and format on the cards in search/. The lab's find/tools/derivefind.py already does the derivation and its tests pin it. Each file should gain a status and a target field, as the architect proposed, so acceptance is a move and not a retype. 2. The three persona stories and the purpose page. front/data/proposals/personas/{founder,security,newsroom}.json are written in full (story, Dinis's note, start here, sections mapped to real slugs). purpose.json is the Why this exists page the site does not have: agenda and disclosure, licences, method, who it is for, the ask. masthead.json holds three heart lines; the current tagline describes a method and no subject. These are words, and words move for free.
what-to-take-in-order

3. Three small live fixes from the review's bug list that are this site's to make: a 404.html with search and the doors; a label on the balance chip (£5 free reading credit, in the meter's balance view, v1.4.2); the feed title and the edition label are sgit.ai's and belong in the sync's text rules or upstream. 4. The reader primitives the pane does not have yet, taken from the article vault as patterns, not code: highlights kept as exact text and re-marked on render (ar-reader.js), a four-column board with keyboard and swipe, and the feedback block's consent and receipt wording (feedback.json). The pane already has the lane the lab only simulated, so this is the one place the live site is ahead and the lab's design is the better face for it.
what-to-take-in-order

5. Decide the direction before porting any layout. The hub's #decisions page holds seven decisions with options (direction, masthead line, doors, article top, feedback, desks, board), kept in the browser and downloadable as JSON. Nothing in the vaults should become the live front page until those are picked, and the lab says so itself. My reading of the screenshots, for what it is worth: Broadsheet is the most finished and closest to the site's existing voice; Briefing's The news, Our view, The evidence, Room for disagreement blocks are the strongest single idea because every block is sourced from something that already exists (the Explainer's short version, the article's In short, the vault links, the Historian's contradictions); Your desk is what the vault pane is becoming. The lab's own Mix option (A for the publication, C for a signed-in reader) is the one that matches where the site has gone since.
what-to-take-in-order

6. The kit, selectively. nr-html.js (the escaping template, NR.url, the safe markdown subset) has tests behind it and is worth adopting as a shared primitive; this site's wire.js, vault-pane.js and search.js each render with their own escaping. NrBase and the gate's render-every-route check are good patterns for any future vault app this site ships. The shell, the direction switcher and the compare view are lab furniture and should not move. The kit's two-theme-per-direction colour blocks are a separate axis from the five themes shipped in v0.12.12 and can be left where they are.
what-not-to-do

- Do not re-run the UX review's measurements as if they were current. Six of its ten bugs and three of its five "fix this week" items have moved. A fourth synthetic-user run against v0.12.13, which the review itself asks for, would be the right way to re-baseline. - Do not port prototype code into the site before the decisions. The vaults are the place to decide and the evidence; the architect's path-to-live section says what moves (components served from the versioned path, tokens, the reader store) and what stays. - Do not copy the vaults into this repository. They are published with read keys and clone in seconds; admin/notes should link them, which this note does.
where-the-material-is

- The zip, extracted to the session's scratch space: HANDOVER.md, lab/BRIEF.md, lab/reviews/architect-kit.md, lab/context/newsroom-ux-review.md (6,200 words), the kit at v0.1.3, the four vault sources, 162 screenshots named <route<direction<width.webp. - The vaults, live: read keys in the hub's data/vaults.json and in the handover. - The decisions: hub #decisions; the review map: hub #map (26 items, 22 prototyped, 4 partial, 2 not in scope).
A design note, 13 October 2026, for v0.12.12 (cards 036, 037, 038). What was decided and why, in the order the decisions were made. The guidance that came out of it is assets/themes/README.md.
the-ask

A reader of the wire replied to the owner's link with two words, "Dark mode!", and the owner asked for the five colour schemes VoiceDebrief ships, done here; then, with a screenshot of the bar wrapping at 2000px, to clean up the top menu; then to use the occasion to improve the documentation and the design guidance.
constraint-one-the-imported-stylesheet-cannot-be-edited

The newsroom's look is assets/newsroom.css, sgit.ai's stylesheet, imported on every sync, and validate.js check 11 fails the build if an imported file changes. It defines fifteen colour tokens in :root and then writes forty-odd literal colours in its rules: #101114 on every heading, #34363c on every paragraph, #fff on every accent fill. Redefining the tokens alone would have produced a dark page with black headings. The answer is a layer that loads after it and shadows exactly those rules: same selector, same specificity, later in the cascade, with a token whose Newsprint value is the literal. The list was generated, not guessed: a twenty-line script parses the stylesheet and prints every rule with a literal and its declarations, and the map in themes.css section B is that list, in file order, so a re-import is a diff and not a hunt. The stylesheets this site owns were rewritten to tokens instead, because they can be.
constraint-two-the-first-paint

A theme that arrives after the first paint is a flash of Newsprint on every page, which is worse than one look. chrome.py only writes the nav and footer blocks, not <head, and the nav block is the top of <body. So the stylesheet and a classic, blocking script are the first three lines of the nav block: by the time the parser reaches the first heading, data-theme is on <html and the theme's rules are loaded. VoiceDebrief puts its script in the head for the same reason and says so.
which-five

Not VoiceDebrief's five copied: the newsroom's own tokens, extended. Newsprint is the look since v0.6.0 and stays the default, pixel for pixel, so nobody who does not open the picker sees a change. Night is the ask: dark, with the teal lifted two steps so it holds 4.5:1 on the dark page. Paper, Blueprint and Ember are the three moods VoiceDebrief found worth having, warm, cool and warm-dark, drawn with this site's structure. Every theme states its contrast and the test measures it rather than trusts it: ink, text, headings and links on the page, and the ink on the accent, all at 4.5:1.
which-five

One naming decision is worth recording. The heading token is --head, not --ink, because the deck viewer in the imported stylesheet already reads var(--ink) as the colour of a dark bar, and a heading token that is near-white in Night would have turned that bar white under its white text. VoiceDebrief's tokens file describes exactly this conflation in its own bridge layer. A token is named for what it is for.
what-stays-literal

The terminal palette and the dark panels on it: a transcript is dark the way a terminal is, in every theme. The vault button's three status dots and the wire's amber "new" flag: signals, not surfaces, and each carries its own dark ink, which was the one place the rewrite had to be undone by hand (a light --fg on an amber fill). The print page: white, always, with the Newsprint tokens restated under @media print.
the-bar

The screenshot showed the problem: nine groups, five tools, the version and (on legacy pages) a "part of sgit.ai" pill, and the two stylesheets collapsing the bar at different widths, 820 and 1200, with neither knowing about the tools this site had added. The fix is one stylesheet for the bar's layout in both looks, loaded with the themes, and three cuts: World News Day under Archive (the people its outreach writes to land on its pages by the links in that outreach, which a top-level group never carried), the parent pill gone (the footer's network line says it), and the tools as one flex item so they move as one and never split. The breakpoints are measured by a sweep of widths and asserted by the test: one row at 1280 and up, Menu below, and on a phone two rows by design: the brand and Menu, then the tools. The first measurement said 1200, on this machine's fonts, and CI's Ubuntu fonts broke the row at exactly that width; a limit measured on one machine is not a limit, so it moved to 1280 with the difference as slack (v0.12.13).
the-gate

A theme with a hole inherits Newsprint's value for it silently. So the test reads themes.css, takes the union of tokens, and fails on any theme missing any; and it reads every stylesheet this site owns and fails on a literal colour outside the allowed signals. This is VoiceDebrief's checkthemes.py rule, carried over because it is the one that keeps the other decisions true after the people who made them have moved on.
what-was-not-done

The imported stylesheet still carries its literals; only the map shadows them, and the map has to be checked against each re-import. The meter is at v1.4.1 for its five literals; the component base and the vault library are vendored and untouched. No theme is offered per persona, though --pc exists and a persona's colour could become a sixth entry. The choice is not carried by the vault between devices, on the view that a theme belongs to a screen, which a reader may disagree with.

13 October 2026, by @newsroom.wire, from the owner's voice memo of the same evening and the work of three agents it fired up for it: an Architect (architecture.md), a Designer (design.md, with mock-ups on the real vault data and screenshots) and a Developer (the graph components and the infographic pipeline, integrated in the releases that follow). The brief, verbatim in parts: "really think about the user experience and how to consume this data, including in as much graphs as possible, including creating infographics about this, an infographic per news item, that top-level view, 'hey, this is what's going on', capture how much it costs and add to the thing, do four different complete UX for each of these wires, actually a fifth one for the top one, and then publish it."
in-short

- One system, five pages. Every wire page keeps one spine: masthead and the row of wires, the status line, the inbox bar first (the job is to empty it), the today band with the edition's hero infographic and the wire's own stat tiles, the lens, a band of charts, the personal brief, the beats with story cards. What differs per wire is only the graph its vault holds: threads as timelines on the Industry Wire, the projects graph on OWASP, the stack with its deadlines on AWS, the ecosystem map and the EN/PT switch on Portugal. No wire gets a colour of its own. - The overview at /wire/ is the fifth page: what the desks released today across the wires, the four wires as tiles with their leads, one lens across all of them, the best of today, small multiples of the week, and what the pictures cost. The Industry Wire moves to /wire/industry/, with the old address kept. - Every graph is drawn from what the vaults already hold, in the browser, live, from createElementNS and text: the desk's own graphs brief lists five, the Architect found eleven more, none needing anything from the desks. One module, wire/graphs.js, pure functions from data to SVG, tested without a browser. - An infographic per story and per edition, generated on the newsroom's side by the morning routine, never by the desks: a 16:9 hero per edition from the editor's note as a document, a 1:1 card per story from its headline and facts; the model per job from the bake-off; the images in the repository for ninety days, then a vault; and a public ledger of what each cost, per image, per edition, per wire, per month, shown on the pages. The key comes from the environment at run time and is never in the repository; without it the run is dry and the pages are complete without pictures. - Honest by construction. Every image carries an AI-image chip, its cost and model, and a disclosure with the full prompt; the card's text says everything the picture says; no quote in an image, no number the story does not carry, the headline exactly.
what-the-data-holds-measured-today

The graphs, and where each is computed. In the browser from the live vault: the provenance strip and graph per story; the projects graph with its zero counts kept visible; the stack as a graph with the deadlines timeline; the persona join as a reach matrix; entity co-occurrence drawn as an honest bar, not a hairball; threads as timelines; sources by day and by tally; the evidence grid (confidence by primary state); corrections over time; coverage independence; the language split. At build, by the morning routine, because they need history, another vault or something paid for: beats per edition over time, the release cadence across wires, and the cost per edition.
the-infographic-pipeline-and-its-cost

The routine runs after the desks publish (they are scheduled from 05:47 to 06:03 London; the routine at 06:56), clones the four vaults, and for each edition that changed generates the hero and the cards for the stories the release note names as added or updated. The key is the image's prompt hash, a pure function of the story's drawn fields, the model, the template version and the style reference, so an unchanged story is never redrawn and a corrected one is. Two sizes only: 16:9 for the hero (1920×1080, the banner size the site already makes) and 1:1 for the card (every model returns a square without cropping). Cards on the cheap concept-slide model, the edition's hero attached to each as the style reference, the bake-off's fix for consistency; heroes on the document model, given the editor's note as the document. The bake-off's prompt rules in every template: never name the platform, no numbers other than those given, no hex codes or type sizes in drawn text, end with "No other text."
the-infographic-pipeline-and-its-cost

The ledger: wire/<slug/infographics/<edition/ledger.json, one row per generation (story, file, job, model, generation id, seconds, cost from OpenRouter's own accounting, prompt hash, style hash, when, bytes, what it supersedes), with totals per edition; and wire/infographics-ledger.json, the sum per wire and per month, shown on every wire page's foot and on the overview as the owner asked. The prompt text is kept beside each image. Caps: three dollars a day and seventy-five a month, checked before every call; expected about $1.80 a day. Images live in the repository as WebP (a card about 100 KB, a hero about 180 KB; two to five megabytes a day); after ninety days the routine moves an edition's images to a newsroom-owned vault with a public read key and leaves a movedto in the ledger.
decisions-taken-and-what-needs-the-owner

Taken: images in the repository, not the vaults (they can be pruned, loaded with a plain img, and never decrypted; a vault's are public for ever); analysis on top of the record, so the newsroom illustrates and the desks never do; the inbox bar before anything visual; chart colours as their own tokens (--viz-) in themes.css, because the site's accent fails the chart contrast rules in two themes; status colour only for deadlines, always with an icon and a word; the What's New firehose on AWS drawn folded under every lens, because "withheld with the reason" is that wire's promise. For the owner: the move of the Industry Wire to /wire/industry/ so that /wire/ can be the overview (the inbox state and the notes carry over; the old address keeps a line saying where it went); the OpenRouter key in the routine's environment, and about two dollars for the five style references and the first live edition.
decisions-taken-and-what-needs-the-owner

For the desks, optional, in the brief: card.claim (a claim of at most eight words per story, for the card; derived from the headline until then), brief.personal.articleready[] on Portugal, and pt twins of the editor's note and the lead's reason.
what-the-first-live-run-taught-14-october
The owner handed the key the same evening and the first editions were made (the ledgers carry every figure). Four things the design above got wrong, corrected in the pipeline and here:
what-the-first-live-run-taught-14-october

- Every image is a square. The tool's generate() takes a prompt and a model and nothing about size; every model behind it returns 1024 by 1024. The prompts asked for 16:9 and 4:5 and got squares, so now they ask for a square and lay the card out for one. The hero reads well as a square; the page shows it at up to 560 px in the header. - Nano Banana 2.1 could not be had. OpenRouter answered every request with "temporarily rate-limited upstream" for the whole evening, for everyone, not for this key. The fallback the bake-off would suggest, Gemini 3.1 Flash Image, made two cards in six seconds each for seven cents, and misspelt both headlines ("patch paph", "IoT T devices"). A card whose headline is not exact breaks the first rule, so the cards now go to Gemini 3 Pro Image: about twenty seconds and fourteen cents each, every word exact in the probe. The pipeline tries the preferred model, waits out a 429 three times, and when the model stays refused for the run falls through to the next preference and records why in the ledger. - The prices. The bake-off's table (10 October) said 0.039 for a card and 0.176 for a hero; OpenRouter billed 0.14 and 0.24. The cap is counted in the billed figures now, and the ledger says which table it used. At these prices the two-dollar cap per wire is a hero and twelve cards, not forty; a first edition of eighty-eight stories (the AWS Wire) gets its lead and its first dozen, and the rest wait for a bigger cap or a cheaper exact model. - Burst and failure. The first run fired every card at once after the hero and spent its whole plan on refusals; now there are six seconds between images, a refusal costs an attempt against the cap, and three failures in a row stop the run.
what-the-first-live-run-taught-14-october

The accountant, the owner's next ask the same evening ("really capture the cost of all these runs, the cost per edition and the cost per work, and provide visibility"): admin/build/accountant.py, a role called @newsroom.accountant that reads every ledger and writes what the wires cost at each release, by wire, edition, month, model and kind, per piece of work, with the key's budget as OpenRouter last reported it, and says what is not counted (the desks' runs, this site's sessions). What held: the hero from the editor's note as a document is the best picture of the set, exactly as the bake-off found; the hero attached to each card keeps the palette and the type; the key never touched a file; the pages are complete without pictures and better with them; and the cost is on the page, to the cent, beside the thing it paid for.
where-the-material-is

The Designer's mock-ups are static pages on the real vault data, drawn by a script in the page under the site's rules, with a theme switch: an overview, the AWS Wire and the OWASP Wire, with screenshots at 390 and 1280 px in Newsprint and Night. They are in the session's scratch space; six screenshots are kept here under wires-ux/shots/. The mock-ups themselves could be published as a vault, as the design lab was, given a write token; none was in the session. The Architect's document and the Designer's are beside this note in full.

13 October 2026, built in newsroom.sgit.ai v0.12.14. Status: a beta with one named reader. It extends the Industry Wire and the wire as an inbox to two more vaults the research agent built on the same pipeline: the OWASP Wire and the AWS Wire. The card is 040 on the engineering board.
in-short

- A wire is a vault plus a config. admin/build/wire-vault.json is the Industry Wire at /wire/; wire-vault.<slug.json is another wire at /wire/<slug/. The config holds the endpoint, the vault id, the public read key, the clone command, the wire's name, a paragraph of what it is, and the named readers with the date and the way they agreed. Nothing else on this site knows a wire by name: wire.py writes every wire's three pages and snapshot, wire.js draws every wire, testwire.mjs tests every wire, and the search indexes every snapshot. - The contract is the same, and a vault may say more. Every vault gives data/bundle.json, data/deliveries.json, data/releases.json and docs/.md as how the wire works says. A vault that describes itself in wire (id, title, cadence, beats, the personal persona) gets its lenses from its own personas, all but the personal one, plus the named readers in the config; without it the page offers the Industry Wire's six. A map or a stack is drawn when it is there and nothing breaks when it is not. - The named reader's agreement is per wire. Each config records it. The agreement of 12 October covered the Industry Wire; on 13 October the owner extended it to the two new wires in chat, and each config says so with the date. - Each wire is its own inbox. The notes already keep the page's path, so a decision at /wire/owasp/ow-09 is not one at /wire/ai-09. The stories seen, the visit and the lens now take a scope too: the Industry Wire's are stored as before, a scoped wire's seen ids as slug:id, its visit and lens beside the Industry Wire's. The device file carries the seen ids as stored, so another device tells them apart.
what-a-vault-adds-beyond-the-edition

A map (data/map.json, the OWASP projects graph): title, intro, and entities, each with id, name, kind, aliases, facts (a flat object of label to value; an http value becomes a link), leaders, standards and notes. The page draws it as a folded section under the bar: each entity with its facts, leaders and standards, and the stories whose own entities values match the entity's name or an alias, case-insensitively. That match is the only thing the page computes; the vault's app does the same. Twenty projects, twelve named by a story in the first edition.
what-a-vault-adds-beyond-the-edition

A stack (data/stack.json, the AWS services a reader runs): persona, what, services (each id, name, aliases, runtime, watch), extraconcerns, deadlines (each what, date, then, source) and later. The join in the vault turns each service into a concern of the stack's persona, so the deliveries already say which items touched which service: a reached delivery to that persona whose connections name the service's id. The page draws the deadlines in the edition's header, soonest first, with the days left and red inside thirty days, and each service as a folded entry with the items that touched it. To change what reaches the reader, the desk edits the file in the vault; nothing on this site changes.
what-is-not-built

- A page of the wires. The strip at the top of each edition names them all; /wire/ is still the Industry Wire, not an index. - One inbox across wires. Each wire's bar counts its own; nothing adds them up. The Vault button's count does, since it counts notes and stories seen wherever they were kept. - The runs. None of the three runbooks is scheduled; the desks publish when asked. - The AWS stack from an account. The vault's later says it: derive the file from what the account runs, with the declared list as an override. Today it is a file the desk seeded.
the-names

The agent that keeps these pages, reading vaults and drawing them on this site, is the newsroom's side of the wire; the owner proposed calling it @newsroom.wire. The agent that writes a vault is what its runbook calls it, the wire's desk: the Industry Wire desk, the OWASP Wire desk, the AWS Wire desk. One reads, the others write, and the read key is the only thing they share.

13 October 2026, built in newsroom.sgit.ai v0.12.58. Card 059. The ask, in chat with two screenshots: the aggregation is the point, so a browser that opens the vault should show the account's balance, recomputed from what it received; the workflow is open a vault or connect a vault, not name a device first; and a browser that sends should be able to file what it sent under a device the reader already has. The pieces it stands on: the activity vault (the device files, the consolidated view, the merge) and send to my vault from any browser (the inbox).
in-short

- Two ways in, nothing to name first. Open your vault with the passkey: the browser reads and writes. Connect with a link: the browser only sends, into the vault's inbox. The locked pane offers both, and asks for no label before either. - Which device is this, asked once, after the open. When the vault already knows devices and this browser is none of them, the pane lists them and offers a new one. Two browsers may share a device. - What the vault holds comes here. After an explicit open, the other devices' records are merged into this browser on their own, and the meter shows the account's balance. Both directions are counted above the tabs: what is only here, and what is in the vault and not here. - A sent batch is filed where the reader says. Where the vault is open, each sending browser's batch has a choice: a device of its own, or one the reader already has, this browser included. The choice is remembered. - Every write is combined with the file as it is, so a shared device never loses one browser's records to the other's.
the-two-workflows

Opening is the full membership; connecting is the push-only one, and the site is not personalised there. That is the trade the ask accepts: what matters in that browser is that the reads, the decisions and the notes are captured, because they are the reader's own intelligence and the reason they come back. The reader's example: an iPad kept light for reading, no tabs, no distractions; read the article, decide, note, and have that count.
the-states-of-a-browser

1. Nothing. The pane's Vault tab offers Open with your passkey and Connect with a link, and I have a recovery code beside the first. A passkey is only offered for making when none answers: soft enforcement, the way in is never a form. 2. Connected. A link is kept in local storage (sgit.inbox.link). The Vault tab says which vault it sends to, takes Send as (the name of this browser, or of a device the reader already has), and offers Send to my vault and Forget the link; the strip above the tabs offers the send on any page. 3. Open, device unknown. The passkey opened the door, the master and the reader vault; the vault knows devices; this browser has never written and is none of them. The pane asks Which device is this? 4. Open, device known. The unlocked view: this device, what is not yet in the vault, what is not yet here, the devices across, the inbox. From a saved session (a page change) the pane returns straight here.
the-states-of-a-browser

The reader moves 1 to 2 by pasting or opening a link; 1 to 3 by the passkey or the code; 3 to 4 by choosing; 4 to 1 by Forget on this device; 2 to 1 by Forget the link. A connected browser that later reaches the passkey moves 2 to 3 like any other.
which-device-is-this

The device id is what a browser writes its file under, and the author on every record it originates. Until now a browser made its own id on first use and showed a label field before the passkey; a second browser on the same iPad, or a second Chrome profile, became a second device whether the reader wanted one or not, and the label had to be typed before anything opened.
which-device-is-this

Now the question is asked once, after the open, and only when there is a choice: the devices the vault knows, with their reads, notes and last update, and A new device with a name. Choosing an existing one makes this browser that device: the id and the label are taken, and the merge that follows brings that device's records in as this browser's own (mergeInto, mergeNotes, mergeWire with own), so the Reading tab, the notes and the meter are what that device had. A new device needs no name; the label can be set in the unlocked view later.
which-device-is-this

Two browsers sharing a device write the same file, so every write is now combine(prev, extract(local)) rather than a plain overwrite: every record of either, the one that knows more where both have it. The file can no longer shrink; a note removed in one browser stays in the vault file. The activity vault's rule, one author per record, holds: the author is the device, and the device is now a bucket the reader names.
what-comes-back-and-when

The pane counted one direction: what was only in this browser, with Update the vault one press away. The other direction was a button under the table across devices, and the screenshot that started this showed the result: a vault with four devices, a browser that had brought in none of them, "the vault has everything of this device" in the Vault tab, and a meter £0.18 off the account. Now inbound() (sync.js) counts what a merge would add, without writing: reads, top-ups, personas, notes and stories seen, from how many other devices. It is shown as Not yet here in the Vault tab, beside Not yet in the vault, with Bring them here beside Update the vault; and in the strip above the tabs, on every page, with the same button.
what-comes-back-and-when

After an explicit open (the passkey, the code, the account just made, the device just chosen) the merge runs on its own: the reader asked for the vault, and the vault is the account. The page reloads once so the meter reads the merged state, and the Vault tab says what arrived. On a page change the saved session opens the vault silently and nothing is merged: a reload under a reader who is reading is not acceptable, so the strip says what is not here and waits for the press.
where-a-sent-batch-is-filed

A browser that connects cannot see the vault's devices, and the link carries no list of them on purpose (it carries where to write and the key to encrypt to, nothing else). So the choice is made where the information is: in the Vault tab, when the batch is listed before it is brought in. Each sending browser gets a File under choice: a device of its own (new, or the row it already has), or any device the vault knows, this browser included, which is always offered even before it has a file.
where-a-sent-batch-is-filed

What is chosen first: what was chosen for that browser last time (aliases in the master's inbox.json, sender id to device id, written only when it changes); else a device whose label matches the name the browser gave itself; else the browser as its own device. Filing under another device re-tags every record with that device and keeps the sender's id as from (refile()), and the file is combined with the target's as every write is. Filing under this browser brings the records in as its own. Soft enforcement throughout: the name on the sending side is free text and only a hint; the reader confirms in the pane; nothing is refused for a name.
not-built

- Consolidating two devices the vault already has into one row (merge files, retire the id). The alias machinery is most of it; the ask was "we might need to", so it waits for the need. Nothing is deleted meanwhile, which is the rule the ask set for payment records. - Automatic sync on a timer or on leaving a page (card 029); the inbound side now runs on an explicit open, the outbound side is still a press. - A choice of device on the sending side. The link would have to carry the devices; it stays minimal. - The table's pennies. Each device's spend is rounded to a tenth of a penny before it is shown at two decimals, so the column can add to a penny less than the total. Top-ups now show a dash in the total when there are none, as the rows do.
tests

admin/build/testsync.mjs: inbound() before and after a merge; a cleared browser taking a device as its own; refile(); a write combined with the file as it is. testpane.mjs: nothing to name before opening; device B asked which device it is, choosing a new one, and the vault's records coming in on their own with the account's balance; device C opening with the recovery code and taking device B as its own: B's read is its own there, A's is tagged A, the id and label are B's, the balance is the account's, nothing left to bring in. testinbox.mjs: the File under choice before anything is brought in, B's batch filed under A itself, A's own notes and one row across the devices, the choice remembered in the master. testnotes.mjs: device B through the chooser.

13 October 2026, built in newsroom.sgit.ai v0.12.7; Ask in v0.12.9. Status: running, on every page through the Search link in the nav. The cards are 031 (search), 032 (a test made robust on the way) and 033 (asking the site). The page is /search/.
in-short

- The owner's guess was right: most of a search engine was already published. Every page has clean HTML with anchored headings and a .md twin; every article has a teaser, topics, tags and a graph whose nodes name its ideas; every article keeps its earlier versions; the wire keeps a snapshot of its headlines. What was missing was an index and a ranking, and both fit in a static site. - The index is built at release. admin/build/searchindex.py reads every page in the sitemap and writes two files: search/docs.json (one entry per page: title, kind, number, date, teaser, topics, tags, the graph's core idea and node labels, headings with anchors; about 290 KB) and search/text.json (the text in paragraphs, each with its anchor; about 4 MB, served compressed). - The ranking runs in the reader's browser. assets/search/search.js fetches the two files from this site and ranks with BM25 over fields and paragraphs. Searching sends nothing anywhere. - It finds what changed. For each article, the paragraphs of its earlier versions that are no longer in it are indexed with the version they read that way in, so a sentence that has since been corrected is still found, and the result links to the version page that shows the change. - Ask: a model that answers from the same index (v0.12.9, card 033): Chrome's built-in model where the browser has it, or the reader's own OpenRouter key, with the passages it was given shown under the answer and cited by number.
what-is-searched-and-how-much-each-part-counts

A page's score is its fields plus its best paragraph plus a third of the next two, multiplied by the square of the share of the query's words it contains at all, so a page with every word beats a page with one word many times; then by its kind (an article counts a little more than a page, the archive less). Pages of every kind are in it: 97 articles, the newsletter, collections, the desk, the decks, the wire's 40 stories (from its snapshot), the engineering cards, this site's notes and the other pages, 375 documents and about 5,600 paragraphs at the time of writing.
the-query

- Words are folded (case, accents) and lightly stemmed, so agents finds agent and thinking finds think. Common words are dropped unless they are all there is. - "Quotes" require the exact phrase, in the page or in an earlier version of it. - A number alone is that article: 97 opens Who owns the words. - The last word is also a prefix, so results come as you type. - Soft phrases: the whole query, and anything typed as one token that is really several, such as agent@riskmandate.ai, count for more where they appear together, without being required. - Filters: everything, articles, the wire, engineering, pages, the archive; and, with the reader's records, hide what I marked done. A result the reader has read says so, and how far; one they decided about says how. The address keeps the query (/search/?q=…&f=articles), so a search can be linked to.
why-not-a-bigger-engine

A search service would need a server and would see every query. A prebuilt inverted index would be larger than the text it indexes at this size. Lunr or a similar library would add a dependency for what is a few hundred lines. The two JSON files are regenerated with the site, cached by the browser like any file, and readable by an agent that wants to rank them its own way.
what-is-not-built

- The live wire. The index holds the wire's snapshot, taken at release; stories added to the vault since are on the wire page, not in search, until the next release. - Search inside the vault pane, over the reader's own notes and reading. - Synonyms and spelling: a misspelt word finds nothing; the prefix helps only from the start of a word.
asking-the-site-card-033-v0-12-9

The search page has an Ask button beside Search. The question is searched with the same index; passagesFor (in assets/search/ask.js) takes the best paragraph of each of the top pages, two from the very best, up to eight, each cut to about 700 characters, current wording only (text that is only in an earlier version is left out, so an answer is never built on a sentence the site has since corrected). They are numbered and given to a model with one instruction: answer only from them, cite them by number, and say so when they do not hold the answer. The answer is shown with the passages under it, each linked to its page and section; a citation is a link to its passage, and a number with no passage behind it stays plain text. What the model is given shows the instruction, the question and the passages, exactly as sent. Which model answers, in order:
asking-the-site-card-033-v0-12-9

1. Chrome's built-in model (the Prompt API: LanguageModel, or the older window.ai.languageModel), when the browser has it. It runs on the reader's machine: no key, nothing sent. The first use may download the model, once; the page shows the progress. 2. The reader's own OpenRouter key, pasted under How questions are answered, with a model (by default openrouter/auto). The key is kept in the tab's session storage, and in local storage only when the reader ticks Keep the key in this browser; Forget the key takes it out of both. It is sent to openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions in the Authorization header, with the question and the passages in the body, and nowhere else: this site has no server to send it to. The page says which model answered and how many characters and tokens were sent. When the built-in model is there but cannot answer, the key is used and the page says why. 3. Neither: the page says so, and Ask shows the passages alone.
asking-the-site-card-033-v0-12-9
?q=…&ask=1 in the address asks on arrival, so a question can be a link.
what-is-not-built

- The key in the master vault, typed once for every device, like the access key. - A conversation: each question is asked fresh, with its own passages. - Tools: the model cannot search again or open a page; sgit.ai's site chat (assets/site-chat.js on sgit.ai) has that, and is the next step if one round of passages is not enough. - Answers kept as notes, sent to the newsroom through the lane like any other note.

13 October 2026, built in newsroom.sgit.ai v0.12.26. Card 049. The request and the brief are the article Sixteen notes I did not want to lose (No. 105). The sending page is /vault/send.html; the link is made in the vault pane's Vault tab.
in-short

- The problem. The vault opens with a passkey, and some browsers cannot reach one: a web view an app opens a link in, a browser signed in to nothing, an old iPad. What they hold stayed there, counted on the Vault button as changes only in this browser. The only way in without the passkey was the recovery code, which opens the master: too much power for a job that only needs to add. - The answer is a lane. Every account can have an inbox: an append lane on the reader vault that any browser can write to and none can read, and a key pair made in the reader's browser whose private half is in the master. The link carries where to write and the key to encrypt to, nothing else. - A browser with the link sends its own device file, the same file the vault already holds for every device, sealed to the key. The vault takes it in the next time it is opened with the passkey: the pane lists what is waiting, opens it, shows it, and on one press writes it into the reader vault as that browser's file, so the merge that already exists brings it in, with that browser as the author. - Nothing new on the server. The append routes (/api/vault/append/ on dev.send.sgraph.ai), the envelope (sgit's hybrid v2) and the device files existed; the pieces new here are the reader's key pair, the link, the sending page and the drain.
the-four-capabilities

The append-lanes API splits what a lane can do into four, and the design puts each where it belongs: The link is https://newsroom.sgit.ai/vault/send.html#sgi1.<reader vault id.<append token.<public key, SPKI, base64url, about 650 characters. The fragment never reaches a server, and the sending page takes it out of the address once it has kept it, so a copied address or a screenshot does not carry it.
the-flow

1. Make the link (the Vault tab, unlocked): a key pair in this browser; a random append token (16 bytes) and enum key (32 bytes); configure on the reader vault with appendanchors: [sha256(token)] and enumkeyhash, with the reader vault's write key and the access key from the master; the record inbox.json written into the master. 2. Send (any browser, vault/send.html, or Send to my vault in the strip above the pane once a link is kept): extract() this browser's own records into one device file, wrap it as {kind: "sgit-newsroom-inbox/v1", to: <key fingerprint, sentat, file}, seal it (a fresh AES-256-GCM key wrapped with RSA-OAEP, the envelope {v: 2, w, i, c}, base64 twice as the API documents), and POST /append/write with the token. The answer is {"ok": true} and nothing else. The browser keeps every record; the time of the send becomes its last update, so the count goes to zero. 3. Drain (the Vault tab, every time it is drawn, and on Look in the lane): list with the enum key, fetch each lane's pending files, open each with the private key, check it. Valid messages are listed by the name the browser gave itself, the time and what they carry; refused ones with the reason. 4. Bring them in: each browser's files combined (combine(): every record of either, the one that knows more where both have it), combined again with the file already in the vault for that browser, written, one publish; mark-processed; then the merge every device already uses, which reloads the page and says what arrived. 5. A new link: a new token, the same key; configure replaces the anchors, so the old token is refused (404). It waits until the lane is empty, so nothing is stranded in a lane no anchor names.
what-is-refused

A message that does not open with the key (sealed to another one), one whose ciphertext was changed (AES-GCM's tag fails), one that opens but is not a newsroom inbox message, is addressed to another key's fingerprint, carries a browser id that is not a plain file name, or has notes that claim another browser. They are listed and can be discarded; nothing in them is merged. What is not refused: a well-formed message from whoever holds the link. That is the brief's model: the link writes, it does not prove who wrote. The drain shows the browser's name, its platform, the time and the counts before anything is brought in, and a new link stops the old one.
choices-and-why

- RSA-OAEP 3072, not 4096. The sgit CLI makes 4096-bit keys. 3072 is 128-bit security, and it keeps the link at about 650 characters and the QR code at 89 modules, which a phone camera reads off a laptop screen; at 4096 the link is about 820 characters and the code 97 modules. - The device file as the message. Inventing a second format for the same records would have needed a second merge. A browser that sends through the inbox is a device like any other: it gets a row across the devices, and its records keep it as their author. - The lane on the reader vault, not a new vault. The brief asks for it there; it keeps the account at four vaults (door, master, reader, the newsroom lane) and the inbox's files out of every commit tree (bare/append/…). - The sending page loads no vault library. It reads local storage, encrypts with Web Crypto and makes one POST, so it works where nothing else of the vault does.
not-built

- Expiry. The append routes have no expiry on a token; a date in the link would be honoured by this page and by nobody else. A new link is the revocation the server enforces. - Signatures. A sender holds no key; the link is the credential, as for the subscribe form. - Purge of processed files (write key and access key; a later release). - The reply lane (card 015): the newsroom answering under a message. The same machinery, pointed the other way. - An A/B test of the link against a pairing flow, which the article proposes.
tests

admin/build/testinbox.mjs: in Node, the link, the envelope, the refusals and combine(); in Chromium, against the mock of the vault API (now with the append routes), browser A with a virtual passkey makes the account and the link (the QR code decoded back with jsQR), browser B with no passkey at all reads, keeps notes and sends twice, three bad messages are appended beside them, A brings B's in and refuses the three, discards them, makes a new link, and the old one can no longer write.

13 October 2026, built in newsroom.sgit.ai v0.12.6. Status: a beta with one named reader. It applies The site is an inbox to the Industry Wire, on the pieces of the feedback loop and the activity vault. The cards are on the engineering board, 023 to 030.
in-short

- The wire is read as an inbox. Every story the reader has not decided about is in it; a decision takes the story out. The state to return to is empty. - New means first seen in this visit. Every story drawn is recorded as seen; a story nobody had drawn for this reader before, on any of their devices, carries a New flag until the visit ends. A reload keeps the visit. - For me and not for me come from the lens the reader reads as, which is now remembered, and from the join the wire's vault records. The bar says how many new stories are for the reader and how many are not, and the not-for-me ones can be checked and corrected. - What changed comes from the vault. When the wire's agent publishes a release note (the release file, below), the bar shows the releases since the last visit; until it does, it shows the head commit's message and says the vault publishes no release notes yet. - Local first, update explicitly, and see what you would lose. Decisions and seen stories are kept in the browser as they happen and reach the reader vault only on Update the vault. Until then the Vault button carries a count, the pane a strip, and the wire a line with Update the vault one press away.
the-workflow

1. The desk updates the vault. The owner asks the wire's agent for a new edition, and for a description of what changed, written as a release (the release file). That is a commit to the wire's vault; this site needs no release to show it. 2. Open the wire. The bar at the top says: since your last visit, N new stories, X for you and Y not for you; what the desk says changed, release by release, with the stories added and updated; and the counts per filter. 3. Work the inbox. At each story, one tap: Done (processed), Read later, Follow up (act on it, or write about it), Not for me, More like this, Wrong. Each is a note with the story's id and takes the story out of the inbox, with undo. Under a lens, the stories withheld from you are listed per beat with the join's reason; on those, Should reach me says the join missed you, and Done clears them. 4. Look back by filter. Inbox, New, Read later, Follow up, Done, Everything. In Everything and Done a decided story folds to its headline. 5. Update the vault. Explicitly, from the wire's bar, the pane's strip or the Vault tab. One file per device, rewritten whole, one commit, as before; it now also carries the stories seen, so another device does not show them as new. 6. Send to the newsroom, when the decisions should reach the desk: the notes go down the reader's own lane (the feedback loop), and the desk reads them with the lane's read key.
the-records

Kinds: done, read-later, follow-up, not-for-me, more-like-this, wrong. A story with any note is decided; the latest note is its state. Notes brought in from another device count as decisions here, and say which device made them.
what-new-means

A visit starts when the wire is opened in a tab that has not opened it before; it lasts as long as the tab. When the edition is drawn, every story not yet in seen is recorded with the time. A story is New when it was recorded in this visit, here. So: the first visit to the wire in a browser shows every story as new; a reload keeps them new; the next visit shows only stories that arrived since. When another device's activity is brought in through the vault, its seen stories come too, tagged with that device, and are not new here.
for-me-and-not-for-me

The lens is the persona the reader reads as. It is taken from the address (#lens=), else the lens chosen last time, else the active persona of the meter when it maps to one of the wire's. Under a lens, the wire's own join (data/deliveries.json, written by the vault's code, not by this page) says which stories reached the reader and which were withheld, with the reason. The bar splits the new stories by it, and every beat lists what was withheld. Without a lens, every story is in the inbox and the bar suggests choosing one.
the-release-file

For the agent that keeps the wire's vault. This is what the owner asks for when they ask you to "describe what changed on the release". On every publish of an edition or a change to one, add an entry at the top of data/releases.json in the vault, in the same commit as the change:
the-release-file

- One entry per publish, newest first, never edited afterwards; a correction is a new entry. - at is the time of the commit, in UTC, ISO 8601. The page shows the entries newer than the reader's last visit, or the latest one when none is newer. - added, updated, withdrawn are story ids from data/bundle.json. The page links each to its story and marks updated stories with an Updated flag. - summary is plain text, a few sentences, written for the named reader: what changed and what deserves attention. No markup; the page draws it as text. - The commit message starts with the release id, so the history and the file agree. Until the file exists, the page shows the head commit's message and says the vault publishes no release notes yet. Nothing else in the vault's contract with this site changes (how the wire works).
local-first-update-explicitly-and-see-what-you-would-lose

Everything here is kept in this browser first, and nothing is sent until the reader presses something. The cost of that rule is that until the reader updates the vault, what they did exists in one browser only, and clearing it loses it. So the site counts what the vault does not have yet (assets/vault-pane/pending.js): reads started, rated or declined, top-ups, notes kept, given words or sent, after this device's last update; and, separately, stories seen. The count of things done is on the Vault button, with an amber dot; the pane has a strip above its tabs that names them, with Update the vault; the wire's bar has the same line. Updating is still an explicit press: automatic or regular sync is a later decision (card 029).
what-is-not-built

- The release file in the wire's vault (card 026): this site reads it; the wire's agent writes it. Until then the head commit's message stands in. - Automatic or regular sync (029), on purpose: explicit first. - The desk reading the decisions (030): a Not for me or a Should reach me is the signal the join needs, and today it reaches the desk only if the reader sends it down their lane and the wire's agent reads that lane. The morning read in the vault's own workflows writes to a feedback file in the vault, which a reader with a read key cannot do; the lane is how it gets there without a write key. - Editions as history. The page reads the vault's current bundle; a story that left the bundle is gone from the page, though the reader's decision about it remains. - The front page (017): it is imported, so the decisions are on the wire and on article pages only.
the-experiments

1. A week of morning reads by the named reader: how long the inbox takes to empty, which decisions are used, how often a Should reach me appears. 2. Two devices: decide on the phone, update, open the wire on the laptop: nothing the phone saw is new, the decisions are there. 3. The first release file from the wire's agent, and whether the summary is what the reader would have wanted to know. 4. The count on the Vault button: whether it is noticed, and how long things stay only in the browser before an update.
the-message-for-the-wire-s-agent

When you publish to the wire's vault, add a release entry at the top of data/releases.json in the same commit: id, time (UTC), edition, title, a short plain-text summary of what changed and what deserves attention, and the story ids added, updated and withdrawn. The schema and an example are in "The release file" at https://newsroom.sgit.ai/admin/notes/2026-10-13the-wire-as-an-inbox.md. newsroom.sgit.ai shows the releases since the reader's last visit at the top of the wire.

13 October 2026, published in newsroom.sgit.ai v0.12.20 at /wire/charter.html. Asked for by the owner in a voice memo of 13 October: publish a charter, the guidelines, the checks and balances, and the principles, so that every agent in the chain and every reader can hold the wires to them. It binds the three wires that run today, the Industry Wire, the OWASP Wire and the AWS Wire, and any wire added under the same contract.
what-a-wire-is-for

A wire is a feed of what happened, in one field, for a reader who has little time and no patience for claims they cannot check. Every story names where it came from, who else covered it, one exact quote with its source, and why it matters. The reader decides what to do with it; the wire does not.
facts-first-analysis-on-top
The record is factual and the analysis sits on it, visibly apart.
facts-first-analysis-on-top

- The facts are the story's headline, date, primary source, coverage, quote and entities. Each is traced to a source the reader can open. A number is dated. A quote is exact, 25 words or fewer when the source's licence asks, and found in the source it is attributed to. - The analysis is the editor's note, the threads, the lead's "why it leads", a story's "why it matters" and the personal brief. It is opinion on top of the record, written by the desk, and it is marked as the desk's. A reader who disagrees with the analysis should still be able to agree with the facts. - What is not known is said. "Primary not fetched" is a valid, visible state. A story whose primary source the desk could not reach says so on the page and is drawn with a dashed border. A confidence level is shown as the desk gave it. - Nothing is reviewed until a person has reviewed it. Every story carries its status as written in the vault, ai-generated, unreviewed until the vault says otherwise. This site never upgrades a status.
corrections-propagate

A correction reaches the reader where they read the claim, not in a note elsewhere. The desk records each correction, dated, in the story's own changes; the edition's header carries the desk's note of what was corrected; the release notes name the stories updated; the page flags them. A correction is never silent and never edits history: the vault keeps every commit, and anyone with the read key can see what was said before. The argument is this site's own.
three-rounds-and-who-enforces-what
The wires run on at least two rounds of agents, with a third asked for on every run.
three-rounds-and-who-enforces-what

1. The desk writes the vault. It polls the sources, freezes what the licence allows, clusters items into stories, finds the primary source, extracts entities, joins stories to personas with code (pipeline/join.py), writes the edition, runs the gate (pipeline/gate.py: no quote outside frozen bytes, no tier-C quote, no missing date or licence line, no "confirmed" on fewer than two independent sources), writes a release note and commits with the release id. The desk holds the vault's write key and nobody else does. Its runbook is in the vault for anyone to read. 2. The newsroom (this site, the agent the owner calls @newsroom.wire) reads the vault with a published read key and draws it. It holds no write key to any wire. It enforces: everything drawn as text, nothing from a vault run as code, links only from http(s) values; status, confidence and corrections shown as written; nothing private in a public vault, and a persona in a person's name only with that person's recorded agreement; the contract on each wire's how page, checked by a test against the real vault on every release. It does not edit stories. A problem in a vault is flagged to the desk, in the brief for the desks, never fixed in place. 3. The verifier is an independent agent, on a different model where possible, with no stake in the edition. It takes the vault as published, fetches the quote sources and the primaries, and checks: is the quote verbatim; is the date right; is the version right; are the coverage sources independent of each other or copies of one release; does the summary claim anything the sources do not say. It writes what it found to data/factcheck-<date.json in the vault, and the desk applies the fixes as dated corrections. This site draws the verifier's record at each story it covers. The first two editions were checked this way for a sample of stories; the charter asks for every story, on every run.
independence

The desk has no advertiser, no publisher relationship and no access beyond the public web; the only person it answers to is the named reader, and that person's persona, brief and stack are public. In that sense the desk is more independent than most editors, and it should stay so: it proposes, the Editor places, and opinionated pieces are written on top, by name, as articles, not inside the wire.
what-we-never-do

- Never publish a claim without a source the reader can open. - Never publish a quote that is not in its source, or longer than the source's licence allows. - Never publish a person's private contact detail, or a story about a named private individual who is not a public figure. A route to someone is an organisation's published role address, under the contact rules this site already keeps. - Never put anything private in a public-read vault: no frozen tier-B bytes, no reader's feedback, no brief for a person who has not agreed. - Never edit another agent's vault, and never fix in place what should be flagged. - Never correct silently, and never remove a story from the record without a withdrawn entry in the release notes. - Never upgrade a story's status, confidence or verification on this side.
public-by-default

Every vault is readable by anyone with its published read key, including its history. Every config on this site, every snapshot, the contract, the runbooks, the release notes, the verifier's records, the brief for the desks and this charter are public. The people and organisations a wire should reach are listed on each wire's reach page, by organisation route only, so that the outreach can be verified by anyone.
the-reader

One named reader so far, by their recorded agreement while the wires are a beta. Their decisions on the wire (done, not for me, should reach me, wrong) are kept in their own browser first, carried by their own vault, and reach the desk only down their own lane. A wrong becomes a correction; the rest become proposed edits to the personas, as a diff for approval. Anyone can read a wire as any public persona; nobody else gets a lens in their name without agreeing to it being public.
holding-the-wires-to-this

The contract and the tests are the barriers. The desk's gate stops a publish that breaks its rules; the newsroom's test fails a release that draws a vault wrongly; the verifier's record says what was checked and what was not. Where the charter asks for something not yet built, the engineering board says so by card: the verifier on every run, the desks reading the reader's lane, the scheduled runs. The charter is changed by a release of this site, with the date, like everything else here.
